name: Afghanistan
catholicPresence: Very few Catholics; almost entirely foreign residents (approx. a few hundred or fewer)
history:
Christianity touched the lands of today's Afghanistan very early. An ancient tradition links the Apostle Thomas with the Indo-Parthian kingdom of Gondophares, whose realm reached into this region, and in later centuries the Church of the East kept bishops in cities such as Herat. Over time these communities faded, and for many centuries there was no lasting Christian presence.

In the twentieth century, when Italy was among the first nations to recognise Afghan independence, it was permitted a chapel within its embassy in Kabul. For decades this small chapel was the only Catholic church in the country, served by Barnabite priests. In 2002 St John Paul II established a mission sui iuris for Afghanistan, and religious sisters, including the Missionaries of Charity, quietly cared for disabled children and the poor.

After August 2021 the remaining priests and sisters were evacuated, and there is no public Catholic life in the country today. Afghan Christians who exist live their faith in hiddenness and danger. The Church holds this people in prayer, honouring decades of humble service and longing for peace, dignity and freedom for every Afghan.

saints.name: St Thomas the Apostle
saints.story: An ancient tradition, preserved in the apocryphal Acts of Thomas, says the Apostle preached at the court of King Gondophares, whose Indo-Parthian kingdom included parts of present-day Afghanistan. Historians treat the story with caution, yet coins confirm Gondophares was a real ruler. Thomas, who once doubted and then confessed 'My Lord and my God', remains a fitting intercessor for a land where faith is lived in hiddenness.

cathedrals.name: Chapel of Our Lady of Divine Providence (Italian Embassy)
cathedrals.story: For most of the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries this modest chapel inside the Italian embassy compound was the only Catholic place of worship in Afghanistan. Barnabite priests celebrated Mass there for diplomats, aid workers and soldiers from many nations. It became the seat of the mission sui iuris created in 2002, a small sign of presence and prayer in a land where public Christian worship has never been possible.

prayerIntention: For the people of Afghanistan, especially women, children and the persecuted: that they may know peace, freedom and the tender closeness of God.

name: Albania
catholicPresence: Approx. 10% Catholic, mostly in the north
history:
Christianity reached the Illyrian coast in apostolic times; St Paul writes that he preached the Gospel 'as far as Illyricum' (Romans 15:19), and Durrës (Dyrrachium) had a bishop from the early centuries. The north of Albania kept strong ties with Rome, and in the fifteenth century Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg resisted the Ottoman advance for decades. Under Ottoman rule many Albanians became Muslim, while Franciscan friars sustained the Catholic communities of the mountains and Shkodër.

In 1967 the communist regime of Enver Hoxha declared Albania the world's first atheist state. Every church and mosque was closed or destroyed, and bishops, priests, religious and lay faithful were imprisoned, tortured and executed. In 2016 thirty-eight of these martyrs were beatified in Shkodër.

When the regime collapsed, the first public Mass was celebrated in Shkodër in November 1990, and St John Paul II visited in 1993 to ordain new bishops. Pope Francis came in 2014 and wept as he heard the testimony of an elderly priest who had survived decades of prison. Today a small but vibrant Church lives in harmony with Muslim and Orthodox neighbours, proud also of St Teresa of Calcutta, a daughter of the Albanian people.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of Good Counsel (Zoja e Shkodrës)

saints.name: St Teresa of Calcutta
saints.story: Born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu to an Albanian family in Skopje, she became a Loreto sister in India and in 1950 founded the Missionaries of Charity to serve the poorest of the poor. Her smile and her long hidden darkness of faith alike speak to the world. Albanians honour her as their most beloved daughter; Tirana's airport and cathedral windows bear her image.

saints.name: Bl. Vinçenc Prendushi
saints.story: A Franciscan friar, poet and translator, he became Archbishop of Durrës. Refusing the communist regime's pressure to break with Rome, he was arrested in 1947, tortured and sentenced to prison, where he died in 1949. He was beatified in Shkodër in 2016 at the head of thirty-eight martyrs of Albania's communist persecution.

saints.name: Bl. Ndre Zadeja
saints.story: A priest, poet and playwright from Shkodër, Dom Ndre Zadeja loved the Albanian language and culture deeply. Shortly after the communists came to power he was arrested and shot in March 1945, among the first clergy to be executed. He is counted among the thirty-eight martyrs beatified in 2016.

saints.name: Bl. Maria Tuci
saints.story: A young teacher and aspirant to the Stigmatine Sisters, Maria Tuci was arrested in 1949 for her faith. She endured brutal treatment in prison and died of her injuries in 1950, aged twenty-two. The only woman among the thirty-eight beatified martyrs, she is remembered as a radiant witness of purity and courage.

cathedrals.name: St Stephen's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in the nineteenth century, this large cathedral is the heart of northern Albanian Catholicism. Under communism it was confiscated and turned into a sports hall. In November 1990 it was the site of the first public Mass after decades of persecution, and in 1993 St John Paul II reconsecrated it and ordained new Albanian bishops there, a moment of resurrection for the whole nation.

cathedrals.name: St Paul's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 2002, this modern cathedral in the capital is a sign of the Church's rebirth after the atheist era. Its simple, light-filled design includes stained glass depicting St Teresa of Calcutta and St John Paul II, the two figures who most marked the Albanian Church's return to public life.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Good Counsel
cathedrals.story: Albanians cherish the tradition that the beloved image of Our Lady of Good Counsel was once venerated in Shkodër before it came to Genazzano in Italy. The shrine was destroyed under communism and later rebuilt, and it draws pilgrims each April to honour Mary as Zoja e Shkodrës, patroness of Albania.

prayerIntention: For the people of Albania: that the witness of their martyrs may bear fruit in reconciliation, honest public life and a Church that is joyful and free.

name: Algeria
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority, mostly foreign residents and students (approx. under 0.1%)
history:
Roman North Africa was one of the great hearts of early Christianity. In what is now Algeria, St Monica was born at Thagaste (Souk Ahras) and her son St Augustine served as bishop of Hippo (Annaba), writing works that shaped the whole Western Church. Councils, martyrs and hundreds of bishoprics flourished here, though the Church was also wounded by the Donatist schism and the Vandal invasion. After the Arab conquest in the seventh century, Christian communities gradually disappeared.

With French colonisation from 1830, a large European Catholic population arrived. Cardinal Lavigerie founded the Missionaries of Africa (White Fathers) in Algiers in 1868, and St Charles de Foucauld lived as a hermit among the Tuareg until he was killed in 1916. The Church's close identification with colonial power is a painful memory, and most Catholics left at independence in 1962.

During the violence of the 1990s, nineteen priests and religious, including Bishop Pierre Claverie and the seven Trappist monks of Tibhirine, chose to stay with their Muslim neighbours and were killed. They were beatified in Oran in 2018. Today a small Church, much of it made up of sub-Saharan students and migrants, lives a vocation of friendship, presence and dialogue.

saints.name: St Augustine of Hippo
saints.story: Born at Thagaste, Augustine searched restlessly for truth before his conversion in Milan. Returning to Africa, he became bishop of Hippo, where he preached, wrote the Confessions and The City of God, and died as the Vandals besieged the city. A Doctor of the Church, he remains one of Christianity's greatest teachers.

saints.name: St Monica
saints.story: A native of Thagaste, Monica prayed with tears for years for the conversion of her son Augustine. She followed him to Italy and saw him baptised shortly before her death at Ostia. She is beloved as patron of mothers and of all who persevere in prayer for those they love.

saints.name: St Charles de Foucauld
saints.story: A French soldier and explorer who returned to faith, Charles became a priest and lived among the Tuareg at Tamanrasset and the Assekrem, praying, learning their language and serving as a 'universal brother'. He was killed outside his hermitage in 1916 and canonised in 2022.

saints.name: Bl. Christian de Chergé and the Monks of Tibhirine
saints.story: Seven Trappist monks of Our Lady of Atlas lived in prayer and friendship with their Muslim neighbours. Refusing to leave during the civil war, they were kidnapped and killed in 1996. Prior Christian's testament, forgiving his future killer, is one of the great spiritual texts of our time. They were beatified in 2018.

saints.name: Bl. Pierre Claverie
saints.story: Born in Algiers, Pierre became a Dominican and later Bishop of Oran, devoted to dialogue with Islam. In August 1996 he was killed by a bomb at his residence together with his young Muslim driver and friend, Mohamed Bouchikhi, their blood mingled. He was beatified with eighteen companions in 2018.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Notre-Dame d'Afrique
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1872 on a hill overlooking the Bay of Algiers, this Romano-Byzantine basilica houses a dark-skinned image of Mary. An inscription in its apse asks: 'Our Lady of Africa, pray for us and for the Muslims.' Christians and Muslims alike come here to pray, making it a living symbol of the Algerian Church's vocation of encounter.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of St Augustine
cathedrals.story: Built at the turn of the twentieth century on a hill above the ruins of ancient Hippo, the basilica honours the great bishop who served here. Its white stone and arches blend Roman and Moorish styles, and it holds a relic of the saint. Restored in the 2010s, it welcomes pilgrims and many curious Algerian visitors.

cathedrals.name: Chapel of Notre-Dame de Santa Cruz
cathedrals.story: High above Oran, this chapel was built after a cholera epidemic in 1849, when the people processed to the mountain to pray for deliverance. Its statue of Mary watches over the city and the sea. It remains a beloved pilgrimage site and a landmark of Oran's skyline.

prayerIntention: For the people of Algeria and for its small Church of encounter: that friendship between Christians and Muslims may grow, and the land of St Augustine know peace and hope.

name: Andorra
history:
The faith came to the Pyrenean valleys of Andorra in late antiquity, and from the early Middle Ages the parishes belonged to the diocese of Urgell. A ninth-century act of consecration of Urgell's cathedral already names Andorran parishes. Over the following centuries small Romanesque churches with slender bell towers rose throughout the valleys, many of which still stand.

In 1278 the paréage agreement made Andorra a co-principality shared by the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix, an arrangement that endures today: the Bishop of Urgell remains one of the two co-princes, alongside the President of France. This unique bond has shaped Andorran identity for more than seven centuries.

The heart of popular devotion is Our Lady of Meritxell, patroness of the country. Her old sanctuary burned in 1972, and a new one designed by Ricardo Bofill was inaugurated in 1976. The 1993 constitution guarantees religious freedom while recognising the special relationship with the Catholic Church. Like much of Europe, Andorra faces secularisation, yet its parishes, feasts and pilgrimages remain woven into family and civic life.

saints.name: St Ermengol of Urgell
saints.story: Bishop of Urgell in the early eleventh century, Ermengol is remembered as a builder of churches and bridges and a pastor to the mountain valleys, including Andorra. He died after falling while working on a bridge. He is the patron of the diocese of Urgell, to which Andorra's parishes belong.

saints.name: St Justus of Urgell
saints.story: The first known bishop of Urgell, Justus took part in Visigothic church councils and wrote a commentary on the Song of Songs. His diocese has shepherded Andorra since its earliest Christian centuries. No canonised saint is known to have been born in Andorra itself, so the Church here looks to the holy bishops of Urgell.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Meritxell
cathedrals.story: The national shrine of Andorra. The old Romanesque-Baroque sanctuary burned in 1972, destroying the original statue of Mary. A new sanctuary by architect Ricardo Bofill, combining stone, arches and light, was inaugurated in 1976. On September 8 Andorrans gather here for their national day.

cathedrals.name: Church of Sant Joan de Caselles
cathedrals.story: A gem of Romanesque architecture, this small church from the eleventh to twelfth centuries has a Lombard bell tower and a striking stucco figure of Christ crucified alongside painted scenes. It shows the simple, enduring faith of the mountain parishes. Andorra has no cathedral of its own: its cathedral is in La Seu d'Urgell, just across the border.

cathedrals.name: Church of Sant Esteve
cathedrals.story: The principal church of the capital, with Romanesque origins and later enlargements, including a round apse with Lombard decoration. It is the parish where many of the country's important liturgies take place.

prayerIntention: For the people of Andorra: that, under the mantle of Our Lady of Meritxell, they may treasure their ancient faith and pass it on with joy to new generations.

name: Angola
history:
The Gospel reached the region in 1491, when Portuguese missionaries baptised the ruler of the Kingdom of Kongo, whose capital Mbanza Kongo lies in today's northern Angola. His son, Afonso I, promoted the faith with conviction, and Afonso's son Henrique was consecrated bishop in 1518, the first bishop from sub-Saharan Africa. Luanda was founded in 1576, and a diocese was established at São Salvador (Mbanza Kongo) in 1596.

The early Church was deeply compromised by the Atlantic slave trade, which carried millions of Angolans to Brazil and beyond; some clergy and institutions profited from it. Missionaries, including Capuchins and later Spiritans, nevertheless built a lasting Christian presence, and Marian devotion took root at Muxima on the Kwanza River.

After independence in 1975, Angola endured a civil war until 2002. The Church suffered under Marxist rule yet worked tirelessly for peace and reconciliation, and Catholic radio and schools became trusted voices. St John Paul II visited in 1992, Benedict XVI in 2009, and Pope Leo XIV in 2026. Today the Angolan Church is young and growing, while challenged by poverty, inequality and the wounds of war.

saints.name: St Peter Claver
saints.story: No canonised saint was born in Angola, but Peter Claver, a Spanish Jesuit in Cartagena, devoted his life to the enslaved Africans arriving by ship, many of them taken from Angola and Kongo. He met them in the holds, nursed the sick, catechised and baptised them, calling himself 'the slave of the slaves forever'. He is a fitting intercessor for a people so wounded by the slave trade.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary of Mama Muxima
cathedrals.story: On a bluff above the Kwanza River stands the white church of Our Lady of the Conception of Muxima, built by the Portuguese around 1599 beside a fort on the slave route. Once a place of sorrow, it has become Angola's most beloved Marian shrine: 'Muxima' means 'heart' in Kimbundu. Hundreds of thousands of pilgrims come each year, especially in September.

cathedrals.name: Ruins of Kulumbimbi Cathedral
cathedrals.story: These stone ruins in the old capital of the Kingdom of Kongo mark one of the oldest church sites in sub-Saharan Africa, built after the conversion of the Kongo kings and later rebuilt as the cathedral of São Salvador. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of Mbanza Kongo, they recall both the early flowering of African Christianity and its entanglement with colonial power.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Remedies
cathedrals.story: The Sé Catedral de Luanda, dedicated to Nossa Senhora dos Remédios, dates from the seventeenth century and is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Luanda. Its white Baroque façade stands at the centre of the capital's Catholic life.

prayerIntention: For the people of Angola: that, healed of the wounds of slavery and war, they may build a nation of justice, peace and shared prosperity, sheltered in the heart of Mama Muxima.

name: Antigua and Barbuda
history:
Christopher Columbus sighted the island in 1493 and named it after Santa María la Antigua, a venerated image of Mary in Seville Cathedral. Yet it was the English who colonised Antigua from 1632, and its sugar economy was built on the labour of enslaved Africans until emancipation in 1834. The Anglican Church was established, and for a long time Catholics were few.

Catholic life grew in the nineteenth century, notably through Portuguese immigrants from Madeira who came as labourers in the 1840s and after, and through later arrivals from neighbouring islands. Parishes and schools developed, serving people of every background.

Today Antigua and Barbuda belongs to the Diocese of St John's–Basseterre, which also covers St Kitts and Nevis, Anguilla, Montserrat and the British Virgin Islands. The community is small but warm, centred on the Holy Family Cathedral in St John's, and active in education and care for the vulnerable. No canonised saint is known to have come from these islands, but the Church here lives the ordinary holiness of family, parish and service.

cathedrals.name: Holy Family Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Diocese of St John's–Basseterre, consecrated in 1987, is a modern church that gathers Catholics from across the island and serves as the mother church of a diocese spread over several Caribbean territories. It is the setting for the diocese's principal celebrations and a sign of the steady growth of the Catholic community in Antigua.

prayerIntention: For the people of Antigua and Barbuda: that their families may be strong, their islands protected from storms, and their small Church a joyful witness of the Holy Family's love.

name: Argentina
history:
The faith arrived with Spanish colonisation in the sixteenth century. Franciscans, Dominicans, Mercedarians and Jesuits evangelised the indigenous peoples, and from the early 1600s the Jesuit reductions among the Guaraní in the northeast created remarkable communities of faith, music and work until the Jesuits were expelled in 1767. The conquest also brought violence, forced labour and devastating epidemics among native peoples.

After independence in 1816, the young nation knew periods of tension between Church and state. In the twentieth century the Church was entangled with political conflict; during the military dictatorship of 1976–1983, some Church leaders were complicit in silence while others, like Bishop Enrique Angelelli, were murdered for defending the poor. The Church later asked forgiveness and helped open archives.

In 2013 Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio of Buenos Aires became Pope Francis, the first pope from the Americas; he died in 2025. Argentines also rejoiced at the canonisations of the Cura Brochero in 2016 and Mama Antula in 2024. Today the Church faces secularisation and economic hardship, yet popular devotion, especially the great youth pilgrimage to Luján, remains strong.

saints.name: St José Gabriel del Rosario Brochero
saints.story: The 'Cura Brochero' rode his mule across the mountains of Córdoba to reach scattered families, built roads, schools and a house for spiritual exercises, and brought his people to God with plain, earthy speech. He contracted leprosy from caring for the sick and died blind. He was canonised in 2016 as Argentina's first native-born saint.

saints.name: St María Antonia de Paz y Figueroa (Mama Antula)
saints.story: After the Jesuits were expelled, this laywoman from Santiago del Estero walked barefoot thousands of kilometres to keep Ignatian spiritual exercises alive, leading tens of thousands through them. In Buenos Aires she founded the Holy House of Spiritual Exercises, which still stands. She was canonised in 2024.

saints.name: Bl. Ceferino Namuncurá
saints.story: Son of a Mapuche chief, Ceferino was educated by the Salesians and dreamed of becoming a priest to serve his people. He fell ill with tuberculosis and died in Rome at eighteen. Beatified in 2007, he is deeply loved, especially in Patagonia, as a bridge between indigenous and Christian identity.

saints.name: Bl. Enrique Angelelli
saints.story: Bishop of La Rioja, he stood with peasants, miners and workers and spoke out against injustice. He died in August 1976 in what was staged as a car accident; Argentine courts later ruled it a murder by agents of the dictatorship. He was beatified in 2019 as a martyr together with two priests and a layman.

saints.name: St Héctor Valdivielso Sáez
saints.story: Born in Buenos Aires to Spanish parents, he became a De La Salle Brother in Spain. During the 1934 revolution in Asturias he was shot together with his fellow Brothers of the school in Turón. He was canonised in 1999 as the first Argentine-born saint.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Luján
cathedrals.story: Argentina's national shrine houses a small clay image of the Immaculate Conception venerated since 1630, when, tradition says, the cart carrying it would not move. The neo-Gothic basilica, built between the 1880s and 1930s, draws millions each year, including the great youth walk from Buenos Aires every October.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral of Buenos Aires
cathedrals.story: Facing the Plaza de Mayo, the cathedral's neoclassical façade with twelve columns hides a richly decorated interior. It holds the mausoleum of General José de San Martín. For many years it was the cathedral of Cardinal Bergoglio, the future Pope Francis, who often prayed and heard confessions here.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Córdoba
cathedrals.story: Dedicated to Our Lady of the Assumption, this cathedral was built over the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and blends Baroque and colonial styles, with a great dome and towers. It is one of the oldest cathedrals in continuous use in Argentina, at the heart of a city long shaped by the Jesuits.

prayerIntention: For the people of Argentina: that, under the protection of Our Lady of Luján, they may find economic justice, care for the poor and a renewed, joyful faith.

name: Armenia
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority, mostly Armenian Catholics (approx. 1–2%); the majority belong to the Armenian Apostolic Church
history:
Armenia was the first nation to adopt Christianity as its state religion, traditionally dated to 301, when St Gregory the Illuminator baptised King Tiridates III. In the fifth century St Mesrop Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet so that the Scriptures and liturgy could be heard in the people's own language. The Armenian Apostolic Church has carried this ancient faith through centuries of invasion and hardship.

Contacts with Rome deepened during the Crusader era, especially in the kingdom of Cilician Armenia. In 1742 the Armenian Catholic Church, in full communion with Rome while keeping the Armenian rite, was formally organised. The Mekhitarist monks, founded by Abbot Mekhitar in the eighteenth century, became renowned for scholarship.

In the genocide of 1915, around a million or more Armenians were killed, among them Archbishop Ignatius Maloyan of Mardin, canonised in 2025. Soviet rule brought further repression. Since independence, Catholics, centred in the northern region around Gyumri, have rebuilt parishes and charitable works in friendship with the Apostolic Church. St John Paul II visited in 2001 and Pope Francis in 2016, and in 2015 St Gregory of Narek was declared a Doctor of the Church.

saints.name: St Gregory the Illuminator
saints.story: According to tradition, Gregory was imprisoned for years in a pit at Khor Virap for his faith before healing King Tiridates III, who then embraced Christianity with his people. As first Catholicos of Armenia, he organised the Church of the first Christian nation. He is venerated by Armenian Apostolic and Catholic Christians alike.

saints.name: St Gregory of Narek
saints.story: A monk of the monastery of Narek, Gregory wrote the Book of Lamentations, a profound dialogue of the soul with God that Armenians have treasured as a book of prayer and healing for a thousand years. In 2015 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church.

saints.name: St Ignatius Maloyan
saints.story: Armenian Catholic Archbishop of Mardin, he was arrested in 1915 during the genocide and urged to convert to Islam to save his life. He refused, encouraged his people, and was shot along with hundreds of others. Beatified in 2001, he was canonised in October 2025.

saints.name: St Mesrop Mashtots
saints.story: A monk and scholar, Mesrop created the Armenian alphabet in the early fifth century so that the Bible could be translated for his people. He founded schools and is honoured by the Armenian Church as a saint and the father of Armenian letters and culture.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Holy Martyrs
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Armenian Catholic Ordinariate for Eastern Europe, rebuilt after the devastating 1988 earthquake and the Soviet era, stands at the heart of Armenia's Catholic community in the north. Pope Francis visited during his 2016 pilgrimage, a moment of great joy for Armenian Catholics.

cathedrals.name: Etchmiadzin Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church, founded in the early fourth century by St Gregory the Illuminator after a vision of Christ descending, and counted among the oldest cathedrals in the world. Though not Catholic, it is the spiritual heart of all Armenian Christianity, and both St John Paul II and Pope Francis prayed here as brothers in faith.

prayerIntention: For the people of Armenia: that the first Christian nation may know lasting peace and security, healing of historical wounds, and ever deeper unity among Christians.

name: Australia
history:
Catholicism came to Australia with the First Fleet in 1788, largely among Irish convicts, yet for years they were denied their own priests. Mass was celebrated only sporadically until 1820, when Fathers John Joseph Therry and Philip Conolly arrived as official chaplains. In 1835 the English Benedictine John Bede Polding became the first bishop, later Archbishop of Sydney.

Through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Irish and then European migrants built a vast network of parishes, schools, hospitals and charities, much of it carried by religious sisters and brothers. St Mary MacKillop co-founded the Sisters of St Joseph in 1866 to educate poor children in the bush, and was canonised in 2010 as Australia's first saint. Relations with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples include both dedicated missions and grave harms, including involvement in policies that separated children from their families.

The Royal Commission into institutional responses to child sexual abuse (2013–2017) revealed terrible failings in Catholic institutions, a source of deep shame and ongoing repair. Today the Church is multicultural and renewed by migrants from Asia, Africa and the Pacific, and its schools educate around one in five Australian children.

saints.name: St Mary MacKillop
saints.story: Born in Melbourne, Mary co-founded the Sisters of St Joseph with Fr Julian Tenison Woods to bring education to poor children in remote areas. She faced fierce opposition and was briefly excommunicated by a bishop in 1871, a decision soon reversed. Faithful and forgiving, she was canonised in 2010 as Australia's first saint.

saints.name: St Peter Chanel
saints.story: A French Marist missionary, Peter Chanel was martyred on the island of Futuna in the Pacific. He was declared protomartyr of Oceania, and the Marists who shared his mission were long based in Sydney. He is widely honoured in Australia's Catholic schools and parishes as a patron of the Church in Oceania.

saints.name: Servant of God Julian Tenison Woods
saints.story: An English-born priest, scientist and explorer, he co-founded the Sisters of St Joseph with Mary MacKillop in Penola, South Australia, in 1866. A tireless missionary across the colonies and a respected geologist, his cause for canonisation has been opened.

saints.name: Servant of God Eileen O'Connor
saints.story: Despite lifelong disability from a spinal condition, Eileen co-founded Our Lady's Nurses for the Poor in Sydney in 1913, sending nurses to care for the sick poor in their homes. She died at twenty-eight. Her cause for canonisation was opened in 2018.

cathedrals.name: St Mary's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Australia's mother church stands on land granted to Catholics in 1821. The present Gothic Revival cathedral, designed by William Wardell after a fire destroyed the earlier church, is built of local golden sandstone. Its twin spires were finally completed in 2000. It hosted World Youth Day celebrations in 2008.

cathedrals.name: St Patrick's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Also designed by William Wardell, this vast bluestone Gothic Revival cathedral was consecrated in 1897 and completed with its spires in 1939. Built largely through the sacrifices of Irish Catholic migrants, its soaring nave and stained glass make it one of the finest nineteenth-century churches in the world.

cathedrals.name: Mary MacKillop Place
cathedrals.story: The shrine where St Mary MacKillop died in 1909 and where her tomb lies in the Memorial Chapel. Pilgrims come from across Australia to pray, especially for the poor, the overlooked and those facing injustice, and to learn the story of the woman who said, 'Never see a need without doing something about it.'

prayerIntention: For the people of Australia: for healing and justice for survivors of abuse, reconciliation with the First Peoples, and a Church humble and faithful in serving all.

name: Austria
catholicPresence: Approx. 50% Catholic, declining but still the largest community
history:
Christianity reached the Roman provinces of Noricum and Pannonia in late antiquity; in the fifth century St Severin cared for the people of the Danube amid the collapse of Roman order. Around 700, St Rupert founded the church and monastery of Salzburg, which became a great centre of mission. Benedictine abbeys such as Melk, Kremsmünster and Admont shaped culture for centuries.

Under the Habsburgs, Austria became a bastion of Catholic Europe, and after the Reformation the Counter-Reformation restored Catholicism, sometimes by coercion of Protestants. In the late eighteenth century Emperor Joseph II dissolved hundreds of monasteries and placed the Church under tight state control. Baroque churches, pilgrimages to Mariazell and great sacred music by Haydn, Mozart and Bruckner express the country's faith.

After the 1938 Anschluss, the Nazi regime persecuted the Church; witnesses like Bl. Franz Jägerstätter and Bl. Restituta Kafka gave their lives. Since the 1990s abuse scandals and secularisation have led many to leave the Church. Yet Austria's parishes, monasteries and Marian shrines remain living places of prayer, and the Church is active in caring for refugees and the poor.

saints.name: St Leopold III
saints.story: Margrave of Austria, Leopold was a devoted husband, father of a large family and a just ruler who founded the monasteries of Klosterneuburg, Heiligenkreuz and Klein-Mariazell. He declined the imperial crown to serve his people. Canonised in 1485, he is the patron saint of Austria.

saints.name: St Severinus of Noricum
saints.story: A monk who came to the Danube lands as Roman authority crumbled, Severinus organised relief for the hungry, ransomed captives and negotiated with barbarian kings. His disciple Eugippius wrote his life, a precious witness to faith in a time of upheaval.

saints.name: St Clement Mary Hofbauer
saints.story: Born in Moravia, Clement became a Redemptorist and worked in Warsaw before settling in Vienna, where he became a tireless confessor, preacher and friend of the poor and of students and intellectuals. He helped renew Catholic life after Josephinism and is honoured as the apostle and patron of Vienna.

saints.name: Bl. Franz Jägerstätter
saints.story: A farmer, husband and father from St Radegund in Upper Austria, Franz refused to fight in Hitler's army, convinced that serving an evil cause was incompatible with his faith. He was executed in Brandenburg in 1943. Beatified in 2007, he is a witness to conscience.

saints.name: Bl. Restituta Kafka
saints.story: A Franciscan sister and surgical nurse in Mödling near Vienna, she refused to remove crucifixes from hospital rooms and was denounced for anti-Nazi writings. She was beheaded in Vienna in 1943 and beatified in 1998.

cathedrals.name: St Stephen's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The Stephansdom, with its soaring Gothic south tower and colourful tiled roof, is the symbol of Vienna. Begun in the twelfth century and largely rebuilt in Gothic style, it was badly damaged by fire in 1945 and restored with contributions from every Austrian province. Its great bell, the Pummerin, rings at the New Year.

cathedrals.name: Salzburg Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Founded on the site of St Rupert's eighth-century church and rebuilt in the seventeenth century in early Baroque style, this cathedral is famous for its bright interior, great dome and the font where Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was baptised. It hosts the cathedral music tradition at the heart of the Salzburg Festival.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Mariazell
cathedrals.story: Austria's national shrine, Mariazell traces its origin to 1157, when a Benedictine monk brought a small wooden statue of Mary to the place. The Gothic-Baroque basilica draws pilgrims from Austria, Hungary and across Central Europe to the Magna Mater Austriae, the Great Mother of Austria.

prayerIntention: For the people of Austria: that, through the intercession of St Leopold and Our Lady of Mariazell, faith may be renewed and the Church be a home for seekers, the wounded and the stranger.

name: Azerbaijan
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic community (approx. a few hundred faithful)
history:
In ancient times, the kingdom of Caucasian Albania, in part of present-day Azerbaijan, embraced Christianity in the fourth century, and its churches and monasteries flourished for centuries; the Udi people are their heirs. Later the region became overwhelmingly Muslim. In the nineteenth century, Catholics from Poland, Germany and elsewhere came to Baku, especially during the oil boom, and a Catholic church was built in the early twentieth century.

Under Soviet rule the church was destroyed in the 1930s and its priest arrested; Catholic life vanished from public view. After independence, a small community re-formed, and Salesian priests arrived in 2000. St John Paul II visited in 2002, and afterwards the state donated land for a new church.

The Church of the Immaculate Conception in Baku was consecrated in 2008, and in 2011 the Holy See established the Apostolic Prefecture of Azerbaijan. Pope Francis visited in 2016. Today a tiny community of local Catholics and foreign workers lives in a largely Muslim society that values religious tolerance, while Christians also pray for peace in the long and painful conflict with Armenia.

cathedrals.name: Church of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: The original Catholic church of Baku, built in the early twentieth century, was demolished by the Soviets in the 1930s. After St John Paul II's 2002 visit, the government provided land for a new church, consecrated in 2008. It is the heart of Catholic life in the country, and Pope Francis celebrated Mass with the local community at the Salesian house in 2016.

prayerIntention: For the people of Azerbaijan and their neighbours in the Caucasus: that lasting peace and reconciliation may take root, and that the small Catholic community may be a sign of friendship and hope.

name: Bahamas
history:
In 1492 Christopher Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas in the Bahamas, but the islands' Lucayan people were soon enslaved and carried away, and within a generation they had vanished, a tragedy of the conquest. English settlers arrived in the seventeenth century, followed by Loyalists and enslaved Africans after the American Revolution, and the Anglican Church was established.

Catholic presence was minimal until the nineteenth century. A permanent Catholic mission was founded in Nassau in the 1880s, and from 1891 Benedictine monks from St John's Abbey in Minnesota took responsibility for the Bahamas, building churches, schools and later St Augustine's Monastery and College. Fr Jerome Hawes, an English architect-priest, designed many island churches and lived his last years as a hermit on Cat Island.

The Diocese of Nassau became an archdiocese in 1999. Today the Bahamian Church is fully local, serves throughout the islands and was tested by Hurricane Dorian in 2019, when parishes and Catholic charities rallied to help devastated communities in Abaco and Grand Bahama. No canonised saint is known from the Bahamas, but the Church honours the faith of its missionaries and families.

cathedrals.name: St Francis Xavier Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in the late nineteenth century as the first Catholic church in the Bahamas, this simple, gracious church became the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Nassau. It stands at the heart of a community that grew from a handful of faithful to a Church present across the islands.

cathedrals.name: The Hermitage, Mount Alvernia
cathedrals.story: On Mount Alvernia, the highest point in the Bahamas, Fr Jerome Hawes built with his own hands a tiny stone hermitage in the style of a medieval monastery, where he lived in prayer until his death in 1956. Reached by a path with Stations of the Cross, it is a place of pilgrimage and quiet beauty.

cathedrals.name: St Augustine's Monastery
cathedrals.story: Designed by Fr Jerome and founded by Benedictine monks from Minnesota, this monastery and its school have been a centre of prayer and education since the mid-twentieth century, forming generations of Bahamian leaders.

prayerIntention: For the people of the Bahamas: for protection from storms, strength for families, and a Church that welcomes all and serves the poor in every island.

name: Bahrain
catholicPresence: Catholic community of migrant workers (approx. 80,000 faithful, mostly from Asia), with very few Bahraini Catholics
history:
Before Islam, the region of Bahrain hosted Christian communities of the Church of the East, with bishops recorded in the fifth and sixth centuries. These communities faded after the coming of Islam, and for many centuries there was no Christian presence.

In modern times, Catholics came as workers in the oil industry and services. In 1939 the Emir granted land for the Sacred Heart Church in Manama, the first Catholic church in the Gulf region. The Catholic community has since grown to many thousands, mostly from India, the Philippines and other countries, worshipping in many languages.

Bahrain belongs to the Apostolic Vicariate of Northern Arabia, whose seat is now in Awali. In 2021 the Cathedral of Our Lady of Arabia was consecrated on land given by King Hamad, the largest Catholic church in the Arabian Peninsula. Pope Francis visited Bahrain in 2022 for a forum on dialogue between East and West. The faithful, many separated from their families for years of work, are a praying, sacrificing Church, honouring Our Lady of Arabia as patroness of the region.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Arabia
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in December 2021 on land donated by the King of Bahrain, this cathedral is the largest Catholic church in the Gulf. Its design evokes a tent, recalling the tent of meeting in the desert, and it can hold more than two thousand worshippers. It is the seat of the Apostolic Vicariate of Northern Arabia.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Church
cathedrals.story: Opened in 1939 on land granted by the then Emir, Sacred Heart is the first Catholic church in the modern Gulf region. Today it welcomes thousands of migrant workers each week, with Masses in many languages, and it remains a beloved home for those far from their families.

prayerIntention: For the Catholics of Bahrain, especially migrant workers far from home: that they may be treated with justice and dignity, and that dialogue and friendship between faiths may flourish.

name: Bangladesh
history:
Catholic missionaries came to Bengal with Portuguese traders in the sixteenth century. Jesuits and Augustinians worked in Chittagong and the Dhaka area from around 1600, and the Holy Rosary Church at Tejgaon, dating to the late seventeenth century, is among the oldest churches in the country. The early community included Portuguese descendants and local converts.

From the nineteenth century, missionaries such as the Holy Cross priests and sisters, PIME fathers and others developed parishes, schools and health care, and the faith took deep root among ethnic minority peoples like the Garo, Santal and others. During the 1971 War of Liberation, some Catholics, including priests, lost their lives, and the Church sheltered refugees.

Today the Catholic Church in Bangladesh is a small minority in a Muslim-majority nation but is widely respected for its schools, hospitals and Caritas relief work after cyclones and floods. St John Paul II visited in 1986 and Pope Francis in 2017, when he met Rohingya refugees. In 2016 Patrick D'Rozario became the country's first cardinal. Christians sometimes face discrimination and land conflicts, yet the Church grows in faith and service.

saints.name: St Teresa of Calcutta
saints.story: Though based in Kolkata, in the wider Bengal region, Mother Teresa served East Bengal too: after the 1971 war she sent sisters to Dhaka to care for war victims, including women who had suffered violence. The Missionaries of Charity continue to serve the poorest in Bangladesh today.

saints.name: Servant of God Theotonius Amal Ganguly
saints.story: Born in Bengal, he became the first Bengali bishop and in 1967 the first Bengali Archbishop of Dhaka. He guided the Church through the 1971 war and the birth of the new nation, devoted to prayer, education and the poor. His cause for canonisation has been opened.

cathedrals.name: St Mary's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Dhaka, built in the mid-twentieth century in the leafy Ramna area, is the centre of Catholic life in the capital. Pope Francis met clergy and religious here in 2017, and it gathers Bengali and tribal Catholics alike.

cathedrals.name: Holy Rosary Church
cathedrals.story: Founded by Portuguese missionaries in the seventeenth century, the Holy Rosary Church is among the oldest churches in Bangladesh. Rebuilt and expanded over time, it now serves one of the largest parishes in the country and keeps alive the memory of the faith's earliest roots in Bengal.

prayerIntention: For the people of Bangladesh: for protection from disasters, dignity for the poor and refugees, and harmony among all faiths in a land of rivers and resilience.

name: Barbados
history:
Barbados was settled by the English in 1627 and quickly became a sugar colony built on the labour of enslaved Africans. The Anglican Church was established, and Catholic worship was suppressed. In the 1650s, under Cromwell, many Irish Catholics were deported to Barbados as indentured labourers, and their faith was harshly restricted.

Catholic life could be practised openly only in the nineteenth century. St Patrick's Church in Bridgetown was built in the 1840s, burned in 1897 and was rebuilt. Religious orders, including Ursuline sisters, helped build Catholic education.

The Diocese of Bridgetown was established in 1970 and today serves Barbados as a small but committed community, active in education, social care and ecumenical friendship with other Christians on the island. No canonised saint is known from Barbados; the Church honours the hidden fidelity of those who kept their faith through centuries of hardship.

cathedrals.name: St Patrick's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: First built in the 1840s as the island's first Catholic church after the end of restrictions, St Patrick's was destroyed by fire in 1897 and rebuilt soon afterwards. A dignified church near the Garrison area, it is the cathedral of the Diocese of Bridgetown and the mother church of Barbadian Catholics.

prayerIntention: For the people of Barbados: that their island may grow in justice, hope and unity, and that the small Catholic community may be a light of service to all.

name: Belarus
catholicPresence: Catholic minority (approx. 7–10%), concentrated in the west and north-west
history:
The lands of Belarus received Christianity from Byzantium through Kievan Rus' in the late tenth century; St Euphrosyne of Polotsk is a beloved early saint. After the Grand Duchy of Lithuania accepted Latin Christianity in 1387, Catholic parishes spread, while the Union of Brest in 1596 brought many Orthodox into communion with Rome as Greek Catholics. Archbishop Josaphat Kuntsevych of Polotsk was killed for the cause of unity in 1623.

Under the Russian Empire, the Greek Catholic Church was abolished in 1839, and Latin Catholics faced restrictions after Polish uprisings. Soviet rule closed nearly all churches and imprisoned or executed many priests; during the Nazi occupation eleven sisters of the Holy Family of Nazareth offered their lives for local families and were shot near Navahrudak in 1943.

After 1991 the Church revived quickly, opening seminaries and restoring churches. Since the contested 2020 elections, Catholic leaders, priests and lay people have faced pressure and arrests; Archbishop Tadeusz Kondrusiewicz was barred from returning for some months. Despite difficulty, Marian devotion, especially at Budslau, sustains a faithful people.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of Budslau
patronSaints.feast: Saturday before the first Sunday of July

saints.name: St Josaphat Kuntsevych
saints.story: A Ruthenian monk who became Archbishop of Polotsk, Josaphat worked tirelessly for unity between the Orthodox and Catholic Churches. Opposition grew violent, and he was killed by a mob in Vitebsk in 1623. Canonised in 1867, he was the first Eastern Catholic saint canonised by Rome.

saints.name: St Andrew Bobola
saints.story: A Jesuit missionary who preached across Polesie, he was captured by Cossacks near Pinsk in 1657 and brutally martyred near Janów (today Ivanava in Belarus). Canonised in 1938, he is honoured as a patron by Belarusian and Polish Catholics.

saints.name: St Euphrosyne of Polotsk
saints.story: A princess of Polotsk who became a nun, Euphrosyne founded monasteries, copied books and promoted learning. She died on pilgrimage in Jerusalem. Venerated in the Orthodox Church and also honoured by Catholics, she is a patroness of Belarus from the time before the division of East and West.

saints.name: Bl. Maria Stella and Companions (Martyrs of Navahrudak)
saints.story: Eleven sisters of the Holy Family of Nazareth offered their lives to God in exchange for local fathers arrested by the Nazis. The men were spared; in August 1943 the sisters were taken away and shot. They were beatified in 2000.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Assumption, Budslau
cathedrals.story: This eighteenth-century Baroque basilica is the national Marian shrine of Belarus, housing the miraculous Budslau icon of Our Lady, given by a papal legate in the seventeenth century. The annual Budslau Fest in early July, now on UNESCO's intangible heritage list, draws tens of thousands of pilgrims.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Holy Name of Mary
cathedrals.story: Originally a seventeenth-century Jesuit church in Minsk's Upper Town, this Baroque church was closed by the Soviets and used as a sports hall. Returned to the Church in 1993 and restored, it became the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Minsk-Mohilev.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St Francis Xavier
cathedrals.story: A masterpiece of Baroque art built by the Jesuits around 1700, with a towering carved wooden altar. It is the cathedral of Grodno, the most Catholic region of Belarus, and its rich interior survived the Soviet era.

prayerIntention: For the people of Belarus: for freedom, justice and reconciliation, for those imprisoned for conscience, and for a Church faithful and free under the care of Our Lady of Budslau.

name: Belgium
catholicPresence: Historically Catholic; approx. half the population baptised Catholic, though regular Mass attendance is now low
history:
Christianity reached the lands of Belgium in late Roman times and took deep root in the seventh century through missionaries such as St Amand, St Lambert and St Hubert. Abbeys, beguinages and great Gothic churches made the region one of the most Catholic in Europe; at Liège St Juliana of Cornillon inspired the feast of Corpus Christi, first celebrated there in 1246.

The Reformation and the wars of the sixteenth century divided the Low Countries, but the southern provinces remained Catholic. After independence in 1830 the Church shaped schools, hospitals, trade unions and the University of Leuven, and Belgian missionaries went out across the world. Among them was St Damien De Veuster, who gave his life among the leprosy patients of Molokai. The Belgian missionary presence in the Congo was also bound up with a colonial system that brought grave abuses, a history the Church is still learning to face honestly.

In recent decades secularisation has emptied many churches, and the abuse crisis, brought painfully into the open from 2010, wounded trust deeply. Yet Marian shrines such as Banneux and Beauraing still draw pilgrims, and migrant communities bring new life to many parishes.

saints.name: St Damien of Molokai (Damien De Veuster)
saints.story: Born in Tremelo, this Picpus Father volunteered in 1873 to serve the exiled leprosy patients of Molokai in Hawaii. He built homes, a church and dignity for the forgotten, nursing, burying and loving them, until he contracted the disease himself and died among them. He was canonised in 2009.

saints.name: St Juliana of Cornillon (of Liège)
saints.story: An Augustinian nun near Liège who, moved by a vision, devoted her life to promoting a feast in honour of the Blessed Sacrament. The feast of Corpus Christi was first kept in the diocese of Liège and later extended to the whole Church. She endured opposition and exile with patience.

saints.name: St John Berchmans
saints.story: Born in Diest, he entered the Jesuits and studied in Rome, where he died aged twenty-two. He became a saint not through great deeds but through faithfulness in small things, cheerful obedience and love of Our Lady. He is a patron of altar servers and young students.

saints.name: St Mutien-Marie Wiaux
saints.story: A Brother of the Christian Schools who taught for nearly sixty years at the college in Malonne. Humble and prayerful, often seen with his rosary, he gave himself to teaching music and drawing and to quiet service. He was canonised in 1989.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St Michael and St Gudula
cathedrals.story: Built over some three centuries from the thirteenth century, this Brabantine Gothic cathedral with its twin white towers stands on a hill above the capital. Its sixteenth-century stained glass and Baroque pulpit are celebrated, and it hosts royal weddings and national ceremonies.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady
cathedrals.story: The tallest Gothic church tower in the Low Countries crowns this cathedral, begun in the fourteenth century. Inside hang several masterpieces by Peter Paul Rubens, including The Raising of the Cross and The Descent from the Cross. It survived iconoclasm, fires and revolution.

cathedrals.name: St Bavo's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: This Gothic cathedral houses the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb, the Ghent Altarpiece completed by the van Eyck brothers in 1432, one of the treasures of Western art. Its luminous panels of saints, prophets and the Lamb upon the altar draw visitors and pilgrims from around the world.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of the Poor
cathedrals.story: In 1933 Our Lady appeared to eleven-year-old Mariette Beco in this village near Liège as the Virgin of the Poor, pointing to a spring for the healing of nations. The apparitions were recognised by the bishop in 1949, and the shrine welcomes many sick and suffering pilgrims.

prayerIntention: For Belgium: that a weary and wounded Church may be healed and renewed, that the young may rediscover the Gospel, and that all who live there may know peace.

name: Belize
catholicPresence: Largest church in the country; approx. a third to 40% Catholic
history:
Catholic presence in Belize grew in the mid-nineteenth century, when refugees fleeing the Caste War in Yucatán settled in the north, bringing their faith with them. Jesuit missionaries began regular work in the colony in 1851, and from the late nineteenth century American Jesuits from Missouri took charge of the mission, founding parishes and schools among Creole, Mestizo, Maya and Garifuna communities.

Catholic schools became one of the backbones of education in the country, and many Belizeans, including political leaders, were formed by them. Feast days, processions and village celebrations blend the faith with the cultures of the many peoples who call Belize home, and the Garifuna Mass with drums and song is especially beloved.

Today the single Diocese of Belize City–Belmopan serves the whole nation. Catholics remain the largest religious community, though evangelical and other churches have grown strongly. The Church continues to serve through schools, social ministry and care for migrants from neighbouring countries.

cathedrals.name: Holy Redeemer Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The mother church of the diocese, standing near the seafront in Belize City. Its parish dates from the early days of the Catholic mission in the nineteenth century, and the cathedral has long been a gathering place for the faithful of the old capital through hurricanes and change.

cathedrals.name: Our Lady of Guadalupe Co-Cathedral
cathedrals.story: When the capital moved inland to Belmopan after Hurricane Hattie devastated Belize City in 1961, the Church followed. This church became the co-cathedral of the diocese, serving the growing, diverse population of the new capital under the patronage of Our Lady of Guadalupe.

prayerIntention: For the people of Belize, in all their beautiful diversity: for unity, safety from storms and violence, and for a Church that serves the poor and the stranger.

name: Benin
catholicPresence: Approx. a quarter of the population Catholic
history:
Portuguese chaplains visited the coast of Dahomey from the seventeenth century, but lasting mission began in 1861, when priests of the Society of African Missions arrived at Ouidah, once a major port of the Atlantic slave trade. The faith grew slowly at first and then steadily through schools, catechists and the first African priests, ordained in the twentieth century.

Benin gave the universal Church Cardinal Bernardin Gantin, who served for many years in the Roman Curia and became Dean of the College of Cardinals. In 1989–1990 Archbishop Isidore de Souza of Cotonou presided over the national conference that led the country peacefully from Marxist one-party rule to democracy, a moment remembered with gratitude.

Catholics today live alongside Muslims, Protestants and followers of Vodun, which remains deeply rooted in the culture. St John Paul II visited in 1982 and 1993, and in 2011 Pope Benedict XVI signed the apostolic exhortation Africae Munus in Ouidah. Vocations are strong, and the national Marian shrine at Dassa-Zoumé draws great crowds each year.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1909, this cathedral stands facing the Temple of Pythons in the historic slave-trading town of Ouidah, a striking sign of faith and coexistence. It recalls the first missionaries who landed here in 1861, and Pope Benedict XVI visited it in 2011.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Apostles
cathedrals.story: Painted in distinctive red and white stripes, the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Cotonou stands in the heart of the country's largest city. It is a lively centre of worship and of the Church's civic witness in Benin's capital of commerce.

cathedrals.name: Marian Shrine of Our Lady of Arigbo
cathedrals.story: Set among the hills of Dassa, where a grotto honours Our Lady of Lourdes, this is the national Marian shrine of Benin. Each August a great pilgrimage brings tens of thousands of the faithful from across the country to pray the rosary and celebrate the Assumption.

prayerIntention: For Benin: for lasting peace and security, for families and the young, and for a Church that is a sign of reconciliation among all its peoples.

name: Bhutan
catholicPresence: Very small Christian presence; Catholics number only a few hundred at most (approx.), with no public church
history:
The first Europeans known to have entered Bhutan were two Portuguese Jesuits, Fr Estêvão Cacella and Fr João Cabral, who arrived in 1627 on their way to Tibet. They were received courteously by the Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, the founder of the Bhutanese state, and stayed for some months before travelling on. Cacella's letter describing the journey is one of the earliest Western accounts of the country.

Centuries later, in 1963, the Canadian Jesuit Fr William Mackey was invited by the royal government to help build a modern school system. He served in Bhutan for more than thirty years as a teacher and educator, respected for his dedication to the Bhutanese people, and Jesuits from India also contributed to education for a time.

Bhutan is a deeply Buddhist kingdom, and public Christian worship and evangelisation are not permitted. The small number of Catholics, many of them foreign workers or from Nepali-speaking families, pray quietly in homes, and the country falls within the pastoral care of the Diocese of Darjeeling in India. Their faith is lived humbly, with gratitude and patience.

saints.name: Fr Estêvão Cacella, SJ (missionary)
saints.story: A Portuguese Jesuit who, with Fr João Cabral, crossed into Bhutan in 1627 and became one of its first European visitors. Welcomed by the Zhabdrung, he described the land and its people with respect in a long letter, before continuing toward Tibet, where he died soon after. He is not a canonised saint, but a pioneer of encounter.

saints.name: Fr William Mackey, SJ (missionary educator)
saints.story: A Canadian Jesuit invited in 1963 to help create Bhutan's modern schools. He served the country for over three decades, founding and guiding schools and training teachers, and was honoured by the state. His witness was one of quiet service rather than preaching, and he was buried in Bhutan.

prayerIntention: For the gentle kingdom of Bhutan: for the happiness and flourishing of its people, and for the few Christians there, that their quiet faith may be a blessing to their neighbours.

name: Bolivia
history:
The Catholic faith came to the Andes with the Spanish conquest in the 1530s. Dominicans, Franciscans, Augustinians, Mercedarians and Jesuits evangelised the Quechua and Aymara peoples, and the Archdiocese of La Plata (Sucre) became a great centre of colonial Church life. The silver mines of Potosí made Spain rich at a terrible human cost through forced labour, a wound some missionaries denounced even then.

Faith took root in Andean culture in a way all its own. In 1583 the Indigenous sculptor Francisco Tito Yupanqui carved the image of Our Lady of Copacabana beside Lake Titicaca, now the patroness of the nation. In the eastern lowlands, the Jesuit missions of Chiquitos and Moxos created towns of music, art and worship; their churches survive today as a World Heritage site.

In modern times the Church accompanied struggles for justice: the Jesuit Fr Luis Espinal was murdered in 1980 for defending democracy and the poor. Today Bolivia remains largely Catholic, with vibrant popular devotion at fiestas and pilgrimages, alongside evangelical growth and debates over relations between Church and state.

saints.name: St Nazaria Ignacia March Mesa
saints.story: Born in Spain, she emigrated to Mexico and then served the poor in Oruro, Bolivia. There in 1925 she founded the Misioneras Cruzadas de la Iglesia, an active order devoted to the Church and to the poor, and helped start Bolivia's first women's labour union. She was canonised in 2018, the saint most closely tied to Bolivia.

saints.name: Fr Martin Schmid, SJ (missionary)
saints.story: A Swiss Jesuit who served for decades in the Chiquitos missions, he was an architect, builder of organs and violins, and composer. He designed several of the beautiful mission churches that still stand and taught Indigenous communities music that is still performed today. He was expelled with the Jesuits in 1767.

saints.name: Fr Luis Espinal, SJ (missionary)
saints.story: A Spanish-born Jesuit priest, journalist and filmmaker who became a Bolivian citizen, he spoke out against corruption and dictatorship. In March 1980 he was kidnapped, tortured and killed by paramilitaries. Pope Francis prayed at the site of his death in 2015, honouring his courage.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Copacabana
cathedrals.story: On the shores of Lake Titicaca, this white Moorish-style basilica with its tiled domes shelters the dark wooden statue of Our Lady carved by Francisco Tito Yupanqui in 1583. The image is so treasured it rarely leaves its chapel. Pilgrims arrive on foot and by boat, and cars are blessed outside.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral and Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe
cathedrals.story: Built from the sixteenth century in the colonial capital, Sucre's cathedral blends Renaissance and Baroque styles. Its adjoining chapel keeps a revered image of Our Lady of Guadalupe painted around 1601 by the Hieronymite friar Diego de Ocaña, famously adorned with gold, pearls and precious stones.

cathedrals.name: Jesuit Mission Churches of Chiquitos
cathedrals.story: In towns such as San Javier, Concepción and San José, eighteenth-century churches built by Jesuits and Indigenous Chiquitano craftsmen still stand, with carved wooden columns and painted façades. Restored in recent decades and listed by UNESCO, they host a celebrated festival of Baroque music.

prayerIntention: For Bolivia: for justice and dignity for its Indigenous peoples and the poor, for peace in its public life, and for a faith that keeps growing under the gaze of Our Lady of Copacabana.

name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
catholicPresence: Catholic minority, approx. 15%, mostly Bosnian Croats
history:
Christianity reached this land in Roman times. In the Middle Ages Bosnia stood between Rome and Constantinople, with its own Bosnian Church, and in the fourteenth century Franciscans came to strengthen Catholic life. When the Ottomans conquered Bosnia in 1463, the friars stayed; Fra Anđeo Zvizdović obtained a charter from Sultan Mehmed II allowing them to minister to their people. For four centuries the Franciscans were almost the only pastors of Bosnian Catholics.

The regular hierarchy was restored in 1881 under Austro-Hungarian rule. The twentieth century brought immense suffering: the Second World War, in which crimes were committed by many sides, then communist persecution, including the killing of dozens of Franciscans at Široki Brijeg in 1945. The war of 1992–1995 brought atrocities against all peoples, and many Catholics were displaced and never returned.

Today the Catholic community is smaller and ageing, but still faithful. Medjugorje draws millions of pilgrims; in 2024 the Holy See gave a positive judgment on its spiritual fruits without ruling on the reported apparitions. Catholics pray for reconciliation in a land of many wounds.

saints.name: Bl. Ivan Merz
saints.story: Born in Banja Luka, this young scholar fought in the First World War, then devoted himself to the liturgy and to forming Catholic youth through the Croatian Eagles movement. He offered his life for the young people he served and died aged thirty-two. St John Paul II beatified him in Banja Luka in 2003.

saints.name: Bl. Drina Martyrs
saints.story: Five Daughters of Divine Charity from the convent in Pale, of Croatian, Slovenian, Hungarian and Austrian origin, were taken by Chetnik soldiers in December 1941. To preserve their chastity they leapt from a window in Goražde and were killed. They were beatified in Sarajevo in 2011.

saints.name: Ven. Petar Barbarić
saints.story: A young man from Herzegovina who studied at the Jesuit seminary in Travnik, hoping to become a priest. Known for his purity, joy and prayer, he died of tuberculosis at twenty-three. He was declared Venerable in 2015 and is a model for the young people of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in 1889 to designs by Josip Vancaš, this neo-Gothic cathedral with twin towers is the largest Catholic church in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was damaged in the siege of Sarajevo, and St John Paul II celebrated Mass in the city in 1997.

cathedrals.name: Church of St James
cathedrals.story: A twin-towered parish church completed in 1969, it became a world pilgrimage centre after reports of Marian apparitions beginning in 1981. Confession lines, evening rosary and Mass draw millions; in 2024 the Holy See encouraged the pastoral fruits of this place of prayer.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Mary, Mother of the Church
cathedrals.story: A modern cathedral consecrated in 1980, built in a bold contemporary style. It was badly damaged by shelling in the war of 1992–1995 and later restored, becoming a sign of the endurance of the Catholic community of Herzegovina.

prayerIntention: For Bosnia and Herzegovina: for healing of memories, justice and reconciliation among all its peoples, and for hope for those who long to stay and build a future there.

name: Botswana
history:
Christianity reached the Tswana peoples in the nineteenth century mainly through Protestant missionaries of the London Missionary Society, among them Robert Moffat and David Livingstone. Several Tswana chiefs, notably Khama III, embraced Christianity, and for a long time Protestant churches shaped the religious life of the Bechuanaland Protectorate.

Catholic missionaries came later, in the twentieth century, working from neighbouring South Africa and Southern Rhodesia and opening missions, schools and clinics. Growth was gradual, and the Church's presence was strengthened after independence in 1966. St John Paul II visited Botswana in 1988, an event warmly remembered by its small Catholic community.

Today Catholics are served by the Diocese of Gaborone and the Diocese of Francistown. When Botswana was struck hard by HIV and AIDS, Catholic parishes, religious sisters and home-based care programmes stood beside the sick, orphans and families. In a peaceful and stable country, the Church continues its quiet work in education, health care and outreach to rural communities and migrants.

cathedrals.name: Christ the King Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Diocese of Gaborone and the mother church of Catholics in the capital. A gathering place for a diverse congregation of Batswana and people from across Africa and beyond, it is the centre of diocesan celebrations and ordinations.

prayerIntention: For Botswana: for continued peace and good governance, for healing and hope for all affected by HIV and AIDS, and for a Church that serves with joy.

name: Brazil
catholicPresence: Largest Catholic population in the world; approx. 55% Catholic
history:
The first Mass on Brazilian soil was celebrated in 1500 by the chaplain of Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet. Jesuits arrived in 1549 with Manuel da Nóbrega, and St José de Anchieta helped found São Paulo, learned the Tupi language and wrote a grammar and catechism in it. Missionaries defended Indigenous peoples at times, yet the colonial Church was also entangled in the brutal enslavement of Africans and Indigenous people, a deep wound in Brazil's history.

In 1717 fishermen in the Paraíba River drew up a small dark clay image of the Immaculate Conception, later known as Nossa Senhora Aparecida, who became patroness of Brazil. Faith mingled with Afro-Brazilian and Indigenous cultures in rich popular devotion. In the twentieth century the Church gave the world figures such as Dom Hélder Câmara and spoke out against the military dictatorship.

Today Brazil has more Catholics than any other country, though the proportion has fallen sharply as evangelical churches grow. Vibrant parishes, base communities, charismatic renewal and the great shrine of Aparecida keep the faith alive.

saints.name: St José de Anchieta
saints.story: Born in the Canary Islands, this Jesuit came to Brazil as a young man and spent over forty years there. He helped found São Paulo, wrote a Tupi grammar, poems and plays, cared for the sick and defended Indigenous people. Called the Apostle of Brazil, he was canonised by Pope Francis in 2014.

saints.name: St Frei Galvão (Antônio de Sant'Anna Galvão)
saints.story: Born in Guaratinguetá, this Franciscan friar founded a convent in São Paulo and was loved as a confessor and peacemaker. His little paper 'pills' bearing a Marian prayer are still given to the sick. In 2007 Pope Benedict XVI canonised him in São Paulo as the first Brazilian-born saint.

saints.name: St Dulce of the Poor (Irmã Dulce)
saints.story: A Franciscan sister from Salvador, Bahia, she began by sheltering the sick in a henhouse beside her convent and built one of Brazil's largest charitable hospitals. Frail herself, she served the poorest for decades. Loved as the 'good angel of Bahia', she was canonised in 2019.

saints.name: St Paulina of the Agonizing Heart of Jesus
saints.story: Born Amabile Visintainer in Italy, she emigrated as a child to Santa Catarina in southern Brazil. There she founded the Little Sisters of the Immaculate Conception to care for the sick and the poor, and bore humiliation with humility. In 2002 she became the first saint canonised from Brazil.

saints.name: Sts Andrew de Soveral, Ambrósio Francisco Ferro and Companions (Martyrs of Natal)
saints.story: Two priests and dozens of lay Catholics, including whole families, were killed at Cunhaú and Uruaçu in Rio Grande do Norte during the Dutch occupation, for refusing to abandon their Catholic faith. Pope Francis canonised them in 2017.

cathedrals.name: National Shrine of Our Lady of Aparecida
cathedrals.story: One of the largest churches in the world, this vast brick basilica houses the small clay image found by fishermen in 1717. Millions of pilgrims come each year, especially on October 12. Popes John Paul II, Benedict XVI and Francis have prayed here, and the Latin American bishops met here in 2007.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral of Our Lady Aparecida
cathedrals.story: Designed by Oscar Niemeyer and dedicated in 1970, this cathedral rises like sixteen concrete hands lifted toward heaven, with a mostly underground nave flooded by light from stained glass between the columns. Angels hang above the congregation. It is an icon of modern sacred architecture.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary of Christ the Redeemer
cathedrals.story: Atop Corcovado mountain, the great statue of Christ with open arms, completed in 1931, watches over Rio. At its base a small chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Aparecida allows Mass to be celebrated. The statue, made of reinforced concrete and soapstone, has become a symbol of Brazil to the world.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lord of Bonfim
cathedrals.story: This eighteenth-century church in Salvador, Bahia, is beloved for its devotion to the crucified Christ. Its famous ribbons are tied around wrists and railings with prayers, and every January the washing of its steps draws enormous crowds in a celebration of faith and Bahian culture.

prayerIntention: For Brazil: for justice for the poor and for Indigenous and Afro-Brazilian peoples, for the protection of the Amazon, and for unity and renewal in the Church under the mantle of Our Lady of Aparecida.

name: Brunei
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority, approx. 2–3%, many of them foreign workers
history:
Brunei is a Malay Muslim monarchy where Islam is the state religion, and Christians form a small minority. Catholic life there grew mainly in the twentieth century, with missionaries serving Chinese, Indigenous and expatriate communities, especially around the oil towns of Seria and Kuala Belait. For many decades Brunei was cared for by dioceses in neighbouring Sarawak.

In 1997 the Holy See established a prefecture apostolic, raised in 2004 to the Apostolic Vicariate of Brunei Darussalam. Its first bishop, Cornelius Sim, a Bruneian who had worked as an engineer before ordination, was named a cardinal by Pope Francis in 2020, a great joy for this tiny flock. He died in 2021.

Catholics in Brunei, many of them Filipino workers, worship freely in their churches, but public religious celebration and evangelisation are restricted, and the visible celebration of Christmas is limited. Within these limits, three parishes sustain a warm and faithful community that prays for the country and lives peaceably among its neighbours.

cathedrals.name: Church of Our Lady of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: The main Catholic church in the capital and the seat of the Apostolic Vicariate of Brunei. Its parish gathers a diverse congregation of Bruneians and foreign workers for Mass in several languages, and it was here that Cardinal Cornelius Sim served his people.

cathedrals.name: St John's Church
cathedrals.story: One of the oldest Catholic parishes in Brunei, serving the oil-producing district of Belait, where many foreign workers and their families have lived and worshipped for generations.

prayerIntention: For Brunei: for peace and the wellbeing of all its people, and for its small Catholic community, especially migrant workers far from home, that they may be strengthened in faith.

name: Bulgaria
history:
Bulgaria embraced Christianity under Khan Boris I in 864, and soon after the disciples of Sts Cyril and Methodius brought the Slavonic liturgy and letters there; Boris even sought ties with Rome before settling within the Byzantine Church. Bulgaria became and remains a predominantly Orthodox land.

Catholic communities took shape from the seventeenth century, when Franciscans ministered among the Paulicians around Plovdiv and in north-western towns such as Chiprovtsi, whose Catholics rose against Ottoman rule in 1688 and were cruelly scattered. In the nineteenth century a Bulgarian Greek Catholic Church also formed. From 1925 to 1934 Archbishop Angelo Roncalli, the future St John XXIII, served in Sofia as papal representative and came to love the Bulgarian people.

Under communism the Church was persecuted. In 1952 Bishop Eugene Bossilkov and three Assumptionist priests were condemned in a show trial and shot. After 1989 freedom returned, St John Paul II beatified the martyrs, and Pope Francis visited in 2019. Today small Latin and Byzantine Catholic communities live in fraternal closeness with their Orthodox neighbours.

saints.name: Bl. Eugene Bossilkov
saints.story: A Passionist priest from a Catholic family near Svishtov, he became Bishop of Nikopol and refused to break with Rome under communist pressure. Arrested in 1952, he was tortured, condemned in a show trial and shot in Sofia. St John Paul II beatified him in 1998 as a martyr.

saints.name: Bl. Kamen Vitchev, Pavel Djidjov and Josaphat Shishkov
saints.story: Three Bulgarian Assumptionist priests, teachers and pastors, arrested by the communist regime and accused of espionage. After torture they were shot in Sofia in November 1952 alongside Bishop Bossilkov. St John Paul II beatified them in Plovdiv in 2002.

saints.name: St John XXIII (Angelo Roncalli)
saints.story: Before becoming Pope, Angelo Roncalli spent nearly ten years in Bulgaria as papal envoy, visiting remote Catholic villages and building friendships with the Orthodox. He later recalled Bulgaria with deep affection. As Pope he opened the Second Vatican Council, and he was canonised in 2014.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St Louis
cathedrals.story: Built in 1861, St Louis is the largest Catholic church in Bulgaria and the seat of the Diocese of Sofia and Plovdiv. Plovdiv has long been the heart of the country's Latin Catholic community, and the cathedral holds the memory of the martyrs beatified in the city in 2002.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St Joseph
cathedrals.story: The original church was destroyed by Allied bombing in 1944. St John Paul II blessed the foundation stone of a new cathedral during his 2002 visit, and the rebuilt church was consecrated in 2006, a sign of the Catholic community's renewal after communism.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Dormition of the Mother of God
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Bulgarian Greek Catholic Church, celebrating the liturgy in the Byzantine rite. It is a reminder of the Eastern Catholic tradition in Bulgaria, which kept faith with Rome through persecution while sharing the spiritual riches of the East.

prayerIntention: For Bulgaria: for its people and families, for unity and friendship between Catholics and Orthodox, and for the gift of hope to the young.

name: Burkina Faso
history:
The Missionaries of Africa, known as the White Fathers, arrived in the Mossi lands in 1900 and founded missions at Koupéla and Ouagadougou, soon joined by the White Sisters. Catechists and families carried the faith to villages, and the Church opened schools and dispensaries that shaped generations. Local vocations followed; in 1965 Paul Zoungrana, Archbishop of Ouagadougou, became the country's first cardinal.

Catholics have long lived in peace with a Muslim majority and followers of traditional religions, often within the same families. St John Paul II visited in 1980 and again in 1990, when he made a heartfelt appeal for the drought-stricken Sahel.

Since about 2015 the country has suffered terrible violence from armed jihadist groups. Thousands have been killed and millions displaced; priests, catechists and worshippers have been killed, and many parishes in the north and east have been forced to close. Christians and Muslims alike are victims. In the midst of this suffering, the Church remains close to the displaced, and the faithful continue to gather in prayer with great courage.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1936, this large cathedral was built with bricks of local earth by the people of Ouagadougou, who carried materials themselves.
