It is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Ouagadougou and the largest church in the country, a place of national celebrations and prayer.

cathedrals.name: Marian Shrine of Our Lady of Yagma
cathedrals.story: A national Marian sanctuary on the outskirts of the capital, where St John Paul II celebrated Mass during his visits. Each year a great pilgrimage draws hundreds of thousands of the faithful to pray to Our Lady for the nation, especially for peace.

prayerIntention: For Burkina Faso: for an end to violence and terror, for the displaced and grieving, and for Christians and Muslims to stand together in peace.

name: Burundi
history:
Catholic missionaries first tried to settle on the shores of Lake Tanganyika in 1879, but the mission did not last. In 1898 the White Fathers founded a lasting mission at Muyaga, and the faith spread rapidly in the twentieth century under German and then Belgian rule. By independence in 1962, Burundi was largely Catholic, with seminaries, schools and a growing local clergy.

Yet Burundi's history has been marked by deep ethnic violence between Hutu and Tutsi: the massacres of 1972, then civil war from 1993. The Church was not spared, and its members were found among both victims and perpetrators. Archbishop Joachim Ruhuna of Gitega was murdered in 1996, and in 2003 the papal nuncio, Archbishop Michael Courtney, was killed. In 1997 forty seminarians at Buta refused to separate into Hutu and Tutsi and were killed together.

The Church has been a strong voice for peace, reconciliation and human rights, sometimes at great cost. Today parishes are full, vocations abundant, and Catholics work for healing in a land that still faces poverty and political tension.

saints.name: The Martyrs of Buta (Servants of God)
saints.story: On 30 April 1997, armed men attacked the minor seminary of Buta and ordered the students to divide by ethnicity. They refused, saying they were all brothers, and forty young seminarians were killed together. A shrine marks the place, and a cause for their beatification has been opened.

saints.name: Archbishop Michael Courtney (nuncio)
saints.story: An Irish diplomat of the Holy See, he served as apostolic nuncio to Burundi and worked tirelessly to bring parties in the civil war to peace talks. In December 2003 he was ambushed and shot. He is remembered in Burundi as a man who gave his life for peace.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of the Martyrs of Fraternity
cathedrals.story: Built at the minor seminary where forty seminarians were killed in 1997, this shrine honours young men who refused to be divided by hatred. It has become a place of pilgrimage and prayer for reconciliation in Burundi and the Great Lakes region.

cathedrals.name: Regina Mundi Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Bujumbura, in the country's largest city on Lake Tanganyika. Dedicated to Mary, Queen of the World, it is the centre of Catholic life in the former capital and has witnessed national moments of mourning and hope.

cathedrals.name: Christ the King Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Gitega, in the historic heart and now capital of Burundi. It is closely linked to the early growth of the Church in the country and to the memory of Archbishop Joachim Ruhuna, who served there.

prayerIntention: For Burundi: for lasting reconciliation, for justice and an end to poverty, and that, like the martyrs of Buta, its people may live as brothers and sisters.

name: Cabo Verde
history:
The islands of Cabo Verde were uninhabited when Portuguese navigators arrived around 1460. Settlement began at Ribeira Grande on Santiago, now Cidade Velha, and the faith came with the first settlers. In 1533 the Diocese of Santiago de Cabo Verde was created, one of the oldest dioceses in sub-Saharan Africa, with jurisdiction for a time over parts of the West African coast.

That early Church grew in a society built on the transatlantic slave trade, for Ribeira Grande was a major hub where enslaved Africans were held, baptised and shipped across the ocean. This painful history is part of the islands' story, alongside the faith that Africans and their Creole descendants made their own and handed on through generations.

The islands knew drought, famine and emigration, and the Church shared these hardships. Today Cabo Verde is among the most Catholic countries in Africa, with two dioceses, Santiago and Mindelo. In 2015 Pope Francis named Bishop Arlindo Furtado of Santiago the country's first cardinal. Popular feasts of patron saints, music and processions keep faith woven into island life.

cathedrals.name: Ruins of the Sé Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Begun in the sixteenth century and completed in the seventeenth, the first cathedral of Cabo Verde was ruined after the town was sacked by French raiders in 1712. Its stone walls still stand above the old town, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of Cidade Velha, a moving witness to the islands' early and complex history.

cathedrals.name: Church of Our Lady of the Rosary
cathedrals.story: Dating from the late fifteenth century, this small church is considered one of the oldest colonial churches in the world. Its Manueline chapel and tombstones recall the first centuries of the faith, and it is still used for worship by the local community.

cathedrals.name: Pro-Cathedral of Our Lady of Grace
cathedrals.story: In the capital Praia, this church serves as the cathedral of the Diocese of Santiago. Standing on the Plateau, the historic centre of the city, it is the heart of Catholic celebrations for the most populous island of the archipelago.

prayerIntention: For Cabo Verde: for its families at home and in the diaspora, for the young seeking a future, and for a joyful faith that remains rooted in the islands.

name: Cambodia
history:
The Portuguese Dominican Gaspar da Cruz visited Cambodia around 1555, among the first Catholic missionaries to reach the kingdom, but he found little openness and soon left. Later missionaries, especially from the Paris Foreign Missions Society from the seventeenth century onward, served small communities, many of them Vietnamese or of mixed descent. Under the French protectorate the Church grew modestly and built schools and a cathedral in Phnom Penh.

The Khmer Rouge regime from 1975 to 1979 tried to erase all religion. The cathedral of Phnom Penh was demolished, churches destroyed, and priests, religious and lay Catholics died alongside about a fifth of the Cambodian people. Bishop Joseph Chhmar Salas, the first Cambodian bishop, died in a labour camp in 1977. A cause for him and his companions has been opened.

Public worship resumed only in 1990. Since then a small Church has been patiently rebuilt, with Khmer liturgy, care for the poor and the disabled, schools and dialogue with the Buddhist majority. Its humble members carry both deep wounds and quiet hope.

saints.name: Servant of God Joseph Chhmar Salas and Companions
saints.story: Ordained bishop in 1975 just before Phnom Penh fell, he became the first Cambodian Catholic bishop. Deported to the countryside by the Khmer Rouge, he shared the suffering of his people and died of exhaustion and hunger in 1977. A cause for him and other victims of the regime has been opened.

saints.name: Fr Gaspar da Cruz, OP (missionary)
saints.story: A Portuguese Dominican who travelled to Cambodia around 1555, he was one of the first Catholic missionaries there. Though his mission there bore little fruit, he went on to China and wrote one of the first European books about it. He died in Portugal caring for plague victims.

cathedrals.name: Site of the former Cathedral of Phnom Penh
cathedrals.story: The neo-Gothic cathedral of Phnom Penh, built under the French protectorate, was entirely demolished by the Khmer Rouge after 1975 and left no trace. Its loss remains a symbol of the suffering of Cambodia's Catholics, who have since rebuilt their communities in humble churches across the country.

prayerIntention: For Cambodia: for healing from the wounds of the past, for justice and dignity for the poor, and for its small Church, that it may be a gentle light among its people.

name: Cameroon
history:
Catholic mission in Cameroon began in 1890, when German Pallottine Fathers led by Fr Heinrich Vieter arrived on the coast and founded the mission of Marienberg. After the First World War the territory was divided between France and Britain; French Spiritans and British Mill Hill Missionaries continued the work, and the faith spread especially in the south and west, carried by catechists and schools.

The Church grew quickly in the twentieth century and produced many priests and religious, including Fr Simon Mpeke, known as Baba Simon, who gave his life to the Kirdi peoples of the north. The years around independence were turbulent, and Church figures were caught up in political conflicts. Later violence also touched the Church: Archbishop Yves Plumey was murdered in 1991, and the Jesuit theologian Fr Engelbert Mveng in 1995.

Today Cameroon is home to a large, lively Church, with full churches, vocations and Catholic universities. It also faces grave suffering from the conflict in the English-speaking regions and attacks by armed groups in the Far North. Bishops and religious work for dialogue and care for the displaced.

saints.name: Servant of God Simon Mpeke (Baba Simon)
saints.story: One of the first Cameroonian priests, ordained in 1935, he left a comfortable ministry in the south to serve the Kirdi peoples of the northern mountains. He lived simply among them, opened schools and cared for the sick, and was loved as Baba Simon. His cause for beatification is under way.

saints.name: Fr Heinrich Vieter, SAC (missionary)
saints.story: A German Pallottine priest who led the first Catholic missionaries to Cameroon in 1890 and became its first vicar apostolic. He founded missions, schools and the first church communities, laying the foundation of the Catholic Church in the country. A cause for his beatification has been opened.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Mary Queen of the Apostles
cathedrals.story: Mvolyé, on a hill in Yaoundé, is the site of the first Catholic mission in the capital, founded in 1901. The modern basilica dedicated to Mary Queen of the Apostles, a place of pilgrimage, honours this beginning of the faith in central Cameroon.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Victories
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Yaoundé, in the centre of the capital. Its striking modern architecture and its position near government buildings make it the stage for national celebrations, ordinations and prayers for the country.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Sts Peter and Paul
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1930s in the great port city, this cathedral is one of the oldest landmarks of Douala and the mother church of the archdiocese, serving a vast and diverse urban population.

prayerIntention: For Cameroon: for peace and dialogue in the English-speaking regions and the Far North, for the displaced and grieving, and for a Church that builds bridges of reconciliation.

name: Canada
history:
Catholic faith arrived with French explorers and settlers in the early seventeenth century. Jesuits, Récollets and Ursulines came to New France; St Marie of the Incarnation founded a school in Quebec in 1639, St Marguerite Bourgeoys taught in Montreal, and St François de Laval became the first bishop in 1674. Jesuit missionaries such as St John de Brébeuf lived among the Huron-Wendat and were killed in the 1640s amid wars between nations. St Kateri Tekakwitha, a Mohawk-Algonquin woman, became the first Indigenous saint of North America.

After the British conquest the Church became the guardian of French Canadian identity, and Irish, Scottish and later many other immigrants brought their faith across the country. Catholic schools, hospitals and religious orders shaped Canadian society.

The Church also took part in the residential school system, which tore Indigenous children from their families and culture, with abuse and many deaths. In 2022 Pope Francis made a penitential pilgrimage to Canada and asked forgiveness. Since Quebec's Quiet Revolution, secularisation has been dramatic, yet immigrant communities, shrines and new movements keep the faith alive.

patronSaints.name: Sts John de Brébeuf, Isaac Jogues and Companions (Canadian Martyrs)

saints.name: St Kateri Tekakwitha
saints.story: Born in a Mohawk village to a Mohawk father and Algonquin Christian mother, she survived smallpox that scarred her face. Baptised at twenty, she faced hostility and moved to the Christian mission of Kahnawake near Montreal, where she lived a life of intense prayer. Called the Lily of the Mohawks, she was canonised in 2012.

saints.name: St André Bessette
saints.story: A frail, barely literate Holy Cross brother, he served for decades as doorkeeper of a college in Montreal. Countless sick people came to him, and he sent them to pray to St Joseph, attributing every healing to him. His devotion gave rise to St Joseph's Oratory. He was canonised in 2010.

saints.name: St Marguerite Bourgeoys
saints.story: From Troyes in France, she came to Ville-Marie, now Montreal, in 1653 and opened its first school in a stone stable. She founded the Congregation of Notre-Dame, an uncloistered community of teaching sisters, and cared for the young women sent to the colony. She was canonised in 1982.

saints.name: St Marguerite d'Youville
saints.story: Born in Varennes, she was widowed young and endured poverty and scorn. She devoted herself to the poor and founded the Sisters of Charity of Montreal, the Grey Nuns, running the General Hospital for the sick, elderly and abandoned. In 1990 she became the first Canadian-born saint.

saints.name: St John de Brébeuf
saints.story: A French Jesuit who spent many years among the Huron-Wendat, learning their language and writing the Huron Carol. In 1649 he was captured during an Iroquois attack on the mission and died under torture. With his companions, the North American Martyrs, he was canonised in 1930.

cathedrals.name: Saint Joseph's Oratory of Mount Royal
cathedrals.story: Born from St André Bessette's tiny chapel of 1904, the great basilica with its vast copper dome rises over Montreal. Pilgrims climb its steps, some on their knees, and leave crutches as thanksgiving. It is the largest church in Canada and a world centre of devotion to St Joseph.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré
cathedrals.story: Near Quebec City, pilgrims have honoured St Anne since the seventeenth century, when shipwrecked sailors are said to have vowed a chapel in thanksgiving. The present Romanesque Revival basilica, with luminous mosaics, receives about a million visitors a year.

cathedrals.name: Notre-Dame Basilica
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1829 to designs by James O'Donnell, this Gothic Revival church dazzles visitors with a deep blue vaulted ceiling studded with gold stars, carved wood and stained glass telling Montreal's religious history. It is one of the most beloved churches in North America.

cathedrals.name: Basilica-Cathedral of Notre-Dame de Québec
cathedrals.story: The seat of the oldest diocese in North America north of Mexico, this cathedral has been rebuilt after sieges and fire across the centuries. St François de Laval is buried here, and in 2014 it received a Holy Door, the first outside Europe.

prayerIntention: For Canada: for truth, healing and reconciliation with Indigenous peoples, for welcome to newcomers, and for renewal of faith in a land of many saints.

name: Central African Republic
catholicPresence: Approx. a quarter to a third of the population Catholic
history:
Catholic missionaries of the Congregation of the Holy Spirit arrived in 1894 and founded the mission of St Paul of the Rapids in Bangui. Under French colonial rule the territory suffered terribly from forced labour by concession companies, and missionaries both shared in and sometimes denounced that system. The faith spread through mission stations, catechists and schools.

In 1938 Barthélemy Boganda was ordained the first priest from Ubangi-Shari; he later left the priesthood to enter politics and became the father of the nation's independence movement, dying in 1959 before independence was achieved. Since independence in 1960 the country has endured coups, dictatorship and poverty.

From 2013 civil war between armed groups, the mostly Muslim Séléka and the anti-balaka militias, brought massacres and displacement, and religion was manipulated to divide communities. Catholic parishes sheltered thousands, Muslims among them, and Cardinal Dieudonné Nzapalainga worked alongside an imam and a Protestant pastor for peace. In November 2015 Pope Francis opened the first Holy Door of the Jubilee of Mercy in Bangui, calling it the spiritual capital of the world.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Notre-Dame of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Built of red brick in the 1930s, the cathedral of Bangui stands at the heart of the capital. Here, on 29 November 2015, Pope Francis opened the Holy Door of the Jubilee of Mercy before it was opened in Rome, a powerful sign of hope for a wounded nation.

prayerIntention: For the Central African Republic: for lasting peace, for disarmament and reconciliation between Christians and Muslims, and for healing for all who have lost loved ones and homes.

name: Chad
catholicPresence: Catholic minority, approx. 20%, mostly in the south
history:
Chad lies where the Sahara meets tropical Africa, and Islam has been present in its north and centre for centuries. Catholic mission came late: missionaries began work in the south during the French colonial period in the 1920s and 1930s, and Jesuits and other congregations later opened missions, schools and health centres among the peoples of the south.

The faith grew quickly among communities such as the Sara, carried by catechists and local leaders. Since independence in 1960 the country has suffered long years of civil war, coups and conflict, and the Church shared in the suffering, as churches and missions were damaged and people fled. The cathedral of N'Djamena itself was badly damaged in the fighting of 1980.

Today the Church in Chad is young and growing, with dioceses across the south and a presence in the Muslim-majority north. It serves through education, healthcare, development and care for refugees from Sudan and the Central African Republic, and it works to maintain good relations between Christians and Muslims in a country marked by poverty and fragility.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Peace
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of N'Djamena was severely damaged during the civil war in 1980 and later rebuilt. Its name, Our Lady of Peace, expresses the longing of Chadian Catholics for an end to conflict, and it remains the heart of Catholic life in the capital.

prayerIntention: For Chad: for peace and stability, for refugees and the hungry, and for friendship between Christians and Muslims in the land where desert meets savannah.

name: Chile
history:
The faith came to Chile with the Spanish conquest, as Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago in 1541 with priests among his company. Mercedarians, Franciscans, Dominicans and Jesuits evangelised the land; Jesuits such as Luis de Valdivia argued for a defensive, more humane policy toward the Mapuche, whose long resistance and suffering under colonisation remain an unhealed wound.

After independence the Church helped shape the new republic and the devotion to Our Lady of Mount Carmel, patroness of the nation's armies. In the twentieth century Chile gave the Church St Teresa of Los Andes and St Alberto Hurtado, whose Hogar de Cristo still shelters the poor. Under the military dictatorship from 1973, Cardinal Raúl Silva Henríquez and the Vicariate of Solidarity defended human rights and the families of the disappeared, at real risk. St John Paul II visited in 1987.

In recent years the Church has been deeply shaken by the revelation of sexual abuse and its cover-up; in 2018 all the bishops offered their resignations to Pope Francis. Trust and practice have declined sharply, yet many Chileans still turn to Mary at shrines such as Maipú and Andacollo.

saints.name: St Teresa of Los Andes
saints.story: Born Juana Fernández Solar in Santiago, a lively young woman who loved sport and her friends, she entered the Carmelite convent of Los Andes at nineteen. She died of typhus less than a year later. Her letters and diary reveal a burning love for Christ. In 1993 she became Chile's first saint.

saints.name: St Alberto Hurtado
saints.story: A Jesuit priest, teacher and writer, he was moved by the homeless children of Santiago to found the Hogar de Cristo in 1944, which became one of Chile's largest charities. He also defended workers' rights. His motto was 'Content, Lord, content'. He was canonised in 2005.

saints.name: Bl. Laura Vicuña
saints.story: Born in Santiago, she moved with her widowed mother to Argentina, where she attended a Salesian school. Grieved by her mother's situation with an abusive man, she offered her life for her mother's conversion and died aged twelve. Her mother returned to the faith. She was beatified in 1988.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral of Santiago
cathedrals.story: Facing the Plaza de Armas, the present cathedral was built from 1748 onward, with the Italian architect Joaquín Toesca shaping its neoclassical façade. It is the fifth church on this site, after earthquakes and fire destroyed earlier ones, and it holds the tombs of archbishops of Santiago.

cathedrals.name: National Shrine of Maipú (Votive Temple)
cathedrals.story: In 1818 Bernardo O'Higgins vowed to build a church to Our Lady of Mount Carmel on the site of the decisive battle of independence. The modern temple, with its tall concrete tower and coloured glass, keeps that promise and is the national shrine of Chile's patroness.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of St Teresa of Los Andes
cathedrals.story: In the Andean foothills, this sanctuary keeps the remains of St Teresa of Los Andes and draws large numbers of young pilgrims, many of whom walk through the night to reach it. It is a place of prayer, confession and encounter with Chile's beloved young saint.

prayerIntention: For Chile: for healing for survivors of abuse and renewal of the Church in humility and truth, for justice for the Mapuche, and for peace and unity among all Chileans.

name: China
history:
The Church of the East reached China in 635, but Catholic mission began with the Franciscan John of Montecorvino, who arrived in Khanbaliq (Beijing) in 1294 and became its archbishop. That mission faded after the Mongol dynasty fell. In 1583 the Jesuit Matteo Ricci entered China, mastered its language and classics, and won respect at the imperial court; St Francis Xavier had died in 1552 on Shangchuan Island waiting to enter.

The Chinese Rites controversy and later imperial bans restricted the faith, and missionaries and Chinese Christians suffered repeated persecution. In the nineteenth century missions expanded under unequal treaties forced on China by Western powers, a link that bred resentment. During the Boxer uprising of 1900 thousands of Catholics were killed; many are among the 120 Martyrs of China canonised in 2000.

After 1949 foreign missionaries were expelled, bishops and priests imprisoned, and a state-controlled Catholic association created, while many faithful worshipped in an unofficial community. Since 2018 a provisional agreement between the Holy See and China on the appointment of bishops has been renewed several times. Chinese Catholics continue to live their faith with great fidelity under real restrictions.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of China
patronSaints.feast: Saturday before the second Sunday of May

saints.name: St Augustine Zhao Rong and Companions (Martyrs of China)
saints.story: One hundred and twenty martyrs, eighty-seven of them Chinese and the others missionaries, killed between 1648 and 1930, many during the Boxer uprising. Augustine Zhao Rong was a soldier converted while escorting a bishop to execution, later a priest who died in prison in 1815. They were canonised in 2000.

saints.name: St Francis Fernández de Capillas
saints.story: A Spanish Dominican who served in Fujian, he was arrested during the upheavals of the fall of the Ming dynasty and beheaded in 1648. He is honoured as the protomartyr of China and is among the 120 martyrs canonised in 2000.

saints.name: Ven. Matteo Ricci
saints.story: An Italian Jesuit who entered China in 1583 and reached Beijing in 1601, he adopted Chinese dress and learning, produced a celebrated world map and befriended scholars such as Xu Guangqi. He is buried in Beijing, the first Westerner granted that honour. He was declared Venerable in 2022.

saints.name: St Francis Xavier
saints.story: The great Jesuit missionary to India and Japan longed to bring the Gospel to China. He died of fever on Shangchuan Island off the coast of Guangdong in December 1552, within sight of the mainland, before he could enter. He is patron of the missions.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (Nantang)
cathedrals.story: Standing on the site where Matteo Ricci established a chapel in 1605, Nantang is the oldest Catholic church site in Beijing. Rebuilt several times after earthquakes, fire and the Boxer uprising, its Baroque façade now faces a busy street, and it is the cathedral of Beijing.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Sheshan
cathedrals.story: On a hill outside Shanghai, this basilica honours Our Lady Help of Christians, whose statue holding the Christ Child aloft crowns its tower. Pilgrims climb the Way of the Cross to the summit, especially in May. Pope Benedict XVI composed a prayer to Our Lady of Sheshan for the Church in China.

cathedrals.name: St Ignatius Cathedral (Xujiahui)
cathedrals.story: Built by the Jesuits and completed in 1910 in the former estate of Xu Guangqi's family, this red-brick Gothic cathedral with twin spires was badly damaged during the Cultural Revolution and later restored. It is the cathedral of the Diocese of Shanghai.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral (Shishi)
cathedrals.story: Built of granite between 1863 and 1888, this soaring Gothic Revival cathedral is known as the Stone House. Its twin spires dominate old Guangzhou, and its restored stained glass makes it one of the most impressive churches in Asia.

prayerIntention: For China: for its immense people and their dignity and freedom, for the unity and fidelity of its Catholics, and for the Church there under the protection of Our Lady of Sheshan.

name: Colombia
history:
The faith arrived with Spanish conquerors and missionaries in the early sixteenth century, and Cartagena and Santa Fe de Bogotá became centres of colonial Church life. In Cartagena, a chief slave port of the Americas, the Jesuit St Peter Claver spent his life serving enslaved Africans as they came off the ships, declaring himself 'the slave of the slaves forever'. Indigenous peoples suffered conquest and decline, and some missionaries raised their voices in defence.

In 1586 an image of Our Lady of the Rosary in Chiquinquirá was said to be miraculously renewed, and she became patroness of Colombia. After independence the Church held great influence, and conflicts between liberals and conservatives often turned on its role. In the twentieth century St Laura Montoya founded missionary sisters to serve Indigenous communities.

Decades of armed conflict between guerrillas, paramilitaries, drug cartels and the state brought immense suffering, and many priests, religious and catechists were killed. The Church has accompanied victims and supported peace efforts, and in 2017 Pope Francis visited and beatified two martyrs of the violence. Faith remains strong and joyful across the country.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of the Rosary of Chiquinquirá

saints.name: St Peter Claver
saints.story: A Spanish Jesuit who arrived in Cartagena in 1610 and devoted forty years to enslaved Africans arriving on the ships, bringing them food, medicine, care and the Gospel. He is estimated to have baptised many thousands. Colombia honours him as patron of human rights.

saints.name: St Laura Montoya
saints.story: Born in Jericó, Antioquia, she was a teacher who felt called to serve Indigenous peoples in the jungles. In 1914 she founded the Missionaries of Mary Immaculate and St Catherine of Siena, living among the Emberá and others with deep respect. In 2013 she became Colombia's first canonised saint.

saints.name: St María Bernarda Bütler
saints.story: A Swiss Franciscan sister who founded the Franciscan Missionaries of Mary Help of Christians in Ecuador, then, exiled by persecution, settled in Cartagena in 1895, where she served the sick and the poor for nearly thirty years. She was canonised in 2008.

saints.name: Bl. Jesús Emilio Jaramillo Monsalve
saints.story: Bishop of Arauca, he defended his people against violence and spoke for peace. In 1989 he was kidnapped and murdered by ELN guerrillas. Pope Francis beatified him as a martyr in Villavicencio in 2017, together with Fr Pedro María Ramírez, killed in 1948.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary of Chiquinquirá
cathedrals.story: This neoclassical basilica in Boyacá keeps the venerated painting of Our Lady of the Rosary with St Anthony and St Andrew, which according to tradition was miraculously restored in 1586. The image is the heart of Colombia's Marian devotion, and St John Paul II prayed before it in 1986.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Las Lajas
cathedrals.story: Built between 1916 and 1949, this neo-Gothic church rises from the bottom of a deep river gorge, joined to a bridge across it. Pilgrims honour an image of Our Lady painted on the rock face, revered since the eighteenth century. It is one of the most breathtaking churches in the world.

cathedrals.name: Primatial Cathedral of Bogotá
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1823 on the Plaza de Bolívar, this neoclassical cathedral stands where the first church of the city was built in 1538. It is the seat of the Primate of Colombia and holds the tomb of the conquistador and founder of Bogotá, Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada.

cathedrals.name: Salt Cathedral of Zipaquirá
cathedrals.story: Carved deep inside a salt mine, this underground church features Stations of the Cross hewn into the salt walls and a great illuminated cross. Though not a cathedral in the canonical sense, it is a beloved place of prayer and pilgrimage, especially honouring the miners.

prayerIntention: For Colombia: for lasting peace and reconciliation, consolation for the victims of violence, and the protection of those who defend life and the land.

name: Comoros
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic minority, well under 1% (approx.), mostly foreign residents
history:
The Comoros islands, between Mozambique and Madagascar, have been overwhelmingly Muslim for many centuries, and Sunni Islam is deeply woven into their culture and law. A Catholic presence came with French colonial rule in the nineteenth century, serving administrators, traders and workers, especially from Madagascar and Réunion.

After independence in 1975 the Holy See created an apostolic administration for the islands, later raised to the Apostolic Vicariate of the Archipelago of the Comoros, which also cares for Catholics on the French island of Mayotte. On the three islands of the Union of the Comoros the Catholic community is tiny, made up largely of Malagasy, African and European residents, and conversion of Comorians is strongly discouraged by society and law.

The Church's mission here is humble: celebrating the sacraments for its small flock, and serving all people through quiet works of education, health care and charity, often carried out by religious sisters. Catholics live their faith discreetly and in respectful friendship with their Muslim neighbours, a small seed of prayer in the Indian Ocean.

cathedrals.name: Catholic Church of Moroni
cathedrals.story: The small Catholic parish in the capital, on the island of Grande Comore, is the heart of the Apostolic Vicariate in the Union of the Comoros. It gathers expatriates, Malagasy and African residents for Mass and prayer, and serves as a modest but faithful witness among a Muslim people.

prayerIntention: For the people of the Comoros: for peace, development and the wellbeing of every family, and for the tiny Catholic community, that it may be a humble sign of love among its neighbours.

name: Costa Rica
catholicPresence: Approx. half the population Catholic; Catholicism is the state religion
history:
Catholic faith arrived with Spanish settlement in the sixteenth century, and the colonial capital Cartago became the religious centre of this small, poor province of the Captaincy General of Guatemala. Missionaries, especially Franciscans, worked among the Indigenous peoples, whose numbers fell sharply through conquest and disease.

In 1635, according to tradition, a young mixed-race woman named Juana Pereira found a small dark stone image of Our Lady on a rock near Cartago. Each time it was taken away it returned to the spot, and a shrine was built there. Our Lady of the Angels, lovingly called La Negrita, became patroness of Costa Rica, and every August hundreds of thousands walk to Cartago in the great romería.

Costa Rica is one of the few countries whose constitution names Catholicism the religion of the state. In the 1940s Archbishop Víctor Sanabria helped bring the Church's social teaching into national life, supporting social security and workers' rights. Today the country is peaceful and without an army, while secularisation and evangelical growth have reduced the Catholic share. Devotion to La Negrita remains a powerful bond of national identity.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of the Angels (La Negrita)

saints.name: Bl. María Romero Meneses
saints.story: Born in Granada, Nicaragua, this Salesian sister spent most of her religious life in San José, Costa Rica. She cared for poor children and families, founded clinics and homes, and taught catechism with great joy and love for Mary Help of Christians. She was beatified by St John Paul II in 2002.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels
cathedrals.story: Rebuilt after the 1910 earthquake, this white basilica in a blend of colonial and Byzantine styles houses the tiny stone image of La Negrita found in 1635. Beneath it, pilgrims collect water from a spring and leave metal ex-votos in thanksgiving. Each August the national pilgrimage converges here.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral of San José
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the capital, rebuilt in the nineteenth century after earlier churches were damaged by earthquakes, has a neoclassical façade and a peaceful interior with colourful stained glass. It stands beside the Central Park and is the seat of the Archdiocese of San José.

cathedrals.name: Ruins of Santiago Apóstol
cathedrals.story: The parish church of Cartago was destroyed by earthquakes several times; the reconstruction begun in 1870 was abandoned after the earthquake of 1910. Its roofless stone walls, now surrounding a quiet garden, are a beloved symbol of Cartago and of the resilience of its people.

prayerIntention: For Costa Rica: for the gift of peace it cherishes, for care for creation and for the poor, and for a living faith under the gentle protection of La Negrita.

name: Croatia
history:
Christianity flourished in Roman Dalmatia, where Salona was an early see; St Domnius was martyred there around 304. The Croats who settled in the region accepted baptism between the seventh and ninth centuries, and their bond with Rome was cherished: Croatia is sometimes called the Bulwark of Christendom. A distinctive tradition of liturgy in Old Church Slavonic, written in Glagolitic script, survived for centuries.

Croatia lived for centuries on the frontier of Ottoman expansion, and its faith was shaped by war and endurance. In 1687 the Croatian Parliament proclaimed St Joseph patron of the kingdom. In the twentieth century Archbishop Aloysius Stepinac of Zagreb was imprisoned by the communists after a show trial; he was beatified in 1998, though his conduct during the Second World War and the Ustaša regime, under which grave crimes were committed, remains debated, especially with Serbian Orthodox.

Communism restricted the Church, yet pilgrimage and family faith endured. The war of independence in the 1990s brought destruction of churches and much suffering. Today the Church plays a major public role, and shrines such as Marija Bistrica draw many pilgrims, though secularisation is growing.

saints.name: St Nikola Tavelić
saints.story: A Franciscan from Šibenik, he served in Bosnia and then in the Holy Land. In 1391 he and three companions publicly proclaimed Christ before the authorities in Jerusalem and were put to death. Canonised in 1970, he was the first Croatian saint.

saints.name: St Leopold Mandić
saints.story: A Croatian Capuchin born in Herceg Novi, in present-day Montenegro, he was very small and frail. He spent decades in a tiny cell in Padua hearing confessions for many hours a day, offering endless mercy, and prayed for the unity of East and West. He was canonised in 1983.

saints.name: St Mark of Križevci
saints.story: A Croatian priest and canon of Esztergom, he was killed in Košice, in present-day Slovakia, with two Jesuit companions by Protestant soldiers during the Thirty Years' War for refusing to renounce the Catholic faith. He was canonised by St John Paul II in 1995.

saints.name: Bl. Alojzije Stepinac
saints.story: Archbishop of Zagreb from 1937, he was arrested by the communist authorities in 1946 and sentenced after a show trial, later held under house arrest until his death. Many Croatians venerate him as a martyr for fidelity to Rome; his wartime record remains disputed. He was beatified in 1998.

saints.name: Bl. Miroslav Bulešić
saints.story: A young priest from Istria who served his people through the hardships after the Second World War. In 1947, while accompanying a bishop administering confirmations in Lanišće, he was attacked and killed by communist activists. He was beatified in 2013 as a martyr.

cathedrals.name: Zagreb Cathedral (Assumption of Mary)
cathedrals.story: Rebuilt in neo-Gothic style after the earthquake of 1880, with twin spires that dominate the skyline, the cathedral is the largest church in Croatia. It holds the tomb of Bl. Alojzije Stepinac. Damaged again in the 2020 earthquake, it is undergoing careful restoration.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St James
cathedrals.story: Built entirely of stone between 1431 and 1535, largely by the master Juraj Dalmatinac and then Nikola Firentinac, its stone vaults and dome were assembled from precisely fitted interlocking slabs. A frieze of seventy-one carved human heads circles its apses. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St Domnius
cathedrals.story: Set inside the mausoleum of the Emperor Diocletian, a persecutor of Christians, this octagonal building became a cathedral dedicated to the martyr Domnius, whom Diocletian's persecution killed. Its Romanesque bell tower rises over the ancient palace, a striking sign of faith overcoming persecution.

cathedrals.name: National Shrine of Our Lady of Marija Bistrica
cathedrals.story: In the hills north of Zagreb, this shrine honours a wooden statue of the Black Madonna hidden during Ottoman raids and rediscovered. It is Croatia's main Marian pilgrimage site, and St John Paul II beatified Alojzije Stepinac here in 1998.

prayerIntention: For Croatia: for faithful families and young people, for reconciliation and honest remembrance among the peoples of the region, and for a Church renewed in holiness.

name: Cuba
catholicPresence: approx. 55–60% baptized Catholic; weekly practice is low
history:
The faith reached Cuba with the Spanish in the early sixteenth century. The first diocese was founded at Baracoa and soon moved to Santiago de Cuba, and the island quickly became a gateway for missions to the Americas. The colonial Church was entangled with conquest and, later, with slavery, yet it also produced prophetic voices: Bartolomé de las Casas, once an encomendero in Cuba, gave up his grant there in 1514 and became a lifelong defender of the Indigenous peoples.

Around 1612, three young men found a small statue of the Virgin floating in the Bay of Nipe. Our Lady of Charity of El Cobre became the heart of Cuban devotion, embraced by Spaniards, Africans and Creoles alike, and in 1916 Pope Benedict XV declared her patroness of Cuba. The priest Félix Varela shaped the island’s conscience in the nineteenth century, teaching that faith and freedom belong together.

After the 1959 revolution, Catholic schools were nationalized, many priests and religious were expelled, and for decades believers faced discrimination under an officially atheist state. A slow thaw followed: the constitution ceased to be atheist in 1992, and Popes John Paul II (1998), Benedict XVI (2012) and Francis (2015) all visited. Today the Church is small in clergy but tenacious, serving the poor through Caritas amid deep economic hardship and emigration.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of Charity of El Cobre

saints.name: St. Anthony Mary Claret
saints.story: A Catalan missionary who served as Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba from 1851 to 1857. He preached tirelessly across the island, founded credit unions and farm schools, defended enslaved people and married couples living without the sacrament, and survived an assassination attempt in Holguín. He later founded the Claretian Missionaries.

saints.name: Bl. José Olallo Valdés
saints.story: Left as an infant at a Havana orphanage, he became a Brother Hospitaller of St. John of God and spent over fifty years nursing the sick in Camagüey, caring for wounded on both sides of the independence war. Beatified in Camagüey in 2008, he is the first Cuban-born person raised to the altars.

saints.name: Ven. Félix Varela
saints.story: Havana-born priest, philosopher and patriot who taught at the San Carlos seminary and argued for the abolition of slavery and Cuban self-government. Exiled, he served the poor Irish immigrants of New York as a parish priest and vicar general. He was declared Venerable in 2012.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Charity of El Cobre
cathedrals.city: El Cobre, near Santiago de Cuba
cathedrals.story: The national shrine, set in the hills above an old copper-mining town, houses the small statue of the Virgin found in the Bay of Nipe in the early 1600s. Pilgrims leave crutches, medals, photographs and letters as offerings. Ernest Hemingway gave his Nobel Prize medal to the shrine, and three popes have prayed here.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Virgin Mary of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Begun by the Jesuits in the mid-eighteenth century and later made the cathedral, its curving baroque façade of coral limestone, studded with fossils from the sea, dominates the Plaza de la Catedral in Old Havana. Its asymmetrical towers and theatrical front make it one of the most beloved baroque buildings in the Caribbean.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: Seat of Cuba’s oldest archdiocese, overlooking Parque Céspedes. The cathedral has been rebuilt several times after earthquakes and pirate raids; the present building, with its twin towers and an angel crowning the façade, dates largely from the early nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Anthony Mary Claret governed the archdiocese from here.

prayerIntention: For the people of Cuba, that under the mantle of Our Lady of Charity families divided by hardship and exile may know hope, freedom and daily bread.

name: Cyprus
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. 1–3%), Maronite and Latin, plus many migrant workers
history:
Cyprus was among the first lands to hear the Gospel. The Acts of the Apostles tells how Paul and Barnabas, himself a Cypriot, preached across the island around AD 45, from Salamis to Paphos, where the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus came to believe. The Church of Cyprus grew strong and was recognized as self-governing in 431; it remains Greek Orthodox and is the faith of most Cypriots today.

When the Crusader Lusignan dynasty ruled from 1192, a Latin hierarchy was imposed and the Orthodox were subordinated, a painful chapter of division that left magnificent Gothic cathedrals in Nicosia and Famagusta. Under Ottoman rule from 1571 those churches became mosques, and the Latin presence shrank to Franciscan friars caring for pilgrims and merchants.

Maronite Catholics, who had come from Lebanon and Syria over many centuries, kept their faith in villages such as Kormakitis; the 1974 division of the island displaced most of them. Today the Catholic community is small: Maronites under their archbishop in Nicosia, and a Latin flock served by Franciscans of the Custody of the Holy Land, swelled by Filipino, Sri Lankan and other migrant workers. Popes Benedict XVI (2010) and Francis (2021) visited, praying for reconciliation on a divided island.

saints.name: St. Barnabas
saints.story: A Levite born in Cyprus, his name means son of encouragement. He vouched for the newly converted Paul to the apostles in Jerusalem and travelled with him on the first missionary journey through Cyprus. Tradition holds that he was martyred at Salamis, where a monastery bearing his name still stands.

saints.name: St. Epiphanius of Salamis
saints.story: Born in Palestine, he became bishop of Salamis (Constantia) in Cyprus around 367 and led the island’s Church for over three decades. A learned, ascetic and fiercely orthodox pastor, he wrote a famous catalogue of heresies and is venerated as a saint in both East and West.

saints.name: St. Spyridon
saints.story: A shepherd who became bishop of Trimythous in Cyprus, remembered for his simplicity, humility and care for the poor. Tradition places him at the Council of Nicaea in 325. His relics now rest in Corfu, and he is honoured by Catholics and Orthodox alike.

cathedrals.name: Holy Cross Catholic Church
cathedrals.story: The main Latin Catholic church of Cyprus, served by Franciscans of the Custody of the Holy Land. The present church dates from the early twentieth century and stands right against the buffer zone that divides Nicosia. Its multilingual Masses gather Cypriots and migrant workers from across Asia and Africa, a living picture of the universal Church.

cathedrals.name: Maronite Cathedral of Our Lady of Graces
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Maronite Archeparchy of Cyprus, heart of a community whose roots on the island go back many centuries. For Maronite families displaced from their villages in 1974, it has become a gathering place where the ancient Syriac liturgy and their own traditions are kept alive.

cathedrals.name: Former Cathedral of Saint Sophia (Selimiye Mosque)
cathedrals.story: Built by the Latin Church between the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, it was where Lusignan kings were crowned and is one of the finest Gothic buildings in the eastern Mediterranean. Converted into a mosque in 1570, it now carries minarets atop its French Gothic towers, a striking reminder of the island’s layered history.

prayerIntention: For Cyprus, the island of Barnabas, that its divided communities may find reconciliation and that Christians of East and West may grow in unity.

name: Czechia
catholicPresence: approx. 7–10% Catholic; one of Europe’s most secular nations
history:
In 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius came to Great Moravia from Byzantium, bringing the liturgy in the Slavic tongue. In Bohemia, Duke Bořivoj and his wife Ludmila were baptized, and their grandson Wenceslas, a gentle and devout prince, was murdered by his brother in the tenth century and venerated as a martyr. The diocese of Prague was founded in 973, and the faith shaped a culture of saints, monasteries and Gothic splendour, crowned by the reign of Charles IV.

The reformer Jan Hus was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415, unleashing the Hussite wars and a long religious division. After the Battle of White Mountain in 1620, the Habsburgs imposed re-Catholicization by force, leaving a baroque landscape of breathtaking beauty but also a wound in the national memory.

Under Communism from 1948, the Church was brutally persecuted: monasteries were seized in a single night in 1950, priests imprisoned, and an underground Church secretly ordained clergy. St. Agnes of Bohemia was canonized on 12 November 1989, days before the Velvet Revolution. Today Czechia is among the least religious nations in Europe, but its Catholic communities are lively, thoughtful and quietly hopeful.

saints.name: St. Wenceslas
saints.story: Duke of Bohemia, raised in the faith by his grandmother St. Ludmila. He ruled with mercy, cared for the poor and built churches. He was murdered by his brother Boleslav on the way to Mass and soon venerated as a martyr and the eternal protector of the Czech lands.

saints.name: St. Agnes of Bohemia
saints.story: A Přemyslid princess who refused royal marriages, including to the Holy Roman Emperor, to give herself to Christ. She founded a hospital and a convent of Poor Clares in Prague and corresponded with St. Clare of Assisi. Her canonization in November 1989 was seen as a sign of the coming freedom.

saints.name: St. John Nepomucene
saints.story: Vicar general of the Archbishop of Prague, he was tortured and thrown from the Charles Bridge into the Vltava on the orders of King Wenceslas IV. Tradition says he refused to break the seal of confession. His statue stands on countless bridges across Central Europe.

saints.name: St. John Neumann
saints.story: Born in Prachatice in southern Bohemia, he emigrated to the United States, joined the Redemptorists and became Bishop of Philadelphia. He built a diocesan Catholic school system and many churches, ministering to immigrants in several languages. He was canonized in 1977.

cathedrals.name: St. Vitus Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Within Prague Castle, this Gothic masterpiece was begun in 1344 under Charles IV and finished only in 1929. It holds the tomb of St. Wenceslas in a chapel lined with semi-precious stones, the silver tomb of St. John Nepomucene, and the crown jewels. Its stained glass includes a celebrated window by Alfons Mucha.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Assumption and Sts. Cyril and Methodius
cathedrals.story: The national pilgrimage site of Moravia, linked by tradition to the mission of Cyril and Methodius. The baroque basilica rises from a medieval Cistercian abbey. Each July thousands gather here; in 1985, a huge pilgrimage became a peaceful protest against the Communist regime, and John Paul II visited in 1990.

cathedrals.name: Church of Our Lady Victorious (Infant Jesus of Prague)
cathedrals.story: An early baroque church in the Malá Strana district, cared for by the Discalced Carmelites. It shelters the small wax statue of the Infant Jesus given in 1628, whose devotion has spread worldwide. Pilgrims from every continent come to see the Child Jesus dressed in liturgical colours.

prayerIntention: For the people of Czechia, that the faith of Wenceslas and Agnes may be rediscovered by a searching generation, and that wounds of the past may be healed in truth and love.

name: Côte d'Ivoire
history:
Early attempts by Capuchin and other French missionaries in the seventeenth century left little lasting trace. The enduring mission began in 1895, when priests of the Society of African Missions (SMA) landed at Grand-Bassam. Many of the first missionaries died of fever within months, but schools, catechists and parishes slowly took root along the coast and then inland. The first Ivorian priests were ordained in the 1930s.

After independence in 1960, the Church grew rapidly and became a respected voice in national life. Bernard Yago, Archbishop of Abidjan, was named the country’s first cardinal in 1983. President Félix Houphouët-Boigny built the vast Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in his home town of Yamoussoukro, consecrated by John Paul II in 1990, a project admired for its grandeur and criticized for its cost in a poor country.

Civil conflict in 2002–2011 and the post-election crisis of 2010–2011 tested the nation deeply. The Catholic Church worked for dialogue and reconciliation alongside Muslim and Protestant leaders, and sheltered displaced people in parishes. Today the Church is vibrant and young, with full seminaries, strong lay movements and a growing role in education and health care across West Africa.

saints.name: Servant of God Melchior de Marion Brésillac
saints.story: A French bishop who founded the Society of African Missions in 1856 to evangelize West Africa. He died of yellow fever in Freetown weeks after arriving, but his missionaries carried the Gospel to Côte d’Ivoire in 1895. His cause for beatification is open; the country has no canonized saints of its own yet.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace
cathedrals.story: Inspired by St. Peter’s in Rome and consecrated by John Paul II in 1990, it is among the largest churches in the world, with a dome rising over 150 metres and vast stained-glass windows made in France. It stands as an awe-inspiring, and much-debated, landmark of Ivorian Catholicism.

cathedrals.name: St. Paul’s Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Designed by the Italian architect Aldo Spirito, this daring modern cathedral looks over the Ébrié Lagoon. A giant tower in the form of St. Paul’s figure supports the roof through cables, like a ship’s mast. Its stained glass depicts African scenes alongside the story of salvation. John Paul II laid the foundation stone in 1980.

prayerIntention: For Côte d’Ivoire, that its people may live in lasting peace and reconciliation, and that its young Church may be a light of hope across West Africa.

name: DR Congo
catholicPresence: approx. 40–50% Catholic; Africa’s largest Catholic population
history:
Portuguese navigators reached the mouth of the Congo River in 1482, and in 1491 the ruler of the Kingdom of Kongo was baptized. His son Afonso I promoted the faith for decades, and Afonso’s son Henrique was consecrated bishop in 1518, the first sub-Saharan African bishop of modern times. That early Church was later weakened by the slave trade, in which Europeans, sadly including Christians, took part.

Modern missions arrived in the late nineteenth century, during the Congo Free State of King Leopold II, whose regime of forced labour killed or maimed millions. Belgian missionaries built schools, hospitals and parishes across the colony, and the Church became deeply woven into Congolese society, though often too closely tied to colonial power. Cardinal Joseph Malula later championed an African Church, and the Zaire Use of the Roman Mass, approved in 1988, brought Congolese song and dance into the liturgy.

The country has endured dictatorship and devastating wars, especially in the east. The bishops and lay movements have defended democracy and human rights at great cost, and martyrs such as Anuarite Nengapeta, Isidore Bakanja and Floribert Bwana Chui witness to its courage. Pope Francis visited Kinshasa in 2023, calling the world to stop plundering Africa.

saints.name: Bl. Isidore Bakanja
saints.story: A young Congolese lay catechist who worked on a Belgian rubber plantation. His agent ordered him to stop sharing his faith and remove his scapular; he refused and was savagely flogged. He died months later, forgiving his tormentor. John Paul II beatified him in 1994.

saints.name: Bl. Marie-Clémentine Anuarite Nengapeta
saints.story: A religious sister of the Holy Family (Jamaa Takatifu) who was killed during the Simba rebellion after resisting a rebel colonel’s assault, choosing death rather than violate her consecrated chastity. She forgave her killer. John Paul II beatified her in Kinshasa in 1985.

saints.name: Bl. Floribert Bwana Chui
saints.story: A young customs officer in Goma and member of the Community of Sant’Egidio, he refused bribes to let spoiled food into the country, saying it would endanger the poor. He was abducted and killed for his integrity. He was beatified in Rome in 2025.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Congo
cathedrals.story: The seat of the Archdiocese of Kinshasa, built in the mid-twentieth century in the Gombe district. Its large, simple nave hosts great national celebrations and moments of mourning, and it has often been a gathering point for lay-led marches calling for peace, justice and free elections.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Sts. Peter and Paul
cathedrals.story: Built in the early twentieth century in the heart of the copper-mining city of Katanga, it is one of the oldest major churches in the country’s interior. It is beloved as a landmark of Lubumbashi and as the spiritual centre of its archdiocese.

prayerIntention: For the Democratic Republic of the Congo, that the violence in the east may end, that its riches may serve its people, and that its martyrs’ courage may inspire justice and peace.

name: Denmark
history:
The Benedictine monk Ansgar, the Apostle of the North, first preached in Denmark around 826. Lasting conversion came when King Harald Bluetooth embraced Christianity around 965, an event proclaimed on the great runestone at Jelling. Medieval Denmark became thoroughly Catholic, with the archdiocese of Lund founded around 1104 as the metropolitan see of all Scandinavia, and magnificent cathedrals at Roskilde, Ribe and Odense. King Canute IV, killed in Odense in 1086, was venerated as a martyr.

In 1536 King Christian III introduced the Lutheran Reformation. Bishops were imprisoned, monasteries dissolved, and Catholic worship forbidden; for three centuries Catholicism survived only in foreign embassy chapels. The scientist Niels Steno, a convert who became a bishop, stands out from this era.

The constitution of 1849 granted religious freedom, and Catholic parishes, schools and religious communities slowly returned. Today the single Diocese of Copenhagen, which also covers the Faroe Islands and Greenland, serves a small but remarkably diverse flock of Danes and of immigrants from Poland, the Philippines, Vietnam, the Middle East and Africa. The Church lives as a minority in a largely secular society, with warm ecumenical relations with the Lutheran national church.

saints.name: St. Ansgar
saints.story: A Benedictine monk from Corbie who became Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen and spent his life evangelizing Denmark and Sweden. Despite repeated setbacks and the burning of Hamburg by Vikings, he persevered, ransoming slaves and founding the first churches in Scandinavia.

saints.name: St. Canute IV (Knud)
saints.story: King of Denmark who supported the Church and founded churches, but whose firm rule provoked a revolt. He was slain with his brother and companions before the altar of St. Alban’s Church in Odense. He was canonized in 1101 and his relics remain in Odense.

saints.name: St. William of Æbelholt
saints.story: A French canon regular invited to Denmark by Bishop Absalon to reform religious life. He founded the abbey of Æbelholt in north Zealand and served there for decades, known for prayer, strict reform and care for the sick. He was canonized in 1224.

saints.name: Bl. Niels Steno
saints.story: A brilliant Danish anatomist and founder of modern geology, he discovered the duct of the parotid gland and principles of rock strata. He converted to Catholicism in Florence, became a priest and bishop, and lived in great poverty serving scattered Catholics in northern Germany. John Paul II beatified him in 1988.

cathedrals.name: St. Ansgar’s Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The Catholic cathedral of Denmark, built in 1842 just after religious freedom began to dawn, in a sober neo-Romanesque style. It is the mother church of all Danish Catholics and home to many language communities. Its quiet interior is a place of prayer in the heart of the capital.

cathedrals.name: Roskilde Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Begun in the twelfth century under Bishop Absalon, this red-brick Gothic cathedral was a great centre of medieval Catholic Denmark and is the burial place of Danish kings. Since the Reformation it has been Lutheran; it is a UNESCO World Heritage site and a moving witness to the shared Christian roots of the nation.

cathedrals.name: St. Canute’s Cathedral
cathedrals.story: A Gothic brick cathedral built over the site where King Canute was martyred, and where his relics and those of his brother are still displayed in the crypt. Now a Lutheran church, it remains the place where Danish Catholics honour their royal martyr.

prayerIntention: For Denmark, that its people may rediscover the living faith of Ansgar, and that its small, many-tongued Catholic community may be a sign of unity and welcome.

name: Djibouti
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic minority (well under 1%), mostly foreign residents
history:
Djibouti is an overwhelmingly Muslim country, and its Catholic community is tiny. Catholic missionaries, especially French Capuchins, arrived in the late nineteenth century as the French colony of Somali Coast developed around the port and the railway to Addis Ababa. A diocese for Djibouti was established in the mid-twentieth century.

Since independence in 1977 the Church has lived as a small, respectful guest. Its members are mostly expatriates, soldiers, and migrants from Ethiopia and elsewhere, together with a handful of local faithful. Conversion is not the Church’s focus; rather, it serves through presence, schools, literacy centres and care for vulnerable people, including the many migrants and refugees who pass through Djibouti on perilous journeys towards Yemen and the Gulf.

The Catholic schools of Caritas Djibouti have educated thousands of Djiboutian children, nearly all of them Muslim, and the Church’s witness of friendship and service is quietly appreciated. Its long-serving bishop, Giorgio Bertin, a Franciscan, also cared for neighbouring Somalia, where the Church has suffered violence. This small Church reminds the world that faith can live as a humble, loving presence at the crossroads of Africa and Arabia.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Good Shepherd
cathedrals.story: The only Catholic cathedral in the country and the spiritual home of its small, international Catholic community. Its distinctive modern structure stands in the capital, where Mass is celebrated for expatriates, migrants and local faithful, and from where the diocese coordinates its schools and charitable works.

prayerIntention: For Djibouti and the migrants who pass through it, that they may find dignity, safety and kindness, and that Christians and Muslims may live together in peace.

name: Dominica
history:
Dominica was named by Columbus on a Sunday in 1493, but its rugged mountains and the resistance of the Kalinago people kept European settlement at bay for over a century. In the 1640s the French Dominican Raymond Breton lived among the Kalinago, learning their language and compiling a dictionary that remains a precious record of their culture.

French planters and priests settled in the eighteenth century, and Catholicism took root among both French settlers and enslaved Africans, whose descendants form most of the population. Britain took the island in 1763, yet the French-Creole Catholic culture endured, as it did in neighbouring islands. The Diocese of Roseau was founded in 1850, and missionaries, notably Belgian Redemptorists and various sisters, built schools and parishes in the villages.

Today Catholics are the majority on the island, though Protestant and evangelical churches have grown. The Church remains close to rural life, its feasts marked by Kwéyòl hymns and processions. Dominica has suffered repeatedly from hurricanes, above all Hurricane Maria in 2017, which devastated homes and churches. Parishes became centres of relief and rebuilding, and the faith of Dominicans has been a source of resilience in recovering their nature island.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Fair Haven
cathedrals.story: The mother church of the Diocese of Roseau, built of volcanic stone in a Gothic Revival and Romanesque style during the nineteenth century. Its stained glass and stone walls have weathered many storms. It stands above the capital as a symbol of Dominican Catholic faith and was restored after hurricane damage.

prayerIntention: For the people of Dominica, that they may be protected from storms, strengthened in rebuilding, and faithful stewards of their beautiful island.

name: Dominican Republic
history:
The island of Hispaniola was the first foothold of the Catholic faith in the Americas. Columbus landed in 1492, and Santo Domingo became the seat of the first dioceses of the New World, established in 1511. Its cathedral, begun in 1512, is honoured as the Primada de América, the first cathedral of the Americas.

The conquest brought catastrophe to the Taíno people, devastated by violence, forced labour and disease. In Advent 1511, the Dominican friar Antonio de Montesinos preached a thunderous sermon in Santo Domingo asking the colonists, are these not human beings? It was the first great public cry for Indigenous rights in the Americas and moved Bartolomé de las Casas to his life’s mission. Enslaved Africans were later brought in great numbers, and their descendants shaped the island’s faith and culture.

During the long Trujillo dictatorship the Church was at first compliant, but in 1960 the bishops issued a courageous pastoral letter denouncing abuses. Devotion to Our Lady of Altagracia, whose image has been venerated since the early sixteenth century, remains the heart of Dominican faith, with crowds of pilgrims travelling to Higüey each January. John Paul II visited three times, including for the fifth centenary of evangelization in 1992. Today the Church is active in education and social works, even as evangelical churches grow.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Santa María la Menor (Catedral Primada de América)
cathedrals.story: Begun in 1512 and consecrated in 1541, it is the oldest cathedral in the Americas. Its plateresque façade of coral-coloured stone and its Gothic rib vaults mark the transition from medieval to Renaissance Spain. It stands in the Colonial Zone, a UNESCO World Heritage site, and is a cherished symbol of the first evangelization.

cathedrals.name: Basilica Cathedral of Our Lady of Altagracia
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1971, this soaring modern basilica rises in a great concrete arch, like hands joined in prayer, above the town where the Virgin of Altagracia has been venerated for five centuries. Her small painting of the Nativity draws enormous crowds every January 21, and John Paul II crowned the image in 1979.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary of Santo Cerro
cathedrals.story: A hilltop shrine dedicated to Our Lady of Mercy, where according to tradition a cross planted by Columbus’s men was the scene of a Marian intercession during a battle in 1495. Pilgrims climb the hill to pray and to look out over the fertile Vega Real valley.

prayerIntention: For the Dominican Republic, that under the care of Our Lady of Altagracia its people may build a society of justice, honesty and welcome, especially for the poor and for migrants.

name: Ecuador
history:
The faith arrived with the Spanish conquest in the 1530s. Franciscans began building their great convent in Quito soon after the city’s founding in 1534, and Dominicans, Mercedarians, Augustinians and Jesuits followed. Quito became one of the artistic capitals of the Spanish empire; the Quito School of painting and sculpture blended European and Indigenous genius in gilded churches of astonishing beauty. Conquest also brought exploitation of Indigenous peoples, which some missionaries denounced and others tolerated.

In the seventeenth century, Mariana de Jesús Paredes, the Lily of Quito, offered her life for her city during earthquakes and epidemics. In 1874, under President Gabriel García Moreno, Ecuador became the first nation officially consecrated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus; García Moreno was assassinated in 1875. The Liberal Revolution of 1895 brought a strongly anticlerical period, with church properties seized and religious expelled.

In the twentieth century, Bishop Leonidas Proaño of Riobamba became known as the bishop of the Indians for his work with Indigenous communities. John Paul II visited in 1985, and Pope Francis in 2015. In 2024 Quito hosted the International Eucharistic Congress, marking 150 years since the consecration to the Sacred Heart. Today the Church faces the challenges of drug-related violence, migration and secularization.

patronSaints.name: Sacred Heart of Jesus
patronSaints.feast: Movable (Friday after the second Sunday after Pentecost)

saints.name: St. Mariana de Jesús Paredes
saints.story: The Lily of Quito lived as a consecrated laywoman in her family home, devoted to prayer, penance and caring for the poor and sick. During an earthquake and epidemic in 1645 she offered her life for the city, and died shortly afterwards. Canonized in 1950, she was declared a national heroine of Ecuador.

saints.name: St. Miguel Febres Cordero
saints.story: Born in Cuenca with a disability in his feet, he joined the De La Salle Brothers and became a renowned teacher, grammarian and member of the Ecuadorian Academy of Language. He wrote textbooks used across Latin America. He died in Spain and was canonized in 1984.

saints.name: St. Narcisa de Jesús Martillo Morán
saints.story: An orphan from a farming family near Guayaquil, she lived as a laywoman of deep prayer, earning her bread as a seamstress and serving the poor. She spent her last years in Lima, where she died. Benedict XVI canonized her in 2008.

saints.name: Bl. Mercedes de Jesús Molina
saints.story: Born near Guayaquil, she devoted herself to orphans and later to missions among the Shuar people of the Amazon. She founded the Sisters of St. Mariana de Jesús to educate girls and care for the poor. John Paul II beatified her in Guayaquil in 1985.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the National Vow (Basílica del Voto Nacional)
cathedrals.story: Built as a perpetual sign of the nation’s consecration to the Sacred Heart, this enormous neo-Gothic basilica was blessed in 1988 although work continued long after. Instead of traditional gargoyles, its exterior features Ecuadorian animals such as tortoises, iguanas and condors. Visitors climb its towers for breathtaking views over Quito.

cathedrals.name: Church of the Society of Jesus (La Compañía)
cathedrals.story: Built by the Jesuits over more than 160 years from 1605, its interior is covered almost entirely in gold leaf, with intricate carvings blending baroque, Moorish and Indigenous motifs. It is among the most splendid baroque churches in the Americas and holds the remains of St. Mariana de Jesús.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (New Cathedral)
cathedrals.story: Begun in 1885, its three great domes covered in blue and white glazed tiles from Czechoslovakia are the emblem of Cuenca. The vast brick interior can hold thousands of worshippers, and its baldachin is modelled on Bernini’s in St. Peter’s. It faces the city’s central park and older cathedral.

prayerIntention: For Ecuador, consecrated to the Sacred Heart, that its people may be freed from violence and fear and find peace, justice and dignity for all, especially its Indigenous and poorest communities.

name: Egypt
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. 0.2–0.3%) among some 10% Christians, most of them Coptic Orthodox
history:
Egypt welcomed the Holy Family in their flight from Herod, and tradition holds that St. Mark the Evangelist founded the Church of Alexandria. Alexandria became a great centre of Christian learning, home to Clement, Origen, Athanasius and Cyril, and the deserts of Egypt gave birth to monasticism through St. Anthony and St. Pachomius. After the Council of Chalcedon in 451, most Egyptian Christians separated from Rome and Constantinople, forming the Coptic Orthodox Church, still the largest Christian community in the Middle East.

Francis of Assisi met Sultan al-Kamil at Damietta in 1219, an encounter remembered as a model of dialogue. Franciscans later served in Egypt, and Catholic communities of several rites took shape; the Coptic Catholic Patriarchate was restored by Leo XIII in 1895. Today Coptic Catholics, Latin, Melkite, Maronite, Armenian, Syriac and Chaldean Catholics form a small but diverse family, running many respected schools and charities.

Egyptian Christians have suffered discrimination and violence, including the church bombings of 2016 and 2017 and the 2015 martyrdom of twenty-one Coptic workers in Libya, whom Pope Francis added to the Roman Martyrology in 2023. Francis visited Cairo in 2017, praying with Coptic Pope Tawadros II and meeting the Grand Imam of Al-Azhar.

saints.name: St. Anthony the Great
saints.story: Hearing the Gospel call to sell all and follow Christ, the young Egyptian gave away his inheritance and withdrew to the desert. His life of prayer and struggle, written by St. Athanasius, inspired countless followers and made him the father of Christian monasticism. His monastery near the Red Sea still stands.

saints.name: St. Athanasius of Alexandria
saints.story: Bishop of Alexandria and Doctor of the Church, he defended the full divinity of Christ against Arianism, enduring five exiles for the faith of Nicaea. His works, including On the Incarnation and the Life of Anthony, shaped Christian theology and spirituality for centuries.

saints.name: St. Pachomius
saints.story: A former Roman soldier who converted after being shown kindness by Christians, he founded the first communal monasteries in Upper Egypt. His rule of shared prayer, work and obedience influenced later monastic rules in both East and West.

saints.name: St. Cyril of Alexandria
saints.story: Patriarch of Alexandria and Doctor of the Church, he championed the title Theotokos, Mother of God, for Mary at the Council of Ephesus in 431. A forceful and sometimes harsh figure in his own time, his theology of Christ’s unity remains foundational.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Heliopolis
cathedrals.story: Built in 1913 for the new garden suburb of Heliopolis by the Belgian Baron Édouard Empain, who is buried in its crypt. Its design was inspired by Hagia Sophia, and it serves a Latin Catholic community. It is a much-loved landmark of Heliopolis and a reminder of Cairo’s cosmopolitan past.

cathedrals.name: Church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus (Abu Serga)
cathedrals.story: A Coptic Orthodox church built over a crypt where, according to tradition, the Holy Family rested during their flight into Egypt. One of the oldest churches in Cairo, it is a pilgrimage site for Christians of every tradition, and a stop on the Holy Family route recognized by the Vatican.

cathedrals.name: Monastery of St. Catherine
cathedrals.story: Founded in the sixth century under Emperor Justinian at the foot of Mount Sinai, at the traditional site of the burning bush. It is Greek Orthodox and among the oldest continuously inhabited monasteries in the world, holding priceless icons and manuscripts. Pilgrims of all faiths revere it.

prayerIntention: For Egypt, land of refuge for the Holy Family, that Christians and Muslims may live together in dignity and peace, and that the blood of its martyrs may bear fruit in reconciliation.

name: El Salvador
history:
Christianity arrived with the Spanish conquest in the 1520s, and the land was named for the Divine Saviour of the World. Colonial El Salvador became a land of indigo and later coffee plantations, where great wealth stood beside deep poverty. Popular Catholic devotion grew strong, with processions, patron feasts and love for Our Lady of Peace.

The twentieth century was marked by injustice and repression, including the massacre of thousands of Indigenous peasants in 1932. In the 1970s many priests and catechists accompanied the poor, and paid with their lives. Jesuit Fr. Rutilio Grande was murdered in 1977, and his friend, Archbishop Óscar Romero, became the voice of the voiceless, until he was shot while celebrating Mass on 24 March 1980. During the civil war of 1980–1992, some 75,000 people died; four American churchwomen were killed in 1980, and six Jesuits with their housekeeper and her daughter at the UCA in 1989.

Romero was canonized in 2018, and Rutilio Grande and his companions beatified in 2022. Today the Church faces the legacy of gang violence, emigration and the growth of evangelical churches, while the witness of its martyrs continues to inspire believers across the world.

patronSaints.name: The Divine Saviour of the World (Transfiguration)

saints.name: St. Óscar Arnulfo Romero
saints.story: Archbishop of San Salvador who, after the murder of his friend Rutilio Grande, became a fearless defender of the poor and the persecuted, pleading in his Sunday homilies for an end to repression. He was shot at the altar of a hospital chapel. Pope Francis canonized him in 2018.

saints.name: Bl. Rutilio Grande
saints.story: A Jesuit priest who formed rural communities in Aguilares to read the Gospel and claim their dignity. He was ambushed and shot along with an elderly man, Manuel Solórzano, and a teenager, Nelson Rutilio Lemus, who were beatified with him in 2022.

saints.name: Bl. Cosme Spessotto
saints.story: An Italian Franciscan who served the people of San Juan Nonualco for decades, building churches and caring for the poor. During the violence he denounced killings of his parishioners. He was shot while praying in his church in 1980 and beatified in 2022.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral of the Holy Saviour
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the capital, rebuilt several times after fires and earthquakes; the present building was completed in 1999. Its crypt holds the tomb of St. Óscar Romero, visited by pilgrims from around the world. Its façade once bore a colourful mural by Fernando Llort, whose removal in 2012 caused controversy.

cathedrals.name: Chapel of the Divine Providence Hospital (Hospitalito)
cathedrals.story: The small chapel of a cancer hospital run by Carmelite sisters, where Archbishop Romero lived in a simple house and where he was shot at the altar on 24 March 1980. His modest home is now a museum, and the chapel is a quiet place of pilgrimage.

cathedrals.name: Church of El Rosario
cathedrals.story: A striking modernist church designed by sculptor Rubén Martínez and completed in 1971. Its arched concrete roof sweeps down to the ground, and sunlight pours through bands of coloured glass, filling the interior with rainbows. It is considered a masterpiece of Latin American religious architecture.

prayerIntention: For El Salvador, that through the prayers of St. Óscar Romero its people may know true peace, justice for the poor and an end to violence.

name: Equatorial Guinea
history:
Catholic missions in what is now Equatorial Guinea began in earnest in the mid-nineteenth century under Spanish rule. Jesuits worked on the island of Fernando Pó (today Bioko), and from 1883 the Claretian Missionaries took charge, founding missions, schools and plantations on the island and later on the mainland of Río Muni. Over the next century most of the population became Catholic, and the faith became deeply rooted in Bubi, Fang and other communities.

After independence in 1968, the regime of Francisco Macías Nguema turned brutally against the Church.
