Priests and missionaries were expelled or imprisoned, religious schools closed, and in the 1970s Catholic worship was effectively banned. Many people fled the country, and tens of thousands died under the dictatorship.

After Macías was overthrown in 1979, the Church was able to rebuild. John Paul II visited in 1982, and native clergy and bishops took up leadership. Today the great majority of the population is Catholic, with three dioceses and the Archdiocese of Malabo. The Church remains an important source of education and hope in a country where oil wealth has not reached most citizens, and where freedoms are limited.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Elizabeth
cathedrals.story: Built in neo-Gothic style in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, its twin towers rise over the capital’s harbour on Bioko island. It is a symbol of Malabo and of the Claretian missions that shaped the country. It was restored after damage and a fire in recent decades.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: A large modern basilica on the mainland, opened in 2011 and inspired by St. Peter’s in Rome. Its scale reflects state sponsorship in a country of great inequality, yet it has become a gathering place for pilgrims and for the diocese’s major celebrations.

prayerIntention: For the people of Equatorial Guinea, that the riches of their land may serve the common good, and that their faith may bear fruit in justice, freedom and peace.

name: Eritrea
history:
Christianity reached the Eritrean highlands through the ancient Kingdom of Aksum in the fourth century, and most Christians in Eritrea today belong to the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Catholic communities of the Ge’ez rite trace their origins to the nineteenth century, when the Italian Vincentian St. Justin de Jacobis lived among the people, respecting their language and liturgy, and formed local clergy. Bl. Ghebre Michael, one of his companions, died for his faith in 1855.

Under Italian colonial rule from 1890, Latin-rite missions also grew, and Catholic schools, hospitals and religious communities spread. After a long war of independence from Ethiopia, Eritrea became independent in 1993. In 2015 Pope Francis established the Eritrean Catholic Church as its own Metropolitan Church sui iuris, centred in Asmara.

The Church in Eritrea lives under heavy restrictions. The government has seized Catholic health clinics and schools in recent years, and many young people have fled indefinite national service and repression. Eritrean Catholics, at home and in a large diaspora, cherish their ancient Ge’ez liturgy and their spiritual heritage. Their bishops have spoken courageously for dialogue, reconciliation and the dignity of every person.

saints.name: St. Justin de Jacobis
saints.story: An Italian Vincentian who served as apostolic vicar in Ethiopia and Eritrea, adopting local customs and the Ge’ez liturgy out of love for the people. He trained native priests, endured imprisonment and exile, and died on the road near Halai in Eritrea. He was canonized in 1975.

saints.name: Bl. Ghebre Michael
saints.story: An Ethiopian monk and scholar who sought the true faith and became Catholic through Justin de Jacobis, who ordained him priest. Arrested under Emperor Tewodros II, he was chained and tortured for refusing to renounce his faith and died a prisoner. He was beatified in 1926.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Rosary (St. Mary’s)
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1923 in a Lombard Romanesque style, its tall red-brick bell tower dominates Harnet Avenue, the main street of Asmara, itself a UNESCO World Heritage city. The cathedral is the heart of Latin Catholic life in the capital and a much-loved landmark.

cathedrals.name: Kidane Mehret Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Eritrean Catholic Church, where the liturgy is celebrated in the ancient Ge’ez rite. Its name means Covenant of Mercy, a beloved Marian title in the Ethiopian and Eritrean traditions. It is the spiritual centre of the Metropolitan Archeparchy of Asmara.

prayerIntention: For Eritrea, that its people may enjoy freedom and peace, that young people need not flee their homeland, and that the Church may serve freely.

name: Estonia
history:
Christianity came to Estonia in the early thirteenth century through the Northern Crusades, when German and Danish forces conquered the land by the sword. The region was dedicated to the Virgin Mary as Terra Mariana, the Land of Mary, a beautiful title but bound up with a violent conversion that left a lasting wound. Monasteries, including the Dominicans in Tallinn and the Bridgettine convent of Pirita, flourished through the late Middle Ages.

The Lutheran Reformation reached Estonia in the 1520s, and Catholicism nearly disappeared for centuries. Under the Russian Empire a small Catholic presence returned, mostly among Poles and other foreigners. In independent Estonia between the world wars, the Jesuit Eduard Profittlich became apostolic administrator and later archbishop; arrested by the Soviets in 1941, he died in prison in 1942 and was beatified in 2025.

Under Soviet occupation the Church survived in a single parish in Tallinn. Since 1991 it has slowly grown, and in 2024 the Apostolic Administration was raised to the Diocese of Tallinn. Today Estonia is one of the least religious countries in the world, yet its small Catholic community, Estonian and international, is lively, prayerful and committed to ecumenism.

saints.name: Bl. Eduard Profittlich
saints.story: A German Jesuit who served in Estonia from 1930, became an Estonian citizen and was ordained archbishop. When the Soviets occupied the country he chose to stay with his flock. Arrested in 1941, he was sentenced to death and died in a prison in Kirov in 1942. He was beatified in Tallinn in 2025.

saints.name: St. Bridget of Sweden
saints.story: The great Swedish mystic and foundress of the Order of the Most Holy Saviour. The Bridgettine convent of Pirita near Tallinn, founded in the fifteenth century, was one of the most important in the region, and Bridgettine sisters returned to Pirita after Estonian independence.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Sts. Peter and Paul
cathedrals.story: The Catholic cathedral of Estonia, located in the Old Town. The church dates from the nineteenth century and was rebuilt in the 1920s. Through Soviet times it remained open as the only Catholic parish in the country, a quiet beacon of faith in difficult years.

cathedrals.name: Pirita Convent
cathedrals.story: The ruins of the great Bridgettine convent founded in the early fifteenth century and destroyed during the Livonian War in 1577. Its tall gable still stands by the sea. Beside the ruins, a new Bridgettine convent built after 1991 welcomes pilgrims and guests.

cathedrals.name: St. Catherine’s Dominican Monastery
cathedrals.story: Founded in 1246, it is among the oldest buildings in Tallinn. The monastery was plundered during the Reformation, but its cloister and church ruins survive in the Old Town and are open to visitors, evoking the medieval Catholic life of the city.

prayerIntention: For Estonia, the Land of Mary, that its people may encounter the living Christ, and that its small Catholic community may grow in faith and joy.

name: Eswatini
history:
Most Swazi people are Christian, many belonging to African Independent and Zionist churches. The Catholic mission began in 1913–1914, when Servite friars from Italy arrived at the invitation of the country’s leaders and established a mission at Mbabane and later elsewhere. Schools, clinics and hospitals followed, and the Servites trained catechists who carried the faith into rural communities.

The Diocese of Manzini covers the whole country. Over the twentieth century, Catholic schools educated many of the nation’s leaders, and Catholic hospitals became pillars of public health. The Church was deeply involved in responding to the HIV and AIDS epidemic, which struck Eswatini harder than almost any country in the world, caring for orphans, the sick and the dying.

Today the Church in Eswatini is small but respected, with a growing number of local clergy and religious. Eswatini is Africa’s last absolute monarchy, and in recent years demands for political reform have met with harsh repression. The Catholic bishops of Southern Africa have joined calls for dialogue, justice and respect for human rights, while parishes continue to serve families facing poverty, unemployment and illness.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: The mother church of the Diocese of Manzini, which embraces all of Eswatini. It is the gathering place for diocesan celebrations, ordinations and the faithful of the country’s main commercial city, and a reminder of the Servite mission that planted the Catholic faith in the kingdom.

prayerIntention: For Eswatini, that its people may find healing from illness and poverty, and that the nation may walk the path of dialogue, justice and peace.

name: Ethiopia
history:
Ethiopia is one of the oldest Christian nations on earth. The faith arrived in the fourth century, when St. Frumentius, a Syrian Christian shipwrecked on the Red Sea coast, helped bring the royal court of Aksum to baptism. The great majority of Ethiopian Christians belong to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose ancient liturgy, monasteries and rock-hewn churches have shaped the nation's soul for sixteen centuries.

Catholic missionaries, chiefly Portuguese Jesuits, arrived in the sixteenth century. Emperor Susenyos embraced Catholicism in 1622, but the attempt to impose Latin customs provoked civil strife, and his son expelled the Jesuits in the 1630s. Later Catholic missionaries were persecuted, and Franciscan friars were martyred at Gondar in 1716. In the nineteenth century St. Justin de Jacobis took a gentler path, respecting the Ge'ez liturgy and Ethiopian traditions, and his work gave birth to the Ethiopian Catholic Church.

Today Catholics are a small community, belonging both to the Ethiopian Catholic Church, which prays in the Ge'ez rite and is led by the Metropolitan Archbishop of Addis Ababa, and to Latin vicariates in the south and west. Catholic schools, clinics and Caritas programmes serve far beyond the Church's numbers, especially amid drought, displacement and the suffering caused by recent armed conflicts, including the war in Tigray.

saints.name: St. Frumentius
saints.story: A young Syrian Christian from Tyre, Frumentius was captured on the Red Sea coast and brought to the court of Aksum, where he won the trust of the royal family. Consecrated bishop by St. Athanasius of Alexandria, he returned to lead the young Church. Ethiopians honour him as Abba Salama, 'Father of Peace', the one who revealed the light.

saints.name: St. Justin de Jacobis
saints.story: An Italian Vincentian priest who came to Ethiopia in 1839, Justin de Jacobis loved its people and its ancient Christian traditions. He adopted local customs, used the Ge'ez liturgy and trained Ethiopian priests. Imprisoned and exiled several times, he died on the road in the lowlands near Halai. He was canonized in 1975.

saints.name: Bl. Ghebre Michael
saints.story: A learned Ethiopian monk and scholar, Ghebre Michael sought the truth through long study and entered communion with the Catholic Church through the friendship of Justin de Jacobis, who ordained him priest. Arrested during a persecution, he was chained, beaten and marched with the army until he died. He was beatified in 1926.

saints.name: Bl. Liberatus Weiss and Companions
saints.story: Three Franciscan friars, Liberatus Weiss, Samuel Marzorati and Michele Pio Fasoli, came to Ethiopia as missionaries. Accused of spreading a foreign faith, they were condemned and stoned to death at Gondar in 1716. They were beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1988.

cathedrals.name: Kidane Mehret Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Ethiopian Catholic Archeparchy of Addis Ababa, dedicated to Kidane Mehret, the Covenant of Mercy, a beloved Ethiopian title of the Virgin Mary. Here the Divine Liturgy is celebrated in the ancient Ge'ez rite with Ethiopian chant and drums, a living sign that Catholic communion embraces the treasures of Ethiopia's own Christian heritage.

prayerIntention: For Ethiopia, ancient land of faith, that its peoples may be healed of war and hunger and that all Christians there may grow in unity and peace.

name: Fiji
history:
Catholic faith reached Fiji in 1844, when Marist missionaries from France landed in the islands, a few years after Methodist missionaries had begun their work. Progress was slow at first, but the Marists, joined later by Marist Sisters and other congregations, founded mission stations, schools and catechist training centres across Viti Levu, Vanua Levu and the outer islands.

The Church grew among both indigenous iTaukei Fijians and, in smaller numbers, among Indo-Fijians whose ancestors came as indentured labourers. The Archdiocese of Suva was established in 1966, and Catholic schools have educated generations of Fiji's leaders. Fiji's history since independence in 1970 has been marked by several coups and ethnic tension, and church leaders have repeatedly called for reconciliation and respect for all communities.

Today Catholics form a lively minority in a largely Christian nation. Fijian hymns, kava ceremonies of welcome and village liturgies give local colour to Catholic worship, and the Pacific Regional Seminary in Suva trains priests for much of Oceania. The Church is also a strong voice on climate change, which threatens Pacific island communities with rising seas and fiercer cyclones.

saints.name: St. Peter Chanel
saints.story: A French Marist priest who was martyred on the nearby island of Futuna, Peter Chanel is the protomartyr and patron of Oceania. Fiji has no saint of its own yet, but Fijian Catholics honour him as a father of the Marist mission that brought the faith to their islands, and his gentle courage is remembered throughout the Pacific.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Completed in the early twentieth century, this sandstone cathedral in the heart of Fiji's capital is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Suva. Its stone was brought from Sydney, and its twin towers have long been a landmark of the city. Sunday Masses ring with the rich harmonies of Fijian choirs.

cathedrals.name: St. Francis Xavier Church, Naiserelagi
cathedrals.story: This hilltop mission church is famous for frescoes painted in the early 1960s by the artist Jean Charlot. They depict a Fijian Black Christ on the cross, surrounded by Fijians and Indo-Fijians offering gifts in their own dress and customs, a moving image of the Gospel taking flesh in Fiji's own peoples.

prayerIntention: For Fiji, that its peoples may live in harmony and mutual respect, and that its islands may be protected and cared for amid a changing climate.

name: Finland
history:
Christianity came to Finland from Sweden in the twelfth century. Tradition remembers St. Henry, an English-born bishop of Uppsala, who accompanied a Swedish expedition and was martyred around 1156; he became Finland's patron. Over the following centuries a Catholic diocese grew at Turku, whose cathedral was the spiritual heart of the land, and Dominican and Bridgettine communities flourished.

The Reformation of the sixteenth century, led in Finland by Mikael Agricola, made the country Lutheran, and for centuries Catholic worship was effectively absent. A small Catholic presence returned in the nineteenth century, when Finland was part of the Russian Empire, and St. Henry's Church in Helsinki was built in 1860. The Diocese of Helsinki was established in 1955 and covers the whole country.

Today Catholics in Finland are few but remarkably diverse, with parishioners from dozens of nations alongside Finnish converts. Relations with the Lutheran and Orthodox churches are warm, and each January an ecumenical delegation travels to Rome around the feast of St. Henry. St. John Paul II visited Finland in 1989.

saints.name: St. Henry of Uppsala
saints.story: An English-born bishop of Uppsala, Henry came to Finland to plant the faith. According to tradition he was killed on the ice of Lake Köyliö by a peasant named Lalli. Venerated as Finland's patron and apostle, he is honoured by Catholics, Lutherans and Orthodox alike.

saints.name: Bl. Hemming of Turku
saints.story: Bishop of Turku for over two decades, Hemming was a careful pastor and a friend of St. Birgitta of Sweden. He strengthened church life, gathered a library and cared for the poor. He was beatified in 1514, shortly before the Reformation, and remains Finland's own medieval blessed.

cathedrals.name: St. Henry's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in 1860 and designed in a modest neo-Gothic style, this small cathedral is the mother church of the Diocese of Helsinki. It became a cathedral in 1955. Its Masses are celebrated in Finnish, Swedish, English and other languages, reflecting the international family of Finnish Catholics.

cathedrals.name: Turku Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1300, this great brick cathedral was the Catholic mother church of medieval Finland and the resting place of St. Henry's relics. Since the Reformation it has been Lutheran and is today the national shrine of the Evangelical Lutheran Church, but its stones still recall the shared Catholic roots of Finnish Christianity.

prayerIntention: For Finland, that its people may find deep peace and hope, and that its Christians may grow together in unity, faith and love.

name: France
catholicPresence: approx. 45% identify as Catholic (far fewer practise regularly)
history:
The Gospel reached Gaul in the first centuries, carried along Roman roads and rivers. The martyrs of Lyon died in 177, and St. Irenaeus became the great teacher of the early Church there. St. Martin of Tours evangelised the countryside in the fourth century, and the baptism of King Clovis at Reims around 500 earned France the title 'eldest daughter of the Church'. Monasteries such as Cluny and Cîteaux, and the Gothic cathedrals of the Middle Ages, made France a heart of Christendom.

France also knew deep wounds: the Wars of Religion between Catholics and Huguenots, the persecution of priests and religious during the Revolution, and the 1905 law separating Church and State. Yet the nineteenth century brought an astonishing flowering of saints, missionary orders and Marian apparitions at Rue du Bac, La Salette and Lourdes, and French missionaries carried the faith across the world.

Today France is largely secular, and Sunday practice is low. The Church has faced the painful 2021 report on clerical sexual abuse with public repentance. Yet new communities, thriving pilgrimages, growing numbers of adult baptisms and the joy that surrounded the reopening of Notre-Dame de Paris in 2024 show a Church still alive and searching.

saints.name: St. Joan of Arc
saints.story: A peasant girl from Domrémy who heard the voices of saints calling her to save France, Joan led armies to lift the siege of Orléans and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims. Captured and tried by a hostile Church court, she was burned at Rouen at nineteen. Later declared innocent, she was canonized in 1920.

saints.name: St. Vincent de Paul
saints.story: A peasant's son who became a priest, Vincent was converted to a life of radical charity. With St. Louise de Marillac he founded the Daughters of Charity, and he founded the Congregation of the Mission to preach to the rural poor. He organised relief for orphans, prisoners and war victims, and is the patron of all charitable works.

saints.name: St. John Vianney
saints.story: The humble Curé of Ars struggled with his studies but became one of the greatest confessors in history. He spent up to sixteen hours a day hearing confessions in his small village church, as pilgrims came from all over France. He is the patron of parish priests.

saints.name: St. Bernadette Soubirous
saints.story: A poor, sickly miller's daughter from Lourdes, Bernadette saw the Virgin Mary eighteen times in 1858 at the grotto of Massabielle, where Mary named herself the Immaculate Conception. Bernadette later became a sister at Nevers, where she lived humbly and suffered much. Lourdes became one of the world's great places of healing and prayer.

saints.name: St. Thérèse of Lisieux
saints.story: A young Carmelite nun who died of tuberculosis at twenty-four, Thérèse taught the 'Little Way' of trust and love in small things. Her autobiography, Story of a Soul, touched millions. She is a Doctor of the Church and patroness of the missions, though she never left her convent.

cathedrals.name: Notre-Dame de Paris
cathedrals.story: Begun in 1163, this Gothic masterpiece with its flying buttresses and rose windows has watched over Paris for more than eight centuries. Devastated by fire in April 2019, it was restored by thousands of craftspeople and reopened in December 2024, a moment of joy and hope for France and the world.

cathedrals.name: Chartres Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Largely rebuilt after a fire in 1194, Chartres preserves one of the most complete collections of medieval stained glass anywhere, bathing its nave in deep blue light. It treasures a relic venerated as the Virgin's veil, and every spring students walk from Paris to Chartres on pilgrimage.

cathedrals.name: Reims Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built on the site where Clovis was baptised, this Gothic cathedral was for centuries the place where French kings were crowned. Famous for its smiling angel sculpture, it was badly shelled in the First World War and lovingly restored, later becoming a symbol of Franco-German reconciliation.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes
cathedrals.story: At the grotto where Mary appeared to Bernadette in 1858, millions of pilgrims come each year, many of them sick or disabled, to pray, bathe in the spring water and join candlelight processions. The basilicas above the grotto and the healing ministry of volunteers make Lourdes a beloved home for the suffering.

prayerIntention: For France, eldest daughter of the Church, that its people may rediscover the living source of their faith and that its Church may be renewed in holiness and humility.

name: Gabon
history:
Portuguese sailors reached the Gabonese coast in the fifteenth century, but lasting Catholic mission began in 1844, when the Holy Ghost Fathers (Spiritans), led by Fr. Jean-Rémi Bessieux, settled at what would become Libreville. They were soon joined by the Sisters of the Immaculate Conception of Castres. Despite tropical disease that claimed many missionaries, they founded schools, parishes and seminaries along the coast and up the Ogooué River.

The Church shaped Gabonese education deeply, and many of the country's leaders were trained in Catholic schools. The Archdiocese of Libreville was established in 1955, and Gabonese priests and bishops gradually took leadership of the Church. Popular devotion has also mingled with traditional beliefs, including Bwiti, a reality pastors have long engaged with patience.

Today Catholics are the largest religious community in Gabon. The Church runs schools and health centres and has spoken for transparency and fair sharing of the nation's oil and timber wealth, which has too often left ordinary families poor. Following the political upheaval of 2023, the bishops have encouraged a peaceful and just transition.

saints.name: Ven. Francis Libermann
saints.story: Born into a Jewish family in Alsace, Francis Libermann became a Catholic and a priest, founding a missionary society later merged with the Holy Ghost Fathers. His vision of missionaries who become 'Black with the Black' shaped the Spiritans who brought the faith to Gabon. He has been declared Venerable. Gabon has no canonized saint of its own yet.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Notre-Dame de l'Assomption
cathedrals.story: The mother church of the Archdiocese of Libreville stands near the heart of the capital, where the Spiritan mission first took root in 1844. It hosts the great celebrations of Gabonese Catholic life, from ordinations to national days of prayer.

cathedrals.name: St. Michael's Church of Nkembo
cathedrals.story: This much-loved parish church in the Nkembo district is celebrated for its wooden columns carved by a local artist with scenes from the Bible, rendered in a distinctly Gabonese style. It is one of the most beautiful expressions of African Catholic art in Central Africa.

prayerIntention: For Gabon, that its natural riches may serve every family, that its leaders may govern justly, and that its Church may be a light of hope.

name: Gambia
history:
The Gambia is a largely Muslim country, known for warm relations between faiths. Portuguese traders brought priests to the river region in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, but no lasting Catholic community formed. Continuous Catholic mission began in 1849, when the Holy Ghost Fathers (Spiritans) arrived in Bathurst, now Banjul, followed by the Sisters of St. Joseph of Cluny.

Irish Spiritans later took charge of the mission, opening schools that became among the most respected in the country and educated Muslims and Christians alike. The Diocese of Banjul was established in 1957 and covers the whole nation; its first Gambian bishop was appointed in 1981.

Today the Catholic community is small but highly visible in education, health care and social service. Catholic and Muslim families often celebrate each other's feasts, and interfaith friendship is a cherished part of national life. The Church continues to serve the poor, including young people tempted by dangerous migration routes.

cathedrals.name: Our Lady of the Assumption Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The mother church of the Diocese of Banjul, which embraces the entire country. It stands in the old capital where the Spiritan mission began in 1849, and gathers Gambian Catholics for the great feasts, ordinations and celebrations of the year.

prayerIntention: For The Gambia, that its spirit of friendship between Muslims and Christians may grow ever stronger, and that its young people may find hope and opportunity at home.

name: Georgia
history:
Georgia embraced Christianity in the fourth century through the witness of St. Nino, a woman from Cappadocia whose prayer and healing led to the conversion of King Mirian and Queen Nana around 326. Tradition also holds that the apostle St. Andrew preached in the region. Christianity became woven into Georgian identity, language and art, and the Georgian Orthodox Church remains the faith of most of the nation.

Catholic presence grew from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries through Franciscan and Dominican missionaries, and later Theatine and Capuchin friars who opened schools and clinics. Communities of Latin, Armenian and Chaldean Catholics took root, especially in the south. During Soviet rule all churches suffered harsh repression; Catholic churches were closed and priests imprisoned or exiled.

Since independence, the Apostolic Administration of the Caucasus, created in 1993, has rebuilt Catholic life. St. John Paul II visited in 1999 and Pope Francis in 2016. Catholics remain a small community whose relations with the Orthodox majority are sometimes delicate, and they serve quietly through Caritas Georgia, caring for the elderly, the poor and families displaced by conflict.

saints.name: St. Nino
saints.story: A young Christian woman from Cappadocia, Nino came to Georgia carrying a cross bound with grapevines and her own hair. Through her prayers the queen and then King Mirian were healed and converted, and Georgia embraced the faith. She is honoured as 'Equal to the Apostles' and as the enlightener of Georgia.

saints.name: St. Andrew the Apostle
saints.story: Brother of St. Peter and the first called of the apostles, Andrew is remembered in Georgian tradition as having preached in the lands of the Caucasus. Georgian Christians count him among the first to bring the Gospel to their land, and his memory links the nation to the apostolic Church.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary
cathedrals.story: The Catholic cathedral of Tbilisi stands in the old city. Built in the nineteenth century on the site of an earlier Catholic church, it was confiscated under Soviet rule and returned to the Church after independence. Restored with care, it now gathers Georgian, Armenian and international Catholics in prayer.

cathedrals.name: Church of Sts. Peter and Paul
cathedrals.story: Built in the late nineteenth century, this was one of very few Catholic churches in Georgia to remain open during Soviet times, sustaining a faithful community through decades of repression. It remains a beloved parish and a symbol of the perseverance of Georgian Catholics.

prayerIntention: For Georgia, ancient Christian land, that its people may live in peace, that the wounds of conflict may heal, and that all Christians there may grow in unity.

name: Germany
history:
Christianity reached the Rhineland in Roman times, with early communities in Trier and Cologne. The great evangelisation of the German lands came in the eighth century through Anglo-Saxon missionaries, above all St. Boniface, the 'Apostle of the Germans', who founded monasteries such as Fulda and was martyred in 754. Under Charlemagne and the Holy Roman Empire, monasteries, cathedrals and universities flourished, and mystics like Hildegard of Bingen and scholars like Albert the Great enriched the whole Church.

In 1517 Martin Luther's protest at Wittenberg began the Reformation, dividing German Christianity and leading to the devastating Thirty Years' War. In the nineteenth century Catholics endured Bismarck's Kulturkampf, and under National Socialism many priests and laypeople suffered, while others failed to resist. Martyrs such as Edith Stein and Bernhard Lichtenberg, and the brave sermons of Bishop von Galen, bear witness to faith under tyranny.

Today the Church in Germany is large and wealthy, with a vast network of hospitals, schools and Caritas services, but it is losing members rapidly. The 2018 study on clerical abuse caused deep pain, and the Synodal Way sought reform amid tension with Rome. Benedict XVI, born in Bavaria, served as pope from 2005 to 2013.

saints.name: St. Boniface
saints.story: Born Wynfrith in England, Boniface became the great missionary of the German lands. He reorganised the Church, founded the abbey of Fulda and, according to tradition, felled the sacred Donar Oak at Geismar. In old age he set out once more to evangelise Frisia, where he was martyred with companions.

saints.name: St. Hildegard of Bingen
saints.story: A Benedictine abbess on the Rhine, Hildegard was a visionary, composer, theologian, healer and adviser to popes and emperors. Her music and writings on creation and the soul still speak today. She was canonized and declared a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

saints.name: St. Albert the Great
saints.story: A Dominican friar and Bishop of Regensburg, Albert was one of the greatest scholars of the Middle Ages, studying theology, philosophy and natural science. He taught St. Thomas Aquinas and is buried in Cologne. He is a Doctor of the Church and patron of scientists.

saints.name: St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein)
saints.story: Born into a Jewish family in Breslau, Edith Stein became a brilliant philosopher, was converted after reading St. Teresa of Ávila, and entered the Carmelites at Cologne. Arrested by the Nazis in the Netherlands, she was murdered at Auschwitz. She is a co-patroness of Europe.

saints.name: Bl. Clemens August von Galen
saints.story: Bishop of Münster during the Nazi era, von Galen preached fearless sermons in 1941 against the killing of the disabled and the persecution of religious. Known as the 'Lion of Münster', he was made a cardinal shortly before his death and beatified in 2005.

cathedrals.name: Cologne Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Begun in 1248 and completed only in 1880, Cologne's soaring Gothic cathedral houses the golden Shrine of the Three Kings. It survived wartime bombing while the city around it was devastated, and stands today as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited landmarks in Germany.

cathedrals.name: Aachen Cathedral
cathedrals.story: At its heart is the octagonal Palatine Chapel built by Charlemagne around 800, where he was buried and where German kings were crowned for centuries. Its gleaming mosaics, Gothic glass choir and the shrine of Charlemagne make it a treasure of European Christian history.

cathedrals.name: Speyer Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Founded in 1030, this massive Romanesque cathedral is one of the largest of its kind in the world. Its vast crypt holds the tombs of medieval emperors and kings, and its calm stone spaces speak of the faith and ambition of the Salian age.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Altötting
cathedrals.story: In the small octagonal Chapel of Grace stands a darkened wooden statue of the Virgin, venerated since the fifteenth century. Pilgrims walk here from across Bavaria, often carrying heavy crosses. Benedict XVI, who grew up nearby, called it the heart of Bavaria.

prayerIntention: For Germany, that its Church may be healed and renewed in faith and unity, and that its people may be generous builders of peace in Europe and the world.

name: Ghana
history:
Catholic worship first arrived on the Gold Coast with the Portuguese, who built São Jorge da Mina at Elmina in 1482 and celebrated Mass there. That early presence did not survive the departure of the Portuguese. Lasting mission began in 1880, when two priests of the Society of African Missions, Fr. Auguste Moreau and Fr. Eugène Murat, landed at Elmina. Many early missionaries died of fever, yet the mission spread inland to Ashanti and the north, where the White Fathers also laboured.

Catechists, Catholic schools and hospitals carried the faith into towns and villages. Ghana's Catholic schools trained much of the nation's leadership, and in the decades around independence in 1957 Ghanaian priests and bishops increasingly took up the leadership of the Church. The Gold Coast's history as a centre of the Atlantic slave trade remains a painful memory the Church has acknowledged.

Today the Catholic Church in Ghana is vibrant, with full seminaries, numerous vocations and Ghanaian missionaries serving abroad. Cardinal Peter Turkson has served in senior Vatican roles. The bishops speak on corruption, illegal mining that poisons rivers, and peaceful democracy.

cathedrals.name: Holy Spirit Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The mother church of the Archdiocese of Accra stands in the capital and hosts the great celebrations of Ghanaian Catholic life. Its liturgies are known for joyful choirs, drums and dancing offertory processions, expressing the warmth of Ghanaian faith.

cathedrals.name: St. Peter's Cathedral Basilica
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Kumasi, in the heartland of the Ashanti people, was raised to the rank of minor basilica. It stands as a sign of the faith that took root in Ashanti through missionaries and local catechists in the early twentieth century.

prayerIntention: For Ghana, that its democracy may remain peaceful and just, its land and rivers be protected, and its vibrant Church continue to bear joyful witness.

name: Greece
history:
Greece received the Gospel from the apostles themselves. St. Paul preached in Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens and Corinth, and his letters to these communities are part of Scripture. St. Andrew, by tradition, was martyred at Patras. Greek became the language of the New Testament and of the great Fathers of the Church, and the Orthodox Church has remained the faith of the Greek people.

A Latin Catholic presence grew after the Fourth Crusade, whose sack of Constantinople in 1204 left a wound in East-West relations that Catholics today acknowledge with sorrow. Under Venetian rule, Catholic communities took root on islands such as Syros, Tinos, Naxos and Corfu, where they still survive. Greek Catholics of the Byzantine rite form a small community as well.

Today Greek Catholics are few, joined by many migrants from the Philippines, Poland, Africa and elsewhere, and by refugees served by Caritas Hellas. St. John Paul II visited Athens in 2001 and asked forgiveness for past wrongs, and Pope Francis visited Lesbos and Athens, embracing refugees. Relations with the Orthodox Church have grown warmer, in hope of greater unity.

saints.name: St. Paul the Apostle
saints.story: On his missionary journeys Paul founded the first Christian communities in Europe at Philippi, Thessalonica and Corinth, and preached on the Areopagus in Athens about the 'unknown God'. His letters to the Thessalonians, Corinthians and Philippians remain among the most treasured texts of the New Testament.

saints.name: St. Dionysius the Areopagite
saints.story: A member of the Athenian council of the Areopagus, Dionysius believed after hearing St. Paul preach, as the Acts of the Apostles records. Tradition honours him as the first bishop of Athens. The Catholic cathedral of Athens bears his name.

saints.name: St. Andrew the Apostle
saints.story: The brother of St. Peter, Andrew is remembered as having preached in Greece and been crucified at Patras on an X-shaped cross. His relics are honoured at Patras, and his feast is a shared joy of Catholic and Orthodox Christians, a sign of the brotherhood of Rome and Constantinople.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral Basilica of St. Dionysius the Areopagite
cathedrals.story: Completed in the 1860s in a neoclassical style near the centre of Athens, this cathedral is the heart of the Catholic Archdiocese of Athens. It welcomes Greek Catholics alongside a large community of migrants and was the setting of papal visits by St. John Paul II and Pope Francis.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. George
cathedrals.story: Crowning the medieval hilltop town of Ano Syros, this cathedral is the mother church of one of Greece's oldest Catholic communities, descended from the Venetian era. From its terrace pilgrims look out over the Aegean, and its feasts are celebrated with great devotion by the island's Catholics.

prayerIntention: For Greece, the land where Paul preached, that its people may know prosperity and peace, and that Catholics and Orthodox may walk ever closer toward unity.

name: Grenada
history:
Catholic faith came to Grenada with French colonists in the seventeenth century, and French Dominicans and Capuchins served the island's settlers and enslaved Africans. The colonial economy rested on slavery, and the Church of that era was bound up in its injustices, a painful history now honestly remembered. After Britain took control in the eighteenth century, Catholics faced restrictions, but the faith endured, especially among Afro-Grenadians.

Irish and other religious congregations later ran schools and parishes, and the Diocese of St. George's in Grenada was established in 1956. The nation's turbulent years, including the 1979 revolution, the killing of Maurice Bishop and the 1983 invasion, left lasting wounds that the churches have helped to heal.

Today Catholics are the largest Christian community on the 'Island of Spice'. In 2004 Hurricane Ivan devastated the island, severely damaging churches including the cathedral, and Catholic communities have patiently rebuilt. Catholic schools remain central to Grenadian life, and the Church continues to serve families facing poverty and the growing threat of climate change.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Built in the early nineteenth century on a hill above the capital's harbour, this stone cathedral is the mother church of the Diocese of St. George's in Grenada. Badly damaged by Hurricane Ivan in 2004, it has been lovingly restored by the faithful as a sign of resilience and hope.

prayerIntention: For Grenada, that its families may flourish, that it may be protected from storms, and that its people may live in reconciliation and peace.

name: Guatemala
history:
Catholicism arrived in Guatemala with the Spanish conquest led by Pedro de Alvarado in 1524, a conquest marked by great violence against the Maya peoples. Friars such as the Dominican Bartolomé de las Casas defended indigenous dignity, and in the Verapaz region missionaries sought peaceful evangelisation. Over centuries, Maya and Catholic traditions intertwined in rich devotion, from the Black Christ of Esquipulas to Holy Week carpets of coloured sawdust in Antigua.

In the nineteenth century liberal governments expelled religious orders and seized Church property. The civil war of 1960–1996 brought terrible suffering, especially to Maya communities; many catechists, priests and religious were killed for standing with the poor. Bishop Juan Gerardi was murdered in 1998, two days after presenting the Church's report documenting wartime atrocities.

Today Catholics remain the largest faith community, although evangelical churches have grown rapidly. The Church continues to defend indigenous peoples, migrants and the land, and the beatified martyrs of El Quiché and Fr. Stanley Rother are honoured as witnesses of a faith that did not abandon the poor.

saints.name: St. Pedro de San José Betancur
saints.story: Born in the Canary Islands, Hermano Pedro came to Santiago de Guatemala (now Antigua), where he cared for the sick, the homeless and poor children. He founded a hospital and the Bethlemite community. In 2002 he became Central America's first canonized saint, at a Mass celebrated in Guatemala by St. John Paul II.

saints.name: Bl. Stanley Rother
saints.story: A farm boy from Oklahoma, Fr. Stanley Rother served the Tz'utujil Maya of Santiago Atitlán for thirteen years, learning their language and sharing their life. During the violence he refused to abandon his people. He was murdered in his rectory in 1981 and beatified in 2017.

saints.name: Bl. José María Gran Cirera and Companions
saints.story: Missionary priests of the Sacred Heart and Maya lay catechists of El Quiché, they were killed during the civil war for their faith and their service to the poor. Ten of these martyrs, including three Maya laymen and a twelve-year-old boy, were beatified in 2021.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Esquipulas
cathedrals.story: This gleaming white baroque basilica, completed in the eighteenth century, houses the beloved Black Christ of Esquipulas, carved in 1594. Pilgrims from across Central America and Mexico come by the hundreds of thousands, especially around January 15, making it one of the great shrines of the Americas.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Facing the central plaza of the capital, this neoclassical cathedral was built from the late eighteenth century after the government moved from earthquake-shattered Antigua. On its pillars are inscribed the names of thousands of victims of the civil war, a solemn place of memory and prayer.

cathedrals.name: Church of La Merced
cathedrals.story: With its exuberant yellow-and-white stucco façade, this baroque church is one of the jewels of colonial Antigua. It is the heart of the city's famous Holy Week processions, when the faithful carry great floats over carpets of flowers and coloured sawdust.

prayerIntention: For Guatemala, that its Maya and all its peoples may live in justice and dignity, and that the blood of its martyrs may bear fruit in lasting peace.

name: Guinea
history:
Guinea is a predominantly Muslim country. Catholic mission began in 1877, when the Holy Ghost Fathers (Spiritans) arrived on the coast, later joined by sisters who opened schools and dispensaries. Missions spread to Conakry, the Forest region and the highlands, where catechists formed communities among peoples such as the Kissi, Toma and Guerzé.

After independence in 1958, the regime of Ahmed Sékou Touré turned against the Church. Foreign missionaries were expelled in 1967, Catholic schools were nationalised, and Archbishop Raymond-Marie Tchidimbo of Conakry was arrested in 1970 and held for nearly nine years, much of it in the notorious Camp Boiro. In 1979 Pope John Paul II named a young Guinean priest, Robert Sarah, as Archbishop of Conakry; he later became a cardinal serving in Rome.

Today the Church in Guinea is fully led by Guinean clergy, small yet resilient, and respected for its schools, health care and peaceful relations with Muslim neighbours. It continues to call for justice, democratic dialogue and an end to poverty in a land rich in minerals but poor in opportunity.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Sainte-Marie
cathedrals.story: Built in the early twentieth century in the capital, this cathedral is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Conakry. It witnessed the Church's endurance through the years of persecution under Sékou Touré and remains the heart of Catholic celebration in Guinea.

prayerIntention: For Guinea, that its people may enjoy peace, justice and a fair share of their land's riches, and that its faithful Church may continue to bear witness with courage.

name: Guinea-Bissau
history:
Portuguese traders and priests reached the coast of Guinea-Bissau in the fifteenth century, and Catholic communities grew in trading towns such as Cacheu and Bissau, often among Creole populations. The region was also caught up in the Atlantic slave trade, a grievous wound in its history. For centuries the mission remained small and largely coastal.

In the twentieth century Franciscan and other missionaries, together with Italian PIME priests, extended the Church inland, opening schools and clinics. The long war of independence against Portugal ended in 1974, and the Diocese of Bissau was established in 1977, followed by the Diocese of Bafatá in 2001.

Today Catholics form a significant minority alongside Muslims and followers of traditional religions. The country has suffered repeated coups and deep poverty, and the Church has often acted as a mediator and a voice for peace. Catholic schools, hospitals and Caritas programmes serve people of every faith, and local vocations continue to grow.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Candelária
cathedrals.story: Standing in the old centre of the capital, this cathedral is the mother church of the Diocese of Bissau. Rebuilt in the twentieth century on the site of an older church, it gathers the faithful for national celebrations and quietly stood as a place of prayer through the country's political crises.

prayerIntention: For Guinea-Bissau, that it may know stable peace and good government, and that its families may be freed from poverty and fear.

name: Guyana
history:
Catholic faith reached Guyana through Portuguese immigrants from Madeira, who arrived in large numbers from the 1830s, and through Jesuit missionaries who served Georgetown, the sugar estates and the Amerindian peoples of the interior. The colonial economy was built first on African slavery and later on indentured labour from India and China, and the Church ministered among these communities in a society marked by deep inequality.

The Diocese of Georgetown, covering the entire country, was established in 1956. Jesuits travelled for weeks by river and on foot to serve villages in the Rupununi and other remote regions. In 1979 Fr. Bernard Darke, a Jesuit priest and photographer for the Catholic Standard, was killed while covering a protest, and the Church's newspaper was long a courageous voice for press freedom.

Today Guyana is a multi-faith nation of Hindus, Christians and Muslims, and Catholics are a respected minority. The Church supports interfaith harmony, Amerindian communities and the poor, and urges that the country's new oil wealth benefit all Guyanese.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (Brickdam Cathedral)
cathedrals.story: After an earlier wooden cathedral burned in 1913, this cathedral on Brickdam was rebuilt in concrete and completed in the 1920s. Its Romanesque style and twin towers make it a landmark of the capital, and it remains the mother church for Catholics across Guyana.

prayerIntention: For Guyana, that its many peoples may live in harmony, and that the riches of its land may bring justice and hope to every family.

name: Haiti
history:
Catholicism came to Hispaniola with Columbus and the Spanish in 1492, and later with the French, who made Saint-Domingue the wealthiest and most brutal slave colony in the Caribbean. Enslaved Africans received baptism, yet the Church of that time was deeply compromised by the slave system. African spiritual traditions blended with Catholic devotion, giving rise to Vodou, which coexists with Catholic practice in many Haitian lives.

After the revolution of 1804, Haiti became the first free Black republic, but for decades it was isolated, and Rome only signed a concordat with the country in 1860. French clergy then rebuilt the Church, founding schools and parishes. In 1882 a smallpox epidemic ended after the people prayed to Our Lady of Perpetual Help, who became Haiti's patroness.

The Church has accompanied Haiti through dictatorship, poverty, political turmoil and disaster. The 2010 earthquake killed Archbishop Joseph Serge Miot and destroyed the Port-au-Prince cathedral. Today, amid gang violence and displacement, priests and religious have been kidnapped and some killed, yet parishes, schools and clinics continue to serve with heroic perseverance.

saints.name: Ven. Pierre Toussaint
saints.story: Born into slavery in Saint-Domingue, Pierre Toussaint was taken to New York, where he became a celebrated hairdresser. After gaining freedom he used his earnings to care for orphans, the sick and the poor, and supported the building of St. Patrick's Old Cathedral. He was declared Venerable in 1996.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1914, this pink and white cathedral was a beloved symbol of the capital until the earthquake of January 12, 2010 left it in ruins. Haitians continue to pray amid its remains, and its rebuilding is a sign of hope for a wounded nation.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Notre-Dame de l'Assomption
cathedrals.story: Overlooking the main square of Haiti's historic northern city, this colonial-era cathedral has been rebuilt after earthquakes and fires. It witnessed the struggle for Haiti's freedom and remains the centre of Catholic life in the north.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, Saut-d'Eau
cathedrals.story: Each July, thousands of pilgrims come to the church at Ville-Bonheur and the nearby waterfall of Saut-d'Eau, where an apparition of the Virgin was reported in the nineteenth century. They pray, bathe in the falls and ask for healing, in a festival that reflects both Catholic and popular Haitian devotion.

prayerIntention: For Haiti, that violence may cease, that its people may be safe and fed, and that through Our Lady of Perpetual Help the nation may rise in hope and dignity.

name: Honduras
history:
Catholicism arrived in Honduras with the Spanish conquest in the 1520s, a conquest that brought violence and disease to the Lenca and other indigenous peoples. Franciscan and Mercedarian friars founded missions, and Comayagua became the seat of the first diocese. Over the centuries, Catholic faith mingled with indigenous and Afro-Caribbean Garífuna cultures.

In 1747 a small clay image of the Virgin was found by a farmworker near the village of Suyapa, and devotion to Our Lady of Suyapa spread throughout the nation; she was later declared patroness of Honduras. In the nineteenth century liberal governments restricted the Church, and priests remained scarce for generations, so lay Delegates of the Word, a movement begun in Honduras in 1966, carried the Gospel to countless rural communities.

Today Catholics remain a large community, though evangelical churches have grown quickly. Honduras faces poverty, gang violence, migration and the killing of environmental defenders. The Church accompanies the poor and migrants, and works for justice and peace, nourished by its deep love for the Virgin of Suyapa.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Suyapa
cathedrals.story: Begun in the mid-twentieth century, this great basilica on the outskirts of the capital honours the tiny image of the Virgin of Suyapa, only a few centimetres tall. Around her feast on February 3, vast crowds of pilgrims come to pray, many having walked through the night.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Comayagua
cathedrals.story: Completed in the early eighteenth century, the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception is a fine example of colonial baroque architecture in Honduras. Its tower holds a medieval clock believed by many to be one of the oldest in the Americas. Comayagua was the country's first episcopal see.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Michael the Archangel
cathedrals.story: Built in the eighteenth century, the capital's cathedral has a white baroque façade and a richly gilded altarpiece. Dedicated to St. Michael, patron of Tegucigalpa, it stands at the heart of the city's public and religious life.

prayerIntention: For Honduras, that through the intercession of Our Lady of Suyapa its people may be freed from violence and poverty, and that its young people may find a future of hope at home.

name: Hungary
history:
Hungary became a Christian kingdom through St. Stephen, its first king, who was crowned around the year 1000 with a crown sent from Rome. He founded dioceses and monasteries, including Pannonhalma, and on his deathbed offered his nation to the Virgin Mary, who has ever since been honoured as Great Lady of the Hungarians. The royal house of the Árpáds gave the Church many saints, including St. Elizabeth and St. Margaret.

Hungary endured the Mongol invasion, a century and a half of Ottoman occupation and the divisions of the Reformation, after which the Catholic restoration rebuilt much of national life. In the twentieth century the Church suffered under Nazi and then Communist rule. Cardinal József Mindszenty was imprisoned and tortured, religious orders were dissolved, and many priests and laypeople were persecuted. Some clergy were also pressured into collaborating with the secret police, a painful legacy still being examined.

Since 1989 the Church has rebuilt schools and communities. Hungary hosted the International Eucharistic Congress in Budapest in 2021, and Pope Francis visited in 2021 and 2023. Practice has declined, yet Hungarian Catholics continue to cherish their saints, pilgrimages and Marian heritage.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady, Great Lady of the Hungarians

saints.name: St. Stephen of Hungary
saints.story: Hungary's first Christian king, Stephen united the Magyar tribes, founded dioceses and monasteries, and wrote counsels to his son on justice and mercy. Before he died he entrusted his crown and people to the Virgin Mary. His incorrupt right hand, the Holy Right, is venerated in Budapest.

saints.name: St. Elizabeth of Hungary
saints.story: A Hungarian princess married to a German landgrave, Elizabeth gave her wealth to the poor and built a hospital. Widowed young, she joined the Franciscan Third Order and served the sick until her death at twenty-four. She is a patroness of charity and of Franciscan tertiaries.

saints.name: St. Margaret of Hungary
saints.story: Daughter of King Béla IV, Margaret was offered to God as a child in thanksgiving for the country's survival of the Mongol invasion. She lived as a Dominican nun on the island in Budapest that now bears her name, choosing the humblest tasks and caring for the sick.

saints.name: Bl. Vilmos Apor
saints.story: Bishop of Győr during the Second World War, Vilmos Apor sheltered Jews and refugees and spoke out against persecution. In 1945 he was shot by a Soviet soldier while protecting women who had taken refuge in his residence. He died days later and was beatified in 1997.

saints.name: Ven. József Mindszenty
saints.story: Cardinal Archbishop of Esztergom, Mindszenty resisted both Nazi and Communist tyranny. Arrested in 1948, tortured and condemned in a show trial, he was freed briefly in 1956, then lived fifteen years in the US embassy in Budapest. He died in exile and was declared Venerable in 2019.

cathedrals.name: Esztergom Basilica
cathedrals.story: Standing high above the Danube, this vast neoclassical basilica, consecrated in 1856, is Hungary's largest church and the seat of its primate. Its great dome dominates the landscape, and its treasury and Renaissance Bakócz Chapel recall a thousand years of Hungarian Christianity.

cathedrals.name: St. Stephen's Basilica
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1905 after decades of construction, this neo-Renaissance basilica is one of Budapest's best-loved landmarks. It houses the Holy Right, the relic of St. Stephen's hand, carried in procession through the city each August 20 on the national feast.

cathedrals.name: Pannonhalma Archabbey
cathedrals.story: Founded by Benedictine monks in 996, Pannonhalma is one of the oldest institutions in Hungary. Monks have prayed on this hilltop for over a thousand years, and its basilica, library and school make it a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a living centre of faith and learning.

prayerIntention: For Hungary, entrusted to the Great Lady of the Hungarians, that its people may grow in faith, mercy and welcome, and live in peace with all their neighbours.

name: Iceland
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. 4%, many of them immigrants)
history:
Iceland's Norse settlers accepted Christianity by decision of the Althing, the national assembly, around the year 1000. Two dioceses were founded at Skálholt and Hólar, and monasteries became centres of learning where the great sagas were written down. St. Thorlak, Bishop of Skálholt, was revered by the people as a holy pastor soon after his death.

The Reformation was imposed by the Danish crown in the sixteenth century. The last Catholic bishop, Jón Arason of Hólar, resisted and was beheaded with two of his sons in 1550, and Catholic practice disappeared for nearly three centuries. In the nineteenth century French priests returned, and the Sisters of St. Joseph of Chambéry built Iceland's first modern hospital, Landakot, in Reykjavík.

Today the Diocese of Reykjavík covers the whole country. Catholics have grown in number in recent decades, largely through immigrants from Poland, the Philippines, Lithuania and elsewhere, alongside Icelandic converts. St. John Paul II visited in 1989, and in 1984 he formally recognised St. Thorlak as patron of Iceland.

saints.name: St. Thorlak (Þorlákur Þórhallsson)
saints.story: Bishop of Skálholt, Thorlak studied in Paris and Lincoln, then returned to reform the Icelandic Church, insisting on clerical integrity and care for the poor. Honoured as a saint by the Althing soon after his death, he was confirmed as patron of Iceland by St. John Paul II in 1984. His feast, Þorláksmessa, is still marked across Iceland.

saints.name: St. Jón Ögmundarson
saints.story: The first Bishop of Hólar in northern Iceland, Jón founded a cathedral school and encouraged learning, prayer and chant. He was venerated as a saint by Icelanders after his death, a local veneration that has never been formally confirmed by Rome.

cathedrals.name: Christ the King Cathedral (Landakotskirkja)
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1929 and designed by architect Guðjón Samúelsson, this neo-Gothic cathedral on Landakot hill was for a time the largest church in Iceland. Its flat-topped tower is a Reykjavík landmark, and its congregation now prays in Icelandic, Polish, English and many other languages.

prayerIntention: For Iceland, that its people may live in peace and wonder at God's creation, and that its growing Catholic community may be a home of welcome for all.

name: India
history:
According to ancient tradition, the apostle St. Thomas reached the coast of Kerala in 52 AD, founded communities and was martyred near Chennai. The St. Thomas Christians kept the faith for centuries with links to the Church of the East. Later, Portuguese explorers arrived in 1498, and St. Francis Xavier preached in Goa and along the southern coasts in the 1540s. Missionaries such as Roberto de Nobili sought to express the faith in Indian culture.

The colonial period also brought harm: the Goa Inquisition, the forced Latinisation of Syro-Malabar Christians, and, too often, the acceptance of caste divisions within the Church. Dalit Catholics still struggle for equal dignity. Yet the Church flourished, especially in the south and northeast, and today India has three Catholic churches: the Latin, Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara.

Catholics are a small minority but run thousands of schools, colleges, hospitals and social services, serving people of every faith. St. Teresa of Kolkata became a symbol of love for the poorest. Christians have faced violence, notably in Kandhamal, Odisha, in 2008 and in Manipur since 2023, yet Indian vocations remain strong and Indian priests and sisters serve across the world.

saints.name: St. Thomas the Apostle
saints.story: The apostle who doubted and then proclaimed 'My Lord and my God', Thomas is remembered by Indian Christians as their father in faith, who came to Kerala and founded seven churches. By tradition he was martyred near Mylapore, Chennai, where the San Thome Basilica stands over his tomb.

saints.name: St. Joseph Vaz
saints.story: A priest born in Goa, Joseph Vaz travelled in disguise to Ceylon, where Catholics were persecuted under Dutch rule, and revived the Church there for over twenty years. He cared for the sick during epidemics and lived in poverty. He was canonized in 2015.

saints.name: St. Kuriakose Elias Chavara
saints.story: A Syro-Malabar priest from Kerala, Chavara co-founded the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate, the first Indian religious congregation for men. He opened schools for children of every caste, introduced a printing press and promoted education for all. He was canonized in 2014.

saints.name: St. Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception
saints.story: A Franciscan Clarist sister from Kerala, Alphonsa endured constant illness and suffering with deep peace, offering everything to Christ. She died young and unknown beyond her convent, yet in 2008 she became the first woman of Indian origin to be canonized.

saints.name: St. Teresa of Calcutta
saints.story: Born in Skopje, Mother Teresa came to India as a Loreto sister and in 1950 founded the Missionaries of Charity to serve the dying and destitute of Kolkata. She became an Indian citizen and a worldwide symbol of compassion. She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and was canonized in 2016.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Bom Jesus
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1605, this baroque Jesuit church holds the body of St. Francis Xavier in a silver casket. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, it draws pilgrims from across India and the world, especially during the exposition of the saint's relics, held about once a decade.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Good Health
cathedrals.story: On the coast of Tamil Nadu, this white Gothic-style basilica honours Marian apparitions remembered from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Millions of pilgrims of many faiths come each year, especially for the feast in September, making it one of the largest Marian shrines in Asia.

cathedrals.name: San Thome Basilica
cathedrals.story: Rebuilt in neo-Gothic style in the 1890s, this basilica is built over the tomb venerated as that of St. Thomas the Apostle. It is one of very few churches in the world built over the tomb of an apostle, and a place of deep devotion for Indian Christians.

cathedrals.name: Sé Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Dedicated to St. Catherine of Alexandria and completed in the early seventeenth century, this is one of the largest churches in Asia. Its golden altarpiece and famous Golden Bell testify to the grandeur of Portuguese-era Goa.

prayerIntention: For India, that its many peoples and faiths may live together in harmony, that the poor and Dalits may be raised up in dignity, and that its Christians may serve in freedom and peace.

name: Indonesia
history:
Catholic faith reached the Indonesian archipelago with Portuguese traders in the sixteenth century. St. Francis Xavier preached in the Moluccas in 1546–1547, and Dominicans evangelised Flores and Solor. When the Dutch East India Company took control, Catholic priests were expelled and Catholic communities in many places passed to Protestantism, though the faith endured on Flores and in parts of Timor.

Catholic mission was permitted again in the nineteenth century. Jesuit Fr. Frans van Lith worked among the Javanese, and in 1904 he baptised the first group of Javanese Catholics at the spring of Sendangsono. Albertus Soegijapranata became the first Indonesian bishop in 1940 and supported the struggle for independence, earning recognition as a National Hero. Catholics suffered during the Japanese occupation, and the violence of 1965–1966 and later conflicts in places such as East Timor and Papua left deep wounds the Church has tried to help heal.

Today Indonesia, the world's largest Muslim-majority country, guarantees recognition of Catholicism as one of its official religions. The Church is strong on Flores, where most people are Catholic, and active in education and health across the nation. Pope Francis visited in 2024, praising Indonesia's commitment to harmony between faiths.

saints.name: St. Francis Xavier
saints.story: The great Jesuit missionary preached in Ambon, Ternate and the Moluccas in 1546 and 1547, baptising many and caring for the sick. Indonesian Catholics honour him as a father of their faith and as the patron of the missions.

saints.name: Bl. Denis of the Nativity and Bl. Redemptus of the Cross
saints.story: Two Discalced Carmelites, the French priest Denis and the Portuguese brother Redemptus, accompanied a Portuguese diplomatic mission to Aceh in Sumatra. They were seized and, refusing to renounce their faith, were martyred in 1638. They were beatified in 1900.

cathedrals.name: Jakarta Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Officially the Church of Our Lady of the Assumption, this neo-Gothic cathedral was consecrated in 1901 with slender spires of iron. It stands directly across from the Istiqlal Mosque, and the two are linked by an underground 'Tunnel of Friendship', which Pope Francis visited in 2024 with the Grand Imam, a beautiful sign of Indonesia's interfaith harmony.

cathedrals.name: Sendangsono Marian Shrine
cathedrals.story: At this spring in the hills of Central Java, Fr. van Lith baptised the first Javanese Catholics in 1904. The grotto and its graceful complex designed by architect Y. B. Mangunwijaya attract many pilgrims, especially in May and October, and it is often called the 'Lourdes of Java'.

prayerIntention: For Indonesia, that its many islands and faiths may live together in harmony and justice, and that its Catholics may be joyful witnesses of fraternity.

name: Iran
history:
Christianity reached Persia in the first centuries, and the Church of the East grew strong under the Parthian and Sasanian empires. It also knew fierce persecution: under King Shapur II in the fourth century, thousands of Christians, including bishops, priests and consecrated women, were martyred. Persian Christians carried the Gospel along the Silk Road as far as China.

Catholic missionaries, among them Dominicans, Augustinians and Discalced Carmelites, worked in Persia from the Middle Ages and especially from the seventeenth century, when Shah Abbas welcomed them to Isfahan. Communities of Armenian Catholics, Chaldean Catholics and Latin Catholics took shape. Since the Islamic Revolution of 1979, Catholic schools have been nationalised, foreign clergy are few, and evangelisation and conversion from Islam are forbidden and can be severely punished.

Today the Catholic Church in Iran is a tiny flock: Chaldean and Armenian Catholics whose families have lived there for generations, together with foreign workers and diplomats. The Archdiocese of Tehran–Isfahan serves Latin Catholics, and in 2024 its archbishop, Dominique Mathieu, was made a cardinal. These Christians pray faithfully, often discreetly, as a small light of hope.

saints.name: St. Simeon bar Sabba'e and Companions
saints.story: Catholicos of the Church of the East at Seleucia-Ctesiphon, Simeon refused to collect a double tax from Christians or to worship the sun. Under King Shapur II he was executed on Good Friday together with many priests and faithful, among the first of a great multitude of Persian martyrs.

saints.name: St. James Intercisus
saints.story: A Persian Christian nobleman, James at first renounced his faith to keep royal favour, then repented after his mother and wife rebuked him. Refusing to deny Christ again, he was put to death by being cut piece by piece, praying as he died. His name, 'Intercisus', means 'cut to pieces'.

saints.name: Sts. Abdon and Sennen
saints.story: According to ancient tradition, these two Persian Christians were brought to Rome as captives, where they cared for the bodies of martyrs and were themselves martyred. Their feast has long been kept in the Roman Church, and they are honoured as Persian witnesses to Christ.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Consolata
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Latin Archdiocese of Tehran–Isfahan, dedicated to Our Lady of Consolation. It gathers a small and international community of Catholics in the Iranian capital, a quiet place of prayer for local faithful, foreign workers and diplomats alike.

cathedrals.name: Chaldean Cathedral of St. Joseph
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Chaldean Catholic Archeparchy of Tehran serves a community whose ancestors have prayed in Aramaic for many centuries. Its liturgy preserves the ancient Syriac traditions of the Church of the East, a living link to the earliest Christians of Persia.

prayerIntention: For Iran, that its people may enjoy freedom, dignity and peace, and that the small Christian flock there may be protected and live their faith without fear.

name: Iraq
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. 0.5%), mostly Chaldean and Syriac Catholics
history:
Iraq, ancient Mesopotamia, is the land of Abraham, of Ur and Nineveh, and of the prophets Jonah and Ezekiel. Christianity arrived very early, and tradition credits the evangelisation of the region to Sts. Addai and Mari, disciples associated with St. Thomas. The Church of the East flourished here for centuries, writing and praying in Syriac, building monasteries and sending missionaries to India and China.

In the sixteenth century part of this Church entered full communion with Rome, becoming the Chaldean Catholic Church, today the largest Catholic community in Iraq, alongside Syriac, Armenian and Latin Catholics. Christians endured massacres, wars and sanctions in the twentieth century. After 2003, violence against Christians surged: Archbishop Paulos Faraj Rahho of Mosul was kidnapped and died in 2008, and in 2010 gunmen attacked Our Lady of Salvation Cathedral in Baghdad, killing dozens of worshippers.

In 2014 the so-called Islamic State drove Christians from Mosul and the Nineveh Plains, destroying churches and monasteries. Many have since emigrated, but some have returned to rebuild. Pope Francis's historic visit in 2021, praying in Mosul, Qaraqosh and Ur, was a moment of consolation for a wounded Church that refuses to disappear.

saints.name: Sts. Addai and Mari
saints.story: Honoured as the apostles of Mesopotamia, Addai and Mari are remembered as the first to bring the Gospel to Edessa and the lands along the Tigris. The ancient Eucharistic prayer that bears their name, still used by Chaldean Catholics, is one of the oldest in Christianity.

saints.name: Sts. Behnam and Sarah
saints.story: According to tradition, Behnam and his sister Sarah, children of an Assyrian prince, were converted and baptised by a hermit, and were martyred for their faith. The monastery of Mar Behnam near Nimrud, cared for by Syriac Catholics, was damaged by the Islamic State and has since been restored by the faithful.

cathedrals.name: Our Lady of Salvation Syriac Catholic Cathedral
cathedrals.story: On October 31, 2010, gunmen attacked this cathedral during Sunday Mass, killing dozens of worshippers and two priests. Restored after the massacre, it now honours the memory of its martyrs, whose cause for beatification has been opened, and Pope Francis prayed here in 2021.

cathedrals.name: Al-Tahira Syriac Catholic Church
cathedrals.story: One of the largest churches in Iraq, the Church of the Immaculate Conception was burned and desecrated by the Islamic State in 2014. Restored by the returning faithful, it welcomed Pope Francis in 2021, when its packed congregation sang in joy where ruins had stood.

cathedrals.name: St. Joseph Chaldean Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The Chaldean Catholic cathedral in Baghdad's Karrada district, where Pope Francis celebrated Mass in the Chaldean rite during his 2021 visit, the first time a pope had done so. It is a spiritual home for Iraq's largest Catholic community.

prayerIntention: For Iraq, cradle of civilisation and of ancient Christian faith, that its peoples may live in security and peace, and that its Christians may remain and flourish in their homeland.

name: Ireland
history:
Christianity reached Ireland before the fifth century, but the island's conversion is linked above all to St. Patrick, a Briton once enslaved there, who returned as a missionary bishop. A distinctive monastic culture followed, with great foundations such as Clonmacnoise and Glendalough, and Irish monks like Columba and Columbanus carried learning and faith to Scotland and continental Europe.

After the Reformation, Irish Catholics endured centuries of persecution under English rule. The Penal Laws barred Catholics from land, education and public life, priests were hunted, and Mass was celebrated secretly at Mass rocks in the countryside. St. Oliver Plunkett was martyred in 1681. The Great Famine of the 1840s killed about a million people and drove millions to emigrate, and Irish emigrants and missionaries helped build the Church across the English-speaking world.

In the twentieth century the Church was central to national life, but revelations of clerical sexual abuse, its cover-up, and harsh treatment in Magdalene laundries, industrial schools and mother-and-baby homes caused profound pain and loss of trust. Today a humbler Irish Church seeks healing, and many still find faith at Knock, Lough Derg and Croagh Patrick.

saints.name: St. Patrick
saints.story: Captured as a youth in Britain and enslaved in Ireland, Patrick turned to God in prayer while tending sheep. After escaping, he returned as a bishop to evangelise the Irish. His Confession reveals a humble, passionate heart. Legend says he used the shamrock to explain the Trinity.

saints.name: St. Brigid of Kildare
saints.story: Founder of a great double monastery at Kildare, Brigid is remembered for her boundless hospitality and generosity to the poor. Many stories tell of her miracles of abundance. The woven rush cross that bears her name is still hung in Irish homes for protection.

saints.name: St. Columba (Colmcille)
saints.story: A monk of royal blood from Donegal, Columba founded monasteries in Ireland before sailing in 563 to Iona, off Scotland. From there he and his monks evangelised the Picts and northern Britain. He was a poet, scholar and lover of books.

saints.name: St. Oliver Plunkett
saints.story: Archbishop of Armagh during the Penal times, Oliver worked tirelessly to restore the Church, often in hiding. Falsely accused in the 'Popish Plot', he was hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn in London in 1681. He was canonized in 1975, and his head is venerated in Drogheda.

saints.name: Ven. Matt Talbot
saints.story: A Dublin labourer who struggled with alcoholism from his teens, Matt Talbot took a pledge of sobriety in 1884 and kept it for forty years through prayer, daily Mass and penance. He is a beloved model for those seeking freedom from addiction and was declared Venerable in 1975.

cathedrals.name: Knock Shrine
cathedrals.story: On August 21, 1879, villagers reported a silent apparition of Our Lady, St. Joseph, St. John and the Lamb of God at the gable of the parish church. Knock became Ireland's national Marian shrine, visited by St. John Paul II in 1979 and Pope Francis in 2018.

cathedrals.name: St. Mary's Pro-Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in the early nineteenth century in a Greek Revival style, at a time when Catholics were only beginning to emerge from the Penal era, this is the Catholic cathedral of Dublin. It is home to the renowned Palestrina Choir, in which the tenor John McCormack once sang.

cathedrals.name: St. Mary's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Designed by Augustus Welby Pugin and begun in 1842, this Gothic Revival cathedral was interrupted by the Great Famine, when it served as a shelter for the starving. Completed later in the century, it is one of the finest Pugin churches in Ireland.

prayerIntention: For Ireland, land of saints and scholars, that its Church may be healed and renewed in humility, and that all its people, north and south, may live in lasting peace.

name: Israel
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. 1%), including Melkite, Latin and Maronite faithful and many migrant workers
history:
This is the land where the faith began. In Nazareth the Word became flesh; in Galilee Jesus called fishermen, healed the sick and preached by the lake; in Jerusalem he died and rose again. The first Christian communities were born here, and pilgrims have come ever since. Byzantine churches covered the holy sites, many later destroyed in wars and conquests. From the fourteenth century the Franciscans of the Custody of the Holy Land have guarded the shrines on behalf of the Catholic Church, and the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem was restored in 1847.

Today Catholics are a small and varied flock. Most local Catholics are Arabic-speaking Melkite Greek Catholics, alongside Latin, Maronite and other Eastern Catholics, and a Hebrew-speaking Catholic community. Tens of thousands of Catholic migrant workers and asylum seekers, many from the Philippines, India and Africa, now fill the churches as well. The Holy See and Israel established diplomatic relations in 1994, and Popes John Paul II, Benedict XVI and Francis came as pilgrims.

Life is not easy for this little Church. Emigration, the long Israeli–Palestinian conflict and the war that began in October 2023 have brought grief to every community in the land, and there have been incidents of harassment and vandalism against Christians and churches. Yet the Church remains, serving through schools, hospitals and parishes, and keeping watch at the places where the Gospel was first lived.

saints.name: St. Mariam Baouardy (Mary of Jesus Crucified)
saints.story: Born in Ibillin in Galilee to a Melkite Catholic family and orphaned young, Mariam became a Discalced Carmelite in France, known as 'the little Arab'. A mystic of great simplicity, she helped found the Carmel in Bethlehem. She was canonized in 2015, among the first modern saints from the Holy Land.

saints.name: St. Marie-Alphonsine Danil Ghattas
saints.story: Born in Jerusalem, she founded the Congregation of the Sisters of the Most Holy Rosary, the first religious order of local Arab women in the Holy Land, devoted to educating girls and spreading the Rosary. She was canonized in 2015 alongside Mariam Baouardy.

saints.name: St. Charles de Foucauld
