saints.story: After his conversion, the former French officer lived for several years in Nazareth as a humble servant of the Poor Clares, seeking the hidden life of Jesus the carpenter. That Nazareth spirituality shaped his later life among the Tuareg of the Sahara. He was canonized in 2022.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Annunciation
cathedrals.story: Built over the grotto venerated as the home of Mary, where the angel Gabriel greeted her. The present basilica, designed by Giovanni Muzio, was completed in 1969 on the remains of Byzantine and Crusader churches. Its walls hold images of Our Lady sent by Catholics from countries all over the world.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Transfiguration
cathedrals.story: Crowning the mountain traditionally identified with the Transfiguration, this Franciscan basilica was designed by Antonio Barluzzi and completed in 1924 over earlier Byzantine and Crusader ruins. Its golden apse mosaic of the transfigured Christ catches the light, and pilgrims climb the winding road to pray where the disciples heard, 'This is my beloved Son.'

cathedrals.name: Stella Maris Monastery
cathedrals.story: On Mount Carmel, linked to the prophet Elijah, stands the Discalced Carmelite monastery and church of Stella Maris. The Carmelite order took its name from hermits who lived on this mountain in the Middle Ages. The present church dates from the nineteenth century, with a cave honoured as Elijah's beneath the altar.

cathedrals.name: Church of the Multiplication
cathedrals.story: Cared for by German Benedictines, this simple church rebuilt in 1982 preserves a beloved fifth-century mosaic of loaves and fishes. It marks the tradition of the feeding of the five thousand. It was badly damaged by an arson attack in 2015 and restored, a quiet witness to both fragility and perseverance.

prayerIntention: For all who live in the land where Jesus walked, that the God of peace would heal its wounds, protect every life, and keep the small Christian communities faithful and unafraid.

name: Italy
history:
The faith reached Italy in the apostolic age. A Christian community already existed in Rome when St. Paul wrote to it, and both Peter and Paul were martyred there under Nero. For nearly three centuries Christians endured waves of persecution, burying their dead in the catacombs, until the Edict of Milan in 313 granted freedom of worship. Rome became the see of the Popes, and Italy the heart of the Latin Church.

From Italy came St. Benedict and Western monasticism, St. Francis and St. Clare, St. Catherine of Siena, and a torrent of art, music and holiness. The story also holds shadows: the worldliness of some Renaissance popes, the long political entanglement of the Papal States, and painful conflict when the new Italian state took Rome in 1870. The Lateran Treaty of 1929 created Vatican City and settled relations between Church and state.

Today Italy remains deeply marked by Catholic culture, with countless parishes, shrines and charitable works, and confraternities and feast-day processions that still fill town squares. Yet Mass attendance has fallen sharply, vocations are fewer, and the Church, like others, has had to face the wounds of abuse. Young witnesses such as Pier Giorgio Frassati and Carlo Acutis, canonized together in 2025, remind Italians that holiness is still possible in ordinary life.

saints.name: St. Francis of Assisi
saints.story: Son of a wealthy cloth merchant, Francis renounced everything to follow the poor Christ. He founded the Friars Minor, preached peace, rebuilt churches, loved creation in his Canticle of the Creatures and received the stigmata. He was proclaimed patron of Italy in 1939 together with St. Catherine of Siena.

saints.name: St. Catherine of Siena
saints.story: A Dominican tertiary and mystic who could barely read in her youth, Catherine became a fearless counsellor of popes, urging Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome. Her Dialogue is a classic of spiritual writing. She is a Doctor of the Church and co-patroness of Italy and of Europe.

saints.name: St. John Bosco
saints.story: A priest of Turin who gathered poor and abandoned boys, giving them faith, schooling and trades. With a 'preventive system' built on reason, religion and loving kindness, he founded the Salesians and, with St. Mary Mazzarello, the Salesian Sisters, who now serve the young worldwide.

saints.name: St. Pio of Pietrelcina (Padre Pio)
saints.story: A Capuchin friar of San Giovanni Rotondo who bore the stigmata for fifty years. He spent long hours in the confessional, founded a hospital, the Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, and drew multitudes to prayer. Investigated and restricted for a time, he remained obedient. He was canonized in 2002.

saints.name: St. Carlo Acutis
saints.story: A Milanese teenager who loved the Eucharist, called it his 'highway to heaven', and used his computer skills to document Eucharistic miracles. He died of leukaemia at fifteen and is buried in Assisi. He was canonized in 2025, the first saint of the millennial generation.

cathedrals.name: Milan Cathedral (Duomo di Milano)
cathedrals.story: Begun in 1386 and finished only in the twentieth century, Milan's Gothic cathedral is one of the largest churches in the world, bristling with spires and thousands of statues. The golden Madonnina crowns its highest spire, and the roof terraces let visitors walk among the pinnacles.

cathedrals.name: Florence Cathedral (Santa Maria del Fiore)
cathedrals.story: Begun in 1296, the cathedral is famous for Brunelleschi's great dome, an engineering marvel completed in the fifteenth century without traditional scaffolding. Its marble façade of white, green and pink, Giotto's bell tower and the Baptistery doors make it a jewel of the Renaissance.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of St. Francis
cathedrals.story: Begun in 1228, two years after Francis died, this double basilica holds his tomb in its crypt. The upper church is adorned with frescoes of his life traditionally attributed to Giotto. Damaged by an earthquake in 1997 and lovingly restored, it remains a place of peace and pilgrimage.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Holy House
cathedrals.story: This Renaissance basilica enshrines the Holy House, venerated by tradition as the house of Mary from Nazareth. For centuries it has been one of Europe's great Marian shrines, visited by saints and popes, and Our Lady of Loreto is patroness of aviators.

prayerIntention: For Italy, that the land of so many saints may rediscover the joy of the Gospel, welcome the stranger, and raise up new generations of holy families, priests and religious.

name: Jamaica
history:
Catholicism first arrived with the Spanish after Columbus reached the island in 1494. Spanish settlers built churches at Sevilla la Nueva on the north coast, but colonization devastated the Indigenous Taíno people, and enslaved Africans were brought to labour on the land, a deep wound the Church acknowledges with sorrow. When England captured Jamaica in 1655, Catholic worship was suppressed for well over a century.

The faith returned slowly from the late eighteenth century, carried by Catholic refugees from Saint-Domingue (Haiti) and others. In the nineteenth century the Jesuits took on the mission, founding schools such as St. George's College in Kingston, and later many religious congregations followed, serving in education, health and among the poor.

Today Catholics are a small part of a largely Protestant nation, but Catholic schools are widely respected and the Church is active in caring for the poor, the sick and the elderly. St. John Paul II visited Jamaica in 1993. The Church faces Jamaica's real struggles, including violent crime and poverty, with steady pastoral presence and a voice for peace.

saints.name: St. John Paul II
saints.story: Jamaica has no canonized saint of its own yet. In 1993 Pope John Paul II made a pastoral visit to Jamaica, encouraging its Catholic community, celebrating Mass in Kingston and speaking of reconciliation and family life. Many Jamaican Catholics remember the visit with great affection.

saints.name: St. Teresa of Calcutta
saints.story: Her Missionaries of Charity serve the poorest in Kingston, caring for the sick, elderly and abandoned. Mother Teresa's spiritual daughters continue her work of quiet, practical love among Jamaicans who have nowhere else to turn.

cathedrals.name: Holy Trinity Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Opened in 1911 after the devastating Kingston earthquake of 1907, this domed cathedral is one of the landmarks of the capital. Its interior is decorated with murals that were restored for its centenary. It is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Kingston and a gathering place for the island's Catholics.

prayerIntention: For the people of Jamaica, that the Lord would bring peace to its communities, protect its young people from violence, and strengthen every family and church on the island.

name: Japan
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. 0.3–0.5%, plus many Catholic migrants)
history:
St. Francis Xavier landed at Kagoshima in 1549, and within decades the faith spread remarkably: by the end of the sixteenth century there were perhaps some 300,000 Japanese Christians, including powerful lords. Then the tide turned. Toyotomi Hideyoshi issued an edict against missionaries in 1587, and in 1597 twenty-six Christians were crucified at Nagasaki. Under the Tokugawa shogunate Christianity was banned from 1614, and thousands were tortured and killed.

For some 250 years, the 'Hidden Christians' kept the faith in secret without priests, passing on prayers and baptism from generation to generation. In 1865, shortly after the Oura Church opened in Nagasaki, a group of villagers quietly revealed to a French priest that they shared his faith, a moment remembered as the 'discovery of the Christians'. Persecution continued until the ban was lifted in 1873.

In 1945 the atomic bomb fell on Urakami, the heart of Nagasaki's Catholic community, destroying the cathedral and killing thousands of faithful. Today Japanese Catholics are few, but their schools, universities and hospitals are widely respected, and migrant Catholics from the Philippines, Vietnam, Brazil and elsewhere bring new life to parishes. The Church in Japan is a strong voice for peace and nuclear disarmament.

saints.name: St. Paul Miki and Companions
saints.story: Paul Miki, a Japanese Jesuit and gifted preacher, was among the twenty-six martyrs crucified on a hill in Nagasaki on 5 February 1597, together with Franciscans, catechists and young boys. From the cross he forgave his executioners. They were canonized in 1862.

saints.name: St. Francis Xavier
saints.story: The Jesuit apostle of Asia arrived in Japan in 1549 and spent about two years there, learning to adapt his preaching to Japanese culture. The communities he founded grew rapidly after his departure. He died on an island off China while hoping to enter that land.

saints.name: St. Lorenzo Ruiz and Companions
saints.story: Lorenzo Ruiz, a Filipino layman and father, was martyred in Nagasaki in 1637 with Dominican missionaries and Japanese Christians. Asked to renounce his faith, he declared he would die for God a thousand times. The sixteen martyrs were canonized in 1987.

saints.name: Bl. Justo Takayama Ukon
saints.story: A samurai lord who chose to lose his lands and status rather than abandon Christ. Exiled to Manila in 1614 with other Christians, he died there weeks after arriving. He was beatified in 2017 as a martyr, honoured for his lifelong fidelity.

cathedrals.name: Oura Church (Basilica of the Twenty-Six Holy Martyrs of Japan)
cathedrals.story: Built by French missionaries and completed in 1864, it is the oldest surviving church in Japan and a National Treasure. Here in 1865 Hidden Christians revealed their faith to Fr. Bernard Petitjean. Dedicated to the twenty-six martyrs, it faces the hill where they died.

cathedrals.name: Urakami Cathedral (St. Mary's Cathedral)
cathedrals.story: Built by descendants of the Hidden Christians, it stood near the hypocentre of the 1945 atomic bomb and was destroyed. The cathedral was rebuilt in 1959. Scorched statues and the bombed bell are preserved, and the 'Bombed Mary', a charred head of Our Lady, is a moving icon of suffering and peace.

cathedrals.name: St. Mary's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Designed by architect Kenzo Tange and completed in 1964, this cathedral replaced a wooden church destroyed in the war. Its soaring stainless-steel walls form a cross of light when seen from above. It is a striking example of modern sacred architecture and the mother church of Tokyo.

prayerIntention: For Japan, that the faith of its martyrs and Hidden Christians may bear fruit in new hearts, and that the nation that suffered nuclear war may be a light of peace for the world.

name: Jordan
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. 1%, Latin and Melkite)
history:
Christianity in Jordan is as old as the Gospel. The east bank of the Jordan River is honoured as 'Bethany beyond the Jordan', where John baptized and where Jesus was baptized. Early Christian communities flourished in cities of the Decapolis, and Byzantine churches with splendid mosaics, many still visible at Madaba and Mount Nebo, testify to a vibrant faith in the first centuries.

After the Islamic conquest in the seventh century, Christians remained as an ancient, mostly Arabic-speaking community. Catholic life was strengthened in the nineteenth century through the restored Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem and the Melkite Greek Catholic Church, which built parishes and schools in towns such as Salt, Madaba, Karak and Amman.

Today Jordan's Christians are a small minority who generally enjoy religious freedom and good relations with their Muslim neighbours, though emigration slowly reduces their numbers. The Church has played a remarkable role in welcoming refugees from Iraq and Syria. Jordan has welcomed papal pilgrims: John Paul II in 2000, Benedict XVI in 2009 and Francis in 2014. Catholic schools and charities are respected far beyond the Christian community.

saints.name: St. John the Baptist
saints.story: The forerunner of Christ preached repentance and baptized in the Jordan River. Tradition locates his ministry at Bethany beyond the Jordan, on the eastern bank, where pilgrims now renew their baptismal promises. Jordanian Christians feel a special closeness to him.

saints.name: St. Elijah the Prophet
saints.story: The prophet Elijah came from Tishbe in Gilead, in today's northern Jordan, and was taken up to heaven near the Jordan River. Honoured as a saint by Christians, especially by the Carmelites, he is remembered at Mar Elias near Ajloun, where ruins of a Byzantine church survive.

cathedrals.name: Memorial of Moses on Mount Nebo
cathedrals.story: On the summit where Moses viewed the Promised Land, the Franciscans care for a basilica built over Byzantine church remains. Its floor holds some of the finest early Christian mosaics in the region. Renovated and reopened in 2016, it offers a sweeping view across the Jordan Valley toward Jerusalem.

cathedrals.name: Baptism Site (Bethany beyond the Jordan)
cathedrals.story: Recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage site, this area preserves ruins of Byzantine churches and baptismal pools. Several Christian churches now stand nearby, including a Latin Catholic Church of the Baptism of the Lord. Popes have prayed here, and pilgrims from around the world come to remember Christ's baptism.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of the Mountain
cathedrals.story: This Marian shrine in northern Jordan recalls the tradition that Jesus, Mary and the disciples rested in a cave here while travelling. It was designated one of the Jubilee pilgrimage sites in 2000 and remains a beloved place of prayer for Jordanian Catholics.

prayerIntention: For the people of Jordan, that this land of the Jordan River may remain a haven of peace and hospitality, and that its ancient Christian communities may flourish among their neighbours.

name: Kazakhstan
history:
Christianity touched the Central Asian steppe in the Middle Ages through the Church of the East, and Franciscan missionaries passed through on their way to the Mongol courts. But the modern Catholic presence in Kazakhstan was born mostly from suffering. Under Stalin, hundreds of thousands of Poles, Germans, Lithuanians, Ukrainians and others were deported to the steppe and to labour camps such as Karlag near Karaganda.

Among the deported and imprisoned were Catholic priests and lay people who kept the faith alive in secret, baptizing, teaching prayers and celebrating Mass in homes. Figures like Bl. Władysław Bukowiński and Bl. Bishop Oleksa Zarytskyi served these scattered flocks at great personal risk. Faithful grandmothers passed on the Rosary when there were no churches.

After independence in 1991, the Church could finally organize openly. Kazakhstan and the Holy See established relations, dioceses were set up, and St. John Paul II visited in 2001. Pope Francis came in 2022 for the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions. Today the Church is small and multi-ethnic, serving through parishes, Caritas and religious communities in a land known for interreligious harmony.

patronSaints.name: Mary, Queen of Peace (National Shrine at Oziornoye)

saints.name: Bl. Władysław Bukowiński
saints.story: A Polish priest arrested by the Soviets and sentenced to labour camps, he chose to stay in Kazakhstan after his release, secretly ministering to Catholics across the steppe from Karaganda. Called the 'apostle of Kazakhstan', he was beatified in Karaganda in 2016.

saints.name: Bl. Oleksa Zarytskyi
saints.story: A Ukrainian Greek Catholic priest, later secretly consecrated a bishop, who ministered tirelessly to deported Catholics in Kazakhstan. He was repeatedly imprisoned and died in a labour camp near Karaganda. He was beatified as a martyr in 2001.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Fatima
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 2012, this neo-Gothic cathedral stands in a city founded around Soviet labour camps where many Catholics suffered. It was built as a memorial to the persecuted and a sign of thanksgiving for freedom. Its twin spires and stained glass make it one of the most beautiful churches in Central Asia.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Mother of Perpetual Help
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Astana, a light-filled modern church in the capital. Pope Francis met bishops, clergy, religious and lay people here during his 2022 visit, encouraging this small Church to remain a joyful and humble witness.

cathedrals.name: National Shrine of the Queen of Peace
cathedrals.story: In the hungry spring of 1941, deported Catholics in this village prayed to Our Lady, and fish appeared in abundance in a nearby lake, saving them from famine. The village became a place of pilgrimage, and in 1995 the shrine was dedicated to Mary, Queen of Peace, patroness of Kazakhstan.

prayerIntention: For Kazakhstan, that the faith kept alive through exile and suffering may grow in freedom, and that its many peoples and religions may live together in lasting peace.

name: Kenya
history:
The first Catholic presence on the Kenyan coast came with the Portuguese after Vasco da Gama reached Malindi in 1498. Augustinian friars served in Mombasa, but the mission ended in tragedy: in 1631 many Christians in Fort Jesus were killed during an uprising, and Catholic life on the coast faded for more than two centuries.

The modern mission began in the late nineteenth century. The Holy Ghost Fathers (Spiritans) established missions on the coast and inland, and from 1902 the Consolata Missionaries arrived in the highlands around Nyeri, followed by the Mill Hill Missionaries in the west and many other congregations. Missionaries built schools and hospitals that shaped generations of Kenyans, though the mission also unfolded within a colonial system whose injustices, including the harsh repression of the Mau Mau period, left lasting wounds.

Today the Catholic Church is one of the largest in Kenya, with millions of faithful, a growing number of Kenyan priests and religious, and a dense network of schools, hospitals and Small Christian Communities. Its bishops have often spoken out for justice, honest elections and peace, especially during times of political violence. Popes John Paul II and Francis both visited, and Kenya now sends its own missionaries abroad.

saints.name: Bl. Irene Stefani
saints.story: An Italian Consolata missionary sister who served in Kenya, caring for wounded African porters during the First World War and later teaching and nursing around Gikondi. Kikuyu people called her 'Nyaatha', mother of mercy. She died after nursing a plague patient and was beatified in Nyeri in 2015.

saints.name: St. Joseph Allamano
saints.story: A priest of Turin who never left Italy, yet founded the Consolata Missionaries, whose very first mission field was Kenya in 1902. His sons and daughters laid the foundations of the Church in central Kenya. He was canonized in 2024.

saints.name: Bl. Leonella Sgorbati
saints.story: An Italian Consolata sister who spent decades in Kenya as a nurse and trainer of nurses, including in Nairobi. She went on to open a nursing school in Mogadishu, where she was shot in 2006, forgiving her killers as she died. She was beatified as a martyr in 2018.

cathedrals.name: Holy Family Minor Basilica
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Nairobi, standing in the city centre. The present building was erected in the mid-twentieth century and later raised to a minor basilica. Popes John Paul II and Francis have prayed here, and it is a busy spiritual home for the capital's Catholics.

cathedrals.name: Holy Ghost Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built by the Holy Ghost Fathers in the early twentieth century, this white cathedral with its twin towers and dome is a landmark of Mombasa. It recalls the coastal roots of Catholic mission in Kenya, from the Portuguese era to the Spiritan missionaries.

cathedrals.name: Subukia National Marian Shrine
cathedrals.story: Set on a hill above the Rift Valley, this national shrine dedicated to Mary draws thousands of pilgrims, especially on Marian feasts. Many come to pray the Rosary along its paths and to collect water from its spring, which some call the 'Lourdes of Africa'.

prayerIntention: For Kenya, that its leaders may govern with justice, its people live in unity across every tribe and faith, and its vibrant Church continue to serve the poor with joy.

name: Kiribati
history:
Protestant missionaries reached the Gilbert Islands in the mid-nineteenth century, and Catholicism arrived soon after through I-Kiribati who had encountered the faith abroad. In 1888 the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart (MSC) arrived and began a mission that spread quickly through the islands, aided by catechists and, later, missionary sisters.

The islands were occupied by Japan during the Second World War, and Tarawa saw one of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific in 1943. Missionaries and islanders alike endured hardship. After the war the Church grew steadily, building schools that formed many of Kiribati's leaders, and local priests and sisters gradually took up the mission.

Today Catholics are the largest Christian community in Kiribati, served by the Diocese of Tarawa and Nauru. Faith is woven into village life, songs and celebrations. Kiribati also faces a grave reality: rising sea levels threaten these low-lying atolls, and the Church has spoken for care of creation and for the dignity of island peoples whose homes are at risk.

saints.name: St. Peter Chanel
saints.story: Kiribati does not yet have saints of its own. St. Peter Chanel, a Marist missionary martyred on Futuna, is the protomartyr of Oceania and is honoured throughout the Pacific as a patron of the island Churches and of missionary courage.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Diocese of Tarawa and Nauru, dedicated to the Sacred Heart in honour of the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart who brought the faith. It is the centre of diocesan celebrations, where full-voiced I-Kiribati choirs fill the liturgy with song.

prayerIntention: For the people of Kiribati, that God would protect their islands and homes, and that the nations of the world may respond with justice and care to the threat of rising seas.

name: Kosovo
history:
Christianity reached this part of the Balkans, the Roman province of Dardania, in the early centuries; the ancient city of Ulpiana had a bishop and Christian martyrs. In the Middle Ages the land became a heartland of the Serbian Orthodox Church, whose ancient monasteries still stand, while Catholic communities, especially among Albanians and in towns such as Prizren and Gjakova, endured alongside them.

Under Ottoman rule many converted to Islam, and some Catholic families lived as hidden or 'crypto-Catholics', outwardly Muslim but secretly baptized and praying in Christian ways. In the twentieth century Catholics shared the sufferings of communist Yugoslavia, and the war of 1998–1999 brought immense loss to Albanians and Serbs alike.

The Catholic Church in Kosovo, now the Diocese of Prizren-Pristina, is small but alive, rooted in Albanian Catholic tradition and in love for Mother Teresa, whose family roots were in this region. The new cathedral in Pristina bears her name. The Church works for reconciliation in a society still marked by ethnic division, and some families have returned openly to the faith of their ancestors.

saints.name: St. Teresa of Calcutta
saints.story: Born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu in Skopje to an Albanian family with roots in Kosovo, she made pilgrimages as a girl to the shrine of Our Lady of Letnica, where she felt her call to religious life. She founded the Missionaries of Charity and was canonized in 2016.

saints.name: Sts. Florus and Laurus
saints.story: According to ancient tradition, these twin brothers were stonemasons martyred at Ulpiana in Dardania, near today's Pristina. They are among the earliest Christians remembered from this land and are honoured by both Catholics and Orthodox.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Mother Teresa
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 2017, this modern cathedral with its tall bell tower was the first Catholic cathedral built in Pristina. Dedicated to St. Teresa of Calcutta, it is a sign of the Albanian Catholic community's renewed confidence and of hope for a peaceful, open society.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Letnica
cathedrals.story: In a mountain village near the border with North Macedonia, this shrine keeps the 'Black Madonna of Letnica'. Catholics, and some Orthodox and Muslims, come in pilgrimage on the feast of the Assumption. Young Gonxhe Bojaxhiu, the future Mother Teresa, prayed here before discerning her vocation.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Perpetual Succour
cathedrals.story: In the historic city of Prizren, long a centre of Albanian Catholic life, this cathedral is the historic seat of the Catholic bishops of the region. It stands among mosques and Orthodox churches in one of the most beautiful old towns of the Balkans.

prayerIntention: For Kosovo, that the wounds of war may be healed, that Albanians, Serbs and all communities may live in mutual respect, and that the Church may be a humble sign of reconciliation.

name: Kuwait
catholicPresence: Expatriate Catholic community (approx. hundreds of thousands of migrant workers; very few citizens)
history:
Kuwait's Catholics are almost all migrants: workers from India, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Lebanon, Egypt and many other countries who have come to work and support families far away. Organized Catholic life began in the mid-twentieth century, when Carmelite missionaries served the growing foreign workforce of the oil era. A church was built in Ahmadi on land given by the Kuwait Oil Company, and Holy Family Cathedral in Kuwait City followed in 1961.

Today Kuwait belongs to the Apostolic Vicariate of Northern Arabia, whose patroness is Our Lady of Arabia. Christians may worship within their church compounds, and the state has allowed this freedom with notable courtesy compared with some neighbours. Yet the churches are small for the numbers: on weekends, Masses in many languages follow one another from morning to night, and courtyards overflow.

This Church is one of quiet faithfulness. Many of its members live with separation from their families, uncertain contracts and sometimes hard working conditions, especially domestic workers. Parishes offer them a home, a language, sacraments and solidarity, and they in turn offer the universal Church a witness of perseverance.

cathedrals.name: Holy Family Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in 1961, this cathedral is the spiritual heart of Catholic life in Kuwait. Mass is celebrated here in many languages, including English, Arabic, Malayalam, Tagalog and others, often back to back throughout the day. Its crowded courtyard is a living picture of the universal Church.

cathedrals.name: Church of Our Lady of Arabia
cathedrals.story: Built on land given by the Kuwait Oil Company, this was one of the first Catholic churches in Kuwait. It houses the venerated statue of Our Lady of Arabia, later proclaimed patroness of the Gulf region, and is a place of Marian devotion for the migrant community.

prayerIntention: For the many migrant Catholics of Kuwait, that they may be treated with justice and dignity, find strength in their faith far from home, and be reunited in joy with those they love.

name: Kyrgyzstan
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic community (well under 0.1%, roughly a few hundred to a thousand faithful)
history:
Christianity first came to the region of today's Kyrgyzstan through the Church of the East along the Silk Road in the early Middle Ages, and medieval Christian gravestones have been found near Lake Issyk-Kul and in the Chüy valley. These communities eventually disappeared. In the Soviet era, many Catholic Germans, Poles, Lithuanians and others were deported to Central Asia, and some settled in Kyrgyzstan, keeping the faith quietly at home.

After independence in 1991 the small Catholic community could organize openly. The Holy See established a mission, later raised to the Apostolic Administration of Kyrgyzstan in 2006, entrusted to the Jesuits. Many of the descendants of deported Catholics emigrated to Germany and elsewhere, so the community today is tiny and diverse.

The Church in Kyrgyzstan lives a simple, humble witness: a few parishes in Bishkek, Talas and Jalal-Abad and some smaller communities, served by priests and sisters from many countries. Registration rules for religious groups can be restrictive. Yet the little flock gathers faithfully, cares for the needy, and prays for the whole nation.

cathedrals.name: Church of St. Michael the Archangel
cathedrals.story: The main Catholic church of Kyrgyzstan and seat of the Apostolic Administration. A modest building rather than a grand cathedral, it grew from the humble beginnings of a community that once prayed in private homes. It is the gathering place for a small, multi-ethnic flock of Kyrgyz, Russians, Germans, Koreans and foreigners.

prayerIntention: For the people of Kyrgyzstan, that they may live in peace and freedom, and that the small Catholic community may be a gentle witness of Christ's love among its neighbours.

name: Laos
history:
Catholic missionaries attempted to enter Laos in the seventeenth century, but lasting mission work began only in the late nineteenth century, led by priests of the Paris Foreign Missions Society (MEP), and later also by the Oblates of Mary Immaculate from Italy and France. Communities grew among Lao, Vietnamese and hill peoples such as the Hmong and Khmu.

The wars that engulfed Indochina brought great suffering. Between 1954 and 1970 a number of priests, missionaries and lay catechists, both foreign and Lao, were killed for their faith. Seventeen of them, including the Lao priest Joseph Thao Tiên and the young catechist Paul Thoj Xyooj, were beatified in Vientiane in 2016. After the communist takeover in 1975 all foreign missionaries were expelled, and the Church's life was severely restricted.

For decades Lao Catholics kept the faith with very few priests. In recent years there has been some greater openness: churches function, local priests are ordained, and in 2017 Bishop Louis-Marie Ling Mangkhanekhoun became the first cardinal from Laos. Restrictions remain, especially in rural areas, but this small Church perseveres with deep faith.

saints.name: Bl. Joseph Thao Tiên
saints.story: One of the first Lao priests, he was arrested by communist forces in 1954 while serving his people and died in captivity. He heads the group of seventeen martyrs of Laos beatified in Vientiane in December 2016.

saints.name: Bl. Mario Borzaga
saints.story: A young Italian Oblate of Mary Immaculate who served among the Hmong in Laos. In 1960 he disappeared with his catechist on a mission journey and was killed. His spiritual diary, 'Diary of a Happy Man', reveals a joyful heart given entirely to God.

saints.name: Bl. Paul Thoj Xyooj
saints.story: A Hmong catechist who accompanied Fr. Mario Borzaga on mission. Captured with him, he reportedly refused to abandon the priest even when offered his freedom, and was killed with him. He is one of the first Hmong blesseds.

saints.name: Bl. Jean-Baptiste Malo
saints.story: A French priest of the Paris Foreign Missions who had served in China before coming to Laos. Arrested in 1954, he died of exhaustion and mistreatment during a forced march in captivity. He was beatified among the martyrs of Laos in 2016.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in the French colonial period, this modest cathedral in the capital is the heart of Catholic life in Laos. Here in 2016 the seventeen martyrs of Laos were beatified, a day of tears and joy for a Church that had long suffered in silence.

prayerIntention: For Laos, that its people may enjoy peace and freedom, and that the small Church, strengthened by its martyrs, may grow in faith and serve all with humility.

name: Latvia
history:
Christianity came to the lands of present-day Latvia in the late twelfth century, when the Augustinian canon St. Meinhard preached among the Livonians and became their first bishop. The mission was soon followed by the armed crusades of the German orders, a violent chapter that brought baptism alongside conquest. Livonia was dedicated to the Virgin Mary as 'Terra Mariana'.

The Reformation turned much of Latvia Lutheran, but the eastern region of Latgale, long under Polish-Lithuanian rule, remained deeply Catholic and is still the heartland of Latvian Catholicism. Under Soviet occupation from 1940 and again after 1944, the Church was persecuted: priests and faithful were deported, churches closed, and religion pushed to the margins of life.

Since independence was restored in 1991, the Catholic Church has rebuilt its parishes and seminaries. St. John Paul II visited in 1993 and Pope Francis in 2018, praying at Aglona, the great Marian shrine of the nation. Today Latvia's Catholics are a significant minority living alongside Lutherans and Orthodox, and ecumenical friendship is a mark of Christian life here.

patronSaints.name: The Blessed Virgin Mary (Terra Mariana), honoured at Aglona

saints.name: St. Meinhard
saints.story: An Augustinian canon from Segeberg in Holstein who came as a missionary to the Livonians along the Daugava river and became the first bishop of Livonia. He preached with patience rather than force. His cult was confirmed by St. John Paul II in 1993, and he is honoured as the apostle of Latvia.

cathedrals.name: Aglona Basilica of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: Built in the eighteenth century by Dominicans in a lakeland setting of Latgale, this white baroque basilica with twin towers keeps a beloved icon of the Mother of God. Each year on 15 August tens of thousands come on pilgrimage. Popes John Paul II and Francis prayed here.

cathedrals.name: St. James's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: A medieval church in Riga's Old Town, first mentioned in the thirteenth century, which became Lutheran after the Reformation and was returned to Catholics in 1923 as the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Riga. Its slender spire is a landmark of the city.

prayerIntention: For Latvia, Mary's land, that its people may live in freedom and peace, heal from the wounds of occupation, and find new life in Christ.

name: Lebanon
catholicPresence: Large Catholic community (approx. a quarter of the population; mostly Maronite, also Melkite, Armenian, Syriac and Latin)
history:
Lebanon's Christian roots go back to the Gospels themselves: Jesus visited the region of Tyre and Sidon, and Christian communities flourished in the coastal cities from the earliest centuries. The Maronite Church traces its origins to the monastic movement around St. Maron in the fourth and fifth centuries. Maronite monks and faithful took refuge in the rugged Qadisha Valley, which became a cradle of hermits and patriarchs, and the Maronites have always remained in communion with Rome.

Over the centuries Lebanon became a mosaic of Christian and Muslim communities. Catholic Eastern Churches, Melkite, Armenian, Syriac and Chaldean, took root alongside the Maronites. Christians shaped modern Lebanon's schools, universities and culture, but also suffered massacres in 1860, famine during the First World War, and the long civil war of 1975–1990, in which Christian militias also bore responsibility for terrible violence.

Today Lebanon's Catholics live amid economic collapse, political paralysis, the devastating Beirut port explosion of 2020, and repeated wars. Emigration has drained the communities. Yet monasteries, schools, hospitals and parishes keep serving everyone, and the shrines of St. Charbel and Our Lady of Lebanon draw Christians and Muslims alike. St. John Paul II called Lebanon 'more than a country: a message' of coexistence.

saints.name: St. Charbel Makhlouf
saints.story: A Maronite monk of the monastery of Annaya who spent his last twenty-three years as a hermit in prayer and silence. After his death, many healings were reported at his tomb, and his body was found incorrupt for decades. Canonized in 1977, he is beloved across Lebanon and the world.

saints.name: St. Rafqa (Rebecca) Choboq Ar-Rayès
saints.story: A Maronite nun who asked God to share in Christ's sufferings and became blind and paralysed, enduring years of pain with peace and gratitude. She was canonized in 2001.

saints.name: St. Nimatullah Kassab Al-Hardini
saints.story: A Maronite monk and teacher, devoted to the Eucharist and to Mary, who taught St. Charbel at the monastery school of Kfifan. Known for humility and hard work, he was canonized in 2004.

saints.name: Bl. Estephan Nehmé
saints.story: A Maronite monk-brother who worked in the fields and gardens of his monasteries, finding God in simple labour. His motto was 'God sees me'. He was beatified in 2010.

saints.name: Bl. Patriarch Estephan Douaihy
saints.story: Maronite Patriarch, historian and reformer who renewed the liturgy and the life of his Church in hard times, often fleeing persecution in the Qadisha Valley. A scholar trained in Rome, he was beatified in 2024.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Lebanon
cathedrals.story: Above the Bay of Jounieh stands a great bronze statue of Mary, Our Lady of Lebanon, erected in 1908 with her arms open over the sea. A modern basilica beside it was built in the late twentieth century. Christians and Muslims come here to pray, and it is the beloved spiritual symbol of the nation.

cathedrals.name: Monastery of St. Maron, Annaya
cathedrals.story: In the mountains above Byblos, this Maronite monastery and the nearby hermitage are where St. Charbel lived and died. His tomb draws countless pilgrims of every faith, many seeking healing and peace. The surrounding cedars and silence speak of his hidden life.

cathedrals.name: St. George Maronite Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The Maronite cathedral in downtown Beirut, completed in the late nineteenth century, was heavily damaged during the civil war and restored, then damaged again by the 2020 port explosion. Its repeated rising from ruins mirrors the resilience of Beirut's people.

prayerIntention: For Lebanon, that its people may know peace, justice and recovery, that its leaders may serve the common good, and that Christians and Muslims may continue to live together as a message of hope.

name: Lesotho
catholicPresence: Largest church in the country (approx. 40–45% Catholic)
history:
Protestant missionaries from the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society reached the Basotho in 1833. Catholic mission began in 1862, when Bishop Marie-Jean-François Allard and Fr. Joseph Gérard, Oblates of Mary Immaculate, received permission from King Moshoeshoe I to settle in a valley the people came to call 'Motse oa 'M'a Jesu', the village of the Mother of Jesus, today's Roma.

Progress was slow at first: Fr. Gérard waited years for his first converts, learning Sesotho and visiting homes on foot and horseback in the mountains. Gradually the faith took root, carried by catechists, sisters and Basotho families. Catholic schools and hospitals spread through the lowlands and the high valleys, and in 1945 Pius XII College at Roma was founded, later becoming the National University of Lesotho.

Today the Catholic Church is the largest in Lesotho, deeply woven into national life through education and health care. It has walked with the Basotho through poverty, political unrest and a severe HIV/AIDS epidemic, caring for the sick and orphaned. St. John Paul II visited in 1988 and beatified Fr. Gérard in Maseru, the first beatification on Southern African soil.

saints.name: Bl. Joseph Gérard
saints.story: A French Oblate missionary who served the Basotho for over fifty years, travelling the mountains on horseback, caring for the sick and dying, and praying for those who rejected the faith. He is buried at Roma. St. John Paul II beatified him in Maseru in 1988.

cathedrals.name: Our Lady of Victories Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Maseru, a large church in the capital and the centre of Lesotho's Catholic life. Great national celebrations, ordinations and the faithful's festive singing in Sesotho fill it with joy.

cathedrals.name: Roma Mission
cathedrals.story: Founded in 1862 by Bishop Allard and Fr. Joseph Gérard, the mission in the 'village of the Mother of Jesus' is the cradle of Catholicism in Lesotho. Bl. Joseph Gérard's tomb is here, and the surrounding valley grew into a centre of schools and the National University.

prayerIntention: For the Basotho people, that God would bless the mountain kingdom with peace, honest leadership and health, and that the Church may continue to serve the poor and the sick with love.

name: Liberia
history:
The first Catholic mission to Liberia came in 1842, when Fr. Edward Barron and companions sailed from the United States to serve freed African Americans and local people. The mission was heroic but short-lived: several missionaries died of fever, and the effort was abandoned. A lasting presence came only in the early twentieth century, when the Society of African Missions (SMA) arrived and began building parishes, schools and clinics.

Catholic schools came to be widely respected, educating many Liberians of all faiths. Liberia's history, however, carries deep wounds, from the tensions between Americo-Liberian settlers and Indigenous peoples to the brutal civil wars of 1989–2003. The Church shared in the suffering: in 1992 five American sisters, Adorers of the Blood of Christ, were killed near Monrovia, and churches sheltering civilians became places of massacre.

Through those years the Church, under leaders such as Archbishop Michael Francis, spoke out courageously for peace and human rights, and Catholic agencies cared for the displaced. During the Ebola epidemic of 2014 Catholic hospitals lost staff and missionaries to the disease. Today the Church remains a small but respected voice for reconciliation, education and care for the poor.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Monrovia in the heart of the capital. It has been a place of refuge and prayer through Liberia's years of war, epidemic and recovery, and the site of Masses for peace and for the nation's healing.

prayerIntention: For Liberia, that the scars of war and Ebola may be healed, that its people may live in lasting peace and justice, and that the Church may be a steady light of hope.

name: Libya
catholicPresence: Very small expatriate Catholic community (no significant local Catholic population)
history:
Christianity reached Libya very early. Simon of Cyrene, who carried the cross of Jesus, came from this land, and Christians from Cyrene appear in the Acts of the Apostles. Ancient tradition, especially in the Coptic Church, holds that St. Mark the Evangelist was born in Cyrene. In late antiquity the region had many bishops and churches, but Christianity gradually faded after the Arab conquests of the seventh century.

In the Italian colonial period from 1911, many Catholic churches were built for Italian settlers, among them cathedrals in Tripoli and Benghazi. After independence and especially after 1969, most Italians left, and the former Tripoli cathedral was converted into a mosque. A small Catholic community remained, mostly foreign workers from Africa, Asia and the Philippines, served by a few priests and religious sisters.

Since 2011 Libya has been torn by conflict, and Christians, especially migrants, have faced grave dangers. In 2015, twenty-one Christian workers, twenty Coptic Egyptians and one Ghanaian, were murdered on a Libyan beach for their faith. The few Catholic communities that remain serve migrants in great need with quiet courage.

saints.name: St. Simon of Cyrene
saints.story: A man from Cyrene in today's Libya who was compelled by Roman soldiers to carry the cross of Jesus on the way to Calvary. His sons Alexander and Rufus are named in Mark's Gospel, suggesting the family became Christians. He is remembered in the fifth Station of the Cross.

saints.name: The Twenty-One Martyrs of Libya
saints.story: Twenty Coptic Orthodox Egyptian workers and one Ghanaian companion, killed by Islamic State militants on a Libyan beach for refusing to deny Christ. In 2023 Pope Francis added them to the Roman Martyrology, honouring their witness as a sign of the shared martyrdom of Christians.

cathedrals.name: Church of St. Francis
cathedrals.story: A Franciscan church in Tripoli that has become the main gathering place of the city's Catholic community since the former cathedral was turned into a mosque. Masses in several languages serve migrant workers from Africa and Asia, and the church has stood by them through years of war and danger.

prayerIntention: For Libya, that its long conflict may end in true peace, and that migrants and all who suffer there may be protected, welcomed and treated with dignity.

name: Liechtenstein
history:
Christianity came to the Alpine Rhine valley in late Roman times, and the region belonged for centuries to the ancient Diocese of Chur. Local tradition honours St. Lucius as the apostle of this region, and St. Florin of Remüs, a holy priest of the ninth century, is remembered in the Alpine valleys nearby. Small churches and chapels, many dedicated to Mary and to local saints, dot the villages.

The Principality of Liechtenstein was formed in the early eighteenth century, and Catholicism became deeply rooted in its identity. The princely family has long been Catholic, and the national day on 15 August coincides with the feast of the Assumption of Mary.

In 1997 Pope John Paul II created the Archdiocese of Vaduz, separating Liechtenstein from Chur. The decision and the appointment of its first archbishop caused considerable controversy and division among the faithful at the time. Today Liechtenstein remains largely Catholic by tradition, though, as elsewhere in Western Europe, regular practice has declined and debates continue about the relationship between Church and state.

saints.name: St. Lucius of Chur
saints.story: Venerated as the first missionary of the region around Chur and the Alpine Rhine. Later legends made him a British king, but historically little is certain beyond his early missionary work. He is honoured as the patron of Liechtenstein and of the Diocese of Chur.

saints.name: St. Florin of Remüs
saints.story: A priest of the Lower Engadine, remembered for his holiness and works of charity; legends tell of water turned into wine for the poor. Venerated throughout the region, he is the patron of the cathedral of Vaduz.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Florin
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1870s in neo-Gothic style to plans by the Viennese architect Friedrich von Schmidt, this church became a cathedral in 1997. Set against the mountains beneath Vaduz Castle, it holds the tombs of members of the princely family.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Maria zum Trost (Dux)
cathedrals.story: A small Marian pilgrimage chapel on a hillside above Schaan, with sweeping views of the Rhine valley. For centuries local people have climbed here to entrust their sorrows and hopes to Mary, Our Lady of Consolation.

prayerIntention: For the people of Liechtenstein, that their prosperity may be shared generously, and that their ancient faith may be renewed in unity and joy.

name: Lithuania
history:
Lithuania was the last pagan land in Europe to embrace Christianity. King Mindaugas was baptized in 1251 and crowned in 1253, but the faith did not take hold. The definitive Christianization came in 1387 when Grand Duke Jogaila, having become King of Poland, brought baptism to Lithuania; Samogitia followed in 1413. Over the following centuries Catholicism became woven into Lithuanian identity, nourished by Jesuit colleges, the university of Vilnius and deep popular devotion.

Under Russian imperial rule in the nineteenth century, Catholics resisted repression, including a ban on Lithuanian books in Latin letters, which were smuggled in by 'book carriers'. Soviet occupation from 1940 and again from 1944 brought fierce persecution: bishops and priests were imprisoned or deported, churches closed or turned into museums. The faithful resisted peacefully, publishing the underground 'Chronicle of the Catholic Church in Lithuania' and planting crosses on the Hill of Crosses again and again after the authorities bulldozed them.

Since independence in 1990 the Church has rebuilt its life. St. John Paul II visited in 1993 and Pope Francis in 2018. Today Lithuania is one of Europe's most Catholic nations, though secularization is advancing and the Church seeks new ways to reach the young.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of the Gate of Dawn, Mother of Mercy

saints.name: St. Casimir
saints.story: A royal prince of Poland and Lithuania who lived with prayer, purity and great love for the poor amid court life. He died young of tuberculosis in Grodno and was buried in Vilnius Cathedral. He is the principal patron of Lithuania.

saints.name: Bl. Jurgis Matulaitis
saints.story: A Lithuanian priest who secretly renewed the Marian Fathers when the order was nearly extinct, served as Bishop of Vilnius in a time of ethnic tension, and worked tirelessly for unity and the poor. He was beatified in 1987.

saints.name: Bl. Teofilius Matulionis
saints.story: A bishop who spent many years in Soviet prisons and camps, yet never stopped serving his people. He died under house arrest, and his death has been recognized as martyrdom. He was beatified in Vilnius in 2017.

saints.name: Bl. Michał Sopoćko
saints.story: A priest in Vilnius and confessor of St. Faustina Kowalska. He arranged for the first image of Divine Mercy to be painted in Vilnius in 1934 and devoted his life to promoting the devotion. He was beatified in 2008.

cathedrals.name: Vilnius Cathedral (Sts. Stanislaus and Ladislaus)
cathedrals.story: Rebuilt in neoclassical style in the late eighteenth century on a site sacred since the Middle Ages, the cathedral holds the baroque chapel of St. Casimir. The Soviets turned it into an art gallery; it was returned to the faithful in 1989, a moment of national rejoicing.

cathedrals.name: Gate of Dawn Chapel
cathedrals.story: Above one of the old city gates hangs the seventeenth-century image of Our Lady of the Gate of Dawn, Mother of Mercy, venerated by Lithuanians, Poles and Belarusians alike. Pilgrims pray in the street below, and many remove their hats as they pass.

cathedrals.name: Divine Mercy Sanctuary
cathedrals.story: This small church keeps the original Divine Mercy image painted in Vilnius in 1934 under the direction of St. Faustina and Bl. Michał Sopoćko. Perpetual adoration and prayer draw pilgrims from around the world.

cathedrals.name: Hill of Crosses
cathedrals.story: A hill covered with tens of thousands of crosses and rosaries, planted by pilgrims since the nineteenth century. During Soviet times it was bulldozed several times, yet crosses always returned overnight. St. John Paul II prayed here in 1993; it is a powerful symbol of faith and endurance.

prayerIntention: For Lithuania, that the faith which endured persecution may be passed on joyfully to new generations, and that the nation may live in freedom, mercy and peace.

name: Luxembourg
catholicPresence: Catholic majority by tradition (approx. 60–65%), though practice is much lower
history:
Christianity reached the land of Luxembourg in late Roman times, and in 698 St. Willibrord, the Anglo-Saxon missionary to the Frisians, founded the abbey of Echternach, which became a great centre of learning and manuscript art. Through the Middle Ages the faith shaped the county and later duchy, and the princely house of Luxembourg gave the Church St. Cunigunde.

In the seventeenth century, amid war and plague, the people turned to Our Lady, Consoler of the Afflicted. She was chosen patroness of the city in 1666 and of the whole land in 1678. The annual 'Octave' pilgrimage in her honour remains a beloved national tradition. The Jesuit church built in the early seventeenth century became the cathedral when Luxembourg became a diocese in 1870, later an archdiocese.

During Nazi occupation, Luxembourg's Church suffered: priests were arrested and some died in concentration camps. In recent decades secularization has advanced rapidly, and in 2015 Church and state agreed on a new separation of their relationship. Pope Francis visited in 2024, encouraging a small but committed Church, increasingly enriched by Portuguese and other immigrant Catholics, to be missionary and close to the poor.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady, Consoler of the Afflicted

saints.name: St. Willibrord
saints.story: An Anglo-Saxon monk who became the apostle of the Frisians and first Archbishop of Utrecht. He founded the abbey of Echternach, where he is buried. Each Whit Tuesday thousands join the 'dancing procession' in his honour, a tradition recognized by UNESCO.

saints.name: St. Cunigunde
saints.story: Daughter of Count Siegfried of Luxembourg and wife of Emperor Henry II, with whom she founded churches and the diocese of Bamberg. After her husband's death she entered a convent as a simple nun. She was canonized in 1200.

cathedrals.name: Notre-Dame Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built as a Jesuit church in the early seventeenth century, blending late Gothic and Renaissance elements, it became a cathedral in 1870. It houses the venerated statue of Our Lady, Consoler of the Afflicted, and the crypt of the grand ducal family. The Octave pilgrimage centres here.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of St. Willibrord
cathedrals.story: Rising on the site of the abbey founded by St. Willibrord in 698, the basilica keeps his tomb in its crypt. Heavily destroyed in 1944, it was rebuilt after the war. It is the destination of the famous dancing procession each Whit Tuesday.

prayerIntention: For Luxembourg, that in prosperity it may not forget the poor and the stranger, and that Our Lady, Consoler of the Afflicted, may lead its people to renewed faith.

name: Madagascar
catholicPresence: Large Catholic community (approx. a third of the population)
history:
The first Catholic missionaries reached Madagascar in the seventeenth century: Portuguese Jesuits briefly, and then French Vincentians at Fort-Dauphin from 1648, but these missions did not last. In the nineteenth century the Merina kingdom welcomed Protestant missionaries, then under Queen Ranavalona I Christianity was banned and many believers, mostly Protestants, were martyred. Catholic missionaries, especially Jesuits, returned from 1861 when the climate eased.

The faith grew through schools and devoted lay people, among them Bl. Victoire Rasoamanarivo, a noblewoman who held the Catholic community together when missionaries were expelled in 1883–1886. French colonization from 1895–1896 brought both expansion and complication; during the unrest of 1896 the Jesuit St. Jacques Berthieu was killed. After independence in 1960 the Church became thoroughly Malagasy in leadership and culture.

Today the Church is a major presence in Madagascar, with vibrant liturgies, many vocations and an enormous network of schools and health centres. In a country marked by deep poverty and political crises, the bishops have often called for justice and reconciliation. Popes John Paul II (1989) and Francis (2019) both visited.

saints.name: St. Jacques Berthieu
saints.story: A French Jesuit missionary who served the Malagasy for nearly twenty years. Captured during the unrest of 1896, he was offered his life if he renounced his faith and refused, and was killed. He was canonized in 2012, becoming Madagascar's first canonized saint.

saints.name: Bl. Victoire Rasoamanarivo
saints.story: A Merina noblewoman who became Catholic as a young woman and endured a difficult marriage with patience. When the missionaries were expelled, she led and protected the Catholic community, opening churches and encouraging the faithful. She was beatified in Antananarivo in 1989.

saints.name: Bl. Lucien Botovasoa
saints.story: A teacher, husband and father of eight, and a Franciscan tertiary in Vohipeno. During the uprising of 1947 he was killed, forgiving his executioners and praying for them. He was beatified in 2018 as a martyr.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (Andohalo)
cathedrals.story: Standing on a hill in the old upper city, this stone cathedral with twin towers was built in the late nineteenth century. It holds the tomb of Bl. Victoire Rasoamanarivo and is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Antananarivo.

cathedrals.name: Akamasoa
cathedrals.story: Not a cathedral but a beloved place of Catholic charity: the 'City of Friendship' founded in 1989 by Fr. Pedro Opeka, a Vincentian priest, on a rubbish dump. Thousands of families now live there with homes, schools and work. Pope Francis visited in 2019.

prayerIntention: For Madagascar, that its people may be freed from poverty and hunger, that its leaders may serve with justice, and that its joyful Church may keep growing in holiness.

name: Malawi
history:
Catholic mission in Malawi began in 1889 when the Missionaries of Africa (White Fathers) arrived, though their first attempt was short-lived. In 1901 the Montfort Missionaries settled in the south at Nzama, and in 1902 the White Fathers returned to establish a mission at Mua in the central region. From these beginnings the Church spread through villages, building schools, hospitals and leprosy centres.

Under colonial rule and after independence in 1964, Catholics grew in number and in the formation of local priests and sisters. Under the long one-party rule of Hastings Banda, freedom was severely restricted. In 1992 the Catholic bishops issued a Lenten pastoral letter, 'Living Our Faith', read in every parish, criticizing injustice and repression. It was a turning point that helped open the way to multiparty democracy in 1994.

Today the Church in Malawi is vibrant, with full churches, many vocations and an extensive network of schools and health facilities. It continues to speak for the poor in a nation facing poverty, food insecurity, climate disasters and corruption, and it remains a respected voice for justice.

cathedrals.name: Maula Cathedral (Our Lady Queen of Africa)
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Lilongwe, dedicated to Mary, Queen of Africa, is the centre of Catholic life in the capital. It hosts great national celebrations, ordinations and Masses for the nation.

cathedrals.name: Mua Mission
cathedrals.story: Founded by the White Fathers in 1902, Mua is one of the oldest Catholic missions in Malawi. It is also known for the KuNgoni Centre of Culture and Art, where the Church has helped preserve and celebrate the traditions of the Chewa, Ngoni and Yao peoples through woodcarving, museum work and dialogue between faith and culture.

prayerIntention: For Malawi, the warm heart of Africa, that its people may be freed from hunger and poverty, that its leaders may serve with honesty, and that the Church may continue to speak for justice.

name: Malaysia
history:
The Catholic faith reached the Malay Peninsula with the Portuguese capture of Malacca in 1511. Churches and a diocese followed, and St Francis Xavier passed through Malacca several times in the 1540s and 1550s on his journeys to the Indies and Japan. When the Dutch took Malacca in 1641, Catholic worship was suppressed for a time, yet a small Portuguese-Eurasian community kept the faith alive, and it remains there today.

In the nineteenth century the Paris Foreign Missions Society (MEP) rebuilt the Church across the peninsula, and from 1808 the College General in Penang trained priests for much of Asia, including future martyrs of Vietnam and China. Missionaries also served in Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo, where many indigenous peoples embraced the faith; today a large share of Malaysian Catholics live there.

The Church in Malaysia is diverse — Chinese, Indian, indigenous, Eurasian and many migrant workers from the Philippines and elsewhere. It lives in a Muslim-majority country where Islam is the religion of the federation and evangelising Muslims is legally restricted, and disputes such as the long court case over Christians' use of the word 'Allah' in Malay have been painful. Even so, parishes are full, and the Church serves through schools, social work and interfaith dialogue.

saints.name: St Francis Xavier
saints.story: The great Jesuit missionary visited Malacca several times between 1545 and 1552, preaching, catechising and caring for the sick. It was in Malacca that he met the Japanese Anjirō, which led to his mission to Japan. After his death his body rested for a time in Malacca's Church of Our Lady on the Hill (now St Paul's Church) before being carried to Goa.

cathedrals.name: St Peter's Church
cathedrals.story: Built in 1710 under Dutch rule, when Catholics were finally permitted to worship, St Peter's is the oldest functioning Catholic church in Malaysia. Its simple façade blends Portuguese and Dutch styles. It is beloved by the Portuguese-Eurasian community, and its Holy Week and Good Friday celebrations draw large crowds.

cathedrals.name: Church of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: The Catholic community of Penang traces its roots to Eurasian Catholics who arrived from Kedah with the founding of the settlement in 1786. The present church dates from the mid-nineteenth century and served for many years as the cathedral of the Diocese of Penang. Its classical white façade is a landmark of historic George Town, a UNESCO World Heritage city.

cathedrals.name: St John's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: First built in 1883 as a modest church, St John's was enlarged in Gothic Revival style and became the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Kuala Lumpur. Its white walls and pointed arches stand close to the city centre, and it serves a congregation celebrating Mass in English, Malay, Tamil and Chinese.

prayerIntention: For Malaysia, that its many peoples may live together in justice, respect and freedom of faith, and that the Church may be a humble and joyful witness of Christ's love.

name: Maldives
catholicPresence: No public Catholic community; a few foreign workers (approx. <0.1%)
history:
The Maldives is constitutionally an Islamic state, and citizenship is tied to the Muslim faith. The islands embraced Islam in the twelfth century, and there is no recorded indigenous Catholic community and no church building in the country, and the public practice of other religions is not permitted. Bringing religious materials for anything beyond personal use is also restricted.

Catholics in the Maldives today are almost entirely foreign workers — teachers, nurses, hotel and construction staff, many from India, Sri Lanka and the Philippines. They pray quietly and privately, often without regular access to the sacraments, and some travel abroad when they can, often to Sri Lanka or India, to attend Mass and receive the sacraments. Many live far from their families for years, sending their earnings home.

This is a hidden and humble presence. The Church honours these believers, who keep the faith far from home, and prays for them, for the Maldivian people, and for genuine freedom of conscience.
prayerIntention: For the people of the Maldives, threatened by the rising seas, and for the Catholic workers who pray there in silence, that they may be sustained by God's grace and that freedom of conscience may grow.

name: Mali
history:
The Catholic mission in Mali began at the end of the nineteenth century, during French colonial expansion. Spiritan (Holy Ghost) Fathers founded a mission at Kita in 1888, and the Missionaries of Africa (White Fathers) soon established communities along the Niger, including at Ségou and Bamako. The missionaries opened schools and clinics, and a small but committed African Church grew, especially among the Bambara, Dogon and Bobo peoples.

In a country that is overwhelmingly Muslim, Catholics have long lived in friendship with their neighbours, and Malian Islam has traditionally been tolerant. Since 2012, however, jihadist insurgencies in the north and centre have brought violence, displacement and fear; Christians have fled some regions, and a Colombian missionary sister, Gloria Cecilia Narváez, was held hostage from 2017 to 2021.

The Church in Mali today is small but respected, known for its schools, health centres and peace work. In 2017 Archbishop Jean Zerbo of Bamako, a peacemaker during the crisis, became Mali's first cardinal. The annual national pilgrimage to Our Lady of Kita gathers thousands of faithful.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1930s in the heart of Bamako, the Cathédrale du Sacré-Cœur is the seat of the Archdiocese of Bamako and one of the oldest Catholic buildings in the capital. Its brick façade stands amid the bustle of the city's markets. It is a meeting place for Catholics from all regions of Mali and for the great celebrations of the national Church.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Kita
cathedrals.story: Kita, the cradle of the Catholic mission in Mali, is home to the national Marian shrine. Each year thousands of pilgrims, many walking for days, gather there to honour Our Lady and entrust Mali to her care. The pilgrimage is the largest Catholic gathering in the country and a moving sign of faith in a land of many trials.

prayerIntention: For Mali, that peace may return to its north and centre, that the displaced may come home in safety, and that Christians and Muslims may continue to live together as brothers and sisters.

name: Malta
history:
Malta treasures its place in the Acts of the Apostles: around AD 60 St Paul was shipwrecked on the island on his way to Rome, was welcomed with 'unusual kindness', and healed the father of Publius, the island's chief man, whom tradition honours as Malta's first bishop. Christian catacombs at Rabat bear witness to the early Church. Under Arab rule from 870, Christianity declined, and it was restored after the Norman conquest of 1091.

In 1530 the islands were given to the Knights of St John, who withstood the Ottoman Great Siege of 1565 and built Valletta, filling it with churches and art. French occupation in 1798 and British rule from 1800 followed, but Maltese Catholic identity remained strong, expressed in parish life, village feasts (festi) and devotion to Mary and St Paul.

In recent decades Malta has become more secular: divorce was introduced after a 2011 referendum, and abuse cases have wounded trust, as they have elsewhere. Yet the faith remains woven into Maltese culture. Malta has given the Church St George Preca and many missionaries, and Archbishop Charles Scicluna has served as a leading Vatican investigator of abuse cases.

patronSaints.name: St Paul the Apostle (Feast of St Paul's Shipwreck)

saints.name: St George Preca
saints.story: A priest from Valletta, Dun Ġorġ founded the Society of Christian Doctrine (M.U.S.E.U.M.) in 1907, forming lay men and women to teach the catechism. He was at first misunderstood and briefly ordered to close his work, but obeyed with humility. Beloved for his holiness, he was canonised in 2007 as Malta's first saint.

saints.name: Bl. Maria Adeodata Pisani
saints.story: Born in Naples to a Maltese noble family, she moved to Malta and entered the Benedictine monastery of St Peter in Mdina. She served as novice mistress and abbess, known for her gentleness, prayer and care for the poor at the monastery gate. She was beatified by Pope John Paul II in Malta in 2001.

saints.name: Bl. Ignatius Falzon
saints.story: A lawyer's son who completed theological studies but never sought priesthood, Nazju Falzon spent his life teaching the catechism in Valletta, especially to the British soldiers and sailors stationed in Malta. Many came to the faith through his patient care. He was beatified in Malta in 2001.

cathedrals.name: St John's Co-Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built by the Knights of St John between 1573 and 1577 to designs by Girolamo Cassar, its plain exterior hides a dazzling Baroque interior painted by Mattia Preti. The floor is paved with marble tombstones of knights, and the oratory holds Caravaggio's 'The Beheading of St John the Baptist', the only work he signed.

cathedrals.name: St Paul's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Tradition places the cathedral on the site of Publius' house, where St Paul healed his father. After the medieval cathedral was damaged in the 1693 earthquake, Lorenzo Gafà rebuilt it in Baroque style, completed in 1702. Its dome crowns the silent walled city of Mdina, and it remains the seat of the Archbishop of Malta.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Ta' Pinu
cathedrals.story: In 1883 Karmni Grima heard Our Lady's voice at a small chapel in the Gozitan countryside, and many healings were attributed to her intercession. The present Romanesque-style basilica was completed in 1931 around the old chapel. Walls filled with votive offerings testify to gratitude, and Pope John Paul II prayed here in 1990.

cathedrals.name: Rotunda of St Mary (Mosta Dome)
cathedrals.story: Built by parishioners between 1833 and 1860, with a dome among the largest in Europe, the Rotunda was inspired by Rome's Pantheon. On 9 April 1942, a German bomb pierced the dome during a service and fell among the faithful without exploding. A replica of the bomb is kept in the church as a sign of gratitude.

prayerIntention: For Malta, the island of St Paul, that its people may keep alive the faith and hospitality first shown to the Apostle, and welcome every stranger who comes to its shores.

name: Marshall Islands
history:
Protestant missionaries from Hawaii brought Christianity to the Marshall Islands in the 1850s, and most Marshallese today belong to Protestant churches. Catholic missionaries arrived during German colonial rule at the end of the nineteenth century, when the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart (MSC) opened a mission based at Jaluit. Their work was disrupted by the First World War and Japanese rule.

After the Second World War, the islands came under United States administration, and American Jesuits served the Catholic communities as part of the mission to the Caroline and Marshall Islands. This era also brought deep suffering: from 1946 to 1958 the United States conducted nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak, displacing communities and leaving lasting harm to health and land. The Church has stood with Marshallese seeking justice.

In 1993 the Apostolic Prefecture of the Marshall Islands was established, entrusted again to the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart. The Catholic community is small but lively, known especially for its schools. Today it shares the anxiety of a nation of low-lying atolls threatened by rising seas, and many Marshallese now live abroad.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: The principal Catholic church of the Marshall Islands and the seat of the Apostolic Prefecture stands on Majuro atoll beside Assumption School. It is the heart of Catholic life in the islands, where Mass is celebrated in Marshallese and English and where families gather for feasts, baptisms and community events.

prayerIntention: For the Marshall Islands, wounded by nuclear testing and threatened by rising seas, that its people may receive justice and care, and that the nations may protect their islands and their future.

name: Mauritania
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic community of foreigners (approx. <0.2%)
history:
Mauritania is an Islamic Republic, and virtually all its citizens are Muslim. The Catholic presence dates from the colonial period, when French Catholics and missionaries lived in the territory. In 1965, soon after independence, the Holy See established the Diocese of Nouakchott, which covers the whole country.

Today the Catholic community is made up of migrants from sub-Saharan Africa, many on their way north, along with expatriates from Europe and elsewhere. There are only a handful of parishes, in Nouakchott, Nouadhibou, Rosso, Atar and a few other towns. Proselytism among Muslims is forbidden, and apostasy from Islam is legally punishable, so the Church lives a quiet presence of prayer and service rather than public mission.

Through Caritas Mauritanie and the work of religious sisters, the Church serves the poor, migrants and people living with disabilities, without regard to religion. It is a small and humble Church, offering friendship and help in the desert, and is respected for its works of charity.

cathedrals.name: St Joseph's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The Cathédrale Saint-Joseph is the seat of the Diocese of Nouakchott, the only Catholic diocese in Mauritania. It is a simple church that gathers a congregation of many nationalities, especially African migrants and students. Here they find a spiritual home, a community, and the sacraments far from their own countries.

prayerIntention: For Mauritania, that its people may be blessed with peace and prosperity, that migrants passing through may be treated with dignity, and that the small Church may continue to serve with love.

name: Mauritius
history:
Catholicism came to Mauritius with French settlement in the eighteenth century. Vincentian (Lazarist) priests arrived in 1722, and the colony, then called Île de France, was organised around a plantation economy built on the forced labour of enslaved Africans and Malagasy. The Church ministered to colonists, yet for a long time it did too little for the enslaved — a painful truth of its history.

After British conquest in 1810 the Catholic Church remained the faith of most Franco-Mauritians and Creoles. Slavery was abolished in 1835, and in 1841 the Spiritan priest Jacques-Désiré Laval arrived. He devoted himself to the freed slaves and the poor, catechising tens of thousands and training lay leaders. He became known as the 'Apostle of Mauritius', and his tomb in Sainte-Croix is a place of pilgrimage for people of every faith.

Today Mauritius is a multi-religious nation, with a Hindu majority and large Muslim and Christian communities. Catholics, many of them Creole, are deeply involved in education and social work. Cardinal Jean Margéot (1916–2009) was the first Mauritian cardinal, and Pope Francis celebrated Mass in Port Louis in 2019, honouring Père Laval's legacy.

saints.name: Bl. Jacques-Désiré Laval
saints.story: A French doctor who became a priest, he joined the Spiritans and arrived in Mauritius in 1841. Living simply among the freed slaves and the poor, he taught the faith, formed lay catechists and cared for the sick. He was the first person beatified by Pope John Paul II, in 1979; his feast on September 9 draws huge crowds.

cathedrals.name: St Louis Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Diocese of Port-Louis stands on a site used for Catholic worship since the eighteenth century. The present building, rebuilt in the twentieth century, has a sober twin-towered façade overlooking a quiet square in the old city. It is the mother church of Mauritian Catholics and the place of the diocese's great celebrations.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Père Laval
cathedrals.story: Bl. Jacques-Désiré Laval rests in the church of Sainte-Croix, where his tomb, with a recumbent effigy, is visited daily by Christians, Hindus and Muslims who come to pray for healing and help. Around his feast on September 9, tens of thousands of pilgrims walk through the night to Sainte-Croix.

cathedrals.name: Marie Reine de la Paix
cathedrals.story: This open-air Marian monument on the slopes above Port Louis, with a statue of Mary, Queen of Peace, overlooks the capital and the harbour. Its terraces have hosted the island's largest gatherings, including the Masses of Pope John Paul II in 1989 and Pope Francis in 2019.

prayerIntention: For Mauritius, that its many cultures and religions may continue to live in harmony, that the poor may be lifted up, and that the example of Père Laval may inspire its people.

name: Mexico
history:
The faith came to Mexico with the Spanish conquest of 1519–1521, an event of great violence and devastation for the indigenous peoples. Franciscans arrived in 1524, followed by Dominicans, Augustinians and Jesuits. Some missionaries — such as Bartolomé de las Casas and Vasco de Quiroga — defended indigenous dignity against abuse. In 1531, Our Lady appeared to the Nahua layman Juan Diego at Tepeyac, leaving her image on his tilma; Our Lady of Guadalupe became the heart of Mexican faith.

After independence, which was begun in 1810 by the priest Miguel Hidalgo, conflicts between Church and state grew. The 1917 Constitution severely restricted the Church, and in 1926 the persecution under President Plutarco Elías Calles provoked the Cristero War. Priests and lay faithful were executed, many crying '¡Viva Cristo Rey!' as they died. Restrictions eased gradually, and full legal recognition came in 1992.

Mexico today has one of the largest Catholic populations in the world, and popular devotion is vibrant. The Church also faces secularisation, the growth of other churches, abuse scandals, and terrible violence linked to organised crime, in which priests and catechists have been murdered.

saints.name: St Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin
saints.story: A humble Nahua layman, Juan Diego saw the Virgin Mary at Tepeyac in December 1531.
