When the bishop asked for a sign, roses bloomed in winter, and when he opened his tilma before the bishop, the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe appeared on it. He spent his last years caring for her chapel. He was canonised in 2002.

saints.name: St Philip of Jesus
saints.story: Born in Mexico City, Felipe de las Casas was a restless young man who became a Franciscan. On his way back to Mexico for ordination, his ship was blown to Japan, where he was arrested with other Christians. He was crucified at Nagasaki in 1597 with St Paul Miki and companions, the first Mexican saint.

saints.name: St Cristóbal Magallanes and Companions
saints.story: A parish priest in Jalisco, Cristóbal Magallanes founded schools and a seminary in hiding during the persecution. Arrested on his way to celebrate Mass, he gave his executioners absolution before being shot in 1927. He and twenty-four other martyrs of the Cristero period, mostly priests, were canonised in 2000.

saints.name: St José Sánchez del Río
saints.story: A fourteen-year-old boy who joined the Cristeros, José was captured and tortured to make him renounce his faith. Forced to walk on flayed feet to the cemetery, he kept crying out '¡Viva Cristo Rey!' and was killed there. He was canonised by Pope Francis in 2016.

saints.name: Bl. Miguel Agustín Pro
saints.story: A joyful Jesuit priest, Miguel Pro ministered in secret in Mexico City during the persecution, using disguises to bring the sacraments. Falsely accused in a plot against a former president, he was executed without trial in 1927. Arms outstretched, he cried 'Viva Cristo Rey!' He was beatified in 1988.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe
cathedrals.story: At the foot of the hill of Tepeyac, the circular modern basilica completed in 1976 enshrines Juan Diego's tilma with the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe. Beside it stands the older baroque basilica of 1709. Millions of pilgrims come every year, many on their knees, especially around December 12, making it one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: Built from 1573 to 1813 on the Zócalo, near the ruins of the great Aztec temple, it is the largest cathedral in the Americas. Its long construction blends Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical styles, with the gilded Altar of the Kings at its heart. It has endured earthquakes and sinking ground, and remains the symbol of Mexican Catholicism.

cathedrals.name: Puebla Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception was consecrated in 1649 under Bishop Juan de Palafox. Its grey stone towers are among the tallest in Mexico, and its interior is rich with onyx, marble and gilded altars. It dominates the historic centre of Puebla, a UNESCO World Heritage city.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of San Juan de los Lagos
cathedrals.city: San Juan de los Lagos, Jalisco
cathedrals.story: Home to a small, beloved image of the Virgin venerated since the sixteenth century, this basilica in the highlands of Jalisco is one of Mexico's most visited shrines after Guadalupe. Its baroque church, built in the eighteenth century, welcomes millions of pilgrims each year, many arriving on foot, especially around Candlemas in early February.

prayerIntention: For Mexico, beloved of Our Lady of Guadalupe, that violence may cease, that the poor, migrants and indigenous peoples may be protected, and that its deep faith may bear fruit in justice and peace.

name: Micronesia
history:
Catholic missions came to the Caroline Islands under Spanish rule, when Spanish Capuchins arrived in Yap and Pohnpei in the 1880s. After Spain sold the islands to Germany in 1899, German Capuchins continued the work, and when Japan took control after the First World War, Spanish Jesuits came in 1921. The Second World War brought great suffering: missionaries were restricted and churches destroyed.

After the war, under United States administration, American Jesuits took over the mission, building schools that formed many of the islands' leaders, such as Xavier High School in Chuuk. Catholicism spread especially in Chuuk, Pohnpei and Yap, alongside Protestant churches established by earlier missionaries from New England and Hawaii.

In 1979 the Diocese of the Caroline Islands was established, with its seat in Chuuk, serving both Micronesia and Palau. Today the Church is woven into island life, with lively parishes, catechists and lay leaders across scattered atolls. It also faces emigration, poverty and the threat of rising seas to low-lying islands.

cathedrals.name: Immaculate Heart of Mary Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The seat of the Diocese of the Caroline Islands stands on Weno, the main island of Chuuk Lagoon. It is the mother church of Catholics in Micronesia and Palau, where the bishop gathers clergy and faithful from islands spread across thousands of kilometres of ocean.

cathedrals.name: Catholic Mission Bell Tower
cathedrals.story: The stone bell tower is the last remnant of a church built by German Capuchin missionaries early in the twentieth century. The church was destroyed during the Second World War, but the tower survived, and it remains a beloved landmark of Kolonia beside the modern Catholic church, a reminder of the mission's endurance.

prayerIntention: For Micronesia, that its islands may be protected from rising seas, that its families may flourish, and that the Church may continue to be a source of faith and unity across the ocean.

name: Moldova
history:
Moldova is an overwhelmingly Orthodox country, and its Catholic community has always been small. Catholics in the region historically included Poles, Germans, Hungarians, Italians and others who settled in Bessarabia, especially in the nineteenth century under Russian rule, when the area belonged to the Diocese of Tiraspol, centred in Saratov.

Under Soviet rule the Church was severely persecuted. Churches were closed or turned to other uses, priests were deported or imprisoned, and Catholics could practise only in secret. A few faithful families kept the faith alive through prayer at home and the occasional visit of a priest.

After Moldova's independence in 1991, the Church slowly revived. An apostolic administration was set up in 1993, and in 2001 Pope John Paul II established the Diocese of Chișinău, covering the whole country, with Bishop Anton Coșa as its first bishop. Today the small community, with parishes in several towns and active social work through Caritas, lives in good relations with the Orthodox majority and serves the poor in one of Europe's poorest nations, including refugees from the war in neighbouring Ukraine.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Divine Providence
cathedrals.story: Built in the nineteenth century for the city's Catholic community, the church suffered during the Soviet period, when Catholic worship was suppressed. Returned to the Church after independence and restored, it became the cathedral of the Diocese of Chișinău. It is the heart of Moldova's small Catholic community, celebrating Mass in Romanian, Russian and other languages.

prayerIntention: For Moldova, that its people may live in peace and dignity, that its young may find hope at home, and that Catholics and Orthodox may witness together to Christ.

name: Monaco
catholicPresence: Majority Catholic (approx. 85–90%); Catholicism is the state religion
history:
Christianity reached the coast of Monaco in late antiquity. According to tradition, the body of St Devota, a young Christian martyred in Corsica around 304, was carried by boat and guided by a dove to the little valley of Les Gaumates, where a chapel was built in her honour. She became the beloved patroness of the Principality.

After the Grimaldi family took the Rock in 1297, Monaco developed as a small Catholic principality. For centuries it belonged to the Diocese of Nice, until Pope Leo XIII established a separate diocese in 1887; it became an archdiocese directly subject to the Holy See in 1981. The constitution names Catholicism as the religion of the State, and the Prince and his family take part in the great feasts.

Today the Church accompanies residents from many nations and a large population of workers. Like much of Western Europe, it faces secularisation, and public debates on questions such as abortion law have brought the Church's moral teaching into the life of the Principality. The feast of St Devota on January 27, with the burning of a boat, remains a moving moment of shared identity.

saints.name: St Devota
saints.story: A young Christian of Corsica, Devota was martyred during the persecution of Diocletian. Tradition says her body was placed in a boat to be taken to Africa, but a storm drove it to Monaco, guided by a dove. Each January a boat is burned in her honour, recalling an attempt to steal her relics.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Saint Nicholas Cathedral)
cathedrals.story: Built from 1875 in white stone in Romanesque-Byzantine style, on the site of a thirteenth-century church dedicated to St Nicholas, the cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Monaco. It holds tombs of the princes, including Prince Rainier III and Princess Grace, and a fine sixteenth-century altarpiece by Louis Bréa.

cathedrals.name: Church of Sainte-Dévote
cathedrals.story: Nestled in a small valley near the harbour where tradition says St Devota's body came to shore, this church, rebuilt in the nineteenth century, keeps the memory of the Principality's patroness. It is the starting point of the January celebrations in her honour, and the place where Princess Grace laid her wedding bouquet in 1956.

prayerIntention: For Monaco, that those blessed with wealth may be generous to the poor of the world, and that the faith of St Devota may remain alive in its families.

name: Mongolia
history:
Christianity was present among the Mongols long ago through the Church of the East, and several medieval Mongol princesses and tribes were Christian. In the thirteenth century Franciscan envoys such as John of Plano Carpini and William of Rubruck visited the Mongol court, and John of Montecorvino became archbishop in Khanbaliq (Beijing) under Mongol rule. These communities later disappeared.

Under communist rule from 1924, all religion was repressed and no Christian community could exist openly. When Mongolia embraced democracy, it established diplomatic relations with the Holy See in 1992, and that year three missionaries of the Congregation of the Immaculate Heart of Mary (CICM), including Fr Wenceslao Padilla, arrived to begin the Church again from nothing.

Today the Church in Mongolia is very young and small, about 1,500 faithful in a handful of parishes, served by missionaries from many countries, with its first Mongolian priests ordained since 2016. It is known for its care of street children, the elderly and the poor. In 2022 Bishop Giorgio Marengo became the youngest cardinal, and Pope Francis visited in 2023, encouraging this tiny flock.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 2002, ten years after the mission began, the cathedral's round design echoes the shape of the traditional Mongolian ger (yurt). It is the seat of the Apostolic Prefecture of Ulaanbaatar and the heart of Mongolia's young Church. Pope Francis met the bishops, clergy and faithful here during his 2023 visit.

prayerIntention: For Mongolia, that its people may grow in peace and prosperity, and that the small Church born again in the steppe may grow in faith, joy and service.

name: Montenegro
history:
Christianity came early to the Adriatic coast of present-day Montenegro, in the Roman province of Dalmatia. The Bay of Kotor, with its old Latin-rite city of Kotor, has had a bishop since early Christian times, and in 809 the relics of the martyr St Tryphon were brought there. The Archdiocese of Bar, on the southern coast, became a metropolitan see in the eleventh century.

Through centuries of Venetian and Ottoman rule, Catholics, mostly Croats and Albanians, lived alongside an Orthodox majority. The coast produced sailors, priests and saints, and its many churches and chapels testify to a deep devotion to Mary and the saints. Under communist Yugoslavia the Church faced restrictions, and during the wars of the 1990s Catholics, like others, suffered tension and emigration.

Since independence in 2006, Montenegro has recognised the Church through a Basic Agreement with the Holy See signed in 2011. Today Catholics are a small but historic community, served by the Archdiocese of Bar and the Diocese of Kotor, and its ancient churches welcome many pilgrims and visitors.

saints.name: St Leopold Mandić
saints.story: Born in Herceg Novi on the Bay of Kotor, Bogdan Mandić became a Capuchin friar. Small and frail, he spent decades in a tiny confessional in Padua, hearing confessions for many hours each day with great mercy. He longed for unity between Catholic and Orthodox Christians. He was canonised in 1983.

saints.name: Bl. Osanna of Cattaro
saints.story: Born to an Orthodox shepherd family near Kotor, Katarina Kosić entered the Catholic Church and became a Dominican tertiary. She lived for decades as an anchoress walled in a cell beside a church in Kotor, praying and counselling visitors. Her prayers were credited with protecting the city during sieges. She was beatified in 1927.

saints.name: St Tryphon
saints.story: A young martyr from Asia Minor who died during the persecution of Decius, Tryphon is not Montenegrin by birth, but his relics have rested in Kotor since 809. He is the patron of Kotor, and his cathedral is the city's spiritual heart. His feast on February 3 is celebrated with ancient traditions.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St Tryphon
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1166, this Romanesque cathedral with two bell towers stands in the medieval heart of Kotor. Rebuilt after earthquakes, including in 1667 and 1979, it keeps frescoes from the fourteenth century and a treasury with the relics of St Tryphon. It is the seat of the Diocese of Kotor and a symbol of the city.

cathedrals.name: Our Lady of the Rocks (Gospa od Škrpjela)
cathedrals.story: According to tradition, sailors found an icon of Mary on a rock in the bay in 1452 and began to build up an islet by sinking stones and ships there. A church was built on the man-made island and rebuilt in the seventeenth century. Every July locals still row out at sunset to throw stones into the sea, continuing the tradition.

prayerIntention: For Montenegro, that its peoples and churches may live together in respect and peace, and that the ancient faith of its coast may be renewed in the young.

name: Morocco
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic community, mostly foreigners (approx. <0.1%)
history:
In Roman times, North Africa was a flourishing Christian land, and present-day Morocco had Christian communities in cities like Tingis (Tangier). There St Marcellus the Centurion was martyred around 298 for refusing to serve in the army after professing his faith. These ancient communities faded after the Arab conquest.

In 1220, five Franciscan friars sent by St Francis of Assisi preached in Marrakesh and were martyred; their witness inspired a young Portuguese canon to become a Franciscan — St Anthony of Padua. Over the centuries, Franciscans and Trinitarians served Christian captives in Morocco. During the French and Spanish protectorates in the twentieth century, a large European Catholic population built churches in many cities, but most left after independence in 1956.

Today the Church in Morocco is small but young and vibrant, made up largely of students and migrants from sub-Saharan Africa alongside Europeans. Proselytism is forbidden, and Moroccan converts face pressure. The Church serves migrants and the poor and is committed to dialogue with Muslims; Pope John Paul II spoke to Muslim youth in Casablanca in 1985, and Pope Francis visited Rabat in 2019.

saints.name: St Marcellus the Centurion
saints.story: A Roman centurion stationed in Tingis (Tangier), Marcellus threw down his military belt during a festival for the emperor's birthday, declaring that as a soldier of Christ he could not take part in pagan rites. He was tried and executed in Tangier. His feast is October 30.

saints.name: Sts Berard and Companions (Franciscan Protomartyrs)
saints.story: Five friars — Berard, Peter, Otho, Accursius and Adjutus — were sent by St Francis to preach to the Muslims. They were beheaded in Marrakesh in 1220. When their relics reached Coimbra, they moved a young Augustinian canon to join the Franciscans; he became St Anthony of Padua. Their feast is January 16.

saints.name: St Charles de Foucauld
saints.story: A French officer who had lost his faith, Charles explored Morocco in 1883–1884 disguised as a Jew. The prayer of Muslims he met stirred his soul and led to his conversion. He became a hermit priest in the Sahara, living as a 'universal brother'. He was canonised in 2022.

cathedrals.name: St Peter's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in the early twentieth century during the French protectorate, the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Rabat is a striking white Art Deco building with two tall towers, standing on Place du Golan in the city centre. Today it welcomes a congregation of many nations, especially African students and migrants.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1961, this modernist cathedral of the Archdiocese of Tangier features a slender tower and bold geometric forms. It serves the Catholic community of northern Morocco, which has roots in the long Spanish presence in the region, and today welcomes migrants who live in the city's neighbourhoods.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Church (Sacré-Cœur)
cathedrals.story: Designed by Paul Tournon and completed in 1930, this white church, popularly called a cathedral, blends Gothic Revival with Moroccan Art Deco motifs. When much of the European population left after independence, it ceased to be used for worship and became a cultural venue, but it remains one of Casablanca's most admired buildings.

prayerIntention: For Morocco, that Christians and Muslims may live in friendship and mutual respect, and that migrants crossing its land may be welcomed with dignity.

name: Mozambique
history:
Catholic presence in Mozambique began with Portuguese sailors and traders after Vasco da Gama's voyage of 1498. Dominicans and Jesuits came in the sixteenth century; the Jesuit Gonçalo da Silveira baptised the ruler of Mwenemutapa in 1561 and was killed soon after. For centuries the Church was small and tied to coastal trading posts.

In the colonial period, especially under the 1940 Concordat, the Church was closely tied to the Portuguese state, which compromised its witness. Some bishops and missionaries spoke out against injustice, and in 1973 missionaries helped reveal the Wiriyamu massacre carried out by colonial forces. After independence in 1975, the Marxist FRELIMO government nationalised schools and church property and restricted religious life.

The Church played a crucial role in ending the civil war (1977–1992): the Community of Sant'Egidio and Archbishop Jaime Gonçalves of Beira mediated the peace accords signed in Rome in 1992. Today the Church is vibrant and growing. It faces severe trials, especially the violent insurgency in Cabo Delgado since 2017, cyclones and poverty. Pope Francis visited Maputo in 2019.

saints.name: Gonçalo da Silveira
saints.story: A Portuguese Jesuit, he travelled up the Zambezi to the court of Mwenemutapa, where he baptised the king and many of his household. Accused by rivals of witchcraft and espionage, he was strangled in 1561. He is honoured as the first martyr of southern Africa, though he has not been beatified.

saints.name: Martyrs of Guiúa
saints.story: During the civil war, in March 1992, catechists and their families who were living and training at the Guiúa Catechetical Centre near Inhambane were killed by armed men. They are remembered as faithful servants of the Gospel in a time of terror. Their cause for beatification has been opened.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1944 in white concrete, with a tall, slender bell tower, this cathedral rises over the centre of Maputo. Its modern lines and stained glass make it a landmark of the city. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Maputo and the site of the nation's great celebrations.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of the Rosary
cathedrals.story: Built in the early twentieth century using stones from the ruined Portuguese fort of São Caetano at Sofala, the Gothic-style cathedral is the seat of the Archdiocese of Beira. It was the church of Archbishop Jaime Gonçalves, a peacemaker in the civil war, and stands in a city often struck by cyclones.

cathedrals.name: Chapel of Our Lady of the Bulwark
cathedrals.story: Built by the Portuguese in 1522 at the tip of the island beside the Fort of São Sebastião, this small chapel is considered the oldest surviving European building in the Southern Hemisphere. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Island of Mozambique, a place of great historic and spiritual meaning.

prayerIntention: For Mozambique, that peace may come to Cabo Delgado, that the displaced may return home, and that the people may recover from war, cyclones and poverty in hope.

name: Myanmar
history:
Catholic contact with Burma began in the sixteenth century through Portuguese traders and soldiers. Descendants of Portuguese captives settled by Burmese kings along the Mu River, the Bayingyi, have kept the faith for centuries. Barnabite missionaries arrived in the 1720s, followed in the nineteenth century by the Paris Foreign Missions Society and the Milan Foreign Missions (PIME), who brought the faith especially to the Karen, Kachin, Chin, Kayah and other ethnic peoples of the hills.

After independence in 1948, the Church grew among these peoples but suffered from civil conflicts. Missionaries were killed, including Bl. Mario Vergara and his catechist Bl. Isidore Ngei Ko Lat in 1950. After the 1962 military coup, Church schools and hospitals were nationalised, and in 1966 most foreign missionaries were expelled. The local Church, poor but faithful, carried on and produced many vocations.

In 2015 Archbishop Charles Maung Bo of Yangon became the country's first cardinal, and Pope Francis visited in 2017. Since the 2021 coup, Myanmar has been torn by civil war. Churches have been shelled, burned and occupied, especially in Kayah, Chin and Sagaing, and many Catholics are displaced. The Church continues to plead for peace and to stand with all who suffer, including the persecuted Rohingya.

saints.name: Bl. Isidore Ngei Ko Lat
saints.story: A young Karen catechist, Isidore helped the missionaries teach the faith and ran a small school. In 1950 he accompanied Fr Mario Vergara to plead for the release of a Catholic held by an armed group; both were killed and their bodies thrown into a river. Beatified in 2014, he is the first Burmese blessed.

saints.name: Bl. Mario Vergara
saints.story: An Italian priest of the PIME missionaries, he served among the Karenni and Karen peoples, building chapels and caring for the sick and orphans despite war and illness. He was killed with his catechist Isidore Ngei Ko Lat in 1950, a martyr for defending his flock. He was beatified in 2014.

saints.name: Bl. Clemente Vismara
saints.story: A PIME missionary and veteran of the First World War, Fr Vismara spent about sixty-five years in the remote mountains of eastern Burma around Kengtung. He founded villages, schools and orphanages and cared for thousands of children. He was known as 'the patriarch of Burma'. He was beatified in 2011.

saints.name: Bl. Paolo Manna
saints.story: An Italian PIME missionary, he served in eastern Burma from 1895 until ill health forced him to return to Italy in 1907. He then devoted his life to awakening missionary zeal in the whole Church and founded the Pontifical Missionary Union. He was beatified in 2001.

cathedrals.name: St Mary's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built between 1895 and 1899 to designs by the Dutch architect Joseph Cuypers, St Mary's is the largest cathedral in Myanmar. Its red-brick Gothic Revival exterior and brightly painted interior survived the 1930 earthquake and the Second World War. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Yangon and was visited by Pope Francis in 2017.

cathedrals.name: Our Lady of Lourdes Shrine
cathedrals.story: This national Marian shrine in the Bago region, with its grotto of Our Lady of Lourdes, is one of the most important pilgrimage places in Myanmar. Each year thousands of Catholics from all ethnic groups gather here, especially in February, to pray for healing, peace and their families.

cathedrals.name: Christ the King Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Diocese of Loikaw became a symbol of the suffering of Myanmar's Catholics after the 2021 coup. Thousands of displaced people sheltered in its compound, and in November 2023 soldiers occupied it, forcing the bishop, priests and refugees to leave. It remains a sign of a Church sharing its people's pain.

prayerIntention: For Myanmar, that the war may end, that the displaced may return home in safety, and that all its peoples may live together in justice, freedom and peace.

name: Namibia
history:
Lutheran missionaries were the first to bring Christianity to much of Namibia, and Lutherans remain the largest church. Catholic missionaries of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate arrived in Windhoek in 1896 during the German colonial period, later joined by other congregations, and missions spread to the north and south, including the Kavango region.

The colonial era brought terrible suffering. Between 1904 and 1908 German forces carried out a genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples, a wound that remains part of Namibia's memory. Under South African rule after the First World War, apartheid policies divided the land. The Catholic Church, together with other churches in the Council of Churches in Namibia, increasingly spoke out for justice, human rights and independence.

Since independence in 1990, the Church has been a respected partner in nation-building, especially through its schools, hospitals and work with people living with HIV. Today it serves a peaceful but unequal society, accompanying the poor, rural communities and young people, and works for reconciliation in a land still marked by its past.

cathedrals.name: St Mary's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in the early twentieth century during the German colonial period, this neo-Romanesque cathedral with twin towers stands near the centre of Windhoek. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Windhoek and the mother church of Catholics in Namibia, where the community gathers for its main celebrations.

prayerIntention: For Namibia, that wounds of the past may be healed through truth and reconciliation, and that all its people may share in its land and its blessings.

name: Nauru
history:
Protestant missionaries reached Nauru first, and the Catholic mission began in the early twentieth century under German rule, when the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart (MSC) arrived. Fr Alois Kayser MSC devoted decades of his life to the Nauruan people, learning their language and helping to put it into writing.

The twentieth century was hard for Nauru. Phosphate mining under colonial administrations stripped much of the island's interior. During the Second World War the Japanese occupied the island and deported many Nauruans to Chuuk, where many died. After independence in 1968, mining brought a brief time of wealth, followed by economic collapse and environmental devastation. In recent years an offshore detention centre for asylum seekers held by Australia has brought international concern.

The Catholic community today is one of the two main churches of the island, part of the Diocese of Tarawa and Nauru, centred in Kiribati. Despite its isolation and small size, it offers schools, worship and community life, and the faith remains a source of strength for Nauruans.

cathedrals.name: Christ the King Church
cathedrals.story: The principal Catholic church of Nauru, in the district of Arubo, is the centre of Catholic life on the island. Here the community gathers for Mass, feasts and celebrations, and it serves as a place of prayer and support for families on this small and isolated island.

prayerIntention: For Nauru, that its land and people may be healed, that those who seek refuge may be treated with dignity, and that its families may find hope for the future.

name: Nepal
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic minority (approx. 8,000 faithful, well under 0.1%)
history:
Catholic missionaries first reached the Kathmandu Valley in the early 18th century, when Italian Capuchins on their way to Tibet opened a small mission among the Newar kingdoms. Their presence was tolerated for some decades, but after the Gorkha conquest of the valley in 1769 the missionaries and their small flock of converts were forced to leave, settling across the border in British India.

For almost two centuries Nepal remained closed to Christian mission. In 1951 the American Jesuit Fr. Marshall Moran was invited to open St. Xavier's School at Godavari, and Catholic presence quietly returned through schools, clinics and works of mercy rather than open preaching. Conversion remained legally restricted, and Catholics lived their faith with great discretion. A Prefecture Apostolic was created in 1983 and raised to an Apostolic Vicariate in 2007.

After the end of the monarchy, Nepal became a secular republic, but challenges remain: in 2009 a bomb attack on the Church of the Assumption in Lalitpur killed worshippers, and anti-conversion laws still weigh on Christians. Today a small, mostly young Church, served by native and foreign priests and sisters, continues to serve the poor, the sick and earthquake survivors with quiet faithfulness.

saints.name: St. Teresa of Calcutta
saints.story: Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity came to Nepal and serve the destitute, the dying and the abandoned in Kathmandu. Though not Nepali, her sisters' humble care for those no one else wants is one of the most visible signs of Catholic love in the country, and she is warmly remembered by Nepali Catholics.

saints.name: Fr. Marshall D. Moran, SJ (missionary, not canonized)
saints.story: An American Jesuit who, invited by the Nepali government, founded St. Xavier's School at Godavari in 1951 and reopened Nepal to a Catholic presence after almost two centuries. Beloved for his friendship with Nepalis of every background, he spent the rest of his life in the country. He is not a canonized saint, but a true father of the Nepali Church.

cathedrals.name: Assumption Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The mother church of Nepal's Catholics, dedicated to Our Lady's Assumption and serving as the cathedral of the Apostolic Vicariate. In 2009 a bomb exploded during Mass here, killing worshippers; the community forgave and rebuilt. Simple in design, it is cherished as the gathering place for the country's small flock at Christmas, Easter and ordinations.

prayerIntention: For the people of Nepal, beneath the Himalayas, that they may live in peace and dignity, and that its small Catholic community may serve the poor freely and joyfully.

name: Netherlands
catholicPresence: Approx. 18–20% Catholic by registration, far fewer practising
history:
The faith came to the Low Countries through missionaries such as St. Servatius in Maastricht in the 4th century and, decisively, the Anglo-Saxon monk St. Willibrord, who became the first bishop of Utrecht around 695. His companion St. Boniface was martyred near Dokkum in 754. For centuries the Church shaped Dutch life, art and piety, giving rise to the Modern Devotion of Geert Groote and Thomas à Kempis' Imitation of Christ.

After the Reformation and the Dutch Revolt, public Catholic worship was forbidden. Catholics, though numerous, worshipped in hidden 'schuilkerken' such as Amsterdam's Our Lord in the Attic, and the Martyrs of Gorkum were hanged in 1572. Full freedom came only in the 19th century, and the hierarchy was restored in 1853. A vibrant Catholic 'pillar' of schools, unions and newspapers followed.

From the 1960s, rapid secularisation emptied many churches, and hundreds have since closed or been repurposed. The 2011 Deetman report revealed grave sexual abuse within Church institutions, for which the bishops apologised. Yet a smaller, more international Church endures, enriched by migrants, pilgrimages and witnesses like St. Titus Brandsma, canonized in 2022.

saints.name: St. Willibrord
saints.story: A Northumbrian monk who came to Frisia in 690 as missionary, was consecrated archbishop of the Frisians in Rome and made Utrecht his see. He founded the abbey of Echternach, where he is buried and still honoured by the dancing procession. He is the Apostle of the Netherlands and its patron.

saints.name: St. Lidwina of Schiedam
saints.story: After a skating accident as a teenager, Lidwina spent the rest of her life bedridden in great pain. She united her suffering with Christ, became known for prayer, visions and wise counsel, and drew visitors from far away. She is patron of the chronically ill and of ice skaters.

saints.name: St. Titus Brandsma
saints.story: A Frisian Carmelite friar, professor and journalist who defended press freedom and instructed Catholic newspapers to refuse Nazi propaganda. Arrested in 1942, he was sent to Dachau, where he comforted fellow prisoners and was killed by lethal injection. He was canonized by Pope Francis in 2022.

saints.name: Bl. Peerke Donders
saints.story: Born to a poor weaver's family in Tilburg, Petrus Donders became a missionary priest in Suriname, where he spent nearly three decades caring for lepers at Batavia, as well as enslaved people and Indigenous communities. He was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1982.

saints.name: The Martyrs of Gorkum
saints.story: Nineteen priests and religious, mostly Franciscans, seized in Gorinchem during the Dutch Revolt and hanged at Brielle after refusing to deny the Real Presence and papal authority. They were canonized in 1867, and a yearly pilgrimage still honours them at Brielle.

cathedrals.name: St. John's Cathedral (Sint-Janskathedraal)
cathedrals.story: The finest example of Brabantine Gothic in the Netherlands, built mainly in the 15th and 16th centuries. Its flying buttresses are crowded with whimsical stone figures, and it houses the miraculous statue of Our Lady of 's-Hertogenbosch (the Zoete Lieve Vrouw), a centre of devotion for centuries.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of St. Servatius
cathedrals.story: Built over the grave of St. Servatius, a 4th-century bishop, this Romanesque basilica is one of the oldest churches in the Netherlands. Its treasury holds the gilded reliquary chest of Servatius, and the septennial Heiligdomsvaart pilgrimage still processes his relics through the city.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady, Star of the Sea (Onze Lieve Vrouwebasiliek)
cathedrals.story: A sturdy Romanesque basilica with a fortress-like westwork, home to the beloved statue of Our Lady Star of the Sea (Sterre der Zee). Candles burn before her day and night, and many Maastricht families bring their joys and sorrows to her chapel.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Bavo
cathedrals.story: A grand cathedral built between 1895 and 1930 by architect Joseph Cuypers, blending Neo-Romanesque, Neo-Gothic and Art Nouveau elements. Its luminous stained glass, mosaics and treasury make it one of the most remarkable Catholic churches of modern Dutch architecture.

prayerIntention: For the Netherlands, that in a secular age its people may rediscover the living God, and that its Church, purified and humbled, may be a home of welcome and hope.

name: New Zealand
history:
Catholicism arrived in Aotearoa New Zealand in January 1838, when the French bishop Jean-Baptiste Pompallier landed at Hokianga with Marist missionaries and celebrated the first Mass at Totara Point. The Marists learned te reo Māori, printed prayers and catechisms at their press in Russell, and many Māori embraced the faith. At the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, Pompallier asked for an assurance of religious freedom, recorded as the so-called fourth article.

The New Zealand Wars and the arrival of large numbers of Irish settlers reshaped the Church through the 19th century. Religious women and men built schools, hospitals and orphanages; among them the French-born Suzanne Aubert, who founded the Daughters of Our Lady of Compassion and is now declared Venerable.

Today the Church is diverse, with Māori, Pākehā, Pacific, Filipino and other communities. It has faced painful truth: the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care documented serious abuse in Catholic institutions, and the bishops have apologised. Pompallier's remains were returned to Hokianga in 2002, a sign of the Church's deep roots in this land.

saints.name: Ven. Suzanne Aubert (Mother Mary Joseph)
saints.story: A French woman who came to New Zealand in 1860, learned te reo Māori and herbal medicine, and served Māori communities on the Whanganui River at Jerusalem (Hiruharama). She founded the Daughters of Our Lady of Compassion and cared for the sick, orphans and the poor in Wellington. She was declared Venerable in 2016.

saints.name: Bishop Jean-Baptiste Pompallier (missionary, not canonized)
saints.story: The first Catholic bishop of New Zealand, who arrived in 1838 and planted the Church among Māori in the north. Respected by many chiefs, he spoke for religious liberty at Waitangi. Though not a canonized saint, he is honoured as the founder of Catholicism in Aotearoa, and his remains rest at Motuti, Hokianga.

saints.name: St. Mary MacKillop
saints.story: Australia's first saint, foundress of the Sisters of St. Joseph of the Sacred Heart. Her sisters came to New Zealand in the 1880s, and she herself visited and established communities here, including in Arrowtown. The Josephites remain loved for their schools and care in rural and poor communities.

cathedrals.name: St Patrick's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Standing on a site used for Catholic worship since the 1840s, the present Gothic Revival cathedral dates from the early 20th century and was beautifully restored in 2007. It is the mother church of the Diocese of Auckland and a quiet sanctuary in the heart of the busy city.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral (Basilica of the Sacred Heart)
cathedrals.story: Opened in 1901 and affectionately called 'the Pro', this Palladian church with its classical portico stands near Parliament. It is the seat of the Archbishop of Wellington and was restored and strengthened after earthquakes, a gracious witness of faith in the capital.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament
cathedrals.story: Designed by Francis Petre and completed in 1905, this Renaissance-style cathedral with its great copper dome was among the finest buildings in the country. It was severely damaged in the 2011 earthquake and later deconstructed, and the diocese is building a new cathedral, a story of loss and hope.

prayerIntention: For Aotearoa New Zealand, that Māori and all peoples may walk together in justice and aroha, and that the Church may heal the wounded and proclaim Christ with humility.

name: Nicaragua
history:
Catholicism came with the Spanish conquest in the 1520s, and the Diocese of León was founded in the 1530s. Its second bishop, the Dominican Antonio de Valdivieso, defended the Indigenous peoples against the abuses of the colonial governors and was murdered in 1550 for this witness, remembered as one of the first bishops killed for justice in the Americas. Over the centuries a deep popular piety took root, above all love for the Immaculate Conception, celebrated each December with the joyful Gritería: 'Who causes so much joy? The Conception of Mary!'

The 20th century brought dictatorship and revolution. Many Catholics took part in the struggle against the Somoza regime and, after 1979, some priests served in the Sandinista government, creating tensions with Rome during Pope John Paul II's 1983 visit.

In recent years the Church has suffered serious persecution from the Ortega–Murillo government: priests and bishops have been imprisoned or exiled, including Bishop Rolando Álvarez, the Missionaries of Charity and the Jesuits were expelled, and Church universities, radios and properties seized. Yet the faithful keep praying, processing and singing to the Purísima.

saints.name: Bl. María Romero Meneses
saints.story: Born in Granada, Nicaragua, she became a Salesian Sister and spent most of her life in Costa Rica, teaching poor girls, opening clinics and building homes for families in need. Known for her joyful prayer and trust in Mary Help of Christians, she was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 2002.

saints.name: Bishop Antonio de Valdivieso (not canonized)
saints.story: A Spanish Dominican and bishop of León who denounced the cruelty of the conquistadors toward Indigenous people and sided with the oppressed. He was stabbed to death in 1550 by men linked to the governor's family. He is honoured in Nicaragua as a martyr for justice, though not formally beatified.

saints.name: Servant of God Fray Odorico D'Andrea
saints.story: An Italian Franciscan who served for decades in San Rafael del Norte in the northern mountains, building schools, roads and clinics and caring tenderly for peasant families. Revered by the people as a saintly pastor, his cause for beatification has been opened.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral Basilica of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: The largest cathedral in Central America, built in the 18th and early 19th centuries in a style blending Baroque and Neoclassical, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011. Its white rooftop domes can be walked upon, and the poet Rubén Darío is buried inside beneath a sorrowing lion.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Granada
cathedrals.story: The bright yellow cathedral on Granada's central square, rebuilt several times after fires and wars, is the city's emblem. Its towers and red domes rise over colonial streets, and it is a beloved centre for the Purísima celebrations and Holy Week processions.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Home to the venerated colonial image of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception of El Viejo, considered the national shrine of Nicaraguan Marian devotion. Each December pilgrims from across the country come to honour her, and the tradition of 'lavada de la plata' (washing the silver) draws thousands.

cathedrals.name: Old Cathedral of Managua (Santiago)
cathedrals.story: An early 20th-century cathedral inspired by Saint-Sulpice in Paris, badly damaged in the 1972 earthquake and left standing as a wounded witness to the city's history. It remains a poignant symbol of Managua's suffering and endurance.

prayerIntention: For Nicaragua, that its persecuted Church may be strengthened, its prisoners and exiles comforted, and its people granted freedom, justice and peace under the mantle of the Purísima.

name: Niger
history:
Niger is a deeply Muslim country, and the Catholic Church there has always been a small, gentle presence. Missionaries of the Society of African Missions (SMA) came to Niamey in the early 1930s, serving mainly the small Christian communities from coastal West Africa, along with French residents. A Prefecture Apostolic of Niamey was created in the 1940s, later a diocese, and in 2001 a second diocese was established at Maradi.

The Church has expressed its faith above all through schools, health care, help during droughts and food crises, and friendship with Muslim neighbours, which many Nigeriens appreciate. Sisters and lay people have run dispensaries and literacy programmes far beyond the Christian community.

In recent years this small flock has known real suffering. In 2015, riots following the Charlie Hebdo cartoons led to the burning of dozens of churches in Zinder and Niamey. Jihadist violence in the Sahel has made rural areas dangerous, and in 2018 the Italian SMA missionary Fr. Pierluigi Maccalli was kidnapped near Bomoanga and held for two years before his release. Still, Catholics in Niger continue to pray, serve and hope.

saints.name: St. Charles de Foucauld
saints.story: Not a missionary in Niger itself, but a hermit who lived among the Tuareg in the Algerian Sahara, a people who also dwell in northern Niger. He sought to be a 'universal brother' through silent presence, prayer and friendship rather than preaching. His spirituality inspires many Christians who live quietly among Muslim neighbours in the Sahel.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Perpetual Help
cathedrals.story: The main Catholic church of Niger and seat of the Archdiocese of Niamey, a modest but dignified building where Nigerien, West African and expatriate Catholics gather together. It has been a place of refuge and prayer during times of unrest and a symbol of the Church's humble presence in the Sahel.

prayerIntention: For the people of Niger, that they may know peace, food security and safety from violence, and that its small Church may be a sign of fraternity with all.

name: Nigeria
history:
Portuguese missionaries reached the kingdoms of Benin and Warri in the 15th and 16th centuries, but these early missions did not endure. Lasting Catholic presence began in the 1860s with the Society of African Missions in Lagos and, from 1885, the Holy Ghost Fathers at Onitsha. Irish missionaries, above all Bishop Joseph Shanahan, built a vast network of schools across the southeast, and education became the great bridge for the Gospel.

The Church grew remarkably in the 20th century. It survived the devastating Biafran war of 1967–1970, during which Catholic relief agencies fed starving families, and it has since produced countless priests and religious who now serve across the world. Bl. Cyprian Michael Iwene Tansi, beatified in 1998, is its first beatified son.

Today Nigeria has one of the most vibrant Catholic communities on earth, with full churches and large seminaries. But it is also a place of grievous suffering: Boko Haram and armed groups have attacked churches and villages, many priests and seminarians have been kidnapped or killed, and the Pentecost 2022 massacre at St. Francis Xavier Church in Owo shocked the world. The faithful continue to worship with courage.

saints.name: Bl. Cyprian Michael Iwene Tansi
saints.story: An Igbo priest from Aguleri ordained in 1937, who served as a zealous, austere pastor in the Onitsha region, caring for families and especially for young women preparing for marriage. Seeking deeper prayer, he became a Cistercian monk at Mount St Bernard Abbey in England. Pope John Paul II beatified him in Onitsha in 1998.

saints.name: Bishop Joseph Shanahan, CSSp (missionary, not canonized)
saints.story: An Irish Holy Ghost Father who led the mission in southeastern Nigeria from 1905, building hundreds of schools and forming catechists. He founded the Missionary Sisters of the Holy Rosary to serve in Nigeria. Though not canonized, he is honoured as a founding father of the Church among the Igbo people.

cathedrals.name: Holy Cross Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The mother church of the Archdiocese of Lagos, rooted in the early SMA mission on Lagos Island. Its Gothic-style twin towers and arches welcome vast congregations, and it remains a historic heart of Catholic life in Nigeria's largest city.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Most Holy Trinity
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Onitsha, near where the Holy Ghost Fathers first landed on the Niger River in 1885. It is a spiritual home for millions of Igbo Catholics and closely linked to the memory of Bl. Iwene Tansi.

cathedrals.name: Our Lady Queen of Nigeria Pro-Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The principal Catholic church of the federal capital, dedicated to Mary as Queen of Nigeria. Large and modern, it hosts national celebrations and prayers for the country, gathering Catholics from every ethnic group in one family of faith.

prayerIntention: For Nigeria, that God may protect its people from violence and kidnapping, heal its divisions, and strengthen its vibrant Church as a sign of reconciliation and hope.

name: North Korea
catholicPresence: Unknown; a state-controlled association claims a few thousand members
history:
Catholicism entered Korea at the end of the 18th century, carried by Korean scholars who encountered it in Beijing, and the faith spread in the north as well as the south despite fierce persecutions in the 19th century. In the early 20th century the north was a lively Christian region: the Diocese of Pyongyang was entrusted to the American Maryknoll missionaries, and German Benedictines built the great Abbey of Tokwon near Wonsan.

After 1945, the communist regime suppressed all religion. Bishop Francis Hong Yong-ho of Pyongyang was arrested in 1949 and never seen again; the Tokwon Benedictines were imprisoned, and many monks and sisters died in camps. Their causes for beatification have been opened as martyrs. Countless Catholics fled south or disappeared.

Today there is no independent Catholic Church in North Korea and no resident priest. A state-run Korean Catholic Association operates Changchung Cathedral in Pyongyang, built in 1988. What remains of hidden faith is known only to God. The Church in South Korea and around the world prays each year for reconciliation and for the 'Church of Silence' in the north.

saints.name: Servant of God Bishop Francis Borgia Hong Yong-ho and companions
saints.story: Bishop of Pyongyang, arrested by communist authorities in 1949 and never heard from again. His cause, with many companion priests, religious and lay faithful killed or vanished in the north, has been opened by the Korean bishops. Their exact fates are mostly unknown.

saints.name: Servant of God Bishop-Abbot Boniface Sauer and companions
saints.story: A German Benedictine who built the Abbey of Tokwon and led the mission in northern Korea. Arrested in 1949, he died in prison in 1950. With dozens of monks and sisters of the Tokwon and Yanji communities who died in prisons and camps, his cause as a martyr has been opened.

cathedrals.name: Changchung Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in 1988 by the state-run Korean Catholic Association, it is the only Catholic church building in North Korea and has no resident priest. Visiting clergy occasionally celebrate Mass. Many see it as a showcase, yet Catholics worldwide pray that it may one day be a true home for a free Church.

cathedrals.name: Former Tokwon Abbey
cathedrals.story: Once a great Benedictine abbey with a church, seminary and printing press, founded by German monks in the 1920s. After the community was arrested in 1949 the buildings were taken over by the state. It is remembered as a place of holiness and martyrdom.

prayerIntention: For the people of North Korea, that they may be freed from fear and hunger, that hidden believers may be strengthened, and that the Korean peninsula may be reconciled in peace.

name: North Macedonia
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. under 1%), Latin and Eastern Catholic
history:
The lands of North Macedonia heard the Gospel very early: St. Paul's vision of 'a man of Macedonia' drew him to the wider region, and in the 9th and 10th centuries Ohrid became a great centre of Slavonic Christianity through St. Clement and St. Naum, disciples of Sts. Cyril and Methodius. Most Christians here belong to the Orthodox tradition.

A small Catholic presence survived through the centuries among merchants, Albanians and Croats, and in the 19th century a Byzantine-rite Catholic community arose among Macedonian Slavs. In Skopje in 1910 was born Anjezë Gonxha Bojaxhiu, baptised in the Sacred Heart parish, who would become St. Teresa of Calcutta. The devastating 1963 Skopje earthquake destroyed the church of her baptism.

Today Catholics form a small community in two jurisdictions: the Latin Diocese of Skopje and the Macedonian Byzantine Catholic Eparchy of the Assumption, centred in Strumica, which became a full eparchy in 2018. Pope Francis visited Skopje in 2019, praying at the Memorial House of Mother Teresa. The Church lives in friendly relations with Orthodox and Muslim neighbours.

saints.name: St. Teresa of Calcutta
saints.story: Born in Skopje to an Albanian Catholic family, Gonxha grew up in the Sacred Heart parish, where she first felt called to mission. She left at 18 to join the Loreto Sisters and later founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta. Canonized in 2016, she is Skopje's most beloved daughter.

saints.name: Sts. Cyril and Methodius
saints.story: Brothers from Thessalonica who brought the Gospel to the Slavs in their own language and created the Glagolitic alphabet. Their disciples spread their work to Ohrid and the Macedonian lands. Co-patrons of Europe, they are venerated by Catholics and Orthodox alike.

saints.name: St. Clement of Ohrid
saints.story: A disciple of Cyril and Methodius who taught thousands of students at Ohrid, translated liturgical texts and became the first bishop of Slavic language in the region. He is honoured as one of the great enlighteners of the Slavs, venerated across Eastern and Western traditions.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Sacred Heart of Jesus
cathedrals.story: The seat of the Latin Catholic bishop of Skopje, rebuilt after the 1963 earthquake destroyed the old parish church where Mother Teresa was baptised and grew up. It is the heart of the capital's small Catholic community.

cathedrals.name: Memorial House of Mother Teresa
cathedrals.story: Opened in 2009 near the site of the old Sacred Heart church, this memorial includes a chapel and exhibits of Mother Teresa's life and relics. Pope Francis prayed here in 2019 with the poor served by her sisters. It is a place of pilgrimage for people of all faiths.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Macedonian Byzantine Catholic Eparchy, where the Eastern Catholic community celebrates the Divine Liturgy in Macedonian. It witnesses to the unity of East and West in the one Catholic Church.

prayerIntention: For North Macedonia, that its peoples may live in harmony and peace, and that, through the intercession of St. Teresa of Calcutta, love for the poor may flourish.

name: Norway
catholicPresence: Approx. 3–4% Catholic (registered), largely of immigrant background
history:
Christianity came to Norway around the turn of the first millennium through missionary kings, above all Olaf Haraldsson, who fell at the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030 and was soon venerated as St. Olav, the 'eternal king of Norway'. His shrine in Nidaros (Trondheim) became one of the great pilgrimage goals of medieval Europe, and the Archdiocese of Nidaros, founded in 1152/53, governed the Church across the North Atlantic.

The Lutheran Reformation was imposed in 1537. Catholic worship was outlawed, the last archbishop fled, and for three centuries Catholic priests were barred from the country. Only with the Dissenter Act of 1845 could Catholics again worship openly, and the constitutional ban on Jesuits was lifted only in 1956. The novelist Sigrid Undset, a convert, helped Norwegians rediscover their Catholic past.

Today the Catholic Church is growing, enriched by Polish, Lithuanian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Eritrean and many other faithful, making it one of the most international communities in the country. Pilgrimage routes to Nidaros have been revived, and every July pilgrims gather for Olsok, the feast of St. Olav.

saints.name: St. Olav (Olaf II Haraldsson)
saints.story: A Viking turned Christian king who worked to make Norway a Christian realm. He fell in battle at Stiklestad in 1030, and reports of miracles soon spread. Venerated as Norway's patron and 'eternal king', his shrine at Nidaros drew pilgrims from all over Europe.

saints.name: St. Hallvard
saints.story: A young man from Lier who, according to tradition, was killed while defending a woman wrongly accused of theft, and whose body was thrown into the fjord weighted with a millstone. It floated, and he was honoured as a martyr for justice. He is the patron saint of Oslo.

saints.name: St. Sunniva
saints.story: According to legend, an Irish princess who fled by sea with companions and settled on the island of Selja, where they died in a cave rather than be captured. Her relics were later moved to Bergen. She is honoured as patron of western Norway and the Diocese of Bjørgvin.

saints.name: St. Eystein Erlendsson
saints.story: Archbishop of Nidaros who strengthened the Church's independence, worked on the great cathedral and wrote of St. Olav's miracles. He was venerated as a saint locally in Norway soon after his death, and his memory is still kept on January 26.

cathedrals.name: St. Olav's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in 1856 as the first Catholic church in Norway after the Reformation, it became a cathedral in 1953. Though modest in size, it is filled each Sunday with Masses in many languages, a living icon of Norway's international Catholic family.

cathedrals.name: St. Olav's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: A new Catholic cathedral consecrated in 2016, a bright modern building that serves the Territorial Prelature of Trondheim, near the site of the medieval Archdiocese of Nidaros. It welcomes pilgrims who walk St. Olav's Way.

cathedrals.name: Nidaros Cathedral (Lutheran, historic pilgrimage site)
cathedrals.story: The magnificent medieval cathedral built over St. Olav's grave, now belonging to the Church of Norway. For centuries it was the goal of Catholic pilgrims, and today Catholics and Lutherans pray together here during Olsok, the feast of St. Olav.

prayerIntention: For Norway, that its people may rediscover the faith of St. Olav, and that its growing, international Church may be a home of unity for all who come there.

name: Oman
catholicPresence: Small Catholic community of migrant workers (approx. 2–4% of residents); very few Omani citizens
history:
Christianity was present in Oman before Islam: the Church of the East had a bishopric in the region in the 5th to 7th centuries, linked to trade routes across the Gulf. These communities gradually disappeared after the arrival of Islam, and for many centuries there was no organised Christian presence.

In modern times the Catholic Church returned with migrant workers. Since the 1970s Sultan Qaboos granted land for churches, and Oman is known in the Gulf for its spirit of tolerance. Catholics, mostly from India, the Philippines, Sri Lanka and other countries, worship in parishes in Muscat, Sohar and Salalah, belonging to the Apostolic Vicariate of Southern Arabia, based in Abu Dhabi. Masses are celebrated in many languages and rites, including Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara.

In 2023 Oman and the Holy See established full diplomatic relations. Catholics live their faith freely within church compounds, though public evangelisation is not permitted. Many are far from their families and work hard for modest wages, and the Church accompanies them as a true home away from home.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of Arabia (patroness of the Vicariates of Arabia)

cathedrals.name: Church of Sts. Peter and Paul
cathedrals.story: The largest Catholic parish in Oman, on land given by the Sultan. On Fridays and Sundays it is crowded with thousands of migrant workers and families praying in English, Malayalam, Tagalog, Konkani and other languages. It is a vivid image of the universal Church far from home.

cathedrals.name: Church of the Holy Spirit
cathedrals.story: A second Muscat parish serving a growing number of Catholics in the capital region, with a busy schedule of Masses, catechism and prayer groups for many nationalities.

cathedrals.name: St. Francis Xavier Church
cathedrals.story: A parish in southern Oman serving migrant Catholics in the Dhofar region. It is a small but faithful community, often far from family, gathering for Mass and fellowship.

prayerIntention: For the people of Oman, that its tradition of tolerance may flourish, and that migrant Catholics far from home may be treated with dignity and find strength in their faith.

name: Pakistan
history:
Catholic presence in the lands of Pakistan dates back to the late 16th century, when Jesuits were invited to the Mughal court of Akbar, including at Lahore, and Carmelites later served in Thatta in Sindh. Lasting growth came in the 19th century, when Capuchin and other missionaries worked in Punjab and Sindh. Many converts came from among the poorest, marginalised communities, and the Church built schools and hospitals that are respected throughout the country to this day.

At independence in 1947 the Church faced a new reality as a small minority in a Muslim-majority state. Christians have often suffered discrimination and poverty. Blasphemy laws have been misused against them, as in the case of Asia Bibi, acquitted in 2018 after years on death row. In 2011 Shahbaz Bhatti, the Catholic federal minister for minorities, was assassinated for defending religious freedom, and churches have been attacked, including the 2015 bombings in Lahore's Youhanabad and the riots in Jaranwala in 2023.

Yet Pakistani Catholics remain deeply devoted, crowding the Marian shrine of Mariamabad and producing priests and religious who serve with courage. Their faith is a witness of steadfast love.

saints.name: Servant of God Akash Bashir
saints.story: A young Catholic security volunteer who, on 15 March 2015, stopped a suicide bomber at the gate of St. John's Church in Youhanabad, Lahore, embracing him and saying he would die but not let him enter. He was killed, saving many worshippers. In 2022 he was declared a Servant of God, the first from Pakistan.

saints.name: Shahbaz Bhatti (not formally beatified)
saints.story: A Catholic politician and Pakistan's federal minister for minorities who defended Christians, Hindus and others against misuse of the blasphemy laws. Aware of death threats, he continued his work and was assassinated in Islamabad in 2011. Many honour him as a witness to faith and justice.

saints.name: Dr. Ruth Pfau (not canonized)
saints.story: A German Catholic religious sister and doctor of the Daughters of the Heart of Mary, who arrived in Karachi in 1960 and dedicated her life to fighting leprosy in Pakistan. Her work helped the country control the disease. On her death she received a state funeral, honoured by the whole nation.

saints.name: Fr. Jerome Xavier, SJ (missionary)
saints.story: A Spanish Jesuit, grand-nephew of St. Francis Xavier, who lived at the Mughal court in Lahore and Agra, writing works on Christ in Persian for Emperor Akbar and Jahangir. He is remembered as one of the first Catholic missionaries in these lands.

cathedrals.name: St. Patrick's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: A Gothic Revival cathedral completed in 1881, with soaring arches and stained glass, at the heart of Karachi's historic Catholic community. It has hosted papal envoys and national celebrations and remains a symbol of the Church's long presence in Sindh.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in the early 20th century, this cathedral in a Romanesque–Byzantine style is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Lahore. It has witnessed both joyful celebrations and times of grief and solidarity after attacks on Christians.

cathedrals.name: National Marian Shrine of Mariamabad
cathedrals.story: Pakistan's most beloved Catholic pilgrimage site, in a village founded by Capuchin missionaries. Every September hundreds of thousands of pilgrims, many walking barefoot, come to honour Mary and seek her help, one of the largest Christian gatherings in the country.

prayerIntention: For Pakistan, that religious freedom and dignity may be secured for all, that Christians may live without fear, and that its people may know peace and prosperity.

name: Palau
history:
Catholicism came to Palau in 1891, during Spanish rule over the Caroline Islands, when Spanish Capuchin missionaries arrived. After Spain sold the islands to Germany in 1899, German Capuchins continued the mission. Under Japanese rule, from 1914, Spanish Jesuits took over and the Catholic community grew steadily, with Palauan catechists playing an essential role.

The Second World War brought great suffering to Palau, with devastating battles on Peleliu and Angaur. Missionaries were interned, and some Spanish Jesuits serving in the islands died at the hands of the Japanese military in 1944. After the war, American Jesuits served the islands and the Church rebuilt its schools and parishes.

Today Palau, independent since 1994, is one of the most Catholic nations in Micronesia. The Church belongs to the Diocese of the Caroline Islands, and parishes in Koror and the outlying states serve Palauan families as well as Filipino and other migrants. Catholic schools such as Mindszenty High School shape young people, and Catholic faith is woven into Palauan family and village life.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Church
cathedrals.story: The main Catholic parish of Palau, at the heart of the islands' largest town. It gathers Palauan and migrant families for Mass, feasts and community events, and is the spiritual centre of the Catholic community in the country.

prayerIntention: For the people of Palau, that their islands and ocean may be protected, their families strengthened, and their Church grow in faith and service.

name: Palestine
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. under 1%), within a Christian community of about 1–2%
history:
Palestine is the land where the Gospel began: Jesus was born in Bethlehem, and Christian communities have lived here without interruption since apostolic times. The Church of the Nativity, built under Constantine and rebuilt by Justinian, is among the oldest churches still in use. Palestinian Christians are among the most ancient Christian communities on earth.

Catholic presence took different forms over the centuries: the Crusader period, then the Franciscan Custody of the Holy Land, entrusted with guarding the holy places since the 14th century. The Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem was restored in 1847, and Melkite Greek Catholics also form an important community. Catholic schools, hospitals and universities, such as Bethlehem University, serve Christians and Muslims alike.

Today Palestinian Christians face hardship: the Israeli occupation, separation barrier and checkpoints, economic struggle and emigration have greatly reduced their numbers. In Gaza, the small community of Holy Family parish has lived through devastating war; Pope Francis called them nearly every evening, and in 2025 the church compound was struck, killing parishioners. These 'living stones' continue to pray for peace in the land of the Prince of Peace.

saints.name: St. Marie-Alphonsine Danil Ghattas
saints.story: Born in Jerusalem to a Palestinian Arab family, she joined the Sisters of St. Joseph and later, inspired by visions of Our Lady, founded the Congregation of the Rosary Sisters, the first Arab women's congregation, devoted to educating girls. She was canonized by Pope Francis in 2015.

saints.name: St. Mariam of Jesus Crucified (Mariam Baouardy)
saints.story: A Melkite Greek Catholic from Galilee, known as 'the Little Arab', a mystic of deep humility and joy. As a Carmelite nun she founded the Carmel of Bethlehem, where she died in 1878 and is buried. She was canonized in 2015.

saints.name: St. Jerome
saints.story: The great Doctor of the Church who spent his last decades in Bethlehem, living in a cave near the grotto of the Nativity and translating the Bible into Latin, the Vulgate. His cave can still be visited beneath St. Catherine's Church.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Nativity
cathedrals.story: Built over the grotto where Christians have venerated Jesus' birth since the 2nd century, first under Constantine in the 4th century and rebuilt under Justinian. Entered through the tiny 'Door of Humility', it is shared by Greek Orthodox, Armenian and Catholic communities and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cathedrals.name: St. Catherine's Church
cathedrals.story: The Franciscan Catholic church adjoining the Basilica of the Nativity, from which the Midnight Mass of Christmas is broadcast to the world. Beneath it lie caves associated with St. Jerome and the Holy Innocents.

cathedrals.name: Holy Family Church
cathedrals.story: The only Catholic parish in Gaza, which during the war became a refuge for hundreds of Christians, Catholic and Orthodox. Pope Francis phoned the parish almost every evening. It stands as a symbol of faith, endurance and hope amid immense suffering.

cathedrals.name: Shepherds' Field Chapel
cathedrals.story: A tent-shaped Franciscan chapel designed by Antonio Barluzzi in the 1950s, marking the fields where tradition says the angels announced Christ's birth to the shepherds. Its light-filled dome recalls the glory that shone around them.

prayerIntention: For the people of Palestine, especially in Gaza and Bethlehem, that war and occupation may end, that justice and peace may embrace, and that Christians may remain as living stones in the land of Christ.

name: Panama
history:
Panama holds a special place in the history of the Church in the Americas: in 1513 the Diocese of Santa María la Antigua del Darién was founded, the first diocese on the American mainland. The faith came with the Spanish conquest, which brought great suffering to Indigenous peoples, and Panama City became a crossroads of the empire, through which treasure, soldiers and missionaries passed between the oceans.

After the old city was destroyed in 1671 during Henry Morgan's raid, the new Panama City was built with its cathedral and churches; tradition tells how the golden altar of San José was saved by being painted black. Popular devotions grew, especially to the Black Christ of Portobelo, honoured each October 21 by pilgrims walking from across the country.

The 20th century brought the canal, migration and political upheaval. During the military regime, the Colombian-born priest Héctor Gallego, who organised peasant cooperatives in Veraguas, disappeared in 1971. In 2019 Panama hosted World Youth Day with Pope Francis, a moment of great joy. Today the Church faces growing evangelical communities and secularisation but remains deeply rooted in Panamanian life.

saints.name: Fr. Héctor Gallego (not canonized)
saints.story: A Colombian priest who served peasants in Santa Fe de Veraguas, helping them form cooperatives and defend their rights. In 1971 he was taken by members of the security forces and never seen again. Remembered with deep affection, he is honoured in Panama as a witness to justice.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral Basilica of Santa María la Antigua
cathedrals.story: Standing in the historic Casco Viejo, this cathedral was built over more than a century and completed in 1796, with twin white towers and stone from the ruins of Old Panama. After a major restoration, its altar was consecrated by Pope Francis during World Youth Day in 2019.

cathedrals.name: Church of San José (Golden Altar)
cathedrals.story: Famous for its magnificent Baroque altar of carved and gilded wood. Tradition holds that it was saved from Henry Morgan's pirates in 1671 by being painted black, and later moved to the new city. It is one of Panama's most beloved churches.

cathedrals.name: Church of San Felipe (Black Christ)
cathedrals.story: Home of the Black Christ of Portobelo, a wooden image of Jesus carrying the cross. Each October 21 tens of thousands of pilgrims, some crawling the final kilometres, come to fulfil promises and give thanks.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Santiago Apóstol
cathedrals.story: One of the oldest churches still in use on the American mainland, in a town founded in the early 1520s. Its colonial altarpieces were carved by Indigenous artisans, and it is a cherished link to the first Christian centuries in Panama.

prayerIntention: For Panama, crossroads of the world, that it may be a land of justice, welcome and peace, and that its young people may follow Christ with joy.

name: Papua New Guinea
history:
The first Catholic missionaries to reach these islands were Marists in 1847 on Woodlark and Murua, followed by priests of the Milan Foreign Missions; the mission was hard, and Bl. Giovanni Mazzucconi was killed in 1855. Lasting foundations came later: the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart arrived at Yule Island in 1885 and in New Britain, and the Divine Word Missionaries began on the north coast of the mainland in 1896. Catechists from local villages carried the faith into the highlands, valleys and islands.

The Second World War brought terrible suffering. Missionaries were killed or interned, and the catechist Peter To Rot of Rakunai kept his community's faith alive during the Japanese occupation until he was imprisoned and killed in 1945. He was beatified in 1995 and canonized in 2025, the first saint of Papua New Guinea.

Today the Catholic Church is the largest single church in the country, running schools and a vast network of health centres. It faces challenges of tribal violence, sorcery-related accusations and poverty, but also great vitality. Pope Francis visited Port Moresby and Vanimo in 2024, praising the joy and resilience of its people.

saints.name: St. Peter To Rot
saints.story: A married catechist from Rakunai on New Britain who, during the Japanese occupation, led prayer, baptised and defended Christian marriage when the occupiers encouraged polygamy. Arrested and imprisoned, he was killed by lethal injection in 1945. Beatified in 1995, he was canonized in 2025, Papua New Guinea's first saint.

saints.name: Bl. Giovanni Battista Mazzucconi
saints.story: A young priest of the Milan Foreign Missions who served on Woodlark Island. After falling ill he left for a time, and on returning in 1855 his ship was attacked and he was killed. He was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1984 as a martyr of the mission in Melanesia.

cathedrals.name: St Mary's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Port Moresby, in the capital city. It gathers Papuans and New Guineans from every province and is a centre for national Church celebrations.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of St. Peter To Rot
cathedrals.story: The home village of Peter To Rot, where his grave and memorial church draw pilgrims from across the country and the Pacific. It is a place to honour a lay catechist whose faithfulness cost him his life.

cathedrals.name: Yule Island Mission
cathedrals.story: The historic landing place of the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart in 1885, from where the faith spread into Papua. Its old mission station remains a symbol of the beginnings of the Church in the south of the country.

prayerIntention: For Papua New Guinea, that through the intercession of St. Peter To Rot, its families may be strengthened, violence may cease, and its Church may grow in joy and holiness.

name: Paraguay
history:
Catholicism came to Paraguay with the Spanish founding of Asunción on the feast of the Assumption, 15 August 1537. Franciscans such as Fray Luis de Bolaños learned Guaraní and translated the catechism into it, and from 1609 the Jesuits established their famous reductions: mission towns where Guaraní peoples lived in community, protected from slave raiders, with remarkable music, art and architecture. In 1628 three Jesuit missionaries, including the Paraguayan-born Roque González, were killed; they are now canonized saints. The expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767 brought the reductions to an end.

After independence, the dictator Francia subjected the Church to state control and cut ties with Rome. The catastrophic War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870) killed a huge proportion of the population, and the Church shared in the nation's slow rebuilding. During the Stroessner dictatorship, bishops and religious increasingly defended human rights.

Today Paraguay is one of the most Catholic countries in Latin America. Pope John Paul II canonized St. Roque González in Asunción in 1988, Pope Francis visited in 2015, and each December 8 huge crowds walk to the Virgin of Caacupé.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of the Miracles of Caacupé

saints.name: St. Roque González de Santa Cruz
saints.story: Born in Asunción, he became a Jesuit and founded several reductions among the Guaraní, defending them against exploitation. He was killed in 1628 with Sts. Alfonso Rodríguez and Juan del Castillo. Canonized in 1988, he is Paraguay's first saint.

saints.name: Bl. María Felicia de Jesús Sacramentado ('Chiquitunga')
saints.story: A joyful young woman from Asunción, active in Catholic Action, who served the poor and the sick before entering the Discalced Carmelites. She died of illness at 34, offering her life with love. She was beatified in Asunción in 2018, the first Paraguayan blessed woman.

saints.name: Fray Luis de Bolaños, OFM (missionary)
saints.story: A Spanish Franciscan who spent decades among the Guaraní, founding early mission towns and translating the catechism into Guaraní. His work laid the foundations for Catholic life in Paraguay and for the later Jesuit reductions.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Caacupé
cathedrals.story: The national shrine of Paraguay, home to the small wooden statue of the Virgin of Caacupé, which tradition says was carved by a Guaraní convert. Each December 8, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims walk from Asunción and beyond to honour her.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the oldest diocese in the Río de la Plata region, rebuilt in its present form in the 19th century. Facing the Plaza de la Independencia, it is the heart of the nation's religious and civic celebrations.

cathedrals.name: Jesuit Mission of La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná
cathedrals.story: The ruins of one of the grandest Jesuit reductions, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its red sandstone church, carved with angels playing instruments, recalls a remarkable chapter of faith, art and Guaraní culture.

prayerIntention: For Paraguay, that its people, rich in faith and the Guaraní heritage, may grow in justice and solidarity under the loving gaze of the Virgin of Caacupé.

name: Peru
history:
The Catholic faith reached Peru with the Spanish conquest that began in 1532. It arrived entangled with violence: the fall of the Inca state, forced labour in the mines and the destruction of ancestral shrines caused immense suffering, and some missionaries, such as the Dominicans in Lima, raised their voices for the dignity of Indigenous peoples. Under St. Toribio de Mogrovejo, Archbishop of Lima, the Third Council of Lima (1582–1583) produced a catechism in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara, and the faith took deep root in Andean culture.

Colonial Lima became a city of saints: Rose of Lima, Martin de Porres, John Macías and Francisco Solano all lived there at the same time. Popular devotion grew around the Lord of Miracles, a mural of the crucified Christ painted by an enslaved man of African origin that survived earthquakes. In the 20th century the Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez helped shape liberation theology, and during the Shining Path violence of the 1980s and 1990s priests and catechists were killed, among them three missionaries beatified in 2015.
