Today Peru remains deeply Catholic, though evangelical churches are growing. In 2025 Robert Prevost, a missionary and former bishop of Chiclayo who holds Peruvian citizenship, was elected Pope Leo XIV.

patronSaints.name: St. Rose of Lima
patronSaints.feast: August 30 (in Peru; August 23 in the universal calendar)

saints.name: St. Rose of Lima
saints.story: Born in Lima, she lived as a Dominican tertiary in a tiny hermitage in her family's garden, devoted to prayer, penance and care for the sick and poor. Canonized in 1671, she was the first saint of the Americas and is patroness of Peru, Latin America and the Philippines.

saints.name: St. Martin de Porres
saints.story: Son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black woman from Panama, he was long excluded because of his mixed race, yet became a Dominican lay brother in Lima. He nursed the sick, fed the poor, cared for animals and was known for his humility and miracles. He was canonized in 1962.

saints.name: St. Toribio de Mogrovejo
saints.story: A Spanish lawyer made Archbishop of Lima, he travelled thousands of kilometres across the Andes to visit his people, learned Quechua, defended Indigenous people against abuse, founded the first seminary in the Americas and convened the Third Council of Lima. He confirmed St. Rose of Lima.

saints.name: St. Francisco Solano
saints.story: A Spanish Franciscan who spent years as a missionary in what are now Argentina and Paraguay, famous for preaching with his violin and learning local languages. He spent his last years in Lima, where he called the city to conversion. He was canonized in 1726.

saints.name: St. John Macías
saints.story: Born in Spain, he worked as a shepherd before coming to Lima, where he became a Dominican lay brother and porter. A friend of Martin de Porres, he distributed food to the poor at the convent door and prayed the Rosary constantly for the souls in purgatory. He was canonized in 1975.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral Basilica of St. John the Apostle and Evangelist
cathedrals.story: Lima's cathedral stands on the Plaza Mayor, on the site chosen by Francisco Pizarro, whose tomb lies inside. Damaged and rebuilt after several earthquakes, it combines Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical elements, with richly carved choir stalls and side chapels. It is the mother church of one of the oldest dioceses in South America.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary and Monastery of Las Nazarenas
cathedrals.story: Home of the Lord of Miracles, a mural of Christ crucified painted in the 17th century by an enslaved Angolan man, which miraculously survived devastating earthquakes. Each October, the 'purple month', vast crowds dressed in purple follow the image through Lima in one of the largest processions in the world.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral Basilica of the Assumption of the Virgin
cathedrals.story: Built over the palace of the Inca Viracocha, using stones from Inca structures, this cathedral holds one of the finest collections of Cusco School paintings, where Andean artists blended European and local imagery, including a famous Last Supper with a guinea pig on the table. It reflects both the encounter and the wounds of conquest.

cathedrals.name: Basilica and Convent of San Francisco
cathedrals.story: A Baroque complex completed in the 17th century, celebrated for its yellow façade, Moorish-style carved ceilings, historic library and catacombs, which served as a burial place for thousands of Lima's faithful. It remains a living Franciscan community and a beloved place of prayer.

prayerIntention: For Peru, that through the intercession of Rose of Lima and Martin de Porres its people may know justice, reconciliation and care for the poorest, from the Andes to the Amazon.

name: Philippines
history:
Christianity arrived in the Philippines with Ferdinand Magellan's expedition in 1521. The first recorded Mass was celebrated on Easter Sunday, 31 March 1521, and in Cebu Rajah Humabon and his wife were baptised; she received an image of the Child Jesus, the Santo Niño, still venerated today. Lasting Spanish rule began with Miguel López de Legazpi in 1565, and Augustinian, Franciscan, Jesuit, Dominican and Augustinian Recollect friars spread the faith across the islands.

The colonial Church was both a source of devotion and of grievance: friars often held great power, and Filipino priests faced discrimination. The execution of three Filipino priests, Gomez, Burgos and Zamora (Gomburza), in 1872 helped inspire the independence movement. In 1902 part of the faithful formed the separate Philippine Independent Church. Under American rule Catholic schools and lay movements flourished, and in 1986 Church leaders, especially Cardinal Jaime Sin, helped the peaceful People Power revolution.

Today the Philippines is one of the world's largest Catholic nations, with fervent devotions such as the Black Nazarene and Simbang Gabi. It faces poverty, migration, political violence and abuse cases, yet Filipino migrants carry the faith across the world. In 2021 the country celebrated 500 years of Christianity.

saints.name: St. Lorenzo Ruiz
saints.story: A husband and father from Binondo, Manila, who served as a calligrapher for the Dominicans. Fleeing a false accusation, he joined missionaries bound for Japan, where they were arrested and tortured in Nagasaki. Refusing to renounce Christ, he died a martyr. Canonized in 1987, he is the first Filipino saint.

saints.name: St. Pedro Calungsod
saints.story: A young catechist from the Visayas who accompanied the Jesuit Bl. Diego Luis de San Vitores on mission in Guam. When they baptised a child against the father's wishes, both were killed. Pedro, still a teenager, could have escaped but stayed by the priest. He was canonized in 2012.

saints.name: Ven. Ignacia del Espíritu Santo
saints.story: A Chinese-Filipino woman from Manila who began a life of prayer and work with other women under Jesuit guidance at a time when Filipina women could rarely enter religious life. Her community became the Religious of the Virgin Mary, the first Filipino women's congregation. She was declared Venerable in 2007.

cathedrals.name: Basilica Minore del Santo Niño
cathedrals.story: Founded by the Augustinians in 1565 on the spot where the image of the Child Jesus was found after a fire, it is the oldest church site in the Philippines. The Santo Niño given in 1521 is enshrined here, and the January Sinulog festival draws millions in dance and prayer.

cathedrals.name: Manila Cathedral (Cathedral Basilica of the Immaculate Conception)
cathedrals.story: Within the walled city of Intramuros, the cathedral has been destroyed by fire, earthquakes and war many times; the present Romanesque-revival building, the eighth on the site, was completed in 1958. It is the mother church of the Philippines and has welcomed popes on their visits.

cathedrals.name: San Agustin Church
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1607, it is the oldest stone church in the Philippines and the only Intramuros building to survive World War II. Part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of Baroque churches, it has a trompe-l'oeil painted ceiling and the tomb of Legazpi.

cathedrals.name: Minor Basilica of the Black Nazarene (Quiapo Church)
cathedrals.story: Home to the dark wooden image of Jesus carrying the cross, brought from Mexico in the 17th century. Each January 9, millions join the Traslación, barefoot devotees surging to touch the image. It is the heart of popular Filipino faith and its longing for Christ in suffering.

prayerIntention: For the Philippines, that its living faith may bear fruit in justice and peace, that the poor and the many Filipinos working abroad may be protected, and that its Church may be holy and humble.

name: Poland
history:
Poland's history as a nation begins with the baptism of Duke Mieszko I in 966. In the year 1000 the Archdiocese of Gniezno was founded at the tomb of St. Adalbert, a missionary martyred by the Prussians. Over the centuries Catholicism became woven into Polish identity, and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was notable in its time for religious tolerance. In 1656, during the Swedish invasion, King John Casimir entrusted the kingdom to Mary as Queen of Poland after the defence of Jasna Góra.

When Poland was partitioned and erased from the map from 1795 to 1918, the Church kept language and hope alive. During World War II the Nazi occupiers murdered thousands of priests and religious; St. Maximilian Kolbe gave his life at Auschwitz, and Poles and Jews suffered terribly, though there were also failures toward Jewish neighbours. Under communism, Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński led the Church's resistance, and in 1978 Karol Wojtyła was elected Pope John Paul II. His 1979 pilgrimage helped give birth to the Solidarity movement.

Today Poland is still one of Europe's most Catholic countries, the land of Divine Mercy devotion, but it is facing rapid secularisation among the young and painful revelations of abuse, calling the Church to humility and renewal.

patronSaints.name: St. Stanislaus of Szczepanów
patronSaints.feast: May 8 (in Poland; April 11 in the universal calendar)

saints.name: St. John Paul II
saints.story: Karol Wojtyła of Wadowice, actor, poet, worker under Nazi occupation, priest and Archbishop of Kraków, was elected pope in 1978. His pontificate helped bring the peaceful fall of communism and reached the whole world through travel, youth days and teaching. He was canonized in 2014.

saints.name: St. Faustina Kowalska
saints.story: A simple sister of Our Lady of Mercy from a poor farming family, she recorded in her Diary revelations of Jesus' Divine Mercy, including the image 'Jesus, I trust in You' and the Chaplet. She died of tuberculosis in Kraków. Canonized in 2000, her message spread worldwide.

saints.name: St. Maximilian Kolbe
saints.story: A Franciscan friar who founded the Militia Immaculatae and the friary of Niepokalanów, using modern media to spread devotion to Mary. Arrested by the Nazis, at Auschwitz he offered his life in place of a condemned father of a family and died in a starvation bunker. He was canonized in 1982.

saints.name: St. Hedwig (Jadwiga) of Poland
saints.story: Crowned 'King' of Poland as a girl, she married Jogaila of Lithuania, leading to the baptism of Lithuania. She cared for the poor, founded hospitals and helped restore the University of Kraków. She died young after childbirth. Pope John Paul II canonized her in 1997.

saints.name: Bl. Jerzy Popiełuszko
saints.story: A Warsaw priest who celebrated monthly 'Masses for the Homeland' for Solidarity supporters, preaching 'overcome evil with good'. He was abducted and murdered by communist security officers in 1984. His funeral drew hundreds of thousands. He was beatified as a martyr in 2010.

cathedrals.name: Jasna Góra Monastery
cathedrals.story: The Pauline monastery that guards the icon of the Black Madonna, revered for centuries. Its successful defence against the Swedes in 1655 became a national symbol. Millions of pilgrims arrive each year, many walking for days in August, making it Poland's spiritual heart.

cathedrals.name: Wawel Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The royal cathedral on Wawel Hill, where Polish kings were crowned and buried. Its Gothic nave holds the shrine of St. Stanislaus, the Renaissance Sigismund Chapel and the great Sigismund Bell. Karol Wojtyła celebrated his first Mass in its crypt and later served as its archbishop.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary of Divine Mercy
cathedrals.story: The convent where St. Faustina lived and died, with the original chapel holding the Divine Mercy image and her relics, and a modern basilica consecrated by John Paul II in 2002. It is a world centre of the Divine Mercy devotion.

cathedrals.name: Gniezno Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The primatial cathedral of Poland, rebuilt in Gothic style, holding the silver shrine of St. Adalbert. Its 12th-century bronze doors depict his life and martyrdom. Here the Archdiocese of Gniezno was founded in 1000, the cradle of the Church in Poland.

prayerIntention: For Poland, that its people may treasure their heritage of faith and Divine Mercy, welcome the stranger, heal wounds of division and abuse, and pass on hope to a new generation.

name: Portugal
history:
Christianity reached the western Iberian Peninsula in Roman times, and Braga became one of its earliest and most important sees; in the 6th century St. Martin of Braga led the Suebi from Arianism to the Catholic faith. Portugal was born as a kingdom during the Reconquest: Afonso Henriques was recognised as king in the 12th century, and the capture of Lisbon in 1147 was followed by the building of its cathedral.

In the age of discovery, Portuguese ships carried missionaries to Africa, Brazil, India and East Asia, and figures such as St. Francis Xavier sailed under Portuguese patronage. This expansion was also bound up with the Atlantic slave trade, and at home Jews were forcibly converted in 1497 and the Inquisition brought great suffering. Later centuries saw the suppression of the Jesuits in 1759, the dissolution of religious orders in 1834, and harsh anticlerical laws after the Republic of 1910.

In 1917 three shepherd children at Fátima reported apparitions of Our Lady calling for prayer, the Rosary and conversion, and Fátima became one of the world's great shrines. Today Portugal remains largely Catholic in culture, though practice has declined. In 2023 Lisbon hosted World Youth Day, welcoming more than a million young pilgrims.

patronSaints.name: The Immaculate Conception (patroness and queen of Portugal)

saints.name: St. Anthony of Lisbon (of Padua)
saints.story: Born in Lisbon as Fernando, he became an Augustinian canon and then a Franciscan after seeing the relics of martyred friars. A powerful preacher and Doctor of the Church, he died near Padua and was canonized within a year. Lisbon celebrates him with joyful street festivals each June.

saints.name: Sts. Francisco and Jacinta Marto
saints.story: Brother and sister from Aljustrel near Fátima who, with their cousin Lúcia, saw Our Lady in 1917. Francisco longed to console Jesus; Jacinta offered sacrifices for sinners. Both died young in the influenza epidemic. Pope Francis canonized them at Fátima in 2017, the youngest non-martyr saints.

saints.name: St. Nuno Álvares Pereira
saints.story: The great military commander who secured Portugal's independence at the Battle of Aljubarrota in 1385. Known for his deep devotion to Mary, after his wife's death he gave away his wealth and became a humble Carmelite brother in Lisbon, serving the poor. He was canonized in 2009.

saints.name: St. John of God
saints.story: Born in Montemor-o-Novo, he lived a restless life as shepherd, soldier and bookseller before a radical conversion in Granada, Spain. He devoted himself to the sick and the mentally ill, founding a hospital whose followers became the Brothers Hospitallers. He is patron of hospitals and nurses.

saints.name: St. Elizabeth of Portugal
saints.story: A princess of Aragon who became queen of Portugal by marrying King Denis. Patient in a difficult marriage, she cared for the poor and sick and more than once made peace between her husband and their son. As a widow she lived near the Poor Clares in Coimbra, where she is venerated.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary of Our Lady of Fátima
cathedrals.story: Built around the Cova da Iria, where the Virgin appeared to three children in 1917. The Chapel of the Apparitions marks the spot, and the basilicas hold the tombs of Francisco, Jacinta and Lúcia. On May 13 and October 13, vast candlelit crowds pray the Rosary together.

cathedrals.name: Lisbon Cathedral (Sé de Lisboa)
cathedrals.story: Begun soon after the city's capture in 1147, this fortress-like Romanesque cathedral survived many earthquakes, including the great one of 1755, with Gothic and Baroque additions. Next to it stands the church built over the birthplace of St. Anthony, who was baptised here.

cathedrals.name: Braga Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The seat of one of the oldest dioceses in the Iberian Peninsula, begun in the 11th–12th centuries and enriched over the centuries with Gothic chapels and Baroque organs. Braga keeps its own ancient liturgical rite and is famous for its solemn Holy Week processions.

cathedrals.name: Sanctuary of Bom Jesus do Monte
cathedrals.story: A hilltop pilgrimage church reached by a monumental Baroque zigzag stairway with chapels and fountains representing the senses and virtues, which pilgrims sometimes climb on their knees. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a beloved image of the ascent to God.

prayerIntention: For Portugal, that the message of Fátima may renew its people in prayer and hope, and that its young people may find in Christ a joyful path of life.

name: Qatar
catholicPresence: Sizeable community of migrant Catholics (estimates vary widely); very few Qatari citizens
history:
Before Islam, Christian communities of the Church of the East lived along the Gulf coast, including the area of Qatar, where Syriac writers such as Isaac of Nineveh were born in the 7th century. These communities faded after the coming of Islam, and for many centuries there was no Christian presence.

In modern times Catholics arrived as workers from the Philippines, India, Sri Lanka, Lebanon, Africa and elsewhere, drawn by Qatar's growing economy. For years they prayed in private homes and schools. In 2008 the Church of Our Lady of the Rosary opened in Doha, the first Christian church built in the country, on land granted by the Emir within a special religious complex. Qatar belongs to the Apostolic Vicariate of Northern Arabia.

Today a very large, multilingual Catholic community gathers there on Fridays and Sundays. Worship is permitted within the compound, but there are no crosses or bells outside and evangelisation is not allowed. Many of the faithful are low-wage migrant workers, and international reports have raised serious concerns about their living and working conditions. For them the parish is a place of consolation, community and dignity.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of Arabia (patroness of the Vicariates of Arabia)

cathedrals.name: Church of Our Lady of the Rosary
cathedrals.story: Opened in 2008 as the first Christian church in Qatar, it stands in the religious complex at Abu Hamour, beside churches of other Christian communities. Its plain exterior carries no outward cross, but inside tens of thousands of migrants pray in many languages each week, filling Masses from early morning to night.

prayerIntention: For Qatar, for peace in the Gulf, and for the many migrant Catholics who live and work there, that their labour may be justly rewarded and their faith kept strong far from home.

name: Republic of the Congo
catholicPresence: Approx. one-third Catholic, the largest single church
history:
The first contact with Christianity on this coast came in the late 15th and 16th centuries through Portuguese sailors and missionaries active in the Kingdom of Kongo and around Loango, but lasting missions came only with French colonisation. From the 1880s the Spiritans (Holy Ghost Fathers) established missions; Bishop Prosper Augouard travelled the Congo River for decades, founding stations and the first cathedral in Brazzaville. The mission brought schools and health care, though it was also bound up with the colonial order.

After independence in 1960, the country adopted a Marxist-Leninist regime in 1969 and the Church faced restrictions. In 1977, after the assassination of President Marien Ngouabi, Cardinal Émile Biayenda, the beloved Congolese Archbishop of Brazzaville, was abducted and killed; his cause for beatification has been opened. Pope John Paul II visited in 1980.

When the one-party state ended, Bishop Ernest Kombo presided over the National Conference of 1991 that prepared the transition to democracy. The civil wars of the late 1990s brought great suffering, and the Church has worked for reconciliation, education and care for the displaced. Today it is a vital presence, alongside many Protestant and revival churches.

saints.name: Servant of God Cardinal Émile Biayenda
saints.story: Born in the Pool region, he became Archbishop of Brazzaville and in 1973 the first Congolese cardinal, known for simplicity, prayer and love for the poor. In March 1977, days after the assassination of the president, he was abducted and murdered. His cause for beatification is under way.

saints.name: Bishop Prosper Augouard, CSSp (missionary)
saints.story: A French Spiritan who arrived in the 1880s and spent nearly forty years as a missionary along the Congo and Ubangi rivers, travelling by steamboat to found missions and building the Sacred Heart Cathedral in Brazzaville. A forceful figure of the colonial era, he laid the foundations of the Church in the country.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1890s under Bishop Augouard, it is one of the oldest cathedrals in Central Africa and the mother church of the Archdiocese of Brazzaville. Cardinal Biayenda is buried here, and it has been a gathering place for prayer in the country's hardest moments.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Sainte-Anne du Congo
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1940s to designs by the French architect Roger Erell, it is famous for its roof of shining green tiles and its tall, pointed arches inspired by both Gothic forms and African tradition. It is one of Brazzaville's best-loved landmarks and a lively parish.

prayerIntention: For the Republic of the Congo, that its people may live in lasting peace and justice, and that the witness of Cardinal Biayenda may inspire reconciliation and courage.

name: Romania
catholicPresence: Catholic minority, approx. 5% (Latin and Greek Catholic)
history:
Christianity reached the lands of present-day Romania in Roman and late antique times, and most Romanians belong to the Orthodox Church. Catholic communities developed in the Middle Ages among Hungarians, Saxons and other peoples of Transylvania and among the Csángós of Moldavia, with the ancient Diocese of Transylvania centred at Alba Iulia. Around 1700 a large part of the Romanian Orthodox clergy of Transylvania entered into union with Rome while keeping their Byzantine liturgy, forming the Romanian Greek-Catholic Church, which became a cradle of Romanian culture and national awakening at Blaj.

Under communism the Church suffered greatly. In 1948 the Greek-Catholic Church was outlawed and its property handed to the Orthodox Church; all its bishops were imprisoned, and several died in prison. Latin Catholic bishops and priests were also jailed and killed. Faith survived in secret, through hidden ordinations and Masses in homes.

After 1989 both Churches were able to rebuild, though disputes over confiscated churches remain painful. Pope John Paul II's visit in 1999 was the first by a pope to a mainly Orthodox country, and in 2019 Pope Francis beatified seven martyred Greek-Catholic bishops at Blaj, praying for unity between Catholics and Orthodox.

patronSaints.name: St. Andrew the Apostle (traditional patron, honoured with the Orthodox)

saints.name: Bl. Iuliu Hossu and six companion bishops
saints.story: Greek-Catholic Bishop of Cluj-Gherla, Hossu read the declaration of union of Transylvania with Romania in 1918. Arrested in 1948 with all his fellow bishops, he refused to renounce communion with Rome and spent his last years under house arrest. Named cardinal in secret, he was beatified with six martyr bishops in 2019.

saints.name: Bl. Vladimir Ghika
saints.story: A Romanian prince and diplomat who converted from Orthodoxy, became a priest and served the poor, the sick and the outcast in Paris and Bucharest. Refusing to leave Romania under communism, he was imprisoned and died in Jilava prison after harsh treatment. He was beatified as a martyr in 2013.

saints.name: Bl. Anton Durcovici
saints.story: Bishop of Iaşi, arrested in 1949 for remaining faithful to Rome. He was held in the prison of Sighet, where he died of hunger and cold, deprived of care. He was beatified as a martyr in Iaşi in 2014.

saints.name: Bl. Veronica Antal
saints.story: A young Franciscan tertiary from a Csángó village in Moldavia who longed to be a nun at a time when convents were closed. Walking home from Mass, she was attacked and killed while resisting rape. She was beatified as a martyr of purity in 2018.

cathedrals.name: St. Michael's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The oldest and most important Latin cathedral in Romania, built mainly in the 13th century in Romanesque and Gothic style and later enlarged. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Alba Iulia and holds the tomb of John Hunyadi, the 15th-century defender of Christian Europe.

cathedrals.name: St. Joseph's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1870s and 1880s in a blend of Romanesque and Gothic revival styles, it is the cathedral of the Latin Archdiocese of Bucharest. In recent years its community defended it against a high-rise built beside it, and it remains a place of prayer and concerts.

cathedrals.name: Franciscan Shrine of Şumuleu Ciuc (Csíksomlyó)
cathedrals.story: A Franciscan church holding a venerated statue of the Virgin, and the destination of a vast Pentecost pilgrimage of Hungarian-speaking Catholics. In 2019 Pope Francis celebrated Mass here on the open hillside in the rain before a large crowd.

prayerIntention: For Romania, that Catholics and Orthodox may grow in mutual love and unity, that the memory of its martyrs may bear fruit, and that all its peoples may live in justice and peace.

name: Russia
history:
The baptism of Prince Vladimir of Kyiv in 988, before the split between East and West, brought Christianity to the lands of Rus', and the Russian people became overwhelmingly Orthodox. Catholics in Russia were mostly foreigners and minorities: merchants, Poles, Lithuanians, Germans, French and Italians. In the 18th and 19th centuries Catholic churches were built in St. Petersburg, Moscow and many provincial cities, and Russia's annexation of Polish and Lithuanian lands brought millions of Catholics under the tsars, who often restricted them.

After 1917 the Soviet state attacked all religion. Catholic churches were closed, and bishops, priests and lay people were shot or sent to the camps; by the late 1930s only a couple of churches serving foreign diplomats remained open. A small Russian Byzantine Catholic community, led by Bl. Leonid Feodorov, was also crushed.

After the fall of communism, Catholic life revived: churches were returned or rebuilt, and in 2002 four dioceses were established, based in Moscow, Saratov, Novosibirsk and Irkutsk. The community remains small and diverse, and relations with the Orthodox Church have known both tension and dialogue, including the 2016 meeting between Pope Francis and Patriarch Kirill. The war against Ukraine has brought new grief and division.

saints.name: Bl. Leonid Feodorov
saints.story: Born in St. Petersburg to an Orthodox family, he became Catholic, was ordained in the Byzantine rite and was named exarch of the Russian Greek Catholic Church. Arrested by the Soviets, he spent years in prisons and the Solovki camp, and died in exile. He was beatified as a martyr in 2001.

saints.name: Bl. Teofilius Matulionis
saints.story: A Lithuanian priest who served Catholics in St. Petersburg and was secretly ordained bishop there. He endured Soviet prisons and the Solovki camp, later became Bishop of Kaišiadorys in Lithuania, and suffered further imprisonment. He was beatified as a martyr in 2017.

saints.name: Servant of God Anna (Mother Catherine) Abrikosova
saints.story: A Moscow woman from a wealthy family who became Catholic and founded a community of Dominican sisters of the Byzantine rite. Arrested in 1923 with her sisters, she spent years in prison and exile and died in a Moscow prison hospital. Her cause for beatification has been opened.

saints.name: Servant of God Walter Ciszek, SJ
saints.story: An American Jesuit of Polish descent who secretly entered the Soviet Union to minister to Catholics. Arrested as a 'Vatican spy', he spent 23 years in prisons and Siberian labour camps, celebrating Mass in secret. His book 'He Leadeth Me' is a classic of trust in God.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: A great red-brick neo-Gothic church built between 1899 and 1911 by Moscow's Polish community. Under Soviet rule it was closed and used as a warehouse and hostel. Returned to the Church and restored, it was consecrated again in 1999 and is now the largest Catholic church in Russia.

cathedrals.name: Church of St. Catherine of Alexandria
cathedrals.story: Built on Nevsky Prospect in the second half of the 18th century, it is the oldest Catholic church in Russia still standing in use. Closed by the Soviets and badly damaged by fire in 1984, it was returned to the Church in the 1990s and lovingly restored.

cathedrals.name: Church of St. Louis of the French
cathedrals.story: Founded for the French community, its present building dates from the 19th century. It was one of the very few Catholic churches that remained open throughout the Soviet era, a lifeline for Catholics of every nation in the capital.

prayerIntention: For Russia, for an end to war and for true peace, for all who suffer, and for unity and love between Catholic and Orthodox Christians.

name: Rwanda
history:
Catholic missionaries, the Missionaries of Africa (White Fathers), arrived in Rwanda in 1900 and founded the mission of Save. Growth was slow at first, but in the 1930s, after the Belgian authorities deposed King Musinga and installed his son, came a wave of mass conversions. King Mutara III Rudahigwa was baptised in 1943 and in 1946 dedicated Rwanda to Christ the King. The Church built schools, hospitals and the first Rwandan seminary, yet it was also closely tied to colonial power and helped harden the categories of Hutu and Tutsi.

In 1994, during the genocide against the Tutsi, around 800,000 people were killed in about a hundred days. Many were murdered in churches where they had sought refuge, and some priests, religious and church members took part in the killing, while others hid and saved people at the cost of their lives. Clergy were also killed, including the Archbishop of Kigali.

In 2016 the Rwandan bishops asked forgiveness for the failings of the Church, and in 2017 Pope Francis implored God's forgiveness for the sins of the Church and its members. Today the Church is involved in healing, reconciliation and education. The apparitions of Our Lady at Kibeho (1981–1989) have been officially approved.

patronSaints.name: Christ the King (Rwanda was dedicated to him in 1946)
Our Lady of Kibeho, Mother of the Word

saints.name: Servant of God Cyprien and Daphrose Rugamba
saints.story: Cyprien, a poet and composer of beloved Rwandan sacred music, and his wife Daphrose, who served street children, founded the Emmanuel Community in Rwanda. They were killed with several of their children in the first days of the genocide. Their cause for beatification was opened in 2015.

saints.name: Sr. Félicitas Niyitegeka
saints.story: A Rwandan religious sister in Gisenyi who sheltered Tutsi refugees during the genocide. Her own brother, a colonel, urged her to escape, but she chose to stay with those in her care, and was killed with them. Rwanda honours her among its national heroes.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Kibeho
cathedrals.story: Built at the site where, from 1981, young students at a girls' school reported apparitions of the Virgin Mary as 'Mother of the Word', calling for prayer, conversion and the Rosary of the Seven Sorrows. The visions also foretold terrible bloodshed. Approved in 2001, it draws pilgrims from across Africa.

cathedrals.name: Kabgayi Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The oldest cathedral in Rwanda, built in the 1920s at the historic heart of the Church in the country, surrounded by schools, a hospital and a printing house. In 1994 thousands of displaced people sheltered here, and nearby the Archbishop of Kigali and other bishops and priests were killed.

cathedrals.name: Nyamata Church Genocide Memorial
cathedrals.story: A Catholic parish church where thousands of people who had taken refuge were killed in April 1994. It is no longer used for worship but kept as a memorial, with the victims' clothes laid on the pews. It is a place of silent prayer, sorrow and the commitment 'never again'.

prayerIntention: For Rwanda, that through Our Lady of Kibeho its people may continue the hard path of healing, truth and reconciliation, and that the Church may serve them in humility.

name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
history:
Saint Kitts was settled by both the English and the French in the 17th century, and the French colonists brought Catholic worship, including a church dedicated to Notre Dame. The island was also a centre of the plantation economy built on the enslavement of Africans, a deep wound in its history. After the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 gave the whole island to Britain, public Catholic worship was forbidden, and the Anglican and later Methodist churches shaped the islands' Christian life.

Catholic life revived in the 19th century after laws against Catholics were eased in 1829. Irish and Portuguese immigrants strengthened the small community; a first resident priest arrived in the 1840s and a church was begun in Basseterre in the 1850s. In 1928 a new stone church was dedicated there, which became a co-cathedral in 1981.

Today Catholics are a small, faithful minority in a mainly Protestant federation, served by a few parishes on Saint Kitts and on Nevis. They belong to the Diocese of Saint John's–Basseterre, whose bishop resides in Antigua, and take part in the life of the wider Caribbean Church through schools, charity and ecumenical friendship.

cathedrals.name: Co-Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Built of grey stone on the site of an earlier 19th-century church and dedicated in 1928, using materials brought from Nevis. It became the co-cathedral of the Diocese of Saint John's–Basseterre in 1981. Its quiet, dignified interior is the spiritual home of the small Catholic community of the federation.

prayerIntention: For the people of Saint Kitts and Nevis, that they may live in peace and solidarity, and that the small Catholic community may be a joyful witness of Christ's love.

name: Saint Lucia
history:
Saint Lucia, named in honour of St. Lucy, was fought over by France and Britain, changing hands many times between the 17th and early 19th centuries. French settlers and missionaries brought the Catholic faith, which took deep root among the enslaved Africans brought to work the plantations and their descendants, and was expressed in the island's French-based Kwéyòl language and culture. Britain took lasting control in 1814, but the people remained largely Catholic.

After emancipation in the 1830s, the Church grew through parishes and schools, and in the 1890s the great Church of the Immaculate Conception was built in Castries. Saint Lucia became a diocese in the 1950s and an archdiocese in 1974, and the Church played a significant role in education and in shaping national identity as the island moved to independence in 1979.

The Saint Lucian painter Dunstan St. Omer helped bring the faith into local form, painting Christ, Mary and the saints as Caribbean people on church walls. Today the Church remains the largest in the country, though evangelical churches are growing, and it faces challenges of youth unemployment, migration and crime. The national day, 13 December, is the feast of St. Lucy.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral Basilica of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1890s and one of the largest churches in the Caribbean, it has a simple exterior and a warm, colourful interior. Its walls were painted by Dunstan St. Omer with saints and biblical scenes in the faces and colours of Saint Lucia. It was named a minor basilica in 1999.

prayerIntention: For Saint Lucia, through the intercession of St. Lucy, that its young people may find hope and work, and that its families and communities may live in peace.

name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
history:
The first Catholic presence in Saint Vincent dates from the 1650s, when French Jesuits, invited by a Carib (Kalinago) chief, lived among the Indigenous people at Barrouallie. The island was long contested by the Kalinago and Garifuna peoples, the French and the British. Britain finally took control, and in 1797 most of the Garifuna were deported to Central America, a painful chapter of the island's history. The plantation economy depended on enslaved Africans, and the Anglican and Methodist churches became predominant.

Catholic life was rebuilt in the 19th century. In 1815 Fr. Joseph Antoine Rendon arrived and built a small wooden church in Kingstown, and Portuguese immigrants from Madeira, who came in the 1840s after emancipation, strengthened the community. From 1919 to 1957 Belgian Benedictine monks served the island; one of them, Dom Charles Verbeke, led a remarkable building programme, including the present cathedral.

The Diocese of Kingstown was established in 1989. Today Catholics are a minority among many Christian denominations, active in schools, social care and ecumenical cooperation, and supporting their people through hurricanes and the 2021 eruption of La Soufrière volcano.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Assumption (St. Mary's Cathedral)
cathedrals.story: A church built in stages from the 1820s and completed in its present form in the 1930s under Dom Charles Verbeke. It is famous for its fanciful mix of Romanesque, Byzantine, Moorish, Venetian and Flemish elements in dark stone, with turrets and arches unlike anything else in the Caribbean. It became the diocese's sole cathedral in 1989.

prayerIntention: For Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, that its people may be protected from disaster, rebuild with hope, and grow in unity, justice and faith.

name: Samoa
history:
Christianity came to Samoa first through Protestant missionaries of the London Missionary Society in 1830, and Congregational and Methodist churches remain strong. Catholic missionaries, French Marist priests sent to evangelise the islands of the Western Pacific, arrived in 1845. They were welcomed by some chiefs, learned the Samoan language and worked patiently despite rivalry and suspicion between missions. In the 1850s Bishop Pierre Bataillon laid the foundation stone of a stone cathedral at Mulivai in Apia.

The Catholic community grew through village catechists, schools and religious sisters, and Samoan Catholics became missionaries to other islands. The Church lived through German and then New Zealand colonial rule and the struggle for independence, achieved in 1962. In 1973 Pio Taofinu'u, Samoa's first Samoan bishop, was named a cardinal, the first from the Pacific Islands. He encouraged the inculturation of the liturgy, including the use of the traditional 'ava ceremony.

Today Samoa's constitution declares the nation founded on God, and Christian faith shapes daily life, village culture and Sunday rest. Catholics form a significant and active minority, and the Archdiocese of Samoa–Apia serves them. Climate change, migration and economic hardship are among the challenges the Church helps families to face.

saints.name: Cardinal Pio Taofinu'u, SM (church leader, not a canonized saint)
saints.story: A Samoan Marist who became Bishop of Apia and, in 1973, the first cardinal from the Pacific Islands. He worked to root the liturgy in Samoan culture and to strengthen the local Church, and later became Samoa's first archbishop. He is remembered with deep affection across Polynesia.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (Mulivai Cathedral)
cathedrals.story: The first stone cathedral was begun in 1852 on Apia's waterfront and completed in 1857. After the old building became unsafe, a new cathedral was built on the same site and opened in 2014. With its white façade facing the sea, it is a landmark of the capital and the heart of Samoan Catholic life.

prayerIntention: For Samoa, that its people may remain founded on God, care for their islands and their families, and grow in unity among all Christians.

name: San Marino
history:
San Marino traces its origins to St. Marinus, a Christian stonemason from the island of Rab in Dalmatia who, according to tradition, came to Rimini in the early 4th century and withdrew to Mount Titano to live as a hermit. A small Christian community gathered around him, and tradition holds that he left them free from any lord but God. From this community grew the world's oldest surviving republic, which counts its founding from the year 301.

Through the centuries San Marino defended its independence, often with the help of its faith. In 1739 the papal legate Cardinal Alberoni occupied the republic, but its liberty was restored on 5 February 1740, the feast of St. Agatha, who became co-patron. Churches and convents, such as the Franciscan friary from the 14th century, shaped its life, and the present Basilica of St. Marinus was built in the 1830s.

The republic belongs to the Diocese of San Marino-Montefeltro, whose seat is in nearby Italy. Catholicism remains part of national identity, and Pope Benedict XVI visited in 2011. Like much of Europe, San Marino faces declining religious practice and has adopted laws that differ from Church teaching, yet its feasts remain deeply rooted.

saints.name: St. Marinus
saints.story: A stonemason from Rab who, by tradition, worked in Rimini, was ordained a deacon and retreated to Mount Titano as a hermit to escape persecution and false accusations. The community that formed around him became the Republic of San Marino. His relics rest in the basilica that bears his name.

saints.name: St. Leo of Montefeltro
saints.story: According to tradition, a fellow stonemason and companion of Marinus from Dalmatia, who became a priest and lived as a hermit on Monte Feltro, where the town of San Leo now bears his name. He is honoured as an evangeliser of the region around San Marino.

saints.name: St. Agatha
saints.story: A young virgin martyr of Catania in Sicily. San Marino adopted her as co-patron because its freedom was restored on her feast, 5 February 1740, after the occupation by Cardinal Alberoni. The anniversary is still kept as a national holiday.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of San Marino (Basilica del Santo)
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1830s on the site of an ancient church, this Neoclassical basilica with a columned portico holds the relics of St. Marinus under the high altar. It is the principal church of the republic, where its civic and religious feasts are celebrated.

cathedrals.name: Church and Friary of St. Francis
cathedrals.story: Founded by the Franciscans in the 14th century, it is the oldest church in the city. Its cloister and museum hold notable paintings, and it has long been a place of prayer and learning for the people of the republic.

prayerIntention: For San Marino, that the freedom born of St. Marinus' faith may be lived in service of every human life, the family and the common good.

name: Sao Tome and Principe
history:
The islands of São Tomé and Príncipe were uninhabited when Portuguese navigators reached them around 1470; São Tomé was named for St. Thomas, on whose feast it was reportedly discovered. The Portuguese brought settlers, including Jewish children forcibly taken from their families, and large numbers of enslaved Africans to work sugar plantations, making the islands a hub of the Atlantic slave trade. The Catholic Church arrived with them, and the Diocese of São Tomé was created in 1534, one of the oldest in sub-Saharan Africa.

For centuries the Church struggled with few priests and the brutal plantation system. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, cocoa plantations relied on forced contract labour from Angola and Cape Verde, which drew international condemnation. Even so, Catholic faith became woven into local culture, festivals and traditional theatre such as the Tchiloli.

After independence in 1975 a one-party Marxist government limited the Church, but religious freedom returned with democracy in 1990. Pope John Paul II visited in 1992. Today Catholics form the majority in this small island nation, alongside growing Protestant and other churches, and the Church works in education, health and the fight against poverty.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Grace (Sé Catedral de Nossa Senhora da Graça)
cathedrals.story: The seat of one of the oldest dioceses in sub-Saharan Africa, with origins in the 16th century and rebuilt and restored several times since. Its simple white façade stands near the presidential palace, and it remains the heart of Catholic life on the islands.

prayerIntention: For São Tomé and Príncipe, that its people may overcome poverty and the wounds of slavery, and live in justice, peace and hope.

name: Saudi Arabia
catholicPresence: Large migrant Catholic population (estimates exceed one million); virtually no Saudi Catholics, and no public worship
history:
Before Islam, Christianity was present in parts of the Arabian Peninsula. In the south-west, the city of Najran, now in Saudi Arabia, had a flourishing Christian community, and in 523 many of its faithful were massacred for refusing to renounce Christ. They are honoured as the Martyrs of Najran, with their leader St. Arethas. Christian Arab tribes also lived in the north and east. After the rise of Islam, these communities gradually disappeared from the peninsula.

In modern times, Catholics have come to Saudi Arabia in great numbers as workers, especially from the Philippines, India, Sri Lanka and other countries, serving in hospitals, homes, construction and industry. They belong to the Apostolic Vicariate of Northern Arabia, whose bishop resides in Bahrain. There are no churches in the country, public non-Muslim worship is not permitted, and Catholics gather discreetly in private, often without a priest; many go long periods without the sacraments.

In recent years there have been signs of dialogue, including a visit by the Vatican's leading official for interreligious dialogue in 2018. Many migrants live far from their families, sometimes in difficult or exploitative conditions. Their quiet faith, prayed in homes and hearts, is a hidden treasure of the Church.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady of Arabia (patroness of the Vicariates of Arabia)

saints.name: St. Arethas (al-Harith) and the Martyrs of Najran
saints.story: Arethas was a leading elder of the Christian community of Najran, in the south of today's Saudi Arabia. When a ruler of Himyar besieged the city and demanded that Christians renounce their faith, Arethas and many men, women and children chose death rather than deny Christ. They are honoured in the Roman Martyrology.

prayerIntention: For the people of Saudi Arabia and for the many hidden Catholics who live and work there, that they may be treated with justice and dignity, and that freedom of worship may one day grow.

name: Senegal
catholicPresence: Catholic minority (approx. 5%) in a mainly Muslim country
history:
Christianity first touched the coast of Senegal through Portuguese navigators and chaplains in the 15th century, and later through French trading posts at Saint-Louis and Gorée. These islands were also centres of the Atlantic slave trade, a tragedy that marked the region deeply. Lasting missionary work began in the 19th century: Bl. Anne-Marie Javouhey's Sisters of St. Joseph of Cluny cared for the sick and taught children, and the Spiritans (Holy Ghost Fathers) founded missions along the coast and in the interior.

The Church grew especially among the Serer and Diola peoples and in the cities, building schools and hospitals. The Marian shrine of Poponguine, founded in 1888, became a national place of pilgrimage. In 1960 Senegal became independent under Léopold Sédar Senghor, a Catholic poet and statesman who led a mainly Muslim nation for twenty years, a sign of the country's remarkable religious harmony. Hyacinthe Thiandoum became the first Senegalese cardinal in 1976.

In 1992 Pope John Paul II visited the 'House of Slaves' on Gorée and asked forgiveness for the sins of Christians in the slave trade. Today Catholics are a small but respected minority, valued for their schools and health care, and Muslims and Christians often share each other's feasts and family ties.

saints.name: Bl. Anne-Marie Javouhey
saints.story: A French foundress of the Sisters of St. Joseph of Cluny, she went to Senegal in 1822, caring for the sick in Saint-Louis and Gorée and dreaming of a local African clergy. She fought for the dignity of enslaved and freed Africans, and her sisters still serve in Senegal. She was beatified in 1950.

saints.name: Bl. Daniel Brottier, CSSp
saints.story: A French Spiritan who served as a missionary in Saint-Louis, Senegal, from 1903. Later, as a chaplain in World War I and director of an orphanage in Paris, he raised funds for the 'Souvenir Africain' cathedral in Dakar, honouring those who died in Africa. He was beatified in 1984.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Our Lady of Victories (Souvenir Africain)
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1936, the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Dakar blends Byzantine and Sudano-Sahelian influences, with a great dome and two towers. Built as a memorial to those who gave their lives in Africa, it is the mother church of Senegal's Catholics.

cathedrals.name: Marian Shrine of Our Lady of Deliverance (Notre-Dame de la Délivrance)
cathedrals.story: A seaside Marian shrine founded in 1888 by Spiritan missionaries. Each year at Pentecost, tens of thousands of pilgrims, many walking from Dakar and beyond, gather to pray with Mary. Muslims sometimes join them, and it is a sign of Senegal's harmony.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Saint-Louis
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1820s in the old colonial capital, it is often called the oldest church in West Africa. Its Neoclassical façade looks onto the historic island town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it has been carefully restored.

prayerIntention: For Senegal, that its precious harmony between Muslims and Christians may endure and grow, and that its people may prosper in peace and justice.

name: Serbia
catholicPresence: Catholic minority (approx. 4%), mostly Hungarians and Croats in Vojvodina
history:
Christianity took root in the region of today's Serbia in Roman times. Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) was an imperial city and early Christian centre, and Singidunum (Belgrade) had believers too. During the persecution under Diocletian, Christians such as Bishop Irenaeus of Sirmium and St. Anastasia were martyred. Later, Slavic peoples settled in the Balkans and received the faith, and from the 13th century, through St. Sava, the Serbian Orthodox Church shaped the nation's identity.

Catholics in Serbia have mainly been Hungarians, Croats, Germans, Slovaks and others, concentrated in Vojvodina, along with a small Greek Catholic community of Ruthenians and others. The Ottoman centuries, the Habsburg era and the wars of the 20th century brought great upheavals; after World War II the German population was expelled and many suffered, and under communism the Church was restricted. The wars of the 1990s deepened wounds between Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats.

Today Catholics form a small, diverse minority, organised in the Archdiocese of Belgrade and dioceses in Vojvodina, and since 2018 a Greek Catholic eparchy. Relations with the Orthodox Church have grown warmer through dialogue, and Catholics pray for healing among the peoples of the Balkans.

saints.name: St. Irenaeus of Sirmium
saints.story: A young bishop of Sirmium who, during Diocletian's persecution, refused to sacrifice to the gods despite the tears of his family. After torture he was beheaded and his body thrown into the Sava river. He is one of the earliest known martyrs of the region.

saints.name: St. Anastasia of Sirmium
saints.story: A Christian woman martyred at Sirmium under Diocletian, honoured since ancient times in East and West. Her relics were later taken to Constantinople, and she is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass. A Mass at dawn on Christmas Day was traditionally associated with her.

saints.name: Sts. Hermylus and Stratonicus
saints.story: Hermylus, a deacon, and Stratonicus, his jailer, who was converted by his courage, were martyred at Singidunum, today's Belgrade, under the emperor Licinius. They were drowned in the Danube. They are venerated in the Eastern and Western Churches.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral Basilica of St. Teresa of Ávila
cathedrals.story: A large Baroque church completed in the late 18th century, with twin towers and a bright interior, and later declared a minor basilica. It is the cathedral of the Diocese of Subotica and the spiritual home of the Hungarian and Croatian Catholics of northern Vojvodina.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Demetrius
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Diocese of Srijem, restored as a diocese in 2008, in the town that was once Roman Sirmium. It recalls the ancient Christian heritage of the city, where martyrs gave their lives in the persecutions of the early 4th century.

prayerIntention: For Serbia, that Orthodox and Catholic Christians may grow in mutual love and unity, and that all the peoples of the Balkans may live in reconciliation and peace.

name: Seychelles
history:
The Seychelles islands were uninhabited until French settlers arrived in the 1770s with enslaved Africans; Britain took control in the early 19th century. For decades there was no resident priest. In 1851 Fr. Léon des Avanchers, a Capuchin from Savoy, arrived, baptised and married many people, and consecrated the mission to Mary, the Immaculate Conception, though he was not allowed to stay. A prefecture was established in 1852, and Savoyard Capuchins took charge of the mission, later followed by Swiss Capuchins.

The Diocese of Port Victoria was created in 1892. Missionaries, brothers and sisters built schools and parishes on Mahé, Praslin and La Digue, and the Catholic faith became the faith of most Seychellois, expressed in Creole culture, music and processions. In 1975 Félix Paul became the first Seychellois bishop, shortly before independence in 1976.

Pope John Paul II visited the Seychelles in 1986. Today Catholics form a clear majority of this small island nation, and the Church remains engaged in education, family life and social care. It faces the challenges of a changing society, including drug abuse, migration and declining practice among the young, and the threat of rising seas to the islands themselves.

patronSaints.name: The Immaculate Conception (to whom the mission was consecrated in 1851)

saints.name: Fr. Léon des Avanchers, OFM Cap (missionary)
saints.story: A Savoyard Capuchin missionary who arrived in the Seychelles in 1851, the first priest to minister there. In a short stay he baptised and married many islanders and consecrated the mission to the Immaculate Conception, laying the foundations of Catholic life before being forced to leave. He later served in East Africa.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Founded in the 19th century and rebuilt after the diocese was created in 1892, the cathedral stands near the clock tower in the heart of the small capital. It was consecrated in 1952, the centenary of the mission. Its bells and Sunday Masses mark the rhythm of Seychellois life.

prayerIntention: For the Seychelles, that its people and its fragile islands may be protected, and that families and young people may find strength and hope in Christ.

name: Sierra Leone
catholicPresence: Catholic minority (approx. 5–10%, estimates vary) in a mainly Muslim country
history:
The first Catholic mission in Sierra Leone was led by the Portuguese Jesuit Baltasar Barreira, who worked on the coast from 1605 and baptised several local rulers, but the mission did not last. Freetown was founded in 1792 as a settlement for freed and formerly enslaved people, and Protestant missions shaped its Christian life. The Catholic mission was re-established in 1859 by Bishop Melchior de Marion Brésillac, founder of the Society of African Missions, who died of yellow fever in Freetown weeks after his arrival, along with several companions. From 1864 the Holy Ghost Fathers took up the mission and built schools that educated generations.

Sierra Leone's civil war (1991–2002) brought atrocities, amputations, child soldiers and mass displacement. Missionaries and local priests stayed with their people, some were kidnapped, and the Church worked tirelessly for peace, the rehabilitation of child soldiers and care for victims. In 2014 the Ebola epidemic struck, and Catholic hospitals and religious lost staff while caring for the sick.

Today Catholics are a minority, but Catholic schools and health care are highly valued. Sierra Leone is known for the peaceful coexistence of Muslims and Christians, who often share families and celebrations.

saints.name: Servant of God Melchior de Marion Brésillac
saints.story: A French missionary bishop who served in India and then founded the Society of African Missions in Lyon. He arrived in Freetown in 1859 to begin a mission, but yellow fever was raging and he died there with several of his companions within weeks. His society went on to serve across West Africa.

saints.name: Fr. Baltasar Barreira, SJ (missionary)
saints.story: A Portuguese Jesuit who, after years in Angola, went to the coast of Sierra Leone in 1605, the first Catholic missionary there. He learned about local customs and baptised several rulers, though his efforts did not leave a lasting Church.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Freetown, built in the late 19th century by the Holy Ghost Fathers in the old centre of the capital. It survived the turmoil of the civil war and is a place of prayer for peace, healing and the nation's future.

prayerIntention: For Sierra Leone, that the wounds of war and epidemic may be healed, that its young people may have hope and opportunity, and that Muslims and Christians may continue to live as brothers and sisters.

name: Singapore
history:
Catholicism in modern Singapore began only two years after the British trading post was founded. In December 1821 Fr. Laurent Imbert of the Paris Foreign Missions, who later died a martyr in Korea, visited and found a small community of about a dozen Catholics. Missionaries from Paris served the growing city, while a Portuguese mission connected to Macau and Goa built its own church, and the two jurisdictions coexisted for many years.

The French missionary Fr. Jean-Marie Beurel built the Church of the Good Shepherd, which later became the cathedral, and brought the De La Salle Brothers and the Sisters of the Infant Jesus, who founded schools that shaped generations of Singaporeans of every faith. Catholics came from many backgrounds: Chinese, Indian, Eurasian, European and later Filipino and other migrants. In 1972 Singapore became its own archdiocese.

Today Singapore is a multi-religious society where the Church lives in harmony with Buddhists, Taoists, Muslims, Hindus and others. Catholic schools, hospitals, hospices and charities are prominent. Archbishop William Goh became the first Singapore-born cardinal in 2022, and in September 2024 Pope Francis visited, celebrating Mass with tens of thousands. Many Catholics are adult converts, and the community continues to grow.

saints.name: St. Laurent Imbert
saints.story: A French priest of the Paris Foreign Missions who visited Singapore in 1821, celebrating Mass for its first small Catholic community. He went on to serve in China and became bishop in Korea, where he gave himself up to protect his flock and was martyred in 1839. He was canonized among the Korean Martyrs in 1984.

saints.name: Fr. Jean-Marie Beurel, MEP (missionary)
saints.story: A French missionary who arrived in Singapore in 1839 and built the Church of the Good Shepherd, now the cathedral. He brought religious brothers and sisters to found schools for boys and girls, laying lasting foundations for Catholic education in Singapore.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Good Shepherd
cathedrals.story: Completed in the 1840s, it is Singapore's oldest Catholic church and a national monument, with a Neoclassical design in the shape of a Latin cross and a slender spire. After major restoration it reopened in 2016. It is the seat of the Archbishop of Singapore.

cathedrals.name: Church of St. Alphonsus (Novena Church)
cathedrals.story: A Redemptorist church famed for its weekly novena to Our Lady of Perpetual Help, attracting thousands of people every Saturday, including many who are not Catholic. Its walls are filled with thanksgiving letters for prayers answered. It was rebuilt and enlarged in recent years.

cathedrals.name: Church of St. Joseph
cathedrals.story: Built by the Portuguese mission in Victoria Street in the early 20th century, this Gothic-style church with fine stained glass recalls the long history of the Portuguese and Eurasian Catholic community in Singapore. It is a national monument.

prayerIntention: For Singapore, that its harmony among religions and peoples may grow, that migrant workers and the vulnerable may be cared for, and that its Church may be a humble sign of Christ.

name: Slovakia
history:
Christianity reached the lands of Slovakia in the 9th century. Around 828 a church was consecrated at Nitra, and in 863 the brothers Cyril and Methodius came to Great Moravia from Byzantium, bringing the liturgy and Scriptures in the Slavic tongue and creating the first Slavic alphabet. Their mission made the Slavs a people of the Gospel, and they remain at the heart of Slovak identity. For many centuries Slovakia was part of the Kingdom of Hungary; Bratislava's cathedral saw the coronation of Hungarian kings. The Reformation and Counter-Reformation brought conflict, including the martyrdom of three priests in Košice in 1619.

In the 20th century, under communism, the Church was severely persecuted. In 1950 religious orders were dissolved overnight, the Greek Catholic Church was banned, and bishops, priests and sisters were imprisoned. A 'secret Church' of hidden priests and lay groups kept the faith alive, and in March 1988 the peaceful Candle Demonstration in Bratislava, calling for religious freedom, foreshadowed the fall of the regime.

Since 1989 the Church has rebuilt in freedom. Pope John Paul II visited three times and Pope Francis in 2021. Slovakia remains a largely Catholic country, though secularisation is growing and the Church is called to renewal.

saints.name: Sts. Melichar Grodziecki, Štefan Pongrácz and Marek Križin (Martyrs of Košice)
saints.story: Two Jesuits, one Polish-Silesian and one Hungarian, and a Croatian canon who served Catholics in Košice. During an anti-Habsburg uprising they were tortured and killed after refusing to renounce their Catholic faith. Pope John Paul II canonized them in Košice in 1995.

saints.name: Bl. Zdenka Schelingová
saints.story: A Sister of Mercy of the Holy Cross and nurse in Bratislava who helped a persecuted priest escape from a prison hospital. Arrested by the communist police, she was tortured and imprisoned, and released only when near death. She was beatified as a martyr in 2003.

saints.name: Bl. Pavol Peter Gojdič
saints.story: A Basilian monk and Greek Catholic Bishop of Prešov, loved for his kindness, who refused to break with Rome when the communists forced his Church into Orthodoxy in 1950. Sentenced to life imprisonment, he died in Leopoldov prison. He was beatified as a martyr in 2001.

saints.name: Bl. Anna Kolesárová
saints.story: A young girl from eastern Slovakia, prayerful and hard-working, who was shot in front of her family by a soldier at the end of World War II when she resisted his attempt to rape her. She was beatified as a martyr in 2018.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Seven Sorrows
cathedrals.story: The national shrine of Slovakia, a Baroque basilica built in the 18th century to house a statue of the Pietà venerated since the 16th century. On her feast, 15 September, crowds of pilgrims gather here, and Pope Francis celebrated Mass at the shrine in 2021.

cathedrals.name: St. Elisabeth Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The largest church in Slovakia, a masterpiece of Gothic architecture begun in the late 14th century and dedicated to St. Elizabeth of Hungary. Its carved portals, soaring nave and medieval altarpiece make it the jewel of eastern Slovakia.

cathedrals.name: St. Martin's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: A Gothic cathedral beneath Bratislava Castle where Hungarian kings and queens were crowned from 1563 to 1830. A gilded replica of the crown tops its spire. Inside, a striking statue of St. Martin sharing his cloak recalls the call to charity.

prayerIntention: For Slovakia, that through Our Lady of Sorrows and the heritage of Sts. Cyril and Methodius, its people may stay faithful, hopeful and united in love.

name: Slovenia
catholicPresence: Approx. 70% Catholic by baptism; practice is lower
history:
The ancestors of the Slovenes in Carantania received the faith in the 8th century through missionaries from Salzburg, notably those sent by St. Virgil, and from the Patriarchate of Aquileia. The Freising Manuscripts, written around the year 1000 and containing prayers and a confession, are the oldest surviving texts in Slovene. For centuries the Slovene lands were part of the Habsburg realm. The Reformation brought the first printed Slovene books, through the Protestant Primož Trubar, before the Counter-Reformation restored Catholicism.

In the 19th century Bishop Anton Martin Slomšek championed the Slovene language, education and Christian culture, and Slovene missionaries such as Frederic Baraga served far abroad. World War II and the communist revolution brought great suffering: priests and lay people were killed by various sides, and after the war thousands of people were executed without trial. Under communist Yugoslavia the Church was restricted and its believers disadvantaged.

Since independence in 1991 the Church has lived in freedom. Pope John Paul II visited in 1996 and 1999, beatifying Slomšek. Today most Slovenes are baptised Catholics, but practice has fallen, and the Church faces secularisation and the legacy of financial scandals in some dioceses, while seeking reconciliation over wartime wounds.

patronSaints.name: Our Lady Help of Christians of Brezje (Marija Pomagaj), honoured at the national shrine

saints.name: Bl. Anton Martin Slomšek
saints.story: Bishop of Lavant who moved his see to Maribor, he was a great educator, writer and pastor, promoting the Slovene language and schools and working for Christian unity. Pope John Paul II beatified him in Maribor in 1999, the first Slovene to be beatified.

saints.name: Bl. Lojze Grozde
saints.story: A young student and member of Catholic Action, devoted to the Eucharist and Mary. On his way home for New Year in 1943 he was captured by communist partisans, who found religious items with him; he was tortured and killed. He was beatified as a martyr in 2010.

saints.name: Ven. Frederic Baraga
saints.story: A Slovene priest who became a missionary among the Ottawa and Ojibwe peoples around the Great Lakes in North America, travelling on snowshoes and writing grammars and prayer books in their languages. He became the first bishop of what is now Marquette, Michigan, and was declared Venerable in 2012.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Mary Help of Christians
cathedrals.story: Slovenia's national Marian shrine, centred on a 19th-century painting of Mary Help of Christians that has drawn pilgrims for generations. Countless votive offerings line its chapel. It is the heart of Slovene Marian devotion.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Nicholas
cathedrals.story: A Baroque cathedral built in the early 18th century, with a green dome and rich frescoes inside. Its bronze doors, added for the 1996 papal visit, depict the history of Christianity among the Slovenes. It is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Ljubljana.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the Assumption, Sveta Gora
cathedrals.story: A hilltop shrine on the border with Italy, linked to a 16th-century apparition of Mary to a shepherdess. Destroyed in World War I, it was rebuilt afterwards and remains a beloved place of pilgrimage with sweeping views over the Soča valley.

prayerIntention: For Slovenia, that its people may be reconciled after past wounds, rediscover the joy of faith, and build a society of hope, family and solidarity.

name: Solomon Islands
history:
The first Christian contact with the Solomon Islands came in 1568, when the Spanish explorer Álvaro de Mendaña reached the islands and planted a cross, but no lasting mission followed. In 1845 Marist missionaries arrived under Bishop Jean-Baptiste Epalle, who was killed soon after landing on Santa Isabel. Disease and violence claimed several more missionaries, and the mission was abandoned. Anglican, Methodist and other Protestant missions became established in the meantime.

In 1898 the Marists returned under Bishop Julian Vidal and began a lasting mission, founding stations on Guadalcanal and other islands. Catechists, sisters and brothers built schools and clinics, and Catholic communities grew. During World War II, when Guadalcanal became a major battlefield, some missionaries, including priests and religious sisters, were killed. After the war the Church grew steadily, and in 1978 Honiara became an archdiocese, the year the new Holy Cross Cathedral was consecrated.

From 1998 to 2003 ethnic tensions brought violence and displacement, and the churches worked together for peace. Today Catholics are the second-largest Christian community in this deeply Christian nation, serving through parishes, schools and health care, and facing challenges of poverty, unrest and rising seas.

saints.name: Bishop Jean-Baptiste Epalle, SM (missionary)
saints.story: A French Marist named Vicar Apostolic of Melanesia and Micronesia, who led the first Catholic mission to the Solomon Islands in 1845. He was attacked and fatally wounded soon after landing on Santa Isabel. His sacrifice is remembered as the beginning of the Catholic Church in the islands.

cathedrals.name: Holy Cross Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1978 on a hill believed to be near where Mendaña's expedition raised the first cross in 1568, giving the cathedral its name. Its design reflects Pacific architecture, with carved altar and lectern by local artisans. It is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Honiara.

prayerIntention: For the Solomon Islands, that its people may live in peace and unity, that its islands and seas may be protected, and that its young people may find hope and opportunity.

name: Somalia
catholicPresence: Tiny Catholic presence (approx. a few hundred faithful or fewer)
history:
Christianity reached the Somali coast only faintly in earlier centuries; the Catholic Church took root mainly under Italian colonial rule from the late 19th century, when missionaries, among them the Consolata Fathers and later Franciscans, served Italian settlers and a small number of Somali converts. A Vicariate was established and, in 1975, the Diocese of Mogadishu, whose cathedral rose in the 1920s as one of the largest churches in Africa.

After independence and especially under the military regime, Catholic schools and works were nationalised and Somali Christians lived their faith in great secrecy. In 1989 Bishop Salvatore Colombo was shot dead in Mogadishu. The civil war that followed destroyed the cathedral, and violence later claimed the lives of faithful servants such as the lay missionary Annalena Tonelli (2003) and Sister Leonella Sgorbati (2006), who forgave her killers as she died.

Today there is no resident bishop; the diocese is cared for from neighbouring Djibouti, and the few Catholics who remain, mostly foreigners and hidden believers, pray quietly. The Church honours Somalia as a land watered by the blood of those who came only to heal and to serve.

saints.name: Bl. Leonella Sgorbati
saints.story: An Italian Consolata Missionary Sister who trained nurses at the SOS hospital in Mogadishu for years. She was shot outside the hospital in 2006; her last words were reportedly 'I forgive, I forgive, I forgive.' She was beatified in 2018 as a martyr, the first person beatified for a death on Somali soil.

saints.name: Bishop Salvatore Colombo (not canonized)
saints.story: An Italian Franciscan who served Somalia for decades and became Bishop of Mogadishu. Beloved for his gentleness and service to the poor, he was shot dead in 1989 in his cathedral area as the country slid into civil war. His witness of faithful presence remains a treasure of the small Somali Church.

saints.name: Annalena Tonelli (lay missionary, not canonized)
saints.story: An Italian laywoman who gave over thirty years to the sick of Kenya and Somalia, especially those with tuberculosis, living simply among Somali people. She was murdered in Borama in 2003. Though not beatified, her life is widely honoured as a pure witness of Christian love offered without any desire to convert by force.

cathedrals.name: Mogadishu Cathedral (ruins)
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1920s under Italian rule in a Norman-Gothic style inspired by Cefalù, it was once among the largest churches in Africa and the seat of the Diocese of Mogadishu. Heavily damaged during the civil war, it stands today as a roofless ruin, yet it remains a poignant symbol of the Church's past presence and of hope for peace.

prayerIntention: For the people of Somalia, worn by long years of war, drought and hunger: that the Lord grant them peace, bread and safety, and console every hidden believer who prays in secret.

name: South Africa
history:
Portuguese navigators planted crosses on South Africa's shores in the 1480s, but under Dutch rule Catholic worship was forbidden at the Cape. Religious freedom came in 1804, and in 1837 Bishop Patrick Raymond Griffith arrived as the first Vicar Apostolic. The Oblates of Mary Immaculate, the Trappists of Mariannhill under Abbot Francis Pfanner, and many congregations of sisters built missions, schools and hospitals across the land.

The Church's story is marked by the long shadow of apartheid. Some Catholic institutions followed the segregated patterns of society, but over time the Church became a courageous voice for justice: Archbishop Denis Hurley of Durban and the bishops' conference denounced apartheid as intrinsically evil, Catholic schools quietly opened to all races, and Regina Mundi church in Soweto sheltered students during the 1976 uprising.

Today the Church is largely Black and deeply rooted in African life, ministering amid poverty, unemployment, HIV and violence. In 2015 Benedict Daswa, a teacher killed for refusing to take part in witchcraft, became the first South African-born blessed, a sign of a faith now truly at home in the soil.

saints.name: Bl. Benedict Daswa
saints.story: A Venda teacher, headmaster, husband and father who converted to Catholicism as a young man. He refused to contribute money to a witch-doctor to hunt the 'witch' blamed for lightning strikes, and was stoned and killed in 1990. Beatified in 2015, he is South Africa's first native-born blessed and a martyr for truth over fear.

saints.name: Bl. Joseph Gérard, OMI
saints.story: A French Oblate who first served among the Zulu in Natal before going on to evangelise the Basotho. Patient through years of little visible fruit, he became known for tireless care of the sick and the poor. Beatified in 1988, he is honoured across Southern Africa as a pioneer missionary.

saints.name: Archbishop Denis Hurley, OMI (not canonized)
saints.story: Archbishop of Durban for over four decades, he was one of the strongest Christian voices against apartheid and a significant participant at the Second Vatican Council. He faced trial and threats for exposing police abuses. Though not canonized, he is remembered as a prophet of justice and reconciliation.

cathedrals.name: St. Mary's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Opened in 1851 near the Houses of Parliament, it is the mother church of Catholicism in South Africa, built soon after the faithful were finally allowed to worship freely. Its simple Gothic Revival lines have watched the whole story of the nation unfold, from colonial times through apartheid to democracy.

cathedrals.name: Regina Mundi Church
cathedrals.story: The largest Catholic church in South Africa, completed in 1962. During apartheid, when political gatherings were banned, it became a place of meeting, mourning and resistance; in 1976 police fired into the church, and the bullet marks remain. Its 'Black Madonna' painting and its history make it a beloved pilgrimage site.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Emmanuel
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1904, this neo-Gothic cathedral stands beside the busy Warwick market area. Under Archbishop Denis Hurley it became known for welcoming people of every race, and today it serves the city's poor and homeless with feeding schemes and pastoral care.

cathedrals.name: Mariannhill Monastery
cathedrals.story: Founded in 1882 by Trappist Abbot Francis Pfanner, Mariannhill grew into one of the largest monasteries in the world and the cradle of a missionary congregation. Its church, schools and workshops shaped generations of Zulu Catholics, and it remains a place of prayer and pilgrimage.

prayerIntention: For South Africa: that the wounds of apartheid, violence and poverty be healed, and that its people, rich in many tongues, walk together in justice, reconciliation and hope.

name: South Korea
history:
The Korean Church is unique in Christian history: it was founded not by missionaries but by lay scholars. Studying Catholic books brought from China, they sent Yi Seung-hun to Beijing, where he was baptized in 1784; on his return he baptized his friends, and a lay community was born. Priests came only years later, often in secret.

The young Church paid dearly. Great persecutions in 1801, 1839, 1846 and 1866 killed perhaps ten thousand believers, from noblemen to servants, mothers and children. In 1984 Pope John Paul II canonized 103 Korean martyrs in Seoul, the first canonization outside Rome in modern times, and in 2014 Pope Francis beatified Paul Yun Ji-chung and 123 companions.

After liberation and the devastation of the Korean War, the Church grew remarkably in the South, earning respect through its defence of human rights during the years of military rule, when Myeongdong Cathedral sheltered protesters. Today South Korean Catholics are numerous, educated and missionary, though they face secularisation and a falling birth rate. In the North, the Church remains silenced, and Korean Catholics pray daily for reunification.

patronSaints.name: Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary

saints.name: St. Andrew Kim Taegon
saints.story: The first Korean-born priest. Sent abroad to study at Macau, he was ordained in Shanghai and returned secretly to serve his people. Arrested while arranging a route for missionaries, he was beheaded near Seoul at age 25. He is patron of the Korean clergy and shares a feast with his fellow martyrs on September 20.

saints.name: St. Paul Chong Hasang
