saints.story: A layman who travelled repeatedly to Beijing, at great risk, to beg for priests for Korea. He wrote a defence of the faith addressed to the government and was martyred in 1839. Together with St. Andrew Kim he leads the 103 Korean martyrs canonized in 1984.

saints.name: Bl. Paul Yun Ji-chung
saints.story: A scholar from Jinsan who became the first Korean Catholic martyr, executed at Jeonju for refusing to perform Confucian ancestral rites in the manner then demanded. He was beatified with 123 companions by Pope Francis in Seoul in 2014.

saints.name: St. Laurent Imbert
saints.story: A French bishop of the Paris Foreign Missions who entered Korea secretly in 1837. When persecution struck, he gave himself up to spare his flock and was beheaded with two fellow priests. He is among the 103 canonized martyrs and is honoured as a true shepherd who laid down his life.

cathedrals.name: Myeongdong Cathedral (Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception)
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1898, this red-and-grey brick Gothic Revival church was one of the first large Western-style buildings in Korea. Relics of martyrs rest in its crypt. In the 1970s and 1980s it became a sanctuary for pro-democracy protesters, making it a symbol of both faith and human dignity.

cathedrals.name: Jeoldusan Martyrs' Shrine
cathedrals.story: On this cliff above the Han River, many Catholics were beheaded during the persecution of 1866; the name means 'Beheading Mountain'. A church and museum now honour the martyrs, and Pope John Paul II prayed here in 1984. It is a place of quiet, heartfelt pilgrimage.

cathedrals.name: Jeondong Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1914 in a Romanesque-Byzantine style on the very spot where Paul Yun Ji-chung and other early martyrs were executed. Its graceful brick facade is among the most beautiful church buildings in Korea, and its history makes it a living memorial of the first Korean martyrs.

cathedrals.name: Seosomun Martyrs' Shrine
cathedrals.story: Just outside Seoul's old west gate stood the main execution ground of the Joseon era, where many Catholics died, including dozens of the canonized martyrs. Today a memorial park and museum honour the largest number of Korean saints martyred at a single site.

prayerIntention: For South Korea and the whole Korean peninsula: that the faith of the martyrs bear fruit in peace, reconciliation and reunification, and that families and the young find true hope in Christ.

name: South Sudan
catholicPresence: Large Catholic community (approx. 35–40%), the country's biggest church
history:
Christianity first flowered along the Nile in the ancient Nubian kingdoms to the north, but the Catholic mission to the peoples of what is now South Sudan began in the 19th century. St. Daniel Comboni, with his vision to 'save Africa through Africa', and the missionaries who followed him laboured among the Dinka, Shilluk, Bari and other peoples, often at the cost of their own lives from disease.

The 20th century brought deep suffering. Khartoum governments pressed Arabisation and Islamisation on the South; in 1964 foreign missionaries were expelled, and through two long civil wars the Church stayed with the people, its catechists and local clergy carrying the faith in displacement camps and in the bush. Churches became places of refuge, schools and food distribution.

Independence in 2011 brought hope, but civil war broke out again in 2013, with terrible ethnic violence. Pope Francis knelt to kiss the feet of the country's rival leaders in 2019, begging them for peace, and in 2023 he made an ecumenical pilgrimage of peace to Juba with the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Moderator of the Church of Scotland. The Church today is young, wounded and resilient.

saints.name: St. Daniel Comboni
saints.story: An Italian missionary who devoted his life to Central Africa, founding missionary institutes of priests and sisters and becoming bishop and Vicar Apostolic of Central Africa, with his seat at Khartoum. He fought the slave trade and believed Africans themselves would be the evangelisers of their continent. He died in Khartoum and was canonized in 2003.

saints.name: St. Josephine Bakhita
saints.story: Born in Darfur, she was kidnapped as a child and sold into slavery many times. In Italy she discovered Christ, won her freedom and became a Canossian sister, known for gentleness and joy. Canonized in 2000, she is beloved throughout both Sudans as a sign that God never forgets the suffering.

saints.name: Bishop Cesare Mazzolari, MCCJ (not canonized)
saints.story: An Italian Comboni missionary who served as Bishop of Rumbek during the civil war, often moving with his scattered people and founding schools and clinics. He died while celebrating Mass shortly after independence. Though not canonized, he is remembered as a shepherd who refused to leave his flock.

cathedrals.name: St. Theresa's Cathedral, Kator
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Juba, a gathering place for the capital's Catholics through war and independence. Its grounds have hosted great celebrations and prayers for peace, and it stands at the heart of the national Church's life as the seat of the metropolitan archbishop.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Mary Help of Christians
cathedrals.story: A large brick cathedral built by the Comboni missionaries in the colonial era, among the most impressive church buildings in the region. During the wars it sheltered thousands of displaced people within its compound, embodying the Church's role as refuge in times of terror.

prayerIntention: For South Sudan, the world's youngest nation: that its leaders choose peace, that hunger and violence end, and that every child may grow up safe in the land of their ancestors.

name: Spain
catholicPresence: Majority Catholic heritage (approx. 55–60% identify as Catholic)
history:
Tradition holds that the Apostle James preached in Hispania and that Our Lady appeared to him on a pillar at Zaragoza; St. Paul hoped to travel there too. By the 4th century the Church was well established, and the Visigothic King Reccared embraced Catholic faith in 589. After the Muslim conquest of 711, Christian kingdoms in the north slowly expanded southward over nearly eight centuries, while the pilgrimage to the tomb of St. James at Compostela bound Spain to the whole of Europe.

The year 1492 brought the fall of Granada, the expulsion of the Jews and the voyage to the Americas. Spain's Golden Age gave the Church giants of holiness, Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross, Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, but also the Inquisition and the violence of conquest overseas, which friars like Bartolomé de las Casas courageously denounced.

The modern era was turbulent: anticlerical laws, and in the Civil War of 1936–39 the killing of thousands of priests, religious and laypeople, followed by decades of a state Church under Franco. Since democracy, Spain has secularised rapidly and faced the pain of abuse revelations, yet its processions, shrines, pilgrimages and missionaries still radiate a deep and living faith.

saints.name: St. Teresa of Ávila
saints.story: A Carmelite nun who reformed her order with fearless determination and founded many convents of the Discalced Carmelites. Her writings, the Interior Castle and her Life, are masterpieces of mystical prayer described with humour and honesty. In 1970 she became the first woman declared a Doctor of the Church.

saints.name: St. John of the Cross
saints.story: Teresa's companion in the Carmelite reform, imprisoned by his own brothers, he wrote some of the most beautiful poetry in the Spanish language in his cell. His Dark Night of the Soul and Spiritual Canticle guide souls through suffering into union with God. He is a Doctor of the Church.

saints.name: St. Ignatius of Loyola
saints.story: A Basque soldier wounded at Pamplona, he was converted while convalescing by reading the lives of Christ and the saints. His Spiritual Exercises taught generations to find God in all things, and he founded the Society of Jesus, which became a great force for education and mission.

saints.name: St. Francis Xavier
saints.story: A Navarrese nobleman and companion of Ignatius, he became one of the greatest missionaries in history, preaching in India, the Moluccas and Japan. He died on an island off the coast of China, longing to enter it. He is patron of the missions.

saints.name: St. Dominic de Guzmán
saints.story: Born in Caleruega in Castile, he founded the Order of Preachers to proclaim the Gospel through study, poverty and preaching. His friars spread across Europe and the world, and the Rosary has long been associated with his devotion to Our Lady.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela
cathedrals.story: Built over the tomb venerated as that of St. James, its Romanesque core was begun in 1075, later clothed in a magnificent Baroque facade. For over a thousand years pilgrims have walked the Camino to embrace the saint's statue and watch the great Botafumeiro censer swing through the nave.

cathedrals.name: Basílica de la Sagrada Família
cathedrals.story: Antoni Gaudí's unfinished masterpiece, begun in 1882, is a forest of stone columns and coloured light telling the whole story of salvation. Gaudí, a man of deep prayer, devoted his last years to it. Pope Benedict XVI consecrated it as a basilica in 2010, and construction continues.

cathedrals.name: Seville Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built from 1401 on the site of the great mosque, whose minaret survives as the Giralda bell tower, it is among the largest Gothic cathedrals in the world. Its golden altarpiece is breathtaking, and it is said to hold the tomb of Christopher Columbus.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar
cathedrals.story: This Baroque basilica on the Ebro enshrines the small wooden image of Mary on a pillar, recalling the ancient tradition of her appearance to St. James. Goya painted part of its domes. Her feast on October 12 is a great national celebration.

prayerIntention: For Spain: that the faith of its saints and martyrs be rekindled in a new generation, and that its families, young people and migrants find in the Church a home of mercy and truth.

name: Sri Lanka
history:
Catholic faith came to Sri Lanka with the Portuguese in the early 16th century, and Franciscans, Jesuits, Dominicans and Augustinians founded many communities along the coasts, especially among fishing peoples. In 1544 hundreds of new Christians on Mannar island were killed for their faith. When the Dutch took the coastal areas in the mid-17th century, they banned Catholic worship and priests.

The faith survived through lay leaders and through St. Joseph Vaz, an Oratorian priest from Goa who entered disguised as a labourer in 1687 and spent over twenty years secretly ministering across the island. Under British rule religious freedom gradually returned, and the Church grew in schools, parishes and great Marian devotion, especially at the jungle shrine of Madhu, honoured by Sinhalese and Tamils alike.

The Church shared the agony of the civil war between government and Tamil separatists, often caring for the displaced on both sides. On Easter Sunday 2019, suicide bombers attacked St. Anthony's Shrine in Colombo, St. Sebastian's Church in Negombo and a church in Batticaloa, as well as hotels, killing over 260 people. Sri Lankan Catholics responded with grief, forgiveness and an enduring demand for truth.

saints.name: St. Joseph Vaz
saints.story: A Goan priest of the Oratory who entered Dutch-ruled Ceylon in disguise to serve Catholics deprived of priests. He travelled barefoot across the island, celebrating Mass at night and caring for the sick during a smallpox epidemic in Kandy. Canonized by Pope Francis in Colombo in 2015, he is called the Apostle of Sri Lanka.

saints.name: Fr. Jacome Gonçalves (not canonized)
saints.story: A Goan Oratorian who continued the work of Joseph Vaz. He wrote numerous religious books, hymns and prayers in Sinhala and Tamil, laying foundations of Catholic literature in both languages. He is honoured as a father of Sri Lankan Catholic culture.

saints.name: The Martyrs of Mannar (not formally canonized)
saints.story: Several hundred newly baptized Christians on Mannar island were killed on the orders of the King of Jaffna for refusing to renounce their faith. Though not formally beatified, they are remembered with great reverence as the first martyrs of the Church in Sri Lanka.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Lanka
cathedrals.story: A national basilica dedicated to Our Lady of Lanka, built in fulfilment of a vow made by the bishops during World War II, asking Mary to protect the island. Completed in the 1970s, it is a great centre of Marian pilgrimage, especially at its annual feasts.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Madhu
cathedrals.story: In the 17th century, Catholics fleeing Dutch persecution carried a statue of Our Lady into the jungle here. The shrine became the island's most beloved pilgrimage site, drawing Sinhalese and Tamils, and even people of other faiths. During the war it sheltered thousands of refugees.

cathedrals.name: St. Anthony's Shrine, Kochchikade
cathedrals.story: A much-loved church where people of all religions come to pray to St. Anthony, especially on Tuesdays. Bombed on Easter Sunday 2019 with great loss of life, it was lovingly restored and reopened within months, a sign of faith that would not be destroyed.

cathedrals.name: St. Lucia's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The seat of the Archbishop of Colombo, completed in the late 19th century in a classical style modelled loosely on St. Peter's in Rome. It is one of the largest churches in South Asia and the heart of the island's Catholic life.

prayerIntention: For Sri Lanka: that the victims of war and of the Easter bombings rest in peace, that justice and healing be given to the grieving, and that Sinhalese and Tamils live together as brothers and sisters.

name: Sudan
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. 2–5%), many from the South and displaced communities
history:
Christianity in Sudan is ancient. From the 6th century the Nubian kingdoms of Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia along the Nile were Christian, building cathedrals adorned with frescoes at Faras and Old Dongola. This Nubian Christianity endured for nearly a thousand years before fading by the 16th century.

Modern Catholic mission began in the 19th century. Daniel Comboni made Khartoum the centre of his work for Central Africa and died there in 1881. During the Mahdist uprising missionaries were held captive for years. St. Josephine Bakhita, kidnapped from Darfur and sold as a slave, would become the Church's most famous Sudanese daughter.

Since independence, Catholics have lived under governments that often favoured an Islamist vision, with restrictions on churches, schools and conversion, and with long wars against the South and in Darfur and the Nuba Mountains. After South Sudan's independence in 2011 the Catholic population in Sudan fell sharply. The war that erupted in 2023 has brought immense suffering, displacement and famine; churches and Christian communities in Khartoum and elsewhere have been damaged, yet priests and sisters have stayed to serve.

saints.name: St. Josephine Bakhita
saints.story: Born in Darfur, she was kidnapped as a small child and so traumatised she forgot her name; 'Bakhita', meaning 'fortunate', was given by her captors. Sold several times and cruelly scarred, she was eventually taken to Italy, where she found Christ and freedom and became a Canossian sister. Canonized in 2000, she is patroness of victims of trafficking.

saints.name: St. Daniel Comboni
saints.story: Missionary bishop and Vicar Apostolic of Central Africa based in Khartoum, he dedicated himself to the peoples of the Sudan, campaigning against the slave trade and founding missionary institutes. Worn out by labour and fever, he died in Khartoum. He was canonized in 2003.

saints.name: Cardinal Gabriel Zubeir Wako (not canonized)
saints.story: For decades Archbishop of Khartoum and the country's first cardinal, he led the Church through war, restrictions and the flight of millions of southerners to the capital. He is honoured, though living and not a saint, as a patient shepherd of a suffering people.

cathedrals.name: St. Matthew's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1908, this Romanesque-style cathedral with its tall bell tower stands near the Blue Nile. It was the heart of Catholic life in the capital for over a century, ministering to Sudanese of many peoples as well as to migrants. It has shared the dangers of the city during the current war.

cathedrals.name: Faras Cathedral (archaeological site)
cathedrals.city: Faras (now submerged, frescoes in Khartoum and Warsaw)
cathedrals.story: A cathedral of the Christian Nubian kingdom whose wonderful wall paintings of Christ, Mary and the saints were rescued by Polish archaeologists before Lake Nasser flooded the site in the 1960s. They testify to centuries of vibrant African Christianity long before the modern missions.

prayerIntention: For Sudan, torn by war and famine: that the fighting cease, that the hungry and displaced find shelter and bread, and that the courage of St. Josephine Bakhita inspire hope in every heart.

name: Suriname
history:
Suriname's Catholic story begins in the colonial era of Dutch rule, when the Reformed Church was dominant and Catholic worship was long restricted. In 1817 a Prefecture Apostolic was established, and missionaries from the Netherlands, first diocesan priests and from 1865 the Redemptorists, began to serve enslaved Africans, free people, Indigenous communities and later the Maroons in the interior.

The most luminous figure of this mission is Bl. Peter Donders, a Dutch priest who spent decades among the lepers of Batavia and among enslaved and Indigenous peoples. After the abolition of slavery in 1863, contract labourers arrived from India, Java and China, and the Church opened schools that helped form a multi-ethnic nation. Sisters and brothers ran hospitals and education across the country.

Since independence in 1975, through military rule in the 1980s and the violence of the interior war, the Church has been a voice for dialogue and human rights. Today Catholics live alongside Hindus, Muslims, Moravians and others in a remarkably peaceful religious landscape, with a single diocese centred on Paramaribo's great wooden cathedral.

saints.name: Bl. Peter Donders, C.Ss.R.
saints.story: A weaver's son from Tilburg who became a priest late and was sent to Suriname in 1842. He spent nearly thirty years caring for the lepers at Batavia, washing their wounds and living as one of them, and ministered to enslaved people and Indigenous villages. He died among his lepers and was beatified in 1982.

saints.name: Bishop Jacobus Grooff (not canonized)
saints.story: A Dutch priest and Vicar Apostolic of Suriname who, together with Peter Donders, defended the dignity of enslaved people and began ministry at the leper colony of Batavia. His outspokenness brought him into conflict with colonial authorities. He is remembered as a pioneer of the Surinamese Church.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral Basilica of Sts. Peter and Paul
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1885, it is one of the largest wooden buildings in the Americas, its tall twin towers and luminous interior of unpainted cedar creating a warm, quiet beauty. After years of decay it was carefully restored and reopened around 2010. It stands in the historic inner city, a UNESCO World Heritage site, and is the heart of Catholic life in the country.

prayerIntention: For Suriname and its many peoples: that peace and respect among its faiths continue to grow, and that the poor, the interior communities and the young find dignity and hope.

name: Sweden
history:
The faith came to Sweden in 829 with St. Ansgar, the 'Apostle of the North', though it took two more centuries to take firm root. Kings embraced Christianity, St. Eric became a royal martyr, and the archdiocese of Uppsala was founded in 1164. The Middle Ages gave Sweden one of the Church's greatest women, St. Bridget, whose order spread across Europe from Vadstena.

With the Reformation under Gustav Vasa from 1527, the Lutheran Church became the state church, monasteries were dissolved and Catholicism was banned for centuries; converting could mean exile. Limited toleration for foreigners came in 1781, and full religious freedom only in the 20th century. Elizabeth Hesselblad, a Swedish convert, refounded the Bridgettine order and later hid Jews in Rome during the war.

Today the single Diocese of Stockholm is remarkably diverse, made up of Swedes alongside Poles, Chaldeans, Croatians, Latin Americans, Eritreans and many others. In 2016 Pope Francis came to Lund to mark the 500th anniversary of the Reformation with Lutherans, and in 2017 Bishop Anders Arborelius became Sweden's first cardinal. In a deeply secular society, the small Church is growing.

saints.name: St. Bridget of Sweden
saints.story: A noblewoman, wife and mother of eight, she turned after her husband's death to a life of prayer and prophetic witness. Her revelations, especially on Christ's Passion, were treasured across Europe. She founded the Order of the Most Holy Saviour and spent her last years in Rome working for the Church's reform. She is co-patroness of Europe.

saints.name: St. Catherine of Vadstena
saints.story: Bridget's daughter, who accompanied her mother to Rome and devoted her life to her mission. After Bridget's death, she brought her relics home to Vadstena and led the new Bridgettine community there, working for the approval of the order.

saints.name: St. Elizabeth Hesselblad
saints.story: Born in Fåglavik, she emigrated to America as a nurse, became Catholic in 1902, and refounded the Bridgettine Order in Rome. During World War II she sheltered Jews in her convent and is recognised by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations. She was canonized in 2016.

saints.name: St. Eric IX of Sweden
saints.story: A Swedish king remembered for supporting the Church and for just rule. According to tradition he was killed at Uppsala after attending Mass on the feast of the Ascension. Venerated as a martyr, he became Sweden's patron, and his relics are still kept in Uppsala Cathedral.

cathedrals.name: St. Eric's Cathedral (Sankt Eriks katedral)
cathedrals.story: Built in 1892 as a parish church and made cathedral of the new Diocese of Stockholm in 1953, it was enlarged in the 1980s to serve a growing, multinational flock. Pope John Paul II visited in 1989. Masses here are celebrated in many languages, reflecting the remarkable diversity of Swedish Catholics.

cathedrals.name: Vadstena Abbey Church (Blue Church)
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1430 for St. Bridget's order, its grey-blue limestone gave it the name 'Blue Church'. Since the Reformation it has been a Lutheran parish church, yet it holds the relics of St. Bridget and St. Catherine and draws Catholic pilgrims, while Bridgettine sisters again live nearby in prayer.

prayerIntention: For Sweden: that its people, so committed to justice and care, may also discover the living God, and that its diverse Catholic community grow in unity and in the spirit of St. Bridget.

name: Switzerland
history:
Christianity reached the Alpine lands under the Roman Empire. Tradition tells of St. Maurice and the Theban Legion martyred at Agaunum, where in 515 the Abbey of Saint-Maurice was founded, one of the oldest monasteries in the West still in continuous use. Irish monks followed: St. Gall's hermitage became the great Abbey of St. Gallen with its famous library, and Einsiedeln became a beloved Marian shrine.

In the 16th century Zwingli in Zurich and Calvin in Geneva led the Reformation, dividing the Confederation into Catholic and Protestant cantons, sometimes at war. St. Peter Canisius strengthened Catholic life from Fribourg. Long before, the hermit St. Nicholas of Flüe had reconciled the quarrelling cantons in 1481, and he is honoured as Father of the Fatherland. Since 1506, Swiss Guards have protected the Pope.

The 19th century brought the brief Sonderbund war and a bitter Kulturkampf against the Church, which slowly healed. Today Swiss Catholicism is marked by a strong role for laypeople in church structures, large numbers of immigrants, declining practice, and difficult reckonings with abuse revealed in a 2023 study, while shrines and monasteries continue to draw seekers.

saints.name: St. Nicholas of Flüe
saints.story: A farmer, soldier, judge and father of ten who, with his wife Dorothea's consent, left home to live as a hermit in the Ranft gorge, reportedly taking no food but the Eucharist for many years. His counsel in 1481 prevented civil war among the cantons. Canonized in 1947, he is patron of Switzerland.

saints.name: St. Marguerite Bays
saints.story: A seamstress from the canton of Fribourg who never married and lived a hidden life of prayer, catechesis and care for the poor and sick in her village. She bore the stigmata and great suffering with serenity. She was canonized in 2019 as a model of lay holiness in ordinary life.

saints.name: St. Peter Canisius
saints.story: A Dutch Jesuit, Doctor of the Church, whose catechisms educated Catholics across German-speaking Europe. He spent his last years in Fribourg, founding the Collège Saint-Michel, and died there; his tomb is in the city. He is honoured as a second apostle of Germany and beloved in Switzerland.

saints.name: St. Maurice and the Theban Legion
saints.story: According to ancient tradition, Maurice commanded a legion of Christian soldiers from Egypt who refused to kill innocent Christians or sacrifice to the gods, and were martyred at Agaunum in the Valais. The town and abbey bear his name, and the Swiss Guards honour him.

cathedrals.name: Einsiedeln Abbey
cathedrals.story: A Benedictine abbey founded in 934 near the hermitage of St. Meinrad, rebuilt in a magnificent Baroque style in the 18th century. Its Chapel of Grace enshrines the Black Madonna, drawing pilgrims for over a thousand years, including those on the Way of St. James.

cathedrals.name: Abbey of Saint-Maurice
cathedrals.story: Founded in 515 on the site of the Theban martyrs' tomb, it is believed to have maintained continuous prayer longer than any other monastery in the West. Its treasury holds extraordinary medieval reliquaries and liturgical objects, a testimony to fifteen centuries of faith.

cathedrals.name: Abbey Cathedral of St. Gallen
cathedrals.story: Grown from the hermitage of the Irish monk St. Gall, the abbey became a great centre of learning. Its late-Baroque cathedral and the breathtaking Abbey Library, holding ancient manuscripts, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Nicholas
cathedrals.story: A Gothic church begun in 1283, with a tall tower dominating the old town. Its Art Nouveau stained-glass windows by the Polish artist Józef Mehoffer are celebrated, and it is the cathedral of the Diocese of Lausanne, Geneva and Fribourg.

prayerIntention: For Switzerland: that, in the spirit of Brother Klaus, it remain a land of peace and reconciliation, and that its Church be renewed in humility, holiness and joyful faith.

name: Syria
catholicPresence: Small Catholic minority (approx. 1–2%) within Syria's ancient Christian community, across several Eastern and Latin rites
history:
Syria is one of the cradles of Christianity. On the road to Damascus Saul of Tarsus met the risen Christ, and in the city Ananias baptized him; nearby Antioch was where believers were first called Christians. The land gave the Church martyrs, monks such as St. Simeon the Stylite, hymn-writers, and the great theologian St. John of Damascus. Syriac Christianity, with its beautiful liturgy and poetry, flourished here.

After the Arab conquest in the 7th century, Christians became a minority but remained part of the country's fabric. Over the centuries several Eastern Churches entered full communion with Rome, so that today Catholics in Syria include Melkite Greek Catholics, Syriac Catholics, Maronites, Armenian Catholics, Chaldeans and Latins. In 1860 eight Franciscans and three Maronite laymen were killed in Damascus; Pope Francis canonized these Martyrs of Damascus in 2024.

The war that began in 2011 devastated the country. Churches were destroyed, priests and bishops kidnapped or killed, among them Jesuit Fr. Frans van der Lugt in Homs, and a large part of Syria's Christians emigrated. After the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, Christians face an uncertain future, but parishes, sisters and charities like Caritas continue to serve everyone in need.

saints.name: St. John of Damascus
saints.story: Born into a Christian family serving the Umayyad court in Damascus, he left public life to become a monk near Jerusalem. He defended the veneration of holy icons during the Iconoclast controversy and summarised the faith of the Fathers in his Fount of Knowledge. He is a Doctor of the Church.

saints.name: St. Simeon Stylites
saints.story: A monk who lived for decades on top of a pillar near Aleppo, praying, fasting and counselling the crowds who came from far away. His extraordinary life drew emperors and peasants alike. The ruins of the great church built around his pillar, Qal'at Sim'an, still stand.

saints.name: Sts. Manuel Ruiz and Companions (Martyrs of Damascus)
saints.story: Eight Franciscan friars and three Maronite brothers, the Massabki, were killed during anti-Christian violence in Damascus in July 1860 after refusing to renounce their faith. Beatified in 1926, they were canonized by Pope Francis in October 2024.

saints.name: Fr. Frans van der Lugt, SJ (not canonized)
saints.story: A Dutch Jesuit who lived in Syria for nearly fifty years. During the siege of Homs he refused to leave the starving people of the Old City, Christians and Muslims alike, and was shot dead in his garden in 2014. He is remembered as a martyr of fidelity and love.

cathedrals.name: Chapel of St. Ananias
cathedrals.story: An underground chapel in the old Christian quarter, venerated as the house of Ananias, who restored Saul's sight and baptized him. Simple and ancient, it is cared for by the Franciscans and is a place of quiet pilgrimage connected to the very beginnings of the Church.

cathedrals.name: Melkite Cathedral of the Dormition of Our Lady
cathedrals.story: The patriarchal cathedral of the Melkite Greek Catholic Church, located in the old city near Bab Sharqi. Rebuilt in the 19th century after the violence of 1860, it is the heart of Syria's largest Catholic community and its rich Byzantine liturgy.

cathedrals.name: Monastery of Mar Musa al-Habashi
cathedrals.story: An ancient desert monastery with remarkable medieval frescoes, revived in the 1980s by Jesuit Fr. Paolo Dall'Oglio as a Syriac Catholic community devoted to friendship between Christians and Muslims. Fr. Paolo disappeared in Raqqa in 2013, but the community continues his witness of hospitality.

prayerIntention: For Syria: that after so much bloodshed, peace and justice may return, that Christians and all communities live in safety and dignity, and that those who fled may one day come home.

name: Taiwan
history:
The first Catholic missionaries reached Taiwan with the Spanish, who held the north of the island from 1626 to 1642; Dominican friars evangelised around Keelung and Tamsui before the Dutch expelled them. Catholic mission resumed only in 1859, when Spanish Dominicans from Manila landed in the south near Kaohsiung and founded communities in places like Wanchin, which would become Taiwan's first basilica.

Under Japanese rule from 1895 the Church grew slowly. After 1949, many priests, sisters and faithful fled mainland China, and the Church expanded rapidly through schools, hospitals and the refounding of Fu Jen Catholic University. Missionaries also brought the faith to many Indigenous peoples, among whom Catholic communities are particularly strong.

The Holy See maintains diplomatic relations with Taiwan, and Taiwanese Catholics are deeply aware of their sisters and brothers in mainland China. Today the Church is small but respected for education, healthcare and service to migrant workers, the elderly and the poor, while facing the challenges of an ageing population and secular society.

saints.name: St. Augustine Zhao Rong and the 120 Martyrs of China
saints.story: Canonized together in 2000, these Chinese believers and foreign missionaries gave their lives for Christ over three centuries. Taiwanese Catholics, many of whose families came from the mainland, honour them deeply as the saints of the Chinese-speaking Church.

saints.name: Fr. Fernando Sainz, OP (missionary, not canonized)
saints.story: A Spanish Dominican who arrived in southern Taiwan in 1859 and is regarded as the founder of the modern Catholic mission on the island. Despite hostility and imprisonment, he established the first communities from which the Church in Taiwan grew.

saints.name: Cardinal Paul Shan Kuo-hsi, SJ (not canonized)
saints.story: Born in Hebei, he became a Jesuit, served as Bishop of Kaohsiung and was made a cardinal in 1998. When diagnosed with cancer, he spent his last years touring Taiwan to speak about life, death and hope, touching many non-Christians.

cathedrals.name: Wanchin Basilica of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Founded by Spanish Dominicans in the 1860s, this white church with Spanish-style towers is among the oldest churches in Taiwan. In 1984 it became the first minor basilica in the country. Its rural setting and long history make it a beloved pilgrimage site.

cathedrals.name: Holy Rosary Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Founded as a simple chapel in 1860 and rebuilt in 1928 in a Gothic and Romanesque style, it is the oldest cathedral in Taiwan. Its white facade and graceful spires have made it a landmark of Kaohsiung's harbourside.

cathedrals.name: Immaculate Conception Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Taipei, a modest city church that serves as the centre for Catholic life in the capital, including Masses for many migrant workers from the Philippines and elsewhere. Its welcoming community reflects the many origins of Taiwan's Catholics, from mainland families to Indigenous believers.

prayerIntention: For Taiwan: that peace be preserved across the Strait, and that its Church, small and faithful, be a light of hope for families, Indigenous peoples and migrant workers.

name: Tajikistan
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic community (approx. a few hundred faithful)
history:
Christianity passed through Central Asia along the Silk Road in the early centuries, and there were Church of the East communities in the region, but they disappeared in later centuries. In the Soviet era, Catholics came to Tajikistan largely as deportees: Germans, Poles and Lithuanians exiled by Stalin, who kept their faith alive in secret, often without priests for decades.

After independence in 1991, a long civil war led many of these Catholics to emigrate. In 1997 Pope John Paul II established a Mission sui iuris, entrusted to the Institute of the Incarnate Word, whose priests and sisters have served the tiny flock ever since.

Today the Church in Tajikistan numbers only a few hundred people, centred on the parish of St. Joseph in Dushanbe, with small communities elsewhere. Religious life is tightly regulated by the state. The Church serves quietly, caring for children with disabilities, the elderly and the poor, and offering a humble presence of friendship in a predominantly Muslim nation.

cathedrals.name: Church of St. Joseph
cathedrals.story: The main Catholic church in Tajikistan and centre of the Mission sui iuris. In this modest building the small community gathers for Mass, catechesis and fellowship, served by missionaries of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, sustaining a faith that survived exile and war.

prayerIntention: For Tajikistan: that its people enjoy peace, prosperity and freedom, and that the small Catholic community be a humble sign of God's love among their Muslim neighbours.

name: Tanzania
history:
Portuguese Augustinians briefly ministered on the Swahili coast in the 16th and 17th centuries, but lasting Catholic mission began in 1868 when the Holy Ghost Fathers (Spiritans) founded a mission at Bagamoyo, where they ransomed and cared for freed slaves. The White Fathers soon arrived in the west around Lake Tanganyika and Lake Victoria, and German Benedictines founded abbeys at Peramiho and Ndanda in the south.

Through German and British colonial rule the Church built schools, hospitals and seminaries that formed much of Tanzania's future leadership. In 1960 Laurean Rugambwa of Bukoba became the first Black African cardinal of modern times. Julius Nyerere, the devout Catholic who led the country to independence and served as its first president, is a Servant of God whose cause for beatification is open, though his socialist policies also had painful economic costs.

Today the Catholic Church is one of the strongest in East Africa, with full seminaries, many vocations, and vibrant parishes. Catholics live peacefully alongside a large Muslim community, and the Church remains a major provider of education and healthcare across the country.

saints.name: Servant of God Julius Nyerere
saints.story: The founding father of Tanzania, a teacher who led the country to independence and served as president for over twenty years. A daily communicant, he worked for national unity across ethnic and religious lines. His cause for beatification was opened in 2005, while his record is also honestly debated.

saints.name: Cardinal Laurean Rugambwa (not canonized)
saints.story: Born in Bukoba, he became the first native African bishop in his region and, in 1960, the first Black African cardinal in modern times. Later Archbishop of Dar es Salaam, he took part in the Second Vatican Council and was much loved for his humility.

saints.name: The founding missionaries of Bagamoyo and the Great Lakes (not canonized)
saints.story: Tanzania has no canonized native saints yet, but its Church honours the missionaries who founded it, especially the Spiritans of Bagamoyo and the White Fathers of Cardinal Lavigerie, who gave their lives, often young, to proclaim the Gospel and fight the slave trade.

cathedrals.name: St. Joseph's Metropolitan Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built by German missionaries between 1897 and 1902 in a Gothic Revival style, its tall white spire faces the harbour and was long a landmark for arriving ships. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Dar es Salaam and a beloved symbol of the city.

cathedrals.name: Bagamoyo Catholic Mission
cathedrals.story: Founded in 1868 by the Holy Ghost Fathers, the oldest mission in East Africa. Here freed slaves found refuge, and here the body of the explorer David Livingstone rested before being taken to England. Its old church and museum make it a place of memory and pilgrimage.

cathedrals.name: St. Joseph's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built by French missionaries between 1893 and 1897, its twin spires rise above the narrow lanes of Stone Town. Its design was inspired by the basilica of Notre-Dame de la Garde in Marseille. It serves the small Catholic community of the largely Muslim islands.

prayerIntention: For Tanzania: that it remain a land of peace between Christians and Muslims, and that its young Church raise up holy families, priests and leaders who serve the poor.

name: Thailand
history:
Portuguese traders and Dominican and Franciscan friars reached the Kingdom of Siam in the 16th century, ministering to foreigners at the royal capital of Ayutthaya. In the 1660s French priests of the Paris Foreign Missions arrived, founding a seminary for all of Asia at Ayutthaya, and King Narai welcomed foreign envoys; but political upheaval in 1688 brought repression, and the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767 scattered the community.

The Church was patiently rebuilt in Bangkok, and in the 19th and 20th centuries missionaries, sisters and brothers founded schools and hospitals that earned wide respect. During the Franco-Thai conflict of 1940–41, Catholics were persecuted as supposed allies of France: at Songkhon seven Catholics, including catechist Philip Siphong and two sisters, were killed, and Fr. Nicholas Bunkerd Kitbamrung died in prison. All are now beatified.

Today Thai Catholics are a small, faithful community, strongest among some ethnic minorities in the north and northeast, and among Vietnamese- and Chinese-descended families. Catholic schools are among the most respected in the country. Pope John Paul II visited in 1984 and Pope Francis in 2019, encouraging friendship with Thailand's Buddhist majority.

saints.name: Bl. Nicholas Bunkerd Kitbamrung
saints.story: The first Thai priest to be beatified. Arrested in 1941 on false charges of spying for France, he was imprisoned at Bang Khwang, where he continued to minister to fellow prisoners and baptized dozens before dying of tuberculosis. He was beatified in 2000.

saints.name: Bl. Philip Siphong Onphitak and Companions (Martyrs of Songkhon)
saints.story: In December 1940, at the village of Songkhon on the Mekong, catechist Philip Siphong was shot, and two Lovers of the Holy Cross sisters together with four young laywomen chose to die rather than renounce their faith. They were beatified in 1989 as Thailand's first martyrs.

saints.name: Bishop Louis Laneau, MEP (missionary, not canonized)
saints.story: A French bishop who spent decades at Ayutthaya, directing the seminary, studying Buddhism, and writing in Thai. Imprisoned after the revolution of 1688, he kept serving the small flock after his release. He is honoured as a founder of the Thai Church.

cathedrals.name: Assumption Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The principal Catholic church of Thailand, built in its present Romanesque form between 1910 and 1918 on a site used by Catholics since the early 19th century. Its golden-hued interior and painted ceilings are striking. Pope John Paul II and Pope Francis both celebrated here.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of the Martyrs of Thailand
cathedrals.story: Built on the banks of the Mekong where the seven martyrs died in 1940, this modern shrine with its distinctive design draws pilgrims from across the country. It honours the courage of a small rural community whose faith did not bend under pressure.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1909 in French Gothic Revival style, it is often described as the largest church in Thailand. The Chanthaburi community grew from Vietnamese Catholics who fled persecution in their homeland, and the cathedral remains a centre of devotion in the east.

prayerIntention: For Thailand: that its people grow in peace and harmony, and that its small Catholic community, rooted in the witness of its martyrs, be a joyful sign of Christ's love to all.

name: Timor-Leste
history:
Portuguese Dominicans began evangelising the island of Timor in the 16th century, working from nearby Solor. Under centuries of Portuguese colonial rule, however, Catholicism remained the faith of a minority, and many Timorese kept their traditional beliefs.

Everything changed with the Indonesian invasion of 1975. During a brutal occupation in which perhaps a quarter of the population died from violence, famine and disease, the Church became the one institution that defended the people. Indonesia required citizens to adopt an official religion, and the Timorese turned in large numbers to Catholicism, with the Mass celebrated in Tetum, as a sign of identity and hope. Pope John Paul II visited in 1989. After the 1991 Santa Cruz massacre, the world began to notice, and in 1996 Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo shared the Nobel Peace Prize.

Independence came after the 1999 referendum, which was followed by murderous violence, including the killing of priests and refugees at the church of Suai. In 2022 it became known that Bishop Belo had been sanctioned by the Vatican over abuse allegations, a deep wound for the faithful. In 2024 Pope Francis celebrated Mass at Tasitolu with around 600,000 people, almost half the nation.

saints.name: Fr. Hilário Madeira, Fr. Francisco Soares, Fr. Tarcisius Dewanto, SJ, and the victims of Suai (not canonized)
saints.story: On 6 September 1999, after the independence vote, militias attacked the church compound in Suai where thousands had sought refuge. Three priests who stayed with their people were killed along with many civilians. They are not beatified, but are remembered as shepherds who gave their lives for their flock.

saints.name: St. John Paul II
saints.story: His 1989 visit to Dili, during the Indonesian occupation, was a turning point: when he kissed a cross placed on the ground rather than the soil itself, many Timorese felt seen. His statue stands at Tasitolu, where he celebrated Mass, and he is deeply loved in Timor-Leste.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 1988 and visited by Pope John Paul II in 1989, it is one of the largest cathedrals in Southeast Asia. Built during the occupation, it became a sanctuary of faith and identity for a suffering people, and remains the heart of the nation's Church.

cathedrals.name: Cristo Rei of Dili
cathedrals.story: A 27-metre statue of Christ standing on a globe atop a hill overlooking the sea, inaugurated in 1996. Pilgrims climb the long stairway lined with Stations of the Cross to pray at the top, and the view over the bay is unforgettable.

cathedrals.name: Church of Santo António de Motael
cathedrals.story: One of the oldest churches in Dili, on the seafront. In 1991 a young man was killed here by Indonesian troops; the memorial procession two weeks later ended in the Santa Cruz massacre, making Motael a place of memory in the struggle for freedom.

prayerIntention: For Timor-Leste: that the young nation, born from great suffering, grow in justice, healing and prosperity, and that its Church be holy, humble and close to the poor.

name: Togo
history:
Catholic mission in Togo began in the 1880s, when the region became a German protectorate. Fathers of the Society of the Divine Word, founded by St. Arnold Janssen, arrived in 1892 and built churches, schools and workshops, laying the foundations of the Church. After World War I, when the territory was divided between France and Britain, the Society of African Missions (SMA) and others continued the work.

The Church grew steadily, especially in the south among the Ewe people, and played a strong role in education. A local clergy emerged, and in 1955 the first Togolese archbishop of Lomé was appointed. During periods of authoritarian rule and political crisis, the bishops have repeatedly called for dialogue, democracy and respect for human rights.

Pope John Paul II visited Togo in 1985, praying at the Marian shrine on the shore of Lake Togo. Today the Church is young and growing, with many vocations, and lives alongside Protestants, Muslims and practitioners of traditional religion, serving through schools, health centres and works of charity.

saints.name: St. Arnold Janssen
saints.story: A German priest who founded the Society of the Divine Word and missionary congregations of sisters. His missionaries were the first to establish the Catholic Church in Togo in 1892. Canonized in 2003, he is honoured as a spiritual father of the Togolese Church.

saints.name: St. Joseph Freinademetz
saints.story: Though he served in China, this Divine Word missionary was a companion of St. Arnold Janssen and a model for the first missionaries of his society, including those sent to Togo. Canonized with Janssen in 2003, he is honoured by the Divine Word family throughout West Africa.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built by German Divine Word missionaries and completed in 1902, its twin Gothic towers in pale stone make it one of the most recognisable landmarks of Lomé. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Lomé and the mother church of Togolese Catholics.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Lake Togo
cathedrals.story: In the historic town of Togoville on the shore of Lake Togo stand an old mission church and a Marian shrine much loved by pilgrims. Pope John Paul II prayed here in 1985, and the site draws pilgrims who cross the lake by canoe.

prayerIntention: For Togo: that its people enjoy peace, freedom and development, and that its young Church grow in holiness, unity and service to the poor.

name: Tonga
history:
Methodist missionaries were the first to bring Christianity to Tonga in the 1820s, and under King George Tupou I the Free Wesleyan Church became the main church of the kingdom. Catholic Marist missionaries arrived in 1842, settling first in the north and later in Tongatapu, and despite early tension they gradually established parishes, schools and a lasting community.

Tongan Catholics developed a deep, joyful faith marked by music, hospitality and strong family life. The country's 1875 constitution guaranteed religious freedom and the sanctity of Sunday. A Vicariate Apostolic was raised to the Diocese of Tonga in 1966, and Tongans became priests, sisters and bishops themselves.

In 2015 Pope Francis made Bishop Soane Patita Paini Mafi the first Tongan cardinal, a great honour for a small Pacific nation. Today the Church serves through schools and parishes on many islands and among the large Tongan diaspora in New Zealand, Australia and the United States, while facing rising sea levels and the after-effects of the 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption and tsunami.

saints.name: St. Peter Chanel
saints.story: A French Marist priest martyred on the neighbouring island of Futuna, the first martyr of Oceania. The Marist mission to Tonga, which arrived a year after his death, shared his spirit, and he is honoured by Catholics across the Pacific, including Tonga.

saints.name: Cardinal Soane Patita Paini Mafi (living, not a saint)
saints.story: Bishop of Tonga and, from 2015, the first Tongan cardinal. Known for his warmth and closeness to his people, he has spoken on behalf of Pacific nations threatened by climate change. He is included here not as a saint but as a sign of the maturity of the Tongan Church.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception of Mary
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Diocese of Tonga in the capital, at the heart of the island's Catholic life. Here Tongan choirs sing in powerful harmony, and the great feasts of the Church are celebrated with the generous hospitality and festivity characteristic of Tongan culture.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of St. Anthony of Padua
cathedrals.story: A modern church distinguished by its traditional Tongan-style roof structure, designated a minor basilica. It serves as a centre for worship and community life, including a library and gathering spaces, and expresses the Gospel in the architecture of the Pacific.

prayerIntention: For Tonga: that its families and communities flourish in faith and love, and that the island nation be protected from storms, rising seas and every disaster.

name: Trinidad and Tobago
history:
Columbus sighted Trinidad in 1498, and under Spanish rule the island received Catholic missions, though colonisation was slow and Indigenous peoples suffered greatly, including in the 1699 Arena uprising and its brutal suppression. In 1783 the Spanish Cedula of Population invited Catholic settlers, many of them French planters with enslaved Africans, transforming the island; Britain took it in 1797, but Catholicism remained the faith of much of the population.

After the abolition of slavery, labourers came from India, China and elsewhere, and the Church, through Dominicans, Benedictines, the Holy Ghost Fathers and many sisters, built schools that shaped the nation's leaders. Devotion took on beautiful local forms, such as the shared veneration of La Divina Pastora at Siparia by Catholics and Hindus.

Trinidad and Tobago gained independence in 1962. Today the Catholic Church is one of the leading churches of a remarkably plural nation of Christians, Hindus and Muslims, serving through its many schools and outreach to the poor, while confronting crime, violence and the needs of migrants from Venezuela.

saints.name: Fr. Marie-Dominique Armand Cothonay, OP (missionary, not canonized)
saints.story: A French Dominican who served in Trinidad in the 1880s and wrote vivid letters about life on the island, its people and the Church. He is one of many missionaries who formed the island's Catholic communities; Trinidad has no canonized saints yet.

saints.name: St. Martin de Porres
saints.story: Though Peruvian, this Dominican brother of African and Spanish descent is deeply loved in Trinidad and Tobago, where many parishes and schools bear his name. His humility and care for the poor and sick speak powerfully to a nation shaped by African heritage.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral Basilica of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: Built between 1816 and 1832 of blue limestone in a Gothic Revival style, it once stood at the water's edge. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Port of Spain, with fine stained glass, and remains the heart of the capital's Catholic life.

cathedrals.name: Mount St. Benedict Abbey
cathedrals.story: Founded in 1912 by Benedictine monks from Brazil, it is the oldest Benedictine monastery in the English-speaking Caribbean. Perched high in the Northern Range with sweeping views, it is a place of prayer, retreat and pilgrimage.

cathedrals.name: La Divina Pastora Church
cathedrals.story: Home to a much-loved statue of the Divine Shepherdess. On Holy Thursday and Good Friday, Hindus come to venerate her as Soparee Mai, while Catholics celebrate her feast later in the year, a rare and moving example of shared devotion.

prayerIntention: For Trinidad and Tobago: that its many peoples live in harmony and peace, that violence give way to justice and opportunity, and that its youth find hope in Christ.

name: Tunisia
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic community (approx. 20,000 or fewer, mostly foreign residents and students)
history:
Roman Africa, with Carthage at its heart, was one of the great homelands of early Christianity. Here the martyrs Perpetua and Felicity died in 203, Tertullian wrote the first Latin theology, and St. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, guided the Church through persecution before his martyrdom in 258. St. Augustine studied and preached in Carthage, and great councils met there. After the Vandal invasion and the Arab conquest of the late 7th century, the ancient Church slowly faded away.

Catholic presence returned with European merchants, captives and redeeming religious orders, and grew greatly under the French protectorate from 1881, when Cardinal Lavigerie built the vast Cathedral of St. Louis at Carthage. At its height, the Church served hundreds of thousands of European settlers.

After independence most of them left, and in 1964 an agreement between the Holy See and Tunisia transferred most church buildings to the state. Today a small, international Church, made up largely of sub-Saharan African students and migrants, lives humbly as a guest in a Muslim country, serving through schools, Caritas and friendship, in the footsteps of the martyrs of Carthage.

saints.name: Sts. Perpetua and Felicity
saints.story: Perpetua, a young noblewoman and nursing mother, and Felicity, a slave who gave birth in prison days before, were martyred in the arena of Carthage with their companions. Perpetua's own prison diary is one of the earliest writings by a Christian woman. They are named in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

saints.name: St. Cyprian of Carthage
saints.story: A wealthy rhetorician converted in mid-life, he became bishop of Carthage and guided the Church through fierce persecution and plague, writing on the unity of the Church and the Lord's Prayer. He was beheaded near Carthage. He is named in the Roman Canon.

saints.name: St. Louis IX of France
saints.story: The saintly king of France died of illness at Carthage during his crusade of 1270. Though his crusades are viewed critically today, he is remembered for personal holiness and care for the poor, and the cathedral of Carthage was dedicated to him.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of St. Vincent de Paul
cathedrals.story: Built in 1897 on the main avenue of Tunis in an eclectic blend of Neo-Romanesque, Gothic and Byzantine styles, it is the seat of the Archdiocese of Tunis and one of the few churches the Church kept after 1964. Today its congregation is international and young.

cathedrals.name: Former Cathedral of St. Louis (Acropolium)
cathedrals.story: Built by Cardinal Lavigerie and consecrated in 1890 on Byrsa Hill, overlooking ancient Carthage. Since 1964 it no longer serves as a church and is used as a cultural centre, but its grand Byzantine-Moorish form recalls both the ancient martyrs and the colonial-era Church.

prayerIntention: For Tunisia: that its people enjoy freedom, work and peace, that migrants be treated with dignity, and that the small Church be a faithful witness of love like the martyrs of Carthage.

name: Turkmenistan
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic community (approx. a few hundred faithful)
history:
In the early Christian centuries, the city of Merv in present-day Turkmenistan was a bishopric of the Church of the East, an important centre on the Silk Road from which missionaries travelled further into Asia. This ancient Christianity disappeared over the following centuries.

Under Soviet rule there was no organised Catholic presence. After independence in 1991, a small number of Catholics, often foreigners or of Polish, German or other descent, sought pastoral care. In 1997 Pope John Paul II established a Mission sui iuris and entrusted it to the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate.

Religious life in Turkmenistan is strictly controlled, and the Catholic community has for many years gathered for Mass in the Chapel of the Transfiguration on the grounds of the Apostolic Nunciature in Ashgabat. The few priests serve a tiny flock with patience and discretion, offering prayer and quiet charity in one of the most closed countries in the world.

cathedrals.name: Chapel of the Transfiguration of the Lord
cathedrals.story: A small chapel within the Apostolic Nunciature, which has served as the main place of Catholic worship in Turkmenistan. Here the Oblate fathers celebrate Mass for local faithful and foreign residents, keeping the flame of faith burning quietly in a tightly controlled society.

prayerIntention: For Turkmenistan: that its people enjoy true freedom, including freedom of conscience, and that the tiny Catholic community be strengthened in faith, hope and love.

name: Tuvalu
history:
Christianity came to Tuvalu in the 19th century, largely through Samoan pastors of the London Missionary Society, and the Congregational Church of Tuvalu became the faith of the great majority, closely woven into island life.

Catholic presence came later and has remained very small. In 1982 a Mission sui iuris of Funafuti was established and served by a small number of missionary priests. The small community gathers on the main atoll of Funafuti, with a handful of faithful on other islands.

Tuvalu, a nation of low-lying atolls, is among the countries most threatened by rising sea levels, and its people have spoken powerfully on the global stage about climate change. The Catholic community, though tiny, shares the concerns and hopes of the whole nation, and the Church worldwide, especially through Pope Francis's Laudato Si', has embraced the cause of the Pacific islands. Catholics here live their faith in close friendship with their Congregational neighbours, sharing in the island traditions of family, singing and community.

cathedrals.name: Catholic Church of the Mission of Funafuti
cathedrals.story: The small Catholic church on Funafuti serves as the centre of the Mission sui iuris, where the few Catholic families of Tuvalu gather for the Eucharist, prayer and fellowship, sustained by missionary priests in a remote and beautiful corner of the Pacific.

prayerIntention: For Tuvalu: that its islands and people be protected from rising seas, that the world act justly on climate change, and that its families live in peace and faith.

name: Türkiye
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic minority (approx. 0.05%, a few tens of thousands across Latin, Armenian, Syriac and Chaldean rites)
history:
Few lands are so woven into the story of the Church. St. Paul was born in Tarsus and preached across Asia Minor; the Book of Revelation addressed the seven churches of Ephesus, Smyrna and their neighbours; tradition holds that the Virgin Mary spent her last years near Ephesus with St. John. The first ecumenical councils, Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon, met here, and Cappadocia gave the Church Sts. Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa.

After the schism of 1054, the fall of Constantinople in 1453 and centuries of Ottoman rule, Christians became minorities. The early 20th century brought immense suffering, including the Armenian genocide of 1915, in which Catholic Armenians such as Archbishop Ignatius Maloyan, now a canonized saint, were also killed, and later population exchanges.

Today's small Catholic community is made up of Levantine families, Armenians, Syriacs, Chaldeans, foreign workers and migrants. Angelo Roncalli, the future St. John XXIII, served in Istanbul as apostolic delegate. Recent decades brought martyrs such as Fr. Andrea Santoro (2006) and Bishop Luigi Padovese (2010). In 2025 Pope Leo XIV went to İznik to commemorate the 1700th anniversary of the Council of Nicaea with other Christian leaders.

saints.name: St. Paul the Apostle
saints.story: Born a Jew in Tarsus in Cilicia, a Roman citizen and Pharisee, he persecuted the Church until the risen Christ met him on the road to Damascus. He became the Apostle to the Gentiles, founding churches across Asia Minor and writing letters that form much of the New Testament.

saints.name: St. Nicholas of Myra
saints.story: Bishop of Myra in Lycia (today's Demre), he is remembered for secret generosity to the poor, especially giving dowries to three young women. Loved in East and West, he became the inspiration for Santa Claus. His relics were taken to Bari in 1087.

saints.name: St. Basil the Great
saints.story: Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a defender of the divinity of the Holy Spirit and a father of Eastern monasticism. He founded a great complex for the sick and poor outside his city. He is a Doctor of the Church.

saints.name: St. Ignatius Maloyan
saints.story: Armenian Catholic Archbishop of Mardin, arrested during the genocide of 1915 and offered his life if he converted to Islam. He refused and was shot with many of his faithful. Beatified in 2001, he was canonized by Pope Leo XIV in October 2025.

cathedrals.name: House of the Virgin Mary (Meryem Ana Evi)
cathedrals.story: A small stone chapel on a wooded hill above Ephesus, identified in the 19th century as the house where Mary may have lived with St. John. Venerated by Christians and Muslims alike and visited by several popes, it is a place of deep peace.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Holy Spirit
cathedrals.story: Built in 1846 in the Harbiye district, it is the cathedral of the Latin Catholics of Istanbul. In its courtyard stands a statue of Pope Benedict XV, honoured for his help to victims of World War I, and Angelo Roncalli often preached here.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of St. Anthony of Padua
cathedrals.story: The largest Catholic church in Istanbul, built in red-brick Venetian Gothic style on İstiklal Avenue and completed in 1912. Run by the Conventual Franciscans, it welcomes Turks, foreigners and migrants, and on Tuesdays many visitors, including Muslims, come to pray to St. Anthony.

cathedrals.name: Church of St. Peter (St. Peter's Grotto)
cathedrals.story: A cave church on the slopes of Mount Starius, traditionally associated with St. Peter and the early Christian community of Antioch, where believers were first called Christians. Its simple facade was added by the Crusaders.

prayerIntention: For Türkiye: that the land of the Apostles and the early Councils be blessed with peace and religious freedom, and that its small Christian communities live in dignity alongside their Muslim neighbours.

name: Uganda
history:
The first Catholic missionaries, White Fathers sent by Cardinal Lavigerie, reached the court of the Kabaka of Buganda in 1879, shortly after Anglican missionaries. Young pages at the royal court eagerly embraced the faith. When Kabaka Mwanga turned against the Christians, who refused his abuses and placed Christ above him, he ordered their deaths: between 1885 and 1887, Catholic and Anglican young men were speared, beheaded or burned alive, most famously at Namugongo on 3 June 1886.

The blood of these martyrs became the seed of an extraordinary Church. In 1964 Pope Paul VI canonized 22 Catholic martyrs, led by Charles Lwanga, and in 1969 he visited Uganda, the first pope to visit sub-Saharan Africa. Religious rivalry between Catholics and Protestants also marked colonial politics, including armed conflict in 1892, a history now largely healed.

The Church suffered with the nation under Idi Amin and later wars, including the long conflict with the Lord's Resistance Army in the north, where Catholic leaders worked courageously for peace and for abducted children. Today Uganda's Church is vibrant and young, and every 3 June millions of pilgrims from across Africa walk to Namugongo.

patronSaints.name: St. Charles Lwanga and the Uganda Martyrs

saints.name: St. Charles Lwanga
saints.story: Head of the royal pages at the court of Kabaka Mwanga, he secretly baptized young catechumens on the night before their arrest and protected the boys in his care from the king's advances. He was burned alive at Namugongo. He is patron of African youth and Catholic Action in Africa.

saints.name: St. Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe
saints.story: Major-domo of the royal household and leader of the Catholic pages, he rebuked the Kabaka for his abuses and for the murder of the Anglican bishop James Hannington. He was beheaded and burned in November 1885, the first Catholic martyr of Uganda.

saints.name: St. Kizito
saints.story: The youngest of the martyrs, about fourteen years old, baptized by Charles Lwanga on the eve of their arrest. He walked to Namugongo cheerfully, encouraging others, and was burned alive with his companions. He is a beloved model for children and young people.

saints.name: Bl. Daudi Okelo and Bl. Jildo Irwa
saints.story: Two young Acholi catechists, about 16 and 12 years old, who went to teach the faith in the remote village of Paimol in northern Uganda. Ordered to stop, they refused to abandon their mission and were speared to death. They were beatified in 2002.

cathedrals.name: Uganda Martyrs Basilica
cathedrals.story: Built on the place where St. Charles Lwanga and companions were burned in 1886, its distinctive design resembles a traditional African hut on 22 copper-clad pillars. Consecrated in 1975 and named a minor basilica, it is the destination of one of Africa's greatest pilgrimages every 3 June.

cathedrals.name: St. Mary's Cathedral, Rubaga
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1925 on Rubaga Hill, where the White Fathers first settled, this great Romanesque-style cathedral is the seat of the Archdiocese of Kampala. It holds the remains of Uganda's first African bishop, Joseph Kiwanuka, and is the mother church of Ugandan Catholics.

cathedrals.name: Munyonyo Martyrs' Shrine
cathedrals.story: Built on the lakeside spot where Kabaka Mwanga ordered the persecution that led to the martyrs' deaths, and where St. Denis Ssebuggwawo was killed. Pope Francis visited in 2015, and the shrine has grown into a major place of prayer and pilgrimage.

prayerIntention: For Uganda: that the courage of its martyrs inspire its young people, that peace and justice grow in every region, and that refugees it welcomes find safety and hope.

name: Ukraine
catholicPresence: Catholic minority (approx. 9–10%), mostly Ukrainian Greek Catholics with a smaller Latin community
history:
In 988 Prince Volodymyr of Kyiv was baptized and brought his people to Christianity in the Byzantine tradition, building on the earlier baptism of his grandmother St. Olga. The faith of Kyivan Rus' shaped Ukraine's culture for a thousand years. In 1596, at the Union of Brest, several bishops of the Kyivan Church entered full communion with Rome while keeping their Eastern liturgy, giving birth to what is now the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church; St. Josaphat Kuntsevych was killed in the conflicts that followed. Latin Catholics, many of Polish descent, also lived in the western lands.

The 20th century was a Golgotha. Under Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky, the Greek Catholic Church became a pillar of national life, and he sheltered Jews during the Holocaust. In 1946 the Soviets forcibly 'liquidated' the Church, arresting all its bishops; many priests and faithful died in the Gulag, and the Church survived underground for over forty years. In 2001 Pope John Paul II beatified a large group of these martyrs in Lviv.

The Church re-emerged in 1989 and has grown strongly. Since Russia's invasion in 2014 and full-scale war from 2022, Catholics of both rites have served the wounded, the displaced and the grieving, and its priests have also suffered imprisonment.

patronSaints.name: Protection of the Most Holy Mother of God (Pokrova)

saints.name: St. Josaphat Kuntsevych
saints.story: A Basilian monk and Greek Catholic Archeparch of Polotsk who worked tirelessly for the unity of the Church after the Union of Brest. Amid fierce tensions, he was killed by a mob in Vitebsk. He was canonized in 1867, the first Eastern Catholic to be formally canonized by Rome.

saints.name: Ven. Andrey Sheptytsky
saints.story: Metropolitan of Lviv for over four decades, a towering spiritual, cultural and national leader. During the Nazi occupation he protested the murder of Jews and helped hide hundreds of Jewish children in monasteries. He was declared Venerable in 2015.

saints.name: Bl. Omelian Kovch
saints.story: A married Greek Catholic priest and father of six who sheltered and baptized Jews to save them from the Nazis. Arrested, he ministered to fellow prisoners in Majdanek, refusing release, until his death there. Beatified in 2001, he is called the 'pastor of Majdanek'.

saints.name: Bl. Mykolai Charnetskyi and companions
saints.story: Bishop Mykolai Charnetskyi and dozens of bishops, priests, religious and laypeople of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church suffered prison, torture and death under the Soviet and Nazi regimes for their fidelity. Pope John Paul II beatified them in Lviv in 2001.

cathedrals.name: St. George's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built between 1744 and 1762 in an elegant Rococo style, it was the mother church of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church for centuries. Seized by the Soviets in 1946 and returned in 1990, it holds the tombs of Metropolitan Sheptytsky and Patriarch Josyf Slipyj.

cathedrals.name: Patriarchal Cathedral of the Resurrection of Christ
cathedrals.story: Consecrated in 2011 on the left bank of the Dnipro, it is the main church of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, whose head moved his seat to Kyiv in 2005. Its modern Byzantine design symbolises the Church's resurrection after decades of persecution.

cathedrals.name: Latin Cathedral Basilica of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: Begun in the 14th century, this Gothic cathedral with rich Baroque chapels is the seat of the Latin Archdiocese of Lviv. Here in 1656 King John Casimir entrusted his kingdom to Mary as Queen. It remains a treasured centre of Latin Catholic life.

cathedrals.name: Zarvanytsia Marian Spiritual Centre
cathedrals.story: A shrine linked to a miraculous icon of the Mother of God venerated since the Middle Ages. Pilgrimages continued secretly under Soviet rule, and today hundreds of thousands come each summer. It is the national Marian shrine of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church.

prayerIntention: For Ukraine: that the war end in a just peace, that the dead rest in God, the wounded be healed, the captives return home, and that the Mother of God cover her people with her protecting veil.

name: United Arab Emirates
catholicPresence: Large migrant Catholic community (approx. 8–10% of residents, nearly all foreign workers)
history:
Christianity was present in eastern Arabia in the early centuries; on Sir Bani Yas island archaeologists have uncovered a Christian monastery dating from around the 7th–8th centuries. That ancient presence faded after the coming of Islam.

The modern Catholic story began with the oil boom. Rulers of the emirates generously gave land for churches: St. Joseph's in Abu Dhabi opened in 1965 and St. Mary's in Dubai in 1967. Millions of migrant workers arrived from India, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Lebanon, Africa and elsewhere, and parishes grew into some of the largest in the world, with Masses in many languages. The UAE is part of the Apostolic Vicariate of Southern Arabia, based in Abu Dhabi.

In 2019 Pope Francis became the first pope to visit the Arabian Peninsula, signing the Document on Human Fraternity with the Grand Imam of Al-Azhar and celebrating Mass for some 180,000 people. In 2023 the Abrahamic Family House, with a church, mosque and synagogue, opened in Abu Dhabi. Catholics worship freely within church compounds, though public evangelisation is not permitted, and many workers face hard conditions far from their families.

cathedrals.name: St. Joseph's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: First opened in 1965 on land given by the ruler, and rebuilt as a larger cathedral in the 1980s, it is the seat of the Apostolic Vicar of Southern Arabia. On weekends its compound overflows with worshippers from dozens of nations, a living icon of the universal Church.

cathedrals.name: St. Mary's Catholic Church
cathedrals.story: Opened in 1967, it is said to be one of the largest Catholic parishes in the world by number of faithful, with tens of thousands attending Masses each weekend in many languages, served by Capuchin friars.

cathedrals.name: St. Francis of Assisi Church, Abrahamic Family House
cathedrals.story: Opened in 2023 as part of the Abrahamic Family House, alongside a mosque and a synagogue, inspired by the 2019 Document on Human Fraternity. Its simple, luminous design invites prayer and dialogue between believers. Visitors of every faith are welcome to see how believers can live side by side.

prayerIntention: For the United Arab Emirates: for the millions of migrant workers far from their families, that they be treated with justice and dignity, and that fraternity between Christians and Muslims continue to grow.

name: United Kingdom
catholicPresence: Catholic minority (approx. 8–10% overall; higher in Scotland and Northern Ireland)
history:
Christianity reached Roman Britain early; St. Alban is honoured as the first British martyr. After the Anglo-Saxon invasions, the faith was rekindled from two directions: Irish monks such as St. Columba at Iona and St. Aidan at Lindisfarne, and St. Augustine, sent by Pope Gregory the Great, who landed in Kent in 597. Medieval England, Scotland and Wales became lands of great abbeys, cathedrals and shrines, from Canterbury, where St. Thomas Becket was martyred, to Walsingham, 'England's Nazareth'.

The Reformation broke this unity. Henry VIII separated the English Church from Rome in 1534, monasteries were dissolved, and under later monarchs Catholic worship was outlawed. Hundreds were executed, among them St. Thomas More, St. John Fisher, St. Margaret Clitherow and St. John Ogilvie in Scotland. Catholics endured centuries of fines and exclusion, though Protestants too suffered under Mary I.

Catholic Emancipation came in 1829, the hierarchy was restored in England and Wales in 1850 and in Scotland in 1878, and Irish immigration and converts like John Henry Newman revitalised the Church. Today the Church is diverse and multi-ethnic, recovering from the grave failures exposed by abuse inquiries, and still bearing the gift of its martyrs, schools and parishes. Northern Ireland's history reminds Catholics and Protestants to keep building peace.

saints.name: St. Thomas More
saints.story: Lawyer, scholar, devoted husband and father, and Lord Chancellor of England. He refused to accept Henry VIII as head of the Church in England and was beheaded, declaring himself 'the King's good servant, but God's first.' He is patron of statesmen and politicians.

saints.name: St. John Henry Newman
saints.story: An Anglican priest and Oxford scholar whose study of the early Church led him into the Catholic Church in 1845. He became an Oratorian and a cardinal, and his writings on conscience, faith and education have influenced the whole Church. He was canonized in 2019 and named a Doctor of the Church in 2025.

saints.name: St. Margaret Clitherow
saints.story: A butcher's wife in York and mother of young children, she hid priests in her home during the persecution. Refusing to plead in court to spare her family and servants from testifying, she was crushed to death. She is called the 'Pearl of York'.

saints.name: St. John Ogilvie
saints.story: A Scottish Jesuit who returned in disguise to minister to Catholics in Edinburgh and Glasgow. Arrested and tortured with sleep deprivation, he refused to betray others and was hanged in Glasgow. Canonized in 1976, he is Scotland's only post-Reformation saint.

saints.name: St. Bede the Venerable
saints.story: A monk of Jarrow in Northumbria who wrote the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, biblical commentaries and works of science. He is the only English Doctor of the Church.

cathedrals.name: Westminster Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The mother church of Catholics in England and Wales, built 1895–1903 in a striking Byzantine style of red brick and white stone. Its vast interior, still being adorned with mosaics, holds Eric Gill's Stations of the Cross. Popes John Paul II and Benedict XVI celebrated Mass here.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of Our Lady of Walsingham
cathedrals.story: In 1061 Richeldis de Faverches is said to have built a replica of the Holy House of Nazareth here after a vision. Destroyed at the Reformation, the shrine was revived in the late 19th and 20th centuries; the Slipper Chapel is now the Catholic National Shrine of England.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral of Christ the King
cathedrals.story: After an immense earlier design by Lutyens was abandoned, this circular modern cathedral, crowned by a lantern of coloured glass, was consecrated in 1967. Affectionately nicknamed 'Paddy's Wigwam' by locals, it embodies the liturgical spirit of Vatican II, with the altar at the centre of the people.

cathedrals.name: St. Andrew's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Opened in 1816 on the banks of the Clyde, it was one of the first Catholic churches built in Scotland after the Reformation and became the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Glasgow, serving a community greatly enlarged by Irish immigration.

prayerIntention: For the United Kingdom: that the faith of its saints and martyrs be renewed, that healing come to all harmed in the Church, and that its nations live in peace, justice and care for the poor.

name: United States
history:
