The first Catholic presence in today's United States came with the Spanish: St. Augustine in Florida was founded in 1565, and Franciscan missions spread through New Mexico, Texas and later California, bringing both faith and the painful disruption of Native peoples' lives. French Jesuits carried the Gospel along the St. Lawrence, the Great Lakes and the Mississippi, and Sts. Isaac Jogues and René Goupil were martyred in New York. In the English colonies, Maryland was founded in 1634 as a refuge for Catholics, though they soon faced restrictions.

After independence, John Carroll became the first bishop, of Baltimore, in 1789. Waves of immigrants from Ireland, Germany, Italy, Poland, Mexico and many other lands built parishes, schools, hospitals and universities, often amid fierce anti-Catholic nativism. Saints like Elizabeth Ann Seton, Frances Cabrini and Katharine Drexel served the poor, immigrants, Native Americans and Black Americans; the Church's own complicity in slavery and segregation is a painful part of the story.

The 20th century saw Catholics enter the mainstream, from John F. Kennedy to a vast network of charities. From 2002 the sexual abuse crisis brought deep shame and reform. In 2025 Robert Prevost of Chicago was elected as Pope Leo XIV, the first pope from the United States, and the Church, increasingly Hispanic and Asian, continues to grow and change.

saints.name: St. Elizabeth Ann Seton
saints.story: A New York socialite, wife and mother of five who, widowed young, became Catholic despite family opposition. She founded the Sisters of Charity and the first free Catholic school for girls in Emmitsburg, Maryland, laying foundations of Catholic education. Canonized in 1975, she was the first native-born American saint.

saints.name: St. Kateri Tekakwitha
saints.story: A Mohawk and Algonquin woman, scarred by smallpox, who embraced Christ despite hostility in her village and fled to a Christian community near Montreal. Known for deep prayer and penance, she died at 24. Canonized in 2012, she is the first Native American saint.

saints.name: St. Katharine Drexel
saints.story: A Philadelphia heiress who gave her fortune and life to serving Native Americans and Black Americans, founding the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament and dozens of schools, including Xavier University of Louisiana. Canonized in 2000, she challenged the racism of her age.

saints.name: St. Frances Xavier Cabrini
saints.story: An Italian sister who came to New York in 1889 to serve Italian immigrants, founding schools, orphanages and hospitals across the Americas. She became a US citizen and, canonized in 1946, the first American citizen to be declared a saint. She is patron of immigrants.

saints.name: Bl. Stanley Rother
saints.story: An Oklahoma farm boy who became a priest and served the Tz'utujil Maya people of Santiago Atitlán in Guatemala. Refusing to abandon them during the civil war, he was murdered in his rectory. Beatified in 2017, he was the first US-born martyr.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception
cathedrals.story: The largest Catholic church in North America, built from 1920 and dedicated in 1959, in Byzantine-Romanesque style. Its chapels honour Marian titles from immigrant peoples all over the world, making it a mosaic of American Catholic history.

cathedrals.name: St. Patrick's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Opened in 1879 on Fifth Avenue, this white marble Gothic Revival cathedral was a bold statement by a once-despised immigrant Church. Its soaring spires and rose window draw millions of visitors, and it is a place of prayer at the heart of Manhattan.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the National Shrine of the Assumption
cathedrals.story: America's first Catholic cathedral, built 1806–1821 and designed by Benjamin Latrobe, architect of the US Capitol. Its neoclassical dome and light-filled interior symbolise religious freedom in the young republic. It is known as America's First Cathedral.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral Basilica of St. Augustine
cathedrals.story: Home to the oldest Catholic parish in the United States, founded in 1565. The present building dates from the 1790s and has been restored after fires. It recalls the first Mass and the long Spanish Catholic heritage of the nation.

prayerIntention: For the United States: that its people overcome division, that every life be protected and every immigrant welcomed, and that its Church be holy, humble and generous in serving the world.

name: Uruguay
catholicPresence: Largest religious group, in a very secular society (approx. 35–40% Catholic)
history:
Catholic faith arrived in the Banda Oriental with Spanish and Portuguese settlers; Jesuit and Franciscan missionaries worked among the Guaraní and other peoples, and Montevideo's Iglesia Matriz was built at the end of the 18th century. Priests took part in the struggle for independence, and in 1825 the Thirty-Three Orientals, who began the final campaign for freedom, entrusted themselves to a small statue of the Virgin, later honoured as the Virgen de los Treinta y Tres.

The 19th century brought tensions between Church and liberal state. Jacinto Vera, the country's first bishop, travelled tirelessly on horseback to every corner of the nation, preaching and administering the sacraments. In the early 20th century Uruguay pursued a strong secularism: crucifixes were removed from hospitals, Christmas was renamed 'Family Day' and Holy Week 'Tourism Week', and in 1917 Church and state were formally separated.

Today Uruguay is the most secular country in Latin America, yet a living Church remains, serving through schools, parishes and social works, and engaging respectfully in public life. The beatification of Jacinto Vera in 2023 brought joy to Uruguayan Catholics and reminded the nation of a shepherd who loved all its people.

patronSaints.name: Virgen de los Treinta y Tres

saints.name: Bl. Jacinto Vera
saints.story: Born on a ship as his family emigrated from the Canary Islands, he became a country priest and then the first bishop of Montevideo. He travelled the whole country on horseback, preaching missions to rural people and caring for the poor. Beatified in 2023, he is Uruguay's first native beatus.

saints.name: Bl. Dolores and Consuelo Aguiar-Mella Díaz
saints.story: Two sisters born in Montevideo who later lived in Madrid. During the Spanish Civil War they were killed for their faith, together with others who had sheltered religious. They were beatified in 2007 among the martyrs of the Spanish persecution.

saints.name: St. Mary Frances of Jesus (Anna Maria Rubatto)
saints.story: An Italian foundress of the Capuchin Sisters of Mother Rubatto who opened houses in Uruguay and died in Montevideo. Her humble service to the sick and poor left a deep mark. She was beatified in 1993 and canonized in 2022, the first saint to have died in Uruguay.

cathedrals.name: Metropolitan Cathedral (Iglesia Matriz)
cathedrals.story: Built between 1790 and 1804 on the Plaza Constitución in the old city, it is the oldest church in Montevideo and seat of the archdiocese. Its neoclassical facade and twin towers have seen the whole history of the nation, and it holds the tombs of bishops and national figures.

cathedrals.name: National Shrine of the Virgen de los Treinta y Tres
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of Florida enshrines the small wooden image before which the patriots of 1825 are said to have prayed. Proclaimed patroness of Uruguay, the Virgin draws national pilgrimages, uniting Uruguayans' faith with the memory of their independence.

prayerIntention: For Uruguay: that its people, so committed to freedom and fairness, open their hearts to God's love, and that the Church serve the poor and the searching with humility and joy.

name: Uzbekistan
history:
Along the Silk Road, cities like Samarkand once had bishops of the Church of the East, and in the 14th century Franciscan missionaries passed through Central Asia; but these communities vanished in later centuries. In the late Russian Empire Catholic soldiers, officials and settlers of Polish, German and Lithuanian origin came to Tashkent, and a church was begun there in 1912.

Under Soviet rule churches were closed and Catholics, joined by exiles and deportees, kept their faith in secret. After independence in 1991, the Church was able to register again. A Mission sui iuris was established in 1997, raised to an Apostolic Administration in 2005, and served by Conventual Franciscans and other religious.

Today Uzbekistan's Catholics are few, spread among several parishes, and include Uzbeks, Koreans, Russians, Poles and foreigners. Religious activity remains regulated, but relations have improved. The restored Sacred Heart Cathedral in Tashkent, with its concerts and liturgies, is a sign of a small Church that perseveres with joy.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Sacred Heart of Jesus
cathedrals.story: Begun in 1912 in Neo-Gothic style by Polish Catholics, it was never fully completed before the revolution. In the Soviet era it was used for other purposes and fell into ruin. Returned to the Church after independence and restored, it was consecrated in 2000 and is now a beloved landmark, famous also for its organ concerts.

prayerIntention: For Uzbekistan: that its people flourish in peace and freedom, and that its small Catholic community be a joyful witness of Christ's love among its Muslim neighbours.

name: Vanuatu
history:
Christianity came to the islands of the New Hebrides in the 19th century, largely through Presbyterian and Anglican missionaries; the first missionary to land, John Williams, was killed on Erromango in 1839. Catholic Marist missionaries arrived in 1887 and gradually founded stations on several islands, particularly in areas associated with French influence under the unusual Anglo-French Condominium.

The Catholic Church grew through schools, catechists and health care, while Presbyterians remained the largest denomination. A local clergy developed slowly, and the Diocese of Port Vila was established in 1966. At independence in 1980 the new nation took as its motto 'In God we stand.'

Today Ni-Vanuatu Catholics, together with other Christians, form the vast majority of a deeply believing nation. The Church accompanies communities through cyclones, earthquakes and the effects of climate change, and promotes education in both English and French, serving islands spread across a vast stretch of ocean, where catechists often lead prayer in villages that see a priest only rarely.

saints.name: St. Peter Chanel
saints.story: A French Marist missionary martyred on Futuna, the first martyr of Oceania. The Marist fathers who brought Catholic faith to Vanuatu belonged to his congregation and carried his spirit, and he is venerated throughout the Pacific islands.

cathedrals.name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Diocese of Port Vila, overlooking the harbour of the capital. It serves as the heart of Catholic life in the country, gathering faithful from many islands and languages, and has been a place of comfort after cyclones and disasters.

prayerIntention: For Vanuatu: that its islands be protected from storms and rising seas, and that its people grow in unity, faith and care for creation.

name: Vatican City (Holy See)
catholicPresence: Entirely Catholic (approx. 100% of its few hundred citizens and residents)
history:
The Vatican Hill, once a place of gardens and a circus of Nero outside ancient Rome, became holy ground when the Apostle Peter was martyred nearby and buried in a cemetery on its slope, around the year 64. Over his tomb, the Emperor Constantine built a great basilica in the 4th century, and for centuries pilgrims from every land came to pray at the tomb of the Prince of the Apostles.

The popes lived mainly at the Lateran for much of the Middle Ages, but from the late 14th century the Vatican became the papal residence. The Renaissance popes rebuilt St. Peter's with the genius of Bramante, Michelangelo, Bernini and others, and filled the Vatican with treasures of art and learning. For over a thousand years popes also ruled the Papal States, a temporal power that ended when Rome was taken by Italy in 1870.

The Lateran Treaty of 1929 created the Vatican City State, the world's smallest country, to guarantee the Holy See's independence. Today it is home to the Pope and the central government of the Church, receiving millions of pilgrims each year. Here the Second Vatican Council met, here saints have been canonized, and here, in May 2025, Pope Leo XIV was elected, the 267th successor of Peter.

saints.name: St. Peter the Apostle
saints.story: The Galilean fisherman whom Jesus called the Rock on which he would build his Church. After denying Christ three times and being forgiven, he led the apostolic community and came to Rome, where he was crucified under Nero. Excavations beneath St. Peter's Basilica found the tomb venerated as his.

saints.name: St. John XXIII
saints.story: Angelo Roncalli, son of peasant farmers, became pope in 1958 at nearly 77 and surprised the world by calling the Second Vatican Council. Loved as 'the Good Pope' for his warmth and humour, he wrote Pacem in Terris. He was canonized in 2014.

saints.name: St. John Paul II
saints.story: Karol Wojtyła of Poland, pope from 1978 to 2005, travelled to more than 120 countries, helped bring down Communism in Eastern Europe without violence, and taught on human dignity and the theology of the body. He was canonized in 2014, and his tomb is in St. Peter's Basilica.

saints.name: St. Paul VI
saints.story: Giovanni Battista Montini guided the Second Vatican Council to its conclusion and its implementation, became the first pope to travel by plane to every continent, and wrote Evangelii Nuntiandi and Humanae Vitae. He was canonized in 2018.

cathedrals.name: St. Peter's Basilica
cathedrals.story: Built from 1506 to 1626 over Constantine's basilica and the tomb of St. Peter, it is one of the largest churches in the world. Michelangelo designed its dome, Bernini its bronze baldachin and the embracing colonnade of the square. Here lie many popes and saints, and from its loggia each new pope first blesses the world.

cathedrals.name: Sistine Chapel
cathedrals.story: Built in the 1470s under Pope Sixtus IV, its walls and ceiling are covered by Michelangelo's Creation and Last Judgement and frescoes by Botticelli, Perugino and others. It is the place where cardinals gather in conclave to elect the pope.

cathedrals.name: Vatican Necropolis (Scavi) and Tomb of St. Peter
cathedrals.story: Beneath the basilica lies a Roman cemetery excavated in the 20th century. At its heart is the humble tomb venerated as St. Peter's, marked by an ancient monument and graffiti of early pilgrims. Visiting it is a moving encounter with the Church's apostolic roots.

prayerIntention: For the Holy Father, Pope Leo XIV, and all who serve the Church at the Vatican: that they be faithful, humble and wise, strengthening their brothers and sisters in faith throughout the world.

name: Venezuela
history:
Catholic faith reached Venezuela with the first Spanish expeditions; in the early 16th century Dominicans and Franciscans founded missions near Cumaná, among the earliest on the South American mainland. Evangelisation was entangled with conquest, the forced labour of Indigenous peoples and later African slavery, though missionaries also defended Indigenous people, and Capuchins and Jesuits founded missions in the Llanos and along the Orinoco. In 1652 Our Lady appeared, according to tradition, to the Indigenous chief Coromoto near Guanare, and she became the beloved patroness of Venezuela.

After independence, led by Simón Bolívar, the Church faced periods of hostility, especially under Antonio Guzmán Blanco in the 1870s, who closed convents and seminaries. In the 20th century it recovered, building schools, universities and social works, and producing saints such as the physician José Gregorio Hernández, beloved as 'the doctor of the poor'.

In recent decades the Church has stood with the people through deep political, economic and humanitarian crisis, which drove millions to emigrate. Bishops have called for dialogue, democracy and respect for human rights, while Caritas and parishes feed the hungry. In October 2025 the canonization of St. José Gregorio Hernández and St. Carmen Rendiles brought immense joy to Venezuelans at home and abroad.

saints.name: St. José Gregorio Hernández
saints.story: A brilliant physician and scientist from Isnotú who studied in Paris and introduced modern medicine to Venezuela, yet treated the poor for free. He tried twice to enter religious life but served God as a lay doctor. Killed by a car while bringing medicine to a patient, he was canonized in 2025.

saints.name: St. Carmen Rendiles
saints.story: Born in Caracas without a left arm, she overcame her disability to found the Servants of Jesus of Venezuela, devoted to the Eucharist, education and parish service. Known for joy and practical charity, she was the first Venezuelan woman canonized, in 2025.

saints.name: Bl. María de San José (Laura Alvarado Cardozo)
saints.story: Foundress of the Augustinian Recollects of the Heart of Jesus, she dedicated her life to orphans, the elderly and the sick, opening homes and hospitals across Venezuela. Her incorrupt body rests in Maracay. She was beatified in 1995, the first Venezuelan blessed.

saints.name: Bl. Candelaria de San José
saints.story: Susana Paz-Castillo Ramírez, from Altagracia de Orituco, cared for the sick in her town during epidemics and founded the Carmelite Sisters of Mother Candelaria. She was beatified in 2008. Her sisters continue her work in hospitals, schools and homes for the elderly in Venezuela and beyond.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of the National Shrine of Our Lady of Coromoto
cathedrals.story: A vast modern shrine consecrated in 1996 by Pope John Paul II near the place of the 1652 apparition. It houses the tiny image of the Virgin that, according to tradition, she left to the chief Coromoto, and draws hundreds of thousands of pilgrims.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Chiquinquirá
cathedrals.story: Home of 'La Chinita', an image of Our Lady that tradition says glowed miraculously on a board found on the shore of Lake Maracaibo in 1709. Her November feast with gaita music is one of the great celebrations of Venezuelan faith.

cathedrals.name: Caracas Cathedral
cathedrals.story: On the Plaza Bolívar, the cathedral's present building dates from the 17th century, rebuilt after earthquakes, with a white colonial facade. It holds the family chapel of Simón Bolívar and is the seat of the Archdiocese of Caracas.

cathedrals.name: Shrine of the Divina Pastora
cathedrals.story: Home of the Divine Shepherdess, whose annual procession to Barquisimeto every 14 January is among the largest Marian processions in the world, drawing millions of pilgrims in thanksgiving for her protection, especially during a cholera epidemic in 1856.

prayerIntention: For Venezuela: that peace, freedom and justice return, that families separated by migration be reunited, and that Our Lady of Coromoto console the hungry and the suffering.

name: Vietnam
history:
Catholic missionaries first reached Vietnam in the 16th century, and from 1615 Jesuits, among them Alexandre de Rhodes, laid the foundations of a lasting Church. Missionaries helped develop the romanised Vietnamese script, quốc ngữ, now used by the whole nation. The Church grew quickly, with catechists playing a crucial role; the young catechist Andrew of Phú Yên was martyred in 1644.

For over two centuries Vietnamese Catholics endured waves of persecution. Under the Nguyễn emperors especially, tens of thousands were killed, priests were hunted, and Christians were branded on the face. The 117 Vietnamese Martyrs canonized in 1988 represent a far greater multitude. French colonial intervention, partly justified by the protection of missionaries, tied the Church in many eyes to foreign rule, a painful legacy.

After 1954 hundreds of thousands of Catholics fled from the North, and after 1975 the communist government restricted the Church, imprisoning clergy such as Archbishop Nguyễn Văn Thuận for thirteen years. Despite limits, the Church has remained vibrant, with packed churches and many vocations, and relations with the Holy See have gradually improved, including the appointment of a resident papal representative in 2023.

patronSaints.name: Vietnamese Martyrs (St. Andrew Dũng-Lạc and Companions)

saints.name: St. Andrew Dũng-Lạc
saints.story: Born to a poor non-Christian family, he was raised by a catechist, became a priest and served his people tirelessly. Arrested repeatedly, he was ransomed by his flock until finally beheaded in Hanoi. He leads the 117 Vietnamese Martyrs canonized by John Paul II in 1988.

saints.name: St. Agnes Lê Thị Thành
saints.story: A wife and mother of six who sheltered priests in her home. Arrested and tortured, she encouraged fellow prisoners and died in prison in Nam Định. She is the only woman among the 117 canonized Vietnamese martyrs.

saints.name: Bl. Andrew of Phú Yên
saints.story: A young catechist baptized by Alexandre de Rhodes. When soldiers came for the missionaries, he declared himself a Christian and was killed with a lance, saying 'Let us pay love with love.' He is Vietnam's protomartyr and was beatified in 2000.

saints.name: St. Théophane Vénard
saints.story: A French priest of the Paris Foreign Missions who served secretly in northern Vietnam. Caught after years in hiding, he was kept in a cage before being beheaded, writing tender letters to his family. St. Thérèse of Lisieux deeply loved him.

saints.name: Ven. Francis Xavier Nguyễn Văn Thuận
saints.story: Coadjutor Archbishop of Saigon, imprisoned for thirteen years, nine in solitary confinement. He celebrated Mass with drops of wine in his hand and wrote messages of hope on scraps of paper, later published as The Road of Hope. Made a cardinal, he was declared Venerable in 2017.

cathedrals.name: Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica of Saigon
cathedrals.story: Built between 1863 and 1880 with red bricks brought from Marseille, its twin bell towers are a landmark of the city. A statue of Our Lady Queen of Peace stands before it. It became a minor basilica in 1962 and is currently being restored.

cathedrals.name: Basilica of Our Lady of La Vang
cathedrals.story: According to tradition, in 1798 Our Lady appeared to persecuted Catholics hiding in the jungle here, teaching them to use local leaves as medicine. The national Marian shrine was heavily damaged in war but remains Vietnam's greatest pilgrimage site, where a new basilica is being raised.

cathedrals.name: St. Joseph's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1886 in neo-Gothic style, reminiscent of Notre-Dame de Paris, on the site of a former pagoda. Its weathered stone towers in the old quarter are among the most recognisable landmarks of Hanoi, and its Masses are crowded with the faithful.

cathedrals.name: Phát Diệm Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Built between 1875 and 1899 under Fr. Trần Lục, this extraordinary stone and wood complex blends Catholic worship with the architecture of Vietnamese pagodas and temples, a remarkable expression of a faith truly rooted in Vietnamese culture.

prayerIntention: For Vietnam: that its Church, strengthened by its martyrs, grow in freedom and joyful witness, and that the nation prosper in justice, peace and care for the poor.

name: Yemen
catholicPresence: Very small Catholic presence (approx. a few thousand at most, mainly foreign workers)
history:
Christianity reached South Arabia in late antiquity, and by the 6th century there were Christian communities in the Himyarite kingdom, notably at Najran, where many Christians were martyred around 523 under King Dhu Nuwas. Churches stood in Sana'a and other towns, but after the coming of Islam Christianity gradually disappeared from the region.

The modern Catholic presence began in Aden, under British rule from 1839, where Catholic soldiers, Indian and Goan workers and others built churches and schools. After independence and the Marxist period in the South, churches were closed, but from the 1970s the Missionaries of Charity of Mother Teresa were invited into the North to care for the sick, the elderly and the disabled, and served in several cities.

The war since 2015 has caused one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. In March 2016 gunmen attacked the Missionaries of Charity home for the elderly in Aden, killing four sisters, Anselm, Marguerite, Reginette and Judith, together with twelve staff and residents; the Salesian priest Fr. Tom Uzhunnalil was kidnapped and held for eighteen months. Churches in Aden have been damaged. The tiny Catholic flock, cared for by the Apostolic Vicariate of Southern Arabia, keeps faith with great courage.

saints.name: St. Arethas and the Martyrs of Najran
saints.story: Christians of Najran, in the Himyarite kingdom of South Arabia, who were massacred for refusing to renounce Christ, including their elder Arethas (Harith). Their martyrdom shook the Christian world of the time. Najran lies today in Saudi Arabia, but the martyrs belong to the ancient Christian story of Yemen's region.

saints.name: The Missionaries of Charity of Aden (not canonized)
saints.story: Sisters Anselm (India), Marguerite (Rwanda), Reginette (Rwanda) and Judith (Kenya), killed on 4 March 2016 while caring for elderly and disabled residents in Aden. Pope Francis called them martyrs of our time. Their deaths reveal the love that stays when everyone else flees.

cathedrals.name: Catholic churches of Aden
cathedrals.story: Built during the British period to serve soldiers, workers and families, Aden's few Catholic churches were long the only Catholic places of worship in Yemen. Damaged or closed during the war, they remain signs of a faith that has quietly persisted under great hardship.

prayerIntention: For Yemen: that the war end, that the starving be fed and the sick healed, and that the sacrifice of all who served its people in love bear fruit in lasting peace.

name: Zambia
history:
Catholic mission in Zambia began in the late 19th century. Jesuits attempted a mission in the Zambezi valley in the 1880s, and in 1891 the White Fathers, led later by Bishop Joseph Dupont, opened missions in the northeast among the Bemba and Mambwe peoples. In 1905 Jesuits founded Chikuni mission in the south, and Capuchins, Franciscans and many congregations of sisters followed.

Under British rule as Northern Rhodesia, the Church built schools and hospitals that educated much of the future national leadership. Zambia became independent in 1964 and in 1991 declared itself a Christian nation. The bishops' conference has repeatedly spoken out on corruption, poverty and democracy, and the Church helped peaceful transitions of power. Archbishop Emmanuel Milingo's healing ministry and later break with the Church caused controversy and pain.

Today the Catholic Church in Zambia is a vibrant, mostly African-led Church with many vocations, small Christian communities, and a strong commitment to social justice through bodies such as the Jesuit Centre for Theological Reflection, serving a nation that still wrestles with poverty and debt.

saints.name: Bishop Joseph Dupont, M.Afr. (missionary, not canonized)
saints.story: A French White Father nicknamed 'Moto Moto' ('fire fire') for his energy, he founded missions among the Bemba in the 1890s and became the first Vicar Apostolic of Nyasa. He is remembered as a founding father of the Catholic Church in northern Zambia.

saints.name: The Uganda Martyrs (venerated in Zambia)
saints.story: Zambia has no canonized native saints yet, but the young martyrs of neighbouring Uganda, led by St. Charles Lwanga, are deeply loved by Zambian Catholics as models of youthful courage, and many parishes, schools and youth groups bear their names.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Child Jesus
cathedrals.story: The cathedral of the Archdiocese of Lusaka, in the capital's city centre. It is a gathering place for the nation's Catholics for great celebrations and prayers for the country, and Pope John Paul II visited Lusaka in 1989.

cathedrals.name: Chikuni Mission
cathedrals.story: Founded by Jesuits in 1905 among the Tonga people, Chikuni grew into a large mission with a church, schools and a hospital, and later a community radio station. It is one of the oldest and most influential Catholic missions in Zambia.

prayerIntention: For Zambia: that its people live in peace and justice, that leaders serve the common good, and that the poor find dignity, work and hope.

name: Zimbabwe
history:
The first Catholic missionary to reach this land was the Portuguese Jesuit Gonçalo da Silveira, who baptized the Mwenemutapa ruler in 1561 and was killed soon after at the court's command. Portuguese Dominicans later served along the Zambezi, but no lasting church remained. Modern mission began in 1879 when Jesuits of the Zambesi Mission arrived, founding Chishawasha near Harare in 1892, followed by Dominican sisters, Trappists, Mariannhill missionaries, Bethlehem Fathers and others.

In colonial Rhodesia the Church built many schools and hospitals, and some missionaries opposed racial injustice. During the liberation war of the 1970s missionaries and Catholics were killed, including the seven missionaries murdered at Musami mission in 1977. After independence in 1980, the Catholic Commission for Justice and Peace courageously documented the Gukurahundi massacres in Matabeleland, publishing Breaking the Silence in 1997.

Today Zimbabwean Catholics live amid economic hardship and political tension, with the bishops repeatedly calling for dialogue and justice. The Church is young and largely Zimbabwean in its clergy, and beloved figures such as the English poet John Bradburne, who cared for lepers at Mutemwa, inspire faith and service.

saints.name: Servant of God John Bradburne
saints.story: An English Franciscan tertiary, poet and wanderer who became warden of the Mutemwa leprosy settlement. He lived among the patients with great tenderness, refusing to leave during the war, and was killed in 1979. His cause for beatification has been opened, and Mutemwa draws pilgrims each year.

saints.name: Fr. Gonçalo da Silveira, SJ (not canonized)
saints.story: A Portuguese Jesuit who travelled up the Zambezi to the court of the Mwenemutapa, where he baptized the ruler and others. Accused by rivals, he was strangled in his sleep. He is remembered as the first Christian martyr of the region.

saints.name: The Musami martyrs (not canonized)
saints.story: Seven missionaries, Jesuit priests and brothers and Dominican sisters, were shot at St. Paul's Mission, Musami, in February 1977 during the liberation war. They had served local people in education and health. Their deaths remain a painful memory and a witness of faithful presence.

cathedrals.name: Cathedral of the Sacred Heart
cathedrals.story: Completed in 1925 in a Romanesque style, it is the seat of the Archdiocese of Harare and the heart of Catholic life in the capital. Its bell tower and simple stone interior have witnessed the nation's journey from colonial rule through independence.

cathedrals.name: St. Mary's Cathedral
cathedrals.story: Dating from the early 20th century, it is one of the oldest Catholic cathedrals in the country and the seat of the Archdiocese of Bulawayo, serving Matabeleland's Catholics through times of hardship and healing. Its congregation has kept praying for reconciliation in a region deeply scarred by the violence of the 1980s.

cathedrals.name: Mutemwa Leprosy Settlement and Shrine
cathedrals.story: The place where John Bradburne lived and served the lepers until his death. Each September thousands of pilgrims climb Chigona hill, where he prayed, and remember a life given completely to the outcast. His many poems and the community he served keep his gentle spirit alive.

prayerIntention: For Zimbabwe: that its people be freed from poverty and fear, that the wounds of past violence be healed in truth, and that leaders serve with justice and mercy.
